`CHANGELOG.md`:

```md
# Changelog

All notable changes to ORRESS are documented here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project uses
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **User-defined types**: a Types view to declare `struct`/`union`/`enum`/`typedef` with a
  form builder (field name, type, array count, pointer), with a live C-layout preview
  (offsets, sizes, padding). Apply a type to a data address from the hex view's right-click
  menu and the Inspector lays the bytes out as named, typed fields. Types persist per
  binary alongside names and comments. The decompiler uses the catalog too: when a
  recovered struct parameter matches a user struct, its fields print with the user's names
  (`p.magic` instead of `p.field_0`), and applied function prototypes override the
  recovered signature. A **Set prototype** editor in the decompiler header pins a
  function's return type and named, typed parameters (a pointer-to-struct parameter then
  prints as field accesses).
- **Symbol demangling** (`orress-demangle`): mangled linker names in the imports, exports
  and function-symbol lists are now shown readable — Rust (legacy `_ZN…E` and v0 `_R…`),
  C++ Itanium (`_Z…`) and MSVC (`?…`). Pure Rust, no C `__cxa_demangle`. GOT/PLT slot
  names are kept raw so exploit `got()`/`plt()` lookups still match.

## [1.2.0] - 2026-10-18

The binary-exploitation release: enough that a student of a Linux pwn/RE course (such as
the *nightmare* course) can work end to end inside ORRESS.

### Added

- **Linux native debugging**: the `ptrace` back end (breakpoints, stepping, registers,
  stack and memory) is now offered in the Debugger panel on Linux (x86-64) as well as
  Windows, and ELF executables are debuggable targets.
- **Exploit-development toolkit** (`orress-pwn`): tubes that talk to a local process or a
  remote TCP service (`send`/`recvuntil`/…), integer packing (`p8`–`p64`/`u*`), cyclic
  (de Bruijn) patterns and offset recovery, a ROP gadget finder, and payload builders —
  format-string writes (`fmtstr`), sigreturn frames (SROP), `execve("/bin/sh")` shellcode,
  `one_gadget`, `ret2csu` and `ret2dlresolve`.
- **Exploit console**: a pwntools-style scripting tab (Rhai) exposing all of the above
  plus symbol/GOT/PLT lookups and gadget search, run on a worker thread with live output.
- **Gadgets panel**: list and filter the binary's ROP gadgets and copy their addresses.
- **glibc heap visualizer** (`orress-heap` + Heap panel): while a Linux program is stopped,
  show the malloc chunks, the tcache, and (with `main_arena`, auto-located from the unsorted
  bin) the fastbins and unsorted/small/large bins.
- **CLI**: `exploit` (run a pwn script headless), `gadgets`, and `one-gadget` subcommands.

## [1.1.0] - 2026-10-18

### Added

- **Project folders** (Zed-style): **File > New Project…** and **Open Project…** root the app at a
  folder, restored on startup. A lazy folder tree sits at the top of the left panel (the open-files
  and analysis-views list stays below it); click a file to open it, right-click to reveal it in the
  OS, make a notes file, or extract an executable's resources.
- **Resource extractor** (new `orress-resources` crate and **Resources** tab): pull native Win32
  resources (icons rebuilt as `.ico`, bitmaps as `.bmp`, manifest, version info, string tables,
  RCDATA), embedded files found by magic-byte signature (PNG/JPEG/GIF/BMP/WAV/ZIP/GZIP/PDF/…), every
  PE section, and overlay data out of a binary, saved into the project folder.
- **Disassembly and decompiler search** (Ctrl+F, F3 / Shift+F3) and right-click menus in the code
  views exposing every action and view.
- **ORRESS Academy, rewritten for beginners**: a full course that assumes only basic Rust, with a
  glossary, per-step goals, "do this" instructions and explained multiple-choice. Level 3 (dynamic
  analysis) is complete — the debugger, breakpoints and stepping, reading and changing a running
  program, patching, emulation and beating anti-debugging — and the course now spans 560 steps.

### Changed

- The **emulator** now models the common SSE2 subset (movdqu/movdqa, pxor/xorps, pcmpeqb,
  pmovmskb, movd/movq, …), so the fixed-length byte comparisons Rust compiles to SIMD now emulate.
- The **Challenge Workbench** bundles its own `challenge-kit`, vendored into each scaffolded
  challenge so it builds offline with no external repository; a Built-in / External toggle keeps the
  escape hatch for a custom checkout.
- The **debugger** can be started again after a program ends, and the CPU simulator shows r8–r15
  when a program uses them.

## [1.0.0] - 2026-10-14

The first public release of ORRESS — the Okiedocus Rusty Reverse Engineering Software Suite.

### Highlights

- **Prebuilt for Windows (x86-64), Linux (x86-64, ARM64) and macOS (Apple Silicon, Intel).**
- **A pure-Rust reverse-engineering IDE** with a Zed-inspired workspace: docks, panes, splits, a
  command palette, and Zed-format keymaps and themes.
- **Loaders and formats**: PE, ELF and Mach-O, plus .NET, Java class/JAR, Android DEX, Python
  `.pyc`, WebAssembly, JavaScript, and ZIP-based containers (ZIP64, JAR, APK).
- **Disassembly and analysis** for x86/x86-64 and ARM64: functions, control-flow graphs, cross
  references, strings, renaming, comments and bookmarks.
- **A decompiler that speaks Rust**, including a *Rust port* mode that turns assembly into
  compilable Rust.
- **Run, debug and solve**: a native debugger (Windows; Linux experimental), an x86-64 emulator
  with time-travel tracing, a symbolic solver, devirtualization, and binary diffing.
- **Malware analysis**: triage with imphash, fuzzy hashes and IOCs, YARA-X scanning, and a sandbox
  that requires a VM, contains the whole process tree and offers a fake network.
- **Built-in tools**: an in-app assembler and patcher, a CyberChef-style transform workbench, a
  code editor with language-server support, a debug-adapter client and an integrated terminal.
- **Extensible**: runs Zed extensions (themes, grammars, language servers, WASM) and Rhai scripts.
- **Learn inside the tool**: the ORRESS Academy — 8 levels, 37 lessons, practice crackmes and a
  CPU simulator.
- **AI, your way**: an assistant on your Claude plan (via the `claude` CLI), the Claude API, any
  OpenAI-compatible or local model, or fully offline; plus an MCP server (`orress-mcp`) that exposes
  ORRESS's engines to AI agents.
- **Team play**: end-to-end-encrypted real-time collaboration through a small relay
  (`orress-relay`), with CTFd and rCTF integration.

### Fixed (since the pre-release builds)

- Mach-O executables now report their real entry point: `LC_MAIN` stores a file offset, which
  is now translated to a virtual address (previously "go to entry" and analysis seeding were off
  on every macOS binary).
- Linux position-independent executables are classified as executables, not libraries.
- Mach-O imports are resolved to their stubs and GOT slots (from the indirect symbol table), so
  calls into system libraries are named in macOS binaries.

### Security

- Extensions run in the wasmtime 36 long-term-support series with path confinement, a filtered
  environment and an execution policy; YARA-X is held on a release built on the same patched
  series.
- Dependencies are checked by `cargo deny` (RustSec advisories, licenses, sources) on every push
  and daily.

[Unreleased]: https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/compare/v1.2.0...HEAD
[1.2.0]: https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/releases/tag/v1.2.0
[1.1.0]: https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/releases/tag/v1.1.0
[1.0.0]: https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/releases/tag/v1.0.0

```

# Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our
community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body
size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender
identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status,
nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual
identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming,
diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our
community include:

* Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
* Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
* Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
* Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes,
  and learning from the experience
* Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall
  community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

* The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of
  any kind
* Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
* Public or private harassment
* Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address,
  without their explicit permission
* Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a
  professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of
acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in
response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive,
or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject
comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are
not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation
decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when
an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces.
Examples of representing our community include using an official email address,
posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed
representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be
reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at
**info@okiedocus.nl**.
All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the
reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining
the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed
unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing
clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the
behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of
actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No
interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with
those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This
includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels
like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent
ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including
sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public
communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or
private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction
with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period.
Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community
standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an
individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the
community.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage],
version 2.1, available at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html][v2.1].

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by
[Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][Mozilla CoC].

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq][FAQ]. Translations are available at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations][translations].

`CONTRIBUTING.md`:

```md
# Contributing to ORRESS

Thanks for helping! Bug reports, test samples, Academy lessons, documentation and code are all
welcome. This guide covers how to get a change merged.

By taking part you agree to follow the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Security problems go
through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), **not** public issues.

## Ways to help

- **Report a bug** — use the *Bug report* issue form. A small reproducer (a file, or the steps
  that produce a wrong disassembly or decompilation) makes a fix far more likely.
- **Suggest a feature** — use the *Feature request* form and describe the problem you are solving,
  not just the feature.
- **Improve the Academy** — lessons are plain TOML in [`academy/lessons/`](academy/lessons).
- **Send code** — see below. For anything larger than a focused fix, open an issue first so we can
  agree on the approach before you spend time on it.

## Setting up

1. Install Rust with [rustup](https://rustup.rs). The repository pins its toolchain in
   [`rust-toolchain.toml`](rust-toolchain.toml); rustup installs it automatically.
2. On Linux, install the GUI libraries:
   `sudo apt install libxkbcommon-dev libgtk-3-dev libwayland-dev`.
3. Build and run:

   ```sh
   cargo run -p orress            # the app (debug build)
   cargo run --release -p orress  # smoother for real binaries
   ```

A full debug build with tests needs several gigabytes of disk space for `target/`.

## Before you open a pull request

CI runs exactly these checks on Windows and Linux; please run them locally first:

```sh
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps
```

and, if you changed dependencies, [`cargo deny check`](https://github.com/EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny).

A good pull request:

- **does one thing** and explains *why* in its description;
- **adds or updates tests** — parsers get a test with real or hand-built bytes, the decompiler gets
  a case in its test module, bug fixes get a regression test;
- **keeps the project pure Rust** — a new dependency that needs a C/C++ toolchain needs a strong
  reason, and every new dependency must pass `cargo deny` (permissive licenses, crates.io only);
- **handles hostile input** — ORRESS opens malware. Never `unwrap()` on data from a file, bound
  allocations and loops by the input size, and prefer returning an error over panicking;
- **updates the docs** — the README, the action's explanation in
  [`crates/orress/src/actions.rs`](crates/orress/src/actions.rs), or the Academy when behaviour
  changes users can see;
- adds an entry under *Unreleased* in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for user-visible changes.

## Where things live

ORRESS is a workspace of focused crates; the app is a thin shell over reusable engines. The
README's [Architecture](README.md#architecture) section maps every crate. A few conventions:

- **Every user-facing operation is an action** with a plain-language explanation in
  `crates/orress/src/actions.rs`. Menus, the command palette, shortcuts and buttons all dispatch
  through it, so a new feature automatically appears everywhere.
- **Views** live in `crates/orress-views`; long-running work (analysis, emulation, scans) runs on a
  worker thread — never block the UI thread.
- **Engines stay UI-free.** Loaders, analysis, the decompiler, the emulator and friends must not
  depend on `egui`, so the CLI and the MCP server can reuse them.
- `unsafe` is forbidden workspace-wide. The only exceptions are two OS interfaces that cannot be
  written without it — the native debugger (`orress-debug`) and the sandbox's Windows Job Objects
  (`orress-sandbox/src/job.rs`) — each opted in explicitly, with a safety comment on every block.

## Commit messages

Use a short imperative summary, optionally prefixed with the area:

```
decompiler: fold signed max/min idioms
loaders: classify PIE executables as executables, not libraries
```

Keep unrelated changes in separate commits.

## Licensing of contributions

ORRESS is dual-licensed under [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE). Unless you
explicitly state otherwise, any contribution you intentionally submit for inclusion in ORRESS, as
defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or
conditions.

Only contribute code you wrote or have the right to submit. Do not paste code from IDA, Ghidra,
Binary Ninja, Zed or other projects unless its license is compatible and it is clearly attributed.

## Malware samples

Never commit live malware. Tests use small hand-built binaries or harmless crackmes. If a bug only
reproduces with a real sample, do not attach it to a public issue — follow the instructions in
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) to share it privately.

```

<div align="center">

<img src="assets/logo-256.png" alt="ORRESS logo" width="160">

# ORRESS

**Okiedocus Rusty Reverse Engineering Software Suite**

A reverse-engineering IDE for CTF players, malware analysts and the curious —
written in pure Rust, with a decompiler that speaks **Rust** and a built-in course that takes you from zero to expert.

[![CI](https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
![MSRV](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSRV-1.95-orange?logo=rust)
![Platforms](https://img.shields.io/badge/platforms-Windows%20%7C%20Linux%20%7C%20macOS-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-green)

<img src="assets/screenshots/decompiler.png" alt="ORRESS disassembly and Rust decompiler side by side" width="860">

</div>

---

## Why ORRESS?

- **Approachable.** Hover anything and ORRESS explains it. The built-in **Academy** (8 levels,
  37 lessons, practice crackmes, a CPU simulator) teaches reverse engineering inside the tool you
  are learning.
- **Complete.** Hex editor, disassembler, graph view, decompiler, debugger, emulator, symbolic
  solver, malware triage, YARA, sandbox, binary diffing, devirtualization, code editor, terminal
  — in one fast native app.
- **Rust all the way down.** Pure-Rust engines (no IDA, Ghidra, Unicorn or Python required). The
  decompiler prints **Rust syntax** and can emit a **compilable Rust port** of a function.
- **Built to be extended.** Every feature is an action reachable from the menu, the command palette
  and a rebindable shortcut. Rhai scripting, an MCP server for AI agents, and **Zed-extension
  compatibility** (themes, grammars, language servers, WASM extensions).
- **Zed-inspired workspace.** Docks, panes, splits, a command palette and Zed-format keymaps and
  themes — built on [egui](https://github.com/emilk/egui).

> **Status: v1.0.** All planned feature milestones are implemented. A few platform-specific features
> are still marked experimental (see [Platform support](#platform-support)); bug reports are very welcome.

## Features

### Load and inspect
- **Formats:** PE, ELF and Mach-O, plus **.NET** (CIL), **Java** `.class`, **Android** DEX/APK
  (smali), **Python** `.pyc`, **WebAssembly** (WAT), **ZIP/JAR** (including ZIP64) and a
  **JavaScript** deobfuscator.
- **Hex editor** with a data inspector, entropy graph, wildcard byte search (`E8 ?? ?? ?? ??`) and
  in-place patching.
- **"What is this file?"** card: format, architecture, protections, compiler/packer detection,
  sections, imports and strings.

### Disassemble and decompile
- Recursive-descent disassembly for **x86, x86-64 and ARM64**, with functions, cross-references,
  jump-table recovery, a control-flow **graph view**, renames, comments and bookmarks saved per file.
- A **decompiler with its own IR** that prints readable Rust: structured control flow, recovered
  types, slices, structs, iterators and SIMD/float support — see [The decompiler](#the-decompiler).
- **Deobfuscation:** opaque-predicate folding and control-flow unflattening.
- An **assembler** (x86-64 and ARM64) for patching instructions in place.

### Run, debug and solve
- **Debugger:** native Windows back end (Win32 Debug API) and a Linux `ptrace` back end
  (experimental), with breakpoints, stepping, registers, stack and memory editing.
- **Emulator:** a pure-Rust x86-64 CPU emulator — run a single function with arguments, with
  common libc calls stubbed out. **Time-travel debugging** lets you scrub backwards and forwards
  through a recorded trace.
- **Solvers:** an instruction-count side-channel solver, **symbolic/concolic execution** with
  SMT-LIB2 export, and one-click **VM devirtualization** that recovers a bytecode VM's key and its
  per-byte checks.
- **Shellcode workbench:** paste a blob (hex, C array, `\x`, base64), disassemble it, emulate it and
  identify API hashes.

### Malware analysis
- **Triage report:** capabilities mapped to **MITRE ATT&CK**, defanged IOCs, hashes (imphash, TLSH,
  ssdeep), config extraction and graded hints, exportable as Markdown.
- **YARA-X** workbench: write, generate and run rules against files, folders or a live process.
- **Sandbox:** a guarded launcher that refuses to run outside a VM, a built-in **fake network**
  (DNS + HTTP), VirtualBox snapshot control and an ETW activity monitor.

### Write code and collaborate
- **Code editor:** multi-cursor, rope-backed, tree-sitter highlighting, **LSP** (rust-analyzer,
  pyright, clangd: diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition, completion), build/run tasks,
  **DAP** source-level debugging and an integrated **terminal**.
- **Workbench:** CyberChef-style recipes (`from_base64 | xor key=0x5a | zlib_inflate`) with a
  **Magic** mode that finds the decoding for you.
- **Binary diffing:** BinDiff-style function matching for patch diffing and variant comparison.
- **Collaboration:** real-time shared sessions (CRDT, presence, follow mode) over a self-hostable,
  end-to-end-encrypted relay, plus **CTFd / rCTF** import and flag submission.
- **Challenge Workbench:** author your own crackme and submit it to a CTF platform from inside
  ORRESS.

## Getting started

**Download:** prebuilt binaries for **Windows** (x86-64), **Linux** (x86-64, ARM64) and **macOS**
(Apple Silicon, Intel) are attached to each
[GitHub release](https://github.com/okiedocus/orress/releases), with a `.sha256` checksum for every
archive. Unpack and run `orress` (the app), or `orress-cli`, `orress-mcp`, `orress-relay`. The macOS
builds are not notarized yet: run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <unpacked folder>` once, or
right-click `orress` → **Open**.

**Build from source:** you need [Rust via rustup](https://rustup.rs) (1.95 or newer). The repository
pins its toolchain (`rust-toolchain.toml`), and rustup installs it automatically on the first build.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/okiedocus/orress.git
cd orress
cargo run --release -p orress                # start the app
cargo run --release -p orress -- crackme.exe # start and open a file
```

**Linux** needs the GUI development libraries first:

```sh
sudo apt install libxkbcommon-dev libgtk-3-dev libwayland-dev   # Debian / Ubuntu
```

Optional extras:

| Want | Install |
|---|---|
| Rust / Python / C language servers in the editor | `rust-analyzer`, `pyright`, `clangd` on your `PATH` |
| AI assistant on your Claude plan | [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code), signed in |
| "Check compiles" button for Rust ports | build with `--features compile-check` |
| Harder symbolic constraints | `z3` (ORRESS exports SMT-LIB2) |

Run the test suite with `cargo test --workspace`.

### Platform support

| | Windows | Linux | macOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| App, analysis, decompiler, emulator, editor | ✅ | ✅ (x86-64, ARM64) | ✅ new — please report issues |
| Native debugger | ✅ 64-bit targets | ⚠️ experimental (`ptrace`, x86-64) | — |
| Sandbox (process-tree containment) | ✅ Job Objects | ✅ process groups | untested |
| ETW activity monitor | ✅ (needs admin) | — | — |

32-bit Windows programs can't be debugged natively yet; use the emulator for those.

## First steps

New to reverse engineering? Open **Learn → Academy** and start at Level 0. Otherwise:

| Do this | How |
|---|---|
| Run any command | `Ctrl+Shift+P` — the command palette |
| Open a file | `Ctrl+O`, or drag it onto the window |
| What is this file? | `Ctrl+I` |
| Strings / functions | `Ctrl+Shift+S` / `Ctrl+Shift+F` |
| Disassembly / go to `main` | `Ctrl+D` / `Ctrl+Shift+M` |
| Graph view | `Space` in the disassembly |
| Rename, comment, bookmark, xrefs | `N`, `;`, `B`, `X` in the disassembly |
| Decompile the current function | `F5` |
| Debug / emulate / shellcode | `F6` / `F7` / `F8` |
| While debugging | `F5` continue · `F10` step over · `F11` step into · `Shift+F5` stop |
| Malware triage / YARA | `Ctrl+Shift+T` / `Ctrl+Shift+Y` |
| Go to an address | `Ctrl+G` (hex by default, `#123` decimal, `+10` relative) |
| Find bytes or text | `Ctrl+F`, then `F3` / `Shift+F3` |
| Show/hide docks | `Ctrl+B` left, `Ctrl+Alt+B` right, `Ctrl+J` bottom |
| Every shortcut | `F1` |

Hover over anything for an explanation; the **Explain** panel keeps the text while you work.

## The decompiler

`F5` opens the decompiler next to the disassembly, and the two follow each other: move through
the listing and the matching line lights up. For the password check of the Academy's second
crackme it prints:

```rust
fn sub_140001100(a1: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if a1.len() != 7 {
        return false;
    }
    if a1[0] != b'R' {
        return false;
    }
    // ...
    return a1[6] == b'3';
}
```

Machine code is lifted into ORRESS's own IR, simplified, structured into
`if`/`while`/`for`/`match`/labelled loops, typed from how values are used and printed as Rust.
Highlights:

- **Rust-shaped types:** pointer + length pairs become `&[T]`/`&str`, read-only and written
  pointers become `&T`/`&mut T`, constant-offset access recovers `#[repr(C)]` structs, and
  signedness is inferred.
- **Idioms, not instructions:** counted loops become `for x in s`, accumulations become
  `.iter().sum()` / `.fold(..)` / `.any(..)`, jump tables become `match`, and `rep movs`/`stos`/`cmps`
  become `memcpy`/`memset`/`memcmp`.
- **Vectorised code folds back:** SSE2 loops, float and integer, with their horizontal-reduce tails
  are *proved* to compute a whole-slice reduction and collapse to a one-line `s.iter()…` call.
- **Floating point and SIMD:** scalar SSE/NEON floats with `f32`/`f64` signatures, and packed SSE as
  lane arrays.
- **Three architectures:** x86-64, x86 and ARM64, sharing one pipeline.
- **Honest output:** what can't be expressed is shown as `read::<u32>(addr)`, `unknown(..)` or
  inline `asm!`, never guessed.

**Rust port mode** turns a function into a *compilable* Rust scaffold. A tiny `orress_rt` prelude
supplies memory helpers. Instructions the lifter can't model are kept as `core::arch::asm!` with
their register inputs and outputs wired up, and every external call or global is stubbed so the
file compiles as-is. Use it as the starting point for porting legacy code to Rust.

## Command line

`orress-cli` runs the same engines from a terminal. Input is a file, or standard input when it is
omitted or `-`.

```sh
orress-cli info crackme.exe [--json]          # what is this file?
orress-cli strings crackme.exe -n 6 --flags   # strings, or only flag-like ones
orress-cli funcs crackme.exe                  # functions found
orress-cli disasm crackme.exe main            # a function by name, `main`, `entry` or 0xADDR
orress-cli decompile crackme.exe main         # ... as Rust
orress-cli vm crackme.exe                     # detect and devirtualize a bytecode VM
orress-cli script crackme.exe solve.rhai      # run a Rhai script (or -e "function_count()")
orress-cli recipe "from_base64 | xor key=0x41" payload.txt
orress-cli magic payload.txt                  # find a decoding automatically
orress-cli patch crackme.exe 0x81a 75 -o cracked.exe
orress-cli ops                                # list every workbench operation
```

There are also [rsbkb](https://github.com/trou/rsbkb)-style shortcuts: `xor`, `b64`, `hex`, `url`,
`rc4`, `hash`, `entropy`, `slice`, `bgrep`, `tsdec`.

## AI integration

**The Assistant panel** (*View → Open View → AI Assistant*) answers questions about the open
binary. Bring your own model:

| Backend | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Claude plan (CLI)** | Runs the `claude` CLI headless with your signed-in account, including Claude Pro/Max — **no API key needed** |
| **Claude API** | Anthropic API key from the field or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| **OpenAI-compatible / local** | OpenAI, Azure, or a local model (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM) by base URL |
| **Offline** | Answers from ORRESS's own static analysis; nothing leaves your machine |

Sending context is **opt-in**: the panel shows exactly what will be sent (an analysis summary,
never the raw file). API keys are kept for the session only unless you tick **Remember key**, which
stores the key in plaintext in `ai.json`.

**MCP server.** `orress-mcp` exposes ORRESS's engines to AI agents such as Claude Code over the MCP
stdio transport. Add it to a project's `.mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "orress": { "command": "cargo", "args": ["run", "-q", "--release", "-p", "orress-mcp"] }
  }
}
```

Tools: `triage`, `strings`, `disassemble` (WASM, `.pyc`, `.class`, .NET, DEX), `detect_vm`,
`deobfuscate_js`, `archive_list` and `binary_diff`. The server only reads the files it is asked to,
and never executes them.

## Malware analysis safely

The **Sandbox** runs a sample as a real process, so detonate live malware only with ORRESS
running **inside a disposable VM**. ORRESS enforces this: the Sandbox refuses to launch unless it
detects a VM.

1. Install a hypervisor on the host: **VirtualBox**, **VMware** or **QEMU/KVM**. These are detected
   unambiguously; on a Windows 11 host, Hyper-V-style detection is ambiguous, see below.
2. Create a throwaway guest, install the guest additions, and set its network to
   **host-only/internal** — never bridged or NAT.
3. Build ORRESS inside the guest and **take a clean snapshot**.
4. Set the guest's DNS server to `127.0.0.1`. In the Sandbox tab, click **Start fake network**,
   choose the sample, confirm, and click **Run in sandbox**. Every DNS query and HTTP request the
   sample makes is answered locally and logged.
5. **Revert to the snapshot** after every run.

> **Hyper-V note:** Windows 11's virtualization-based security makes a *physical* host report the
> `Microsoft Hv` hypervisor too, so ORRESS treats Hyper-V as unconfirmed by default. If you really
> are inside a Hyper-V guest, untick **Refuse to run outside a VM** in the Sandbox policy.

Static analysis (triage, YARA, disassembly, emulation) never executes the sample and is safe on any
machine.

## Configuration

**Help → Open Config Folder** opens the config folder (`%APPDATA%\okiedocus\ORRESS\config` on
Windows, `~/.config/orress` on Linux).

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `settings.json` | Theme, zoom, Explain Mode, recent files, language-server overrides |
| `keymap.json` | Your shortcuts in **Zed's keymap format**; they override the defaults |
| `themes/*.json` | Custom themes — ORRESS themes or **Zed theme families** directly |
| `lsp/*.json` | Language-server adapter manifests (add or override a server for any language) |
| `extensions/<name>/` | Installed **Zed extensions** (themes, grammars, language servers, WASM) |
| `projects/*.orress` | Your names, comments, bookmarks and patches, saved per file (by SHA-256) |
| `academy.json` | Academy progress |

Example `keymap.json`:

```json
[
  { "context": "Global", "bindings": { "ctrl-p": "command_palette::Toggle" } },
  { "context": "Hex", "bindings": { "ctrl-w": null } }
]
```

Action names are listed on the Keyboard Shortcuts page (`F1`). Extensions can be installed from a
git URL or a local folder via the command palette → **Manage Extensions**.

## Architecture

ORRESS is a Cargo workspace of focused crates; the app is a thin shell over reusable engines.

| Layer | Crates |
|---|---|
| **App & UI** | `orress` (app), `orress-workspace` (docks, panes), `orress-views` (every view), `orress-ui`, `orress-theme`, `orress-actions` (actions, keymaps), `orress-settings` |
| **Loading** | `orress-loaders` (PE/ELF/Mach-O), `orress-bytes`, `orress-archive`, `orress-dotnet`, `orress-java`, `orress-dex`, `orress-pyc`, `orress-wasm`, `orress-js` |
| **Analysis** | `orress-arch` (decoding), `orress-analysis` (functions, CFG, xrefs), `orress-decompiler`, `orress-asm` (assembler), `orress-diff`, `orress-vm` (devirtualization) |
| **Dynamic** | `orress-debug`, `orress-emu` (emulator + time travel), `orress-sym` (symbolic execution) |
| **Malware** | `orress-triage`, `orress-sandbox` |
| **Editor & tools** | `orress-editor`, `orress-lsp`, `orress-dap`, `orress-term`, `orress-transforms` (workbench) |
| **Extend & connect** | `orress-ext` (Zed extensions, WASM host), `orress-script` (Rhai), `orress-ai`, `orress-mcp`, `orress-collab`, `orress-relay`, `orress-ctf`, `orress-challenge` |
| **Learn & project** | `orress-academy`, `orress-project` (documents, annotations) |
| **Binaries** | `orress` (GUI), `orress-cli`, `orress-mcp`, `orress-relay` |

Every user-facing operation is an **action** with a plain-language explanation
(`crates/orress/src/actions.rs`). Menus, the palette, shortcuts and buttons all dispatch through
the same path, so a new feature shows up everywhere at once. Academy lessons are TOML files in
[`academy/lessons/`](academy/lessons) and the practice crackmes are Rust programs in
[`academy/crackmes/`](academy/crackmes).

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the setup, the
checks CI runs, and the project's conventions. Everyone taking part follows the
[Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Release notes are in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## Security

ORRESS opens hostile files by design. Please report vulnerabilities **privately** as described in
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) — not as public issues. Dependencies are checked against the RustSec
advisory database and a license policy ([`deny.toml`](deny.toml)) on every push and daily.

option. ORRESS follows Zed's design but contains no Zed source code.

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution you intentionally submit for inclusion in
ORRESS shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

`SECURITY.md`:

```md
# Security Policy

ORRESS is built to open hostile files: malware, crackmes and deliberately malformed binaries.
Bugs that let such input escape the analysis are taken seriously.

## Supported versions

| Version | Supported |
|---|---|
| 1.x (latest minor release) | ✅ security fixes |
| < 1.0 | ❌ |

Fixes land on `main` and ship in the next patch release.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Please do not open a public issue for security problems.**

- Preferred: GitHub's private reporting — the **Security** tab → **Report a vulnerability**.
- Or email **info@okiedocus.nl** with `ORRESS security` in the subject.

Include the ORRESS version (or commit), your OS, what you did, what happened, and ideally a
reproducer. If the reproducer is a malicious or malformed sample, send it as a password-protected
archive (password `infected`) and say so.

What to expect:

- an acknowledgement within **3 working days**;
- an assessment and a planned fix or mitigation within **14 days**;
- credit in the release notes and the advisory, unless you prefer to stay anonymous.

Please give us a reasonable chance to release a fix before you disclose publicly; we aim to
coordinate disclosure within **90 days**.

## What counts as a vulnerability

In scope — for example:

- **Parsing untrusted files.** A crafted PE, ELF, Mach-O, archive, .NET, Java, DEX, `.pyc`,
  WASM or JavaScript file that causes memory corruption, code execution, writes outside expected
  locations, or an unbounded hang or allocation that static analysis should survive.
- **Extensions.** A WASM extension (including Zed extensions) that escapes its sandbox: reading or
  writing files outside the directories it was granted, reading environment secrets, or running
  commands beyond the extension policy.
- **The sandbox and debugger.** A sample that escapes process-tree containment, survives a kill,
  or runs when the "refuse outside a VM" policy should have stopped it.
- **The MCP server** (`orress-mcp`) and the **collaboration relay** (`orress-relay`): crashes or
  resource exhaustion from remote input, data leaking between rooms, or breaking the end-to-end
  encryption of collaboration sessions.
- **AI integration.** Anything that sends file contents, keys or other data to a model provider
  without the user's explicit opt-in.
- Vulnerable dependencies that are reachable in ORRESS.

Out of scope:

- Malware doing what malware does when you deliberately run it in the **Sandbox** outside a VM
  after turning off the VM check, or on a bridged network. See *Malware analysis safely* in the
  README.
- Results that are simply wrong (a bad decompilation or a missed YARA match) — please file those
  as normal bugs.
- Code you choose to run yourself: the terminal, Run/Debug tasks, scripts, or language servers
  you configured.
- Prompt-injection text inside a binary that changes what an AI model *says*, as long as it
  cannot make ORRESS act or leak data.

## Hardening already in place

- Pure-Rust parsers with size and recursion limits; parsers are tested against truncated and
  hostile input.
- Extensions run in wasmtime with path confinement, a filtered environment and an execution
  policy; runaway guests are interrupted.
- The Sandbox requires a detected VM by default, contains the whole process tree (Windows Job
  Objects, Unix process groups), and offers a fake network.
- AI context is opt-in and previewed before sending; API keys are not stored unless you ask.
- CI runs `cargo deny` (RustSec advisories, licenses, crate sources) on every push and pull
  request and again daily, so a newly published advisory turns the build red. Dependabot keeps
  dependencies and CI actions current, and CI actions are pinned to commit SHAs.

```

`academy/AUTHORING.md`:

```md
# Writing Academy lessons

The Academy is a **complete course**. Its learner knows **basic Rust** (variables, functions,
`if`/`loop`/`match`, `Vec`, `String`, `&str`, structs, `cargo run`) and **nothing else**: not
hexadecimal, not what a register is, not what a debugger does, not how an `.exe` is built.
Everything beyond basic Rust is taught here, in order, before it is used.

Lessons live in `academy/lessons/*.toml`, the glossary in `academy/glossary/*.toml`. Both are
found automatically (see `crates/orress-academy/build.rs`). Run
`cargo test -p orress-academy` after every change: it validates every lesson and glossary file.

## The rules

1. **Never use a word before it is taught.** If a step says "register", either a previous lesson
   taught it, or this step explains it in a sentence and it is in the glossary. When unsure,
   explain again: repetition is cheaper than confusion.
2. **Explain first, then ask.** A step that asks something is preceded by text that teaches
   everything needed to answer it. No step tests knowledge a lesson did not give.
3. **Every task says exactly what to do.** A step whose `check` is anything other than
   `continue` or `choice` must have `instructions`: a numbered list of concrete actions that
   name the exact menu, button, panel, view, key or field. ("In the **Project** panel on the
   left, click **Strings**.", not "Open the strings.") The tests enforce that the list exists;
   you are responsible for it being precise and *true* (check the UI code, see below).
4. **Explain the why.** After each task, `success` says what the learner just saw and why it
   matters. Wrong multiple-choice answers get an `explain` entry saying why they are wrong.
5. **Rust is the anchor.** Show the Rust code first, then what it becomes. The learner can
   read Rust; use it to explain everything else.
6. **Small steps.** One idea per step. A step's `text` is roughly 120-350 words. A lesson has
   about 6-14 steps. Split a lesson that grows past that.
7. **Worked examples before exercises.** Walk through one example completely, then let the
   learner do a similar one.
8. **Hints go from a nudge to almost the answer**, at most three. The last hint should make the
   step solvable for anyone who read the text.
9. **Plain language.** Short sentences. Active voice. Address the learner as "you". No
   "simply", "just", "obviously", "trivially". Not everyone's first language is English.
10. **Characters:** the UI font cannot show `→ ← ✔ ✓ ● ○` (a test rejects them). Write `->`.

## Lesson format

```toml
id = "l1-crackme1"          # stable: progress is saved by id; do not rename existing ids
level = 1                   # 0-7, see LEVELS in src/lesson.rs
order = 11                  # sort order inside the level (unique within the course)
title = "Your first crackme"
summary = "One line shown in the overview."
goals = [                   # "In this lesson you will learn to ..." (3-5 items)
    "find readable text inside a program with the Strings view",
    "jump from a string to the code that uses it",
]
badge = "First Crack"       # optional
reveal_source = "crackme01" # optional: show the crackme's source after the lesson

[[steps]]
title = "Open the strings"
goal = "See every piece of readable text inside the program."   # one line, optional
text = '''
Markdown teaching text. Use **bold** for UI names and `code` for code, values and keys.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Optional: extra depth for the curious, folded under "Learn more". Never needed to continue.
'''
instructions = [
    "In the **Project** panel on the left, click **Strings**.",
    "In the filter box at the top of the Strings view, type `pass`.",
]
spotlight = "tree.Strings"  # optional; must be a known target (see lesson.rs tests)
check = { kind = "view", view = "Strings" }
hints = ["...", "...", "..."]
success = '''Shown once the step is done: what you saw, and why it matters.'''
```

### Checks (`check = { kind = ... }`)

| kind | completes when | fields |
|---|---|---|
| `continue` (default) | the learner presses Next | |
| `choice` | the right option is picked | `options`, `correct` (0-based), `explain` (one per option, recommended) |
| `answer` | the typed answer matches | `answers`, `number` (42 = 0x2a = 0b101010), `case_sensitive` |
| `secret` | typed text has this SHA-256 | `sha256` (hides passwords from people reading the file) |
| `action` | a command runs | `id`, e.g. `view::Decompiler` (ids: `crates/orress/src/actions.rs`) |
| `view` | a file view gets focus | `view`: Disassembly, Graph, Functions, Info, Hex, Sections, Imports, Strings |
| `open_crackme` | a practice program is opened | `name`: crackme01 ... crackme08 (the step shows an Open button) |
| `sim` | the CPU simulator program ends with these registers | `expect = [["rax", 15]]`, `requires = ["add"]`; needs `solution` (+ usually `sim_code`) |
| `cursor_in_main` | the cursor is inside the detected `main` | |
| `renamed` | the learner renamed something | |
| `commented` | the learner added a comment | |

Prefer checks that prove the learner **did and understood** something: an `answer` whose value
they can only get by actually looking (an address, a constant, a byte count, a password) teaches
more than "open view X". Verify such answers against the real crackme (see below).

Widgets (`widget = ...`): `number_converter`, `ascii_table`.

## Glossary format

One file per level: `academy/glossary/<level>-<name>.toml`. Define a term in the **earliest
level that uses it**; later levels reuse it. Every term and alias must be unique across all
files (a test checks), and every `see` entry must exist.

```toml
[[term]]
term = "register"
aliases = ["registers"]    # spellings in lesson text that should match (plural, short forms)
short = "A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU that instructions work on."
text = '''
Longer Markdown explanation for a beginner, ideally with a Rust comparison and an example.
'''
see = ["rax", "CPU"]
```

Each step automatically lists the glossary terms its text mentions ("Words in this step"), so
every technical word a lesson uses should be in the glossary. Avoid terms that are also common
English words in other senses, or give them a specific spelling (`"call (instruction)"` would
never match; prefer `call instruction` and use that phrase in the text).

## Verifying against the real app

Never guess what the UI looks like or what a crackme contains.

- **UI**: views are in `crates/orress-views/src/`, the workspace and project tree in
  `crates/orress-workspace/src/`, menus and commands in `crates/orress/src/app.rs` and
  `crates/orress/src/actions.rs`, default key bindings in `crates/orress-actions/src/keymap.rs`
  and `assets/keymaps/` (if present). Name buttons and menus exactly as they are labelled.
- **Crackmes**: sources in `academy/crackmes/*.rs`, binaries in `academy/crackmes/bin/`.
  Check what ORRESS shows with the CLI, e.g.
  `target/debug/orress-cli.exe strings academy/crackmes/bin/crackme01.exe`,
  `... disasm academy/crackmes/bin/crackme02.exe main`,
  `... decompile academy/crackmes/bin/crackme03.exe <name or 0xaddress>`,
  `... funcs`, `... info`, `... vm`. Run `orress-cli.exe --help` for the rest.

## Adding a practice program

Write `academy/crackmes/crackmeNN.rs` (a small Rust program: start with a `//!` comment that says
which lesson uses it and how it is solved), then run
`powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File academy\crackmes\build.ps1`. It builds only crackmes that
have no `.exe` yet; `-Only crackmeNN` rebuilds one after its source changed (that changes the file
hash, so learners lose names they saved for it, and addresses quoted in lessons must be rechecked).
Every source with a built
`bin/crackmeNN.exe` is embedded automatically and can be used with `open_crackme`. Keep the
build flags from `build.ps1` (stripped, opt-level=1) so lessons match what learners see.
Programs must be harmless: no network, no file changes outside their own folder, nothing that
persists.

## Testing

`cargo test -p orress-academy` validates everything. The test `every_lesson_file_is_valid`
lists all broken files at once (`file name: lesson id step N: problem`), so you can see your own
files' problems even while other files are being edited.

`academy/crackmes/build.ps1`:

```ps1
# Builds the Academy crackmes with rustc. The resulting .exe files are committed in
# bin/ and embedded in ORRESS, so users do not need to build anything.
#
#   powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File academy\crackmes\build.ps1
#       builds only the crackmes that have no bin\<name>.exe yet (new ones)
#   ... build.ps1 -Only crackme05[,crackme06]
#       rebuilds these, after changing their source
#
# Rebuilding is not byte-identical (the linker writes a timestamp and a PDB id), and
# ORRESS keeps a learner's names and comments per file hash, so a rebuilt crackme loses
# them. Only rebuild a crackme whose source changed, and check that the addresses its
# lessons quote still match (orress-cli disasm / strings).
#
# opt-level=1 keeps the code close to the source (opt-level=0 adds a lot of noise,
# higher levels merge and reorder too much for beginners). panic=abort and stripped
# symbols keep the files small; the lessons teach you to find main without names.

param([string[]]$Only = @())

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$here = Split-Path -Parent $MyInvocation.MyCommand.Path
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force (Join-Path $here "bin") | Out-Null

# Every crackmeNN.rs here; ORRESS embeds each one that has a built bin\crackmeNN.exe.
$names = Get-ChildItem (Join-Path $here "crackme*.rs") | ForEach-Object { $_.BaseName } | Sort-Object
foreach ($n in $Only) {
    if ($names -notcontains $n) { throw "no source $n.rs in $here" }
}
foreach ($name in $names) {
    $src = Join-Path $here "$name.rs"
    $exe = Join-Path $here "bin\$name.exe"
    $wanted = if ($Only.Count -gt 0) { $Only -contains $name } else { -not (Test-Path $exe) }
    if (-not $wanted) { continue }
    rustc --edition 2024 -C opt-level=1 -C panic=abort -C debuginfo=0 -C strip=symbols `
        -C codegen-units=1 --remap-path-prefix "$here=crackmes" $src -o $exe
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "building $name failed" }
    Remove-Item -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue (Join-Path $here "bin\$name.pdb")
    Write-Host "built $exe"
}

```

`academy/crackmes/crackme01.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #1 (Level 1, lesson "Your first crackme")
//!
//! The password is stored as plain text, so the Strings view is enough to find it.

use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #1 ===");
    print!("Password: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    // Remove the line ending: Enter adds "\n" (or "\r\n" on Windows).
    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    // `black_box` keeps the password as text in the program's data. Without it, the
    // compiler turns the comparison into two 8-byte numbers (try it!).
    if line == std::hint::black_box("open_sesame_101") {
        println!("Correct! You cracked your first program.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong password. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme02.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #2 (Level 1, lesson "Byte by byte")
//!
//! The password is never stored as a string: each byte is compared on its own, so it
//! only appears as numbers (character codes) inside `cmp` instructions.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps this a separate function you can find and rename.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(s: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if s.len() != 7 {
        return false;
    }
    // `black_box` stops the compiler from merging the checks into one big comparison,
    // so every character stays a separate `cmp`.
    black_box(s)[0] == b'R'
        && black_box(s)[1] == b'3'
        && black_box(s)[2] == b'v'
        && black_box(s)[3] == b'3'
        && black_box(s)[4] == b'r'
        && black_box(s)[5] == b's'
        && black_box(s)[6] == b'3'
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #2 ===");
    print!("Password: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    // Remove the line ending: Enter adds "\n" (or "\r\n" on Windows).
    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_password(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You read the password byte by byte.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong password. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme03.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #3 (Level 2+, "XOR-encoded password")
//!
//! The password is never stored, not even as character codes. Each input byte is
//! XOR'd with a rolling 4-byte key and compared to a constant ciphertext. Three ways
//! to beat it, each taught by a lesson:
//!
//!   * Keygen (Level 2): XOR is its own inverse, so password[i] = CIPHER[i] ^ KEY[i % 4].
//!   * Symbolic execution (Level 4): the check is a byte-wise transform-and-compare.
//!   * Side channel (Level 4): the loop bails on the first wrong byte, so a correct
//!     byte makes it run further -> instruction counting recovers it one byte at a time.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const KEY: [u8; 4] = [0x5a, 0x1c, 0x7e, 0x33];
const CIPHER: [u8; 8] = [0x15, 0x4e, 0x2c, 0x76, 0x09, 0x4f, 0x4a, 0x01];

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps this a separate function you can find and rename.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(s: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if s.len() != CIPHER.len() {
        return false;
    }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < CIPHER.len() {
        // `black_box` stops the compiler from precomputing the comparison, so each
        // byte stays a real xor-then-compare you can see in the disassembly.
        if black_box(s[i] ^ KEY[i % 4]) != CIPHER[i] {
            return false; // bail on the first wrong byte: the side channel
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #3 ===");
    print!("Key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_password(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You decoded the XOR'd key.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong key. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

```

`academy/crackmes/crackme04.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #4 (Level 3, "Beating anti-debugging")
//!
//! This one fights back. It checks whether a debugger is attached with the Windows
//! API `IsDebuggerPresent`, and if so it bails out *before* ever telling you the
//! password was right. Run it under the debugger and it always says "detected";
//! the real check never gets to speak.
//!
//! Beat it the way the lesson teaches:
//!   * Patch and go  - find the `if debugger_present() { ... }` branch and NOP / invert
//!     it, so the bail never happens.
//!   * Emulate       - run check_password in the Emulator, where there is no real
//!     debugger to detect.
//!
//! The password itself is an ordinary fixed string, so once the guard is gone the
//! check is easy; the whole challenge is getting past the anti-debug branch.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

#[cfg(windows)]
#[link(name = "kernel32")]
unsafe extern "system" {
    fn IsDebuggerPresent() -> i32;
}

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps the anti-debug check a separate, findable function.
#[inline(never)]
fn debugger_present() -> bool {
    #[cfg(windows)]
    {
        unsafe { IsDebuggerPresent() != 0 }
    }
    #[cfg(not(windows))]
    {
        false
    }
}

#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(s: &[u8]) -> bool {
    s == black_box(b"n0_debugger_here")
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #4 ===");
    print!("Password: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    let ok = check_password(line.as_bytes());

    // The anti-debug gate: under a debugger, refuse to reveal success.
    if debugger_present() {
        println!("Debugger detected. Nice try.");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    if ok {
        println!("Correct! You slipped past the anti-debugging.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong password. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

```

`academy/crackmes/crackme05.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #5 (Level 5, "VM-based obfuscation" / "Reversing a custom VM")
//!
//! The password check is not written as native code — it's a tiny **bytecode virtual
//! machine**. `check_password` is a classic fetch-decode-execute dispatch loop: it reads
//! an opcode from CODE, jumps to the handler for it, runs it, and loops back. The real
//! logic (XOR, rotate, compare) lives in the CODE array as data.
//!
//! That shape — one dispatcher block that many handler arms branch back to, inside a loop —
//! is exactly what ORRESS's VM detector looks for, so Triage flags it as VM-based
//! obfuscation. To solve it you map the opcodes (the "Reversing a custom VM" lesson), then
//! read the bytecode to recover the key.
//!
//! ISA: a stack machine over bytes.
//!   0 PUSHIN i : push input[i]        5 ROL n : a=pop; push rotate_left(a, n)
//!   1 PUSHIM v : push v               6 EQ    : b=pop; a=pop; fail unless a == b
//!   2 XOR      : b=pop; a=pop; a^b    7 DUP   : push top
//!   3 ADD      : b=pop; a=pop; a+b    8 LEN n : fail unless input.len() == n
//!   4 SUB      : b=pop; a=pop; a-b    9 HALT  : success

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const CODE: [u8; 83] = [
    8, 8, 0, 0, 1, 59, 2, 5, 1, 1,
    154, 6, 0, 1, 1, 167, 2, 5, 3, 1,
    86, 6, 0, 2, 1, 30, 2, 5, 5, 1,
    40, 6, 0, 3, 1, 100, 2, 5, 2, 1,
    81, 6, 0, 4, 1, 194, 2, 5, 7, 1,
    218, 6, 0, 5, 1, 89, 2, 5, 4, 1,
    115, 6, 0, 6, 1, 141, 2, 5, 6, 1,
    58, 6, 0, 7, 1, 16, 2, 5, 2, 1,
    209, 6, 9,
];

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps the interpreter a single findable function. The dispatch loop
/// below is the VM: one `match` (the dispatcher) that every handler arm loops back to.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(input: &[u8]) -> bool {
    let mut stack = [0u8; 32];
    let mut sp = 0usize;
    let mut pc = 0usize;
    loop {
        // `black_box` hides the opcode from the optimiser, so it can't fold the VM away or
        // prove any handler unreachable — every opcode stays a real arm of the dispatch.
        let op = black_box(CODE[pc]);
        pc += 1;
        match op {
            0 => {
                let i = CODE[pc] as usize;
                pc += 1;
                match input.get(i) {
                    Some(&b) => {
                        stack[sp] = b;
                        sp += 1;
                    }
                    None => return false,
                }
            }
            1 => {
                stack[sp] = CODE[pc];
                sp += 1;
                pc += 1;
            }
            2 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a ^ b;
            }
            3 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a.wrapping_add(b);
            }
            4 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a.wrapping_sub(b);
            }
            5 => {
                let n = u32::from(CODE[pc]);
                pc += 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = stack[sp - 1].rotate_left(n);
            }
            6 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 2;
                if a != b {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            7 => {
                stack[sp] = stack[sp - 1];
                sp += 1;
            }
            8 => {
                let n = CODE[pc] as usize;
                pc += 1;
                if input.len() != n {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            9 => return true,
            _ => return false,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #5 ===");
    print!("Key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_password(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You devirtualized the check.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong key. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

```

`academy/crackmes/crackme06.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #6 (Level 5, a second custom VM)
//!
//! Like crackme05 this is a bytecode VM, but built differently on purpose: a stack of 16-bit values,
//! a different opcode set, and a 2-byte little-endian immediate operand (PUSHI). It exists to prove
//! ORRESS's VM analysis isn't over-fit to crackme05's exact shape.
//!
//! ISA (stack of u16):
//!   0 HALT             success
//!   1 PUSHI  lo hi     push the 16-bit little-endian immediate
//!   2 PUSHIN idx       push input[idx] (zero-extended)
//!   3 ADD              pop b, pop a, push a + b
//!   4 MUL              pop b, pop a, push a * b
//!   5 XOR              pop b, pop a, push a ^ b
//!   6 EQ               pop b, pop a, fail unless a == b
//!   7 SUB              pop b, pop a, push a - b
//!
//! The check: for each input byte, ((input[i] ^ K[i]) * M[i]) & 0xffff == C[i] (M[i] odd, so solvable).

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const CODE: [u8; 113] = [
    2, 0, 1, 17, 0, 5, 1, 143, 0, 4, 1, 151,
    67, 6, 2, 1, 1, 126, 0, 5, 1, 59, 0, 4,
    1, 14, 17, 6, 2, 2, 1, 44, 0, 5, 1, 213,
    0, 4, 1, 187, 65, 6, 2, 3, 1, 90, 0, 5,
    1, 39, 0, 4, 1, 119, 7, 6, 2, 4, 1, 147,
    0, 5, 1, 97, 0, 4, 1, 197, 86, 6, 2, 5,
    1, 8, 0, 5, 1, 171, 0, 4, 1, 105, 39, 6,
    2, 6, 1, 225, 0, 5, 1, 29, 0, 4, 1, 167,
    16, 6, 2, 7, 1, 64, 0, 5, 1, 243, 0, 4,
    1, 105, 48, 6, 0,
];

#[inline(never)]
fn check_key(input: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if input.len() != 8 {
        return false;
    }
    let mut stack = [0u16; 32];
    let mut sp = 0usize;
    let mut pc = 0usize;
    loop {
        let op = black_box(CODE[pc]);
        pc += 1;
        match op {
            0 => return true,
            1 => {
                stack[sp] = u16::from_le_bytes([CODE[pc], CODE[pc + 1]]);
                sp += 1;
                pc += 2;
            }
            2 => {
                let idx = CODE[pc] as usize;
                pc += 1;
                match input.get(idx) {
                    Some(&b) => {
                        stack[sp] = u16::from(b);
                        sp += 1;
                    }
                    None => return false,
                }
            }
            3 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a.wrapping_add(b);
            }
            4 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a.wrapping_mul(b);
            }
            5 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a ^ b;
            }
            6 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 2;
                if a != b {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            7 => {
                let b = stack[sp - 1];
                let a = stack[sp - 2];
                sp -= 1;
                stack[sp - 1] = a.wrapping_sub(b);
            }
            _ => return false,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #6 ===");
    print!("Key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_key(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You devirtualized the second VM.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong key. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #7 (Level 5, a register-based VM)
//!
//! A third bytecode VM, deliberately *register*-based rather than stack-based, to prove ORRESS's VM
//! analysis isn't tied to a stack machine. Four virtual registers, uniform 3-byte instructions
//! `[opcode, rd, arg]`.
//!
//! ISA (regs: [u8; 4]):
//!   0 HALT              success
//!   1 LOADIN rd, idx    rd = input[idx]
//!   2 XORI   rd, imm    rd ^= imm
//!   3 ADDI   rd, imm    rd += imm
//!   4 ROLI   rd, amt    rd = rd.rotate_left(amt)
//!   5 CMPI   rd, imm    fail unless rd == imm
//!   6 SUBI   rd, imm    rd -= imm
//!   7 MOV    rd, rs     rd = rs
//!
//! The check: for each input byte, rotate_left(input[i] ^ K[i], R[i]) == C[i]. Key "r3g_v4lz".

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const CODE: [u8; 99] = [
    1, 0, 0, 2, 0, 92, 4, 0, 1, 5, 0, 92,
    1, 0, 1, 2, 0, 18, 4, 0, 2, 5, 0, 132,
    1, 0, 2, 2, 0, 169, 4, 0, 3, 5, 0, 118,
    1, 0, 3, 2, 0, 126, 4, 0, 4, 5, 0, 18,
    1, 0, 4, 2, 0, 3, 4, 0, 5, 5, 0, 174,
    1, 0, 5, 2, 0, 241, 4, 0, 6, 5, 0, 113,
    1, 0, 6, 2, 0, 107, 4, 0, 7, 5, 0, 131,
    1, 0, 7, 2, 0, 141, 4, 0, 1, 5, 0, 239,
    0, 0, 0,
];

#[inline(never)]
fn check_key(input: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if input.len() != 8 {
        return false;
    }
    let mut regs = [0u8; 4];
    let mut pc = 0usize;
    loop {
        let op = black_box(CODE[pc]);
        let rd = CODE[pc + 1] as usize;
        let arg = CODE[pc + 2];
        pc += 3;
        match op {
            0 => return true,
            1 => match input.get(arg as usize) {
                Some(&b) => regs[rd] = b,
                None => return false,
            },
            2 => regs[rd] ^= arg,
            3 => regs[rd] = regs[rd].wrapping_add(arg),
            4 => regs[rd] = regs[rd].rotate_left(u32::from(arg)),
            5 => {
                if regs[rd] != arg {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            6 => regs[rd] = regs[rd].wrapping_sub(arg),
            7 => regs[rd] = regs[arg as usize],
            _ => return false,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #7 ===");
    print!("Key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_key(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You devirtualized the register VM.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong key. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme08.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #8 (Level 5/7, "Control-flow flattening")
//!
//! `check_password` is **control-flow-flattened**: its logic isn't a straight line of
//! `if`s — every step is a `match` arm of one dispatcher loop, and each arm sets a `state`
//! variable to pick the next arm. `black_box(state)` stops the optimiser from collapsing the
//! state machine back into structured control flow, so the compiled binary really does run a
//! dispatch loop with a jump table on `state` — the shape obfuscators (OLLVM) emit.
//!
//! The original control flow is a simple per-byte check: `rotate_left(input[i] ^ K[i], i+1)`
//! must equal `C[i]` for each of the 8 bytes. ORRESS's decompiler undoes the flattening
//! (relinking each arm to its real successor and dropping the dispatcher), so the recovered
//! pseudocode reads as the straight-line check it started as — look for the
//! "deobfuscated by ORRESS" note. Key: "unfl4tt3".

use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const K: [u8; 8] = [0x3b, 0xa7, 0x1e, 0x64, 0xc2, 0x59, 0x8d, 0x10];

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps the flattened interpreter one findable function.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(input: &[u8]) -> bool {
    // The expected transformed bytes: rotate_left(K[i] ^ key[i], i+1) for key = "unfl4tt3".
    const C: [u8; 8] = expected();
    // One state per original basic block (no loop counter), so the compiler emits a real
    // dispatcher with a case per state — the control-flow-flattening shape — rather than a
    // tidy loop. Each arm checks one byte and sets the next state.
    let mut state: u32 = 0;
    loop {
        match state {
            0 => {
                if input.len() != 8 {
                    return false;
                }
                state = 1;
            }
            1 if rotate_left(input[0] ^ K[0], 1) == C[0] => state = 2,
            2 if rotate_left(input[1] ^ K[1], 2) == C[1] => state = 3,
            3 if rotate_left(input[2] ^ K[2], 3) == C[2] => state = 4,
            4 if rotate_left(input[3] ^ K[3], 4) == C[3] => state = 5,
            5 if rotate_left(input[4] ^ K[4], 5) == C[4] => state = 6,
            6 if rotate_left(input[5] ^ K[5], 6) == C[5] => state = 7,
            7 if rotate_left(input[6] ^ K[6], 7) == C[6] => state = 8,
            8 if rotate_left(input[7] ^ K[7], 8) == C[7] => state = 9,
            9 => return true,
            _ => return false,
        }
    }
}

const fn rotate_left_const(v: u8, n: u32) -> u8 {
    v.rotate_left(n)
}

fn rotate_left(v: u8, n: u32) -> u8 {
    v.rotate_left(n)
}

/// Computes the expected transformed bytes at compile time from the real key "unfl4tt3".
const fn expected() -> [u8; 8] {
    let key = *b"unfl4tt3";
    let mut out = [0u8; 8];
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < 8 {
        out[i] = rotate_left_const(key[i] ^ K[i], (i + 1) as u32);
        i += 1;
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #8 ===");
    print!("Key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_password(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You unflattened the check.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong key. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme09.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #9 (Level 2, lesson "Writing a keygen")
//!
//! A keygen-me: the serial number is not fixed but computed from the name you type, so
//! every name has its own serial. `check_serial` adds up the character codes of the name,
//! starting from 0x1000, and XORs the sum with 0xBEEF:
//!
//!   serial = (0x1000 + name[0] + name[1] + ...) ^ 0xBEEF
//!
//! The lesson asks for the serial of the name `alice`: 0x1000 + 510 = 0x11FE, and
//! 0x11FE ^ 0xBEEF = 0xAF11 = 44817. A keygen in Rust:
//!
//!   let sum = name.bytes().fold(0x1000u32, |s, c| s + u32::from(c));
//!   println!("{}", sum ^ 0xBEEF);

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

/// Reads one line and removes the line ending.
#[inline(never)]
fn read_line() -> String {
    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);
    line.to_owned()
}

/// Reads a line and turns it into a number.
#[inline(never)]
fn read_serial() -> u32 {
    match read_line().trim().parse() {
        Ok(n) => n,
        Err(_) => {
            println!("A serial number is a number, like 12345.");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps the check a separate function you can find and rename.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_serial(name: &[u8], serial: u32) -> bool {
    if name.len() < 3 {
        return false;
    }
    let mut sum: u32 = 0x1000;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < name.len() {
        // `black_box` keeps the loop a real loop you can read.
        sum = sum.wrapping_add(u32::from(black_box(name[i])));
        i += 1;
    }
    (sum ^ 0xBEEF) == serial
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #9 (keygen-me) ===");
    print!("Name: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();
    let name = read_line();
    print!("Serial number: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();
    let serial = read_serial();

    if check_serial(name.as_bytes(), serial) {
        println!("Correct! That serial belongs to {name}.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong serial for this name. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #10 (Level 2, "Static analysis": the practice program for the
//! lessons on file formats, navigation, naming, the graph view and the decompiler)
//!
//! A small "licence checker" with a clear structure, so every static-analysis view has
//! something to show: `main` prints, reads a line and calls `is_valid`, which checks the
//! length and the first character and then calls `checksum`, a loop that adds up the
//! character codes. The graph view shows the if/else in `main` and the loop in `checksum`.
//!
//! Solve it in the decompiler lesson: a valid code is 6 characters long, starts with `K`,
//! and its character codes add up to 500 (0x1F4). `KUUUUU` works (75 + 5 * 85 = 500), and
//! so does any other code with the same sum.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

/// The sum every valid code must reach.
const TARGET: u32 = 500;

/// Adds up the character codes. `#[inline(never)]` keeps it a separate function, and
/// `black_box` keeps the loop a real loop you can see in the graph view.
#[inline(never)]
fn checksum(code: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    let mut sum: u32 = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < code.len() {
        sum = sum.wrapping_add(u32::from(black_box(code[i])));
        i += 1;
    }
    sum
}

#[inline(never)]
fn is_valid(code: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if code.len() != 6 {
        return false;
    }
    if code[0] != b'K' {
        return false;
    }
    // `black_box` hides that the length is 6, so `checksum` stays a general loop.
    checksum(black_box(code)) == TARGET
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #10 ===");
    print!("Licence code: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if is_valid(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Licence accepted. Welcome!");
    } else {
        println!("Invalid licence code.");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme11.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #11 (Level 3, lesson "Reading memory at runtime")
//!
//! The password is never stored, not as text and not as character codes: `decode_secret`
//! builds it in memory only while the program runs, from scrambled bytes and a changing
//! key. Reading the file does not show it; watching the running program does.
//!
//! Solve it with the debugger: put a breakpoint on the first instruction of
//! `check_password`, run, type any input, and when it stops look at memory at the address
//! in `r8` (the third argument: a pointer to the decoded 12-byte secret).
//! The Emulator also works: run `decode_secret` and read the scratch buffer after the run.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

/// The password, scrambled: byte i is XOR'd with a key that changes after every byte
/// (key = key * 5 + 3, starting at 0x5c).
const ENC: [u8; 12] = [
    0x2b, 0xfb, 0x7a, 0x2a, 0x18, 0x6c, 0x33, 0x79, 0x1b, 0x25, 0xc3, 0xff,
];

/// Decodes the password into `out`. `#[inline(never)]` keeps it a separate function.
#[inline(never)]
fn decode_secret(out: &mut [u8; 12]) {
    // `black_box` stops the compiler from decoding at compile time, which would put the
    // password straight back into the file.
    let enc = black_box(&ENC);
    let mut key: u8 = 0x5c;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < out.len() {
        out[i] = enc[i] ^ key;
        key = key.wrapping_mul(5).wrapping_add(3);
        i += 1;
    }
}

/// Compares every byte (no early exit), so only the result tells you anything.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(input: &[u8], secret: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if input.len() != secret.len() {
        return false;
    }
    let mut same = true;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < secret.len() {
        if black_box(input[i]) != secret[i] {
            same = false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    same
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #11 ===");
    print!("Password: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    let mut secret = [0u8; 12];
    decode_secret(&mut secret);

    if check_password(line.as_bytes(), &secret) {
        println!("Correct! You read the secret while the program was running.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong password. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}
