`academy/crackmes/crackme12.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #12 (Level 3, lesson "Practice: three guards")
//!
//! Three anti-debugging checks, and they fail silently: if any of them sees a debugger,
//! the program decodes a decoy password instead of the real one and always answers
//! "Wrong". Reading memory under the debugger without beating the checks shows the decoy.
//!
//!   1. `api_check`    - asks Windows with `IsDebuggerPresent`.
//!   2. `peb_check`    - reads the `BeingDebugged` byte of the PEB itself (`gs:[0x60]`,
//!                       then the byte at offset 2), no API call at all.
//!   3. `timing_check` - measures a short loop with `Instant` (QueryPerformanceCounter);
//!                       if it took longer than half a second, someone was stepping.
//!
//! Beat it the way the lessons teach:
//!   * Change registers: break right after each check's `call`, set `rax` to 0, continue.
//!     Then break at `check_password` and read the real secret at `r8`.
//!   * Patch: make each check return 0, save a patched copy.
//!   * Emulate: run `decode_secret` in the Emulator with a 16-character input and
//!     "pass input length" off (so the decoy flag, arg1, is 0). The scratch buffer shows
//!     the real password, and no check ever runs.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

const REAL: [u8; 16] = [
    0x4a, 0x44, 0x8b, 0xcc, 0x06, 0x76, 0xe0, 0x61, 0x3d, 0xde, 0xc9, 0x42, 0x7a, 0x10, 0x4c, 0x28,
];
const DECOY: [u8; 16] = [
    0x54, 0x4c, 0xdf, 0xca, 0x31, 0x5d, 0xa2, 0x6a, 0x3d, 0x89, 0xc1, 0x55, 0x63, 0x16, 0x4a, 0x3a,
];

#[cfg(windows)]
#[link(name = "kernel32")]
unsafe extern "system" {
    fn IsDebuggerPresent() -> i32;
}

/// Guard 1: the Windows API.
#[inline(never)]
fn api_check() -> bool {
    #[cfg(windows)]
    {
        unsafe { IsDebuggerPresent() != 0 }
    }
    #[cfg(not(windows))]
    {
        false
    }
}

/// Guard 2: the PEB's BeingDebugged byte, read directly.
#[inline(never)]
fn peb_check() -> bool {
    #[cfg(all(windows, target_arch = "x86_64"))]
    {
        let peb: *const u8;
        // SAFETY: on 64-bit Windows, gs:[0x60] always holds the address of this process's
        // PEB, and byte 2 of the PEB is BeingDebugged.
        unsafe {
            std::arch::asm!("mov {}, gs:[0x60]", out(reg) peb, options(nostack, readonly, preserves_flags));
            *peb.add(2) != 0
        }
    }
    #[cfg(not(all(windows, target_arch = "x86_64")))]
    {
        false
    }
}

/// Guard 3: a timing check. The loop takes microseconds; stepping through it takes ages.
#[inline(never)]
fn timing_check() -> bool {
    let start = Instant::now();
    let mut sum: u64 = 0;
    for i in 0..black_box(1000u64) {
        sum = sum.wrapping_add(black_box(i));
    }
    black_box(sum);
    start.elapsed() > Duration::from_millis(500)
}

/// Decodes the real password (or, if `decoy` is true, the decoy) into `out`.
#[inline(never)]
fn decode_secret(out: &mut [u8; 16], decoy: bool) {
    let enc = if decoy { black_box(&DECOY) } else { black_box(&REAL) };
    let mut key: u8 = 0x3a;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < out.len() {
        out[i] = enc[i] ^ key;
        key = key.wrapping_mul(5).wrapping_add(3);
        i += 1;
    }
}

/// Compares every byte (no early exit).
#[inline(never)]
fn check_password(input: &[u8], secret: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if input.len() != secret.len() {
        return false;
    }
    let mut same = true;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < secret.len() {
        if black_box(input[i]) != secret[i] {
            same = false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    same
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #12 ===");
    print!("Password: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    // The three guard results are OR'd together into one `watched` flag (the compiler
    // combines them with `or`), which is then checked once near the end.
    let mut watched = false;
    if api_check() {
        watched = true;
    }
    if peb_check() {
        watched = true;
    }
    if timing_check() {
        watched = true;
    }

    let mut secret = [0u8; 16];
    decode_secret(&mut secret, black_box(watched));

    // Silent failure: when watched, even the right password is "wrong".
    if check_password(line.as_bytes(), &secret) && !watched {
        println!("Correct! Three guards down. You beat the anti-debugging.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong password. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme13.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #13 (Level 4, "Practice: break a real cipher")
//!
//! The flag is checked by *encrypting* your input with the TEA block cipher and comparing the
//! result (as hex text) with a stored ciphertext. Nothing here is custom: it is textbook TEA,
//! recognisable by its "delta" constant 0x9E3779B9 (twice in the disassembly of the encryption
//! function; the decompiler writes the `add` as `-= 0x61c88647`, the same number in two's
//! complement).
//!
//! Solve it the way the lesson teaches:
//!   1. Recognise the algorithm from the constant in the encryption function.
//!   2. Find the 16-byte key (a readable string the encryption function uses).
//!   3. Find the stored ciphertext (48 hex digits in the Strings view).
//!   4. In the Workbench: `from_hex | tea_decrypt key=<the key>` gives the flag.
//!
//! Flag: flag{te4_h4s_a_g0ld_k3y}

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

/// The TEA key: 16 bytes, read as four little-endian 32-bit words.
static KEY: [u8; 16] = *b"t1ny_crypt0_k3y!";

/// TEA-encrypted flag, as lowercase hex text.
static EXPECTED: &str = "0c0b5df889a72f0143b197b070de2a2c09c4c9db4af2ad80";

/// Encrypts one 8-byte block with TEA (32 cycles). `#[inline(never)]` keeps it a separate
/// function you can find.
#[inline(never)]
fn tea_encrypt(v: &mut [u32; 2], k: &[u32; 4]) {
    const DELTA: u32 = 0x9E37_79B9;
    let (mut v0, mut v1) = (v[0], v[1]);
    let mut sum: u32 = 0;
    for _ in 0..32 {
        sum = sum.wrapping_add(DELTA);
        v0 = v0.wrapping_add(
            (v1 << 4).wrapping_add(k[0]) ^ v1.wrapping_add(sum) ^ (v1 >> 5).wrapping_add(k[1]),
        );
        v1 = v1.wrapping_add(
            (v0 << 4).wrapping_add(k[2]) ^ v0.wrapping_add(sum) ^ (v0 >> 5).wrapping_add(k[3]),
        );
    }
    v[0] = v0;
    v[1] = v1;
}

#[inline(never)]
fn check_flag(input: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if input.len() != 24 {
        return false;
    }
    let key = black_box(&KEY);
    let mut k = [0u32; 4];
    for (i, word) in k.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        *word = u32::from_le_bytes([key[4 * i], key[4 * i + 1], key[4 * i + 2], key[4 * i + 3]]);
    }
    let mut hex = String::new();
    for block in input.chunks(8) {
        let mut v = [
            u32::from_le_bytes([block[0], block[1], block[2], block[3]]),
            u32::from_le_bytes([block[4], block[5], block[6], block[7]]),
        ];
        tea_encrypt(&mut v, &k);
        for word in v {
            for byte in word.to_le_bytes() {
                hex.push_str(&format!("{byte:02x}"));
            }
        }
    }
    hex == black_box(EXPECTED)
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #13 ===");
    print!("Flag: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_flag(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Correct! You decrypted the flag.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong flag. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme14.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #14 (Level 4, "Symbolic execution")
//!
//! The 12-character key is checked two characters at a time. For each pair (a, b):
//!
//!   x = a ^ KA[j]        y = b ^ 0x3c
//!   (x ^ y) == MIX[j]   and   x.rotate_left(1) + y == ROT[j]      (the addition wraps at 256)
//!
//! Every condition mixes two input bytes, so you cannot read one character off a single
//! comparison the way you could in crackme03, and the instruction-counting side channel gets
//! confused. Symbolic execution does not care: it collects the twelve conditions and the solver
//! finds the only input that satisfies all of them.
//!
//! Solve it the way the lesson teaches: in the Emulator's **Symbolic solve** section, enter
//! `check_key` (0x1400012c0) as the function, 12 as the input length, the block that sets the
//! return value 0x600d (0x140001478) as the target and the shared failure exit (0x140001489) as
//! the avoid address. The solver collects 12 constraints and recovers the key.
//!
//! Key: s0lv3_m3_n0w

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const KA: [u8; 6] = [0x5a, 0x13, 0xc7, 0x2e, 0x91, 0x64];
const MIX: [u8; 6] = [0x25, 0x35, 0x97, 0x4c, 0x9c, 0x1f];
const ROT: [u8; 6] = [0x5e, 0x48, 0x4c, 0x95, 0xef, 0xf3];

/// Returns 0x600d ("good") for the right key and 0 otherwise. It takes a fixed-size array,
/// so the only argument is a pointer to the 12 bytes.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_key(key: &[u8; 12]) -> u32 {
    let mut j = 0;
    while j < 6 {
        // `black_box` stops the compiler from folding the checks together.
        let x = black_box(key[2 * j]) ^ KA[j];
        let y = black_box(key[2 * j + 1]) ^ 0x3c;
        if x ^ y != MIX[j] {
            return 0;
        }
        if x.rotate_left(1).wrapping_add(y) != ROT[j] {
            return 0;
        }
        j += 1;
    }
    black_box(0x600d)
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #14 ===");
    print!("Key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }

    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    let ok = match <&[u8; 12]>::try_from(line.as_bytes()) {
        Ok(key) => check_key(key) == 0x600d,
        Err(_) => false,
    };
    if ok {
        println!("Correct! The solver was right.");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong key. Try again!");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

```

`academy/crackmes/crackme15.rs`:

```rs
//! crackme15 - HARMLESS malware-like TRAINING SAMPLE (Level 6, Malware analysis).
//!
//! THIS PROGRAM DOES NOTHING HARMFUL. It only prints a message and exits with code 0.
//! It touches no network, no registry, no other processes and no files. It exists so the
//! Academy's malware lessons (triage, IOC extraction, YARA, reporting) have a realistic
//! target to analyse safely.
//!
//! To make triage interesting it deliberately *contains the indicators an analyst looks for*,
//! but never acts on any of them:
//!   - suspicious strings: a fake C2 URL on the reserved, non-routable `.invalid` TLD, a
//!     registry Run-key path, a browser User-Agent and a mutex name;
//!   - an XOR-encoded configuration blob in the `ExampleRAT` demo format (marker `ORCFG`,
//!     2-byte little-endian length, then `key=value;` text XOR-ed with 0x5A) that ORRESS's
//!     Triage config extractor decodes;
//!   - imports that malware uses for process injection (`VirtualAllocEx`,
//!     `WriteProcessMemory`, `CreateRemoteThread`, `OpenProcess`), HTTP C2 (`InternetOpenA`,
//!     `HttpSendRequestA`), persistence/crypto (`RegCreateKeyExA`, `RegSetValueExA`,
//!     `CryptEncrypt`) and dynamic API resolution (`LoadLibraryA`, `GetProcAddress`) - all of
//!     which are merely *referenced* (their addresses are read into a checksum) and never
//!     called. No injection, no network, no registry write, no encryption ever happens.
//!
//! Used by: the Level 6 lessons l6-malware-triage and l6-static-deep-dive.
//! Solution: there is nothing to "solve" - you analyse it. The decoded C2 host is
//! `update.example.invalid` and the distinctive marker string is `ORRESS_TRAINING_SAMPLE_v1`.

// Suspicious-looking indicators. All inert: `.invalid` never resolves, and nothing here is
// ever connected to, written or executed.
static MARKER: &str = "ORRESS_TRAINING_SAMPLE_v1";
static C2_URL: &str = "http://cdn.example.invalid/beacon";
static USER_AGENT: &str = "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0) ORRESS-Trainer/1.0";
static RUN_KEY: &str = r"HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run";
static MUTEX: &str = r"Global\ORRESS-TRAIN-01";

// XOR-encoded (0x5A) ExampleRAT config: ORCFG + u16 length + encoded "key=value;" text.
static CONFIG: &[u8] = &[79,82,67,70,71,121,0,57,104,103,50,46,46,42,96,117,117,47,42,62,59,46,63,116,63,34,59,55,42,54,63,116,51,52,44,59,54,51,62,117,61,59,46,63,116,42,50,42,97,42,53,40,46,103,98,110,110,105,97,57,59,55,42,59,51,61,52,103,14,8,27,19,20,19,20,29,119,104,106,104,108,97,55,47,46,63,34,103,21,8,8,31,9,9,119,14,8,27,19,20,119,106,107,97,40,57,110,49,63,35,103,9,105,57,40,105,46,14,40,59,51,52,51,52,61,17,63,35];

// Imports that process-injecting malware pulls in. Declared and referenced, NEVER called.
#[link(name = "kernel32")]
unsafe extern "system" {
    fn VirtualAlloc();
    fn VirtualAllocEx();
    fn WriteProcessMemory();
    fn CreateRemoteThread();
    fn OpenProcess();
    fn LoadLibraryA();
    fn GetProcAddress();
}
#[link(name = "wininet")]
unsafe extern "system" {
    fn InternetOpenA();
    fn HttpSendRequestA();
}
#[link(name = "advapi32")]
unsafe extern "system" {
    fn RegCreateKeyExA();
    fn RegSetValueExA();
    fn CryptEncrypt();
}

fn main() {
    // Reference every suspicious import's ADDRESS (never call it), so the functions appear in
    // the import table for an analyst to find. `black_box` stops the optimiser removing them.
    let imports: [*const (); 12] = [
        VirtualAlloc as *const (),
        VirtualAllocEx as *const (),
        WriteProcessMemory as *const (),
        CreateRemoteThread as *const (),
        OpenProcess as *const (),
        LoadLibraryA as *const (),
        GetProcAddress as *const (),
        InternetOpenA as *const (),
        HttpSendRequestA as *const (),
        RegCreateKeyExA as *const (),
        RegSetValueExA as *const (),
        CryptEncrypt as *const (),
    ];
    let mut checksum: usize = 0;
    for p in imports {
        checksum ^= p as usize;
    }

    // Keep the indicator strings and the config in the binary without acting on them.
    std::hint::black_box((
        MARKER,
        C2_URL,
        USER_AGENT,
        RUN_KEY,
        MUTEX,
        CONFIG,
        checksum,
    ));

    println!("{MARKER}");
    println!("This is a HARMLESS training sample for the ORRESS Academy.");
    println!("It contains malware-like indicators but does nothing harmful: it has not");
    println!("touched the network, the registry, any process or any file. Analyse it safely.");
}

`academy/crackmes/crackme17.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #17 (Level 7, "Time-travel debugging" and "Binary diffing")
//!
//! "KeyVault 1.0": a small licence-key checker with a security bug. Crackme #18 is version
//! 1.1 of the same program, with the bug fixed. Diffing the two shows exactly what changed.
//!
//! The key is never stored as text. Each key byte is XORed with 0x5c, its position is added,
//! and the result is compared with the bytes in `ENC`. Key: "ORR-DIFF-7".
//!
//! The bug: `check_key` only compares as many bytes as you type. An empty key, or any start
//! of the real key ("O", "ORR-"), is accepted. Version 1.1 first checks the key's length and
//! shape in a new function, `key_shape_ok`.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const KEY_LEN: usize = 10;
/// The encoded key, computed at compile time: the plain key is not in the binary.
const ENC: [u8; KEY_LEN] = encode(*b"ORR-DIFF-7");

const fn encode(key: [u8; KEY_LEN]) -> [u8; KEY_LEN] {
    let mut out = [0u8; KEY_LEN];
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < KEY_LEN {
        out[i] = (key[i] ^ 0x5c).wrapping_add(i as u8);
        i += 1;
    }
    out
}

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps this a separate function you can find, record and diff.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_key(key: &[u8]) -> bool {
    // Only printable characters (space to `~`) can be part of a key.
    for &b in key {
        if !(0x20..=0x7e).contains(&b) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    // BUG: the loop below runs over the bytes you typed, not over the whole key.
    // `black_box` on the length keeps this a real loop (the compiler does not unroll it).
    let len = black_box(key.len());
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len {
        if i >= KEY_LEN {
            return false;
        }
        // `black_box` keeps each byte a real xor-add-compare in the machine code.
        if black_box(key[i] ^ 0x5c).wrapping_add(i as u8) != ENC[i] {
            return false; // stops at the first wrong byte
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #17: KeyVault 1.0 ===");
    print!("Licence key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_key(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Access granted. Welcome to KeyVault.");
    } else {
        println!("Access denied.");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

```

`academy/crackmes/crackme18.rs`:

```rs
//! ORRESS Academy - Crackme #18 (Level 7, "Binary diffing" and the final project)
//!
//! "KeyVault 1.1": crackme #17 with its security bug fixed. A binary diff of #17 against #18
//! shows one changed function (`check_key`) and one added function (`key_shape_ok`).
//!
//! The fix: before the byte loop, `key_shape_ok` checks that the key is exactly 10 bytes long
//! and has a `-` at positions 3 and 8. The key is the same as in #17: "ORR-DIFF-7", stored
//! encoded: ENC[i] = (key[i] ^ 0x5c) + i. A keygen reverses it: key[i] = (ENC[i] - i) ^ 0x5c.

use std::hint::black_box;
use std::io::{self, BufRead, Write};

const KEY_LEN: usize = 10;
/// The encoded key, computed at compile time: the plain key is not in the binary.
const ENC: [u8; KEY_LEN] = encode(*b"ORR-DIFF-7");

const fn encode(key: [u8; KEY_LEN]) -> [u8; KEY_LEN] {
    let mut out = [0u8; KEY_LEN];
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < KEY_LEN {
        out[i] = (key[i] ^ 0x5c).wrapping_add(i as u8);
        i += 1;
    }
    out
}

/// New in 1.1: the key must have the right length and two dashes.
#[inline(never)]
fn key_shape_ok(key: &[u8]) -> bool {
    key.len() == KEY_LEN && key[3] == b'-' && key[8] == b'-'
}

/// `#[inline(never)]` keeps this a separate function you can find, record and diff.
#[inline(never)]
fn check_key(key: &[u8]) -> bool {
    // FIX: reject keys of the wrong length or shape before comparing anything.
    if !key_shape_ok(key) {
        return false;
    }
    // Only printable characters (space to `~`) can be part of a key.
    for &b in key {
        if !(0x20..=0x7e).contains(&b) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    // `black_box` on the length keeps this a real loop (the compiler does not unroll it).
    let len = black_box(key.len());
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len {
        if i >= KEY_LEN {
            return false;
        }
        // `black_box` keeps each byte a real xor-add-compare in the machine code.
        if black_box(key[i] ^ 0x5c).wrapping_add(i as u8) != ENC[i] {
            return false; // stops at the first wrong byte
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn main() {
    println!("=== ORRESS Academy - Crackme #18: KeyVault 1.1 ===");
    print!("Licence key: ");
    io::stdout().flush().ok();

    let mut input = String::new();
    if io::stdin().lock().read_line(&mut input).is_err() {
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    let line = input.strip_suffix('\n').unwrap_or(&input);
    let line = line.strip_suffix('\r').unwrap_or(line);

    if check_key(line.as_bytes()) {
        println!("Access granted. Welcome to KeyVault.");
    } else {
        println!("Access denied.");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
}

see = ["instruction", "assembly language", "disassembler"]

[[term]]
term = "instruction"
aliases = ["instructions"]
short = "One small command for the CPU, such as add two numbers, copy a value, compare, or continue somewhere else."
text = '''
A program is a long list of instructions. Each one does very little, but a CPU runs billions per second. In machine code an instruction is one or more bytes (1 to 15 on x86-64); in assembly it is a short line of text like `add rax, rbx`.
'''
see = ["opcode", "machine code", "assembly language"]

[[term]]
term = "opcode"
aliases = ["opcodes"]
short = "The number that says which operation an instruction performs."
text = '''
In the Academy's toy machine, opcode `1` means "add" and `2` means "multiply". Real CPUs work the same way: the first byte(s) of an instruction say what it does, the following bytes say with which values.
'''
see = ["instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "instruction pointer"
aliases = ["program counter"]
short = "The place where the CPU keeps the address of the next instruction to run."
text = '''
After each instruction the CPU moves the instruction pointer to the next one. A jump or a call changes it, which is how `if`, loops and function calls work underneath. On x86-64 it is the register `rip`.
'''
see = ["CPU", "instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "execute"
aliases = ["executes", "executed", "executing", "execution"]
short = "To run an instruction or a program: the CPU fetches, decodes and does what the instructions say."
see = ["CPU", "instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "assembly language"
aliases = ["assembly"]
short = "The text form of machine code: one short line per instruction, like add rax, rbx."
text = '''
Assembly is written for people; the CPU only sees the bytes. Each assembly line corresponds to exactly one machine code instruction:

```text
48 01 D8    add rax, rbx
```

Level 1 teaches you to read x86-64 assembly.
'''
see = ["machine code", "disassembler", "instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "register"
aliases = ["registers"]
short = "A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU that instructions work on, like rax or rcx."
text = '''
An x86-64 CPU has 16 general registers of 64 bits each, with names such as `rax`, `rbx`, `rcx` and `rdx`. Think of them as the CPU's own local variables. Some have a fixed job: on Windows the first argument of a function arrives in `rcx`, and the return value is left in `rax`. Level 1 explains them in detail.
'''
see = ["CPU", "instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "disassembler"
aliases = ["disassemble", "disassembled", "disassembling"]
short = "A tool that turns machine code bytes back into readable assembly text."
text = '''
The **Disassembly** view of ORRESS is a disassembler: it shows each instruction with its address and adds comments, for example the text of a string an instruction uses.
'''
see = ["machine code", "assembly language"]

[[term]]
term = "architecture"
aliases = ["architectures", "CPU architecture", "instruction set"]
short = "A family of CPUs that understand the same machine code, such as x86-64 or ARM64."
text = '''
A program is built for one architecture. The same bytes mean different things on different architectures, so an x86-64 program cannot run directly on an ARM64 CPU. In Rust you choose it with the build target, for example `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.
'''
see = ["x86-64", "ARM64", "32-bit"]

[[term]]
term = "x86-64"
aliases = ["x64", "AMD64", "x86_64"]
short = "The 64-bit architecture of almost all Windows PCs and most servers. The Academy's crackmes are x86-64 programs."
see = ["architecture", "ARM64"]

[[term]]
term = "32-bit"
aliases = ["64-bit"]
short = "The size of the numbers and addresses a CPU works with most easily. Modern computers are 64-bit."
text = '''
On a 64-bit computer, registers and addresses are 64 bits (8 bytes), and a Rust `usize` is 8 bytes. On a 32-bit computer they are 4 bytes. Older programs and small devices are often 32-bit.
'''
see = ["architecture", "usize"]

[[term]]
term = "system call"
aliases = ["system calls", "syscall", "syscalls"]
short = "The low-level way a program asks the operating system to do something, such as read a file."
text = '''
Most programs do not make system calls themselves; they call library functions (on Windows in DLLs such as `kernel32.dll`), which make the system calls for them.
'''
see = ["operating system", "library"]

[[term]]
term = "library"
aliases = ["libraries"]
short = "A collection of ready-made functions that programs can use."
text = '''
Rust's standard library is one; on Windows the operating system offers its functions in DLLs such as `kernel32.dll`. A library can be copied into the program (static linking) or loaded when the program starts (dynamic linking).
'''
see = ["standard library", "static linking", "dynamic linking", "API"]

[[term]]
term = "API"
aliases = ["APIs"]
short = "Application programming interface: the set of functions a library or system offers to programs."
text = '''
The Windows API is the set of functions Windows offers, such as `WriteConsoleW` to write text to the console. Which API functions a program uses tells a lot about what it does.
'''
see = ["library", "operating system"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- numbers

[[term]]
term = "bit"
aliases = ["bits"]
short = "The smallest unit of data: a single 0 or 1. A bit has two possible values."
text = '''
A bit is like a switch: off (0) or on (1). Eight bits make a byte. Every extra bit doubles the number of values: 1 bit has 2 values, 2 bits have 4, 8 bits have 256.

```rust
let flags: u8 = 0b0000_0101;   // bits 0 and 2 are set
```
'''
see = ["byte", "binary"]

[[term]]
term = "byte"
aliases = ["bytes"]
short = "Eight bits: a number from 0 to 255 (0x00 to 0xFF). Memory is a long row of bytes."
text = '''
A byte is written as two hex digits, from `00` to `FF`. In Rust it is a `u8`. Every byte in memory has its own address; bigger values use several bytes next to each other.

```rust
assert_eq!(u8::MAX, 0xFF);
assert_eq!(b'A', 0x41);   // the character A is the byte 0x41
```
'''
see = ["bit", "hexadecimal", "memory"]

[[term]]
term = "nibble"
aliases = ["nibbles"]
short = "Four bits, half a byte: exactly one hex digit."
see = ["hexadecimal", "bit"]

[[term]]
term = "decimal"
aliases = ["base 10"]
short = "The everyday number system with the ten digits 0 to 9, where each place is worth ten times the next."
see = ["binary", "hexadecimal"]

[[term]]
term = "binary"
aliases = ["base 2", "binary number", "binary numbers"]
short = "The base-2 number system with only the digits 0 and 1, written with 0b in Rust. Also an informal word for a compiled program."
text = '''
Each place is worth twice the place to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To read a binary number, add the place values where there is a 1:

```rust
assert_eq!(0b1011, 8 + 2 + 1);   // 11
println!("{:b}", 11);            // prints 1011
```

Reversers also say "a binary" for a compiled program file, because it holds machine code instead of text.
'''
see = ["bit", "decimal", "hexadecimal"]

[[term]]
term = "hexadecimal"
aliases = ["hex", "base 16"]
short = "The base-16 number system with digits 0-9 and A-F, written with 0x. Two hex digits are exactly one byte."
text = '''
A is 10, B is 11 ... F is 15. Each place is worth 16 times the place to its right: `0x2A` = 2 x 16 + 10 = 42. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so binary converts to hex group by group: `0b1101_0110` = `0xD6`.

```rust
assert_eq!(0x2A, 42);
println!("{:x} {:#X}", 42, 42);   // 2a 0x2A
```

Addresses, bytes and constants in ORRESS are all shown in hex.
'''
see = ["binary", "byte", "nibble"]

[[term]]
term = "place value"
aliases = ["place values"]
short = "What a digit is worth because of its position: in decimal 1, 10, 100; in binary 1, 2, 4; in hex 1, 16, 256."
see = ["decimal", "binary", "hexadecimal"]

[[term]]
term = "unsigned"
aliases = ["unsigned integer", "unsigned integers", "u8", "u16", "u32", "u64"]
short = "An integer type for zero and positive numbers only, like Rust's u8 to u64."
text = '''
| type | bytes | largest value |
|---|---|---|
| `u8` | 1 | `0xFF` (255) |
| `u16` | 2 | `0xFFFF` (65535) |
| `u32` | 4 | `0xFFFF_FFFF` |
| `u64` | 8 | `0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF` |

The largest value always has all bits set.
'''
see = ["signed", "byte"]

[[term]]
term = "signed"
aliases = ["signed integer", "signed integers", "i8", "i16", "i32", "i64"]
short = "An integer type that can also be negative, like Rust's i8 to i64. Stored in two's complement."
text = '''
An `i8` goes from -128 to 127. If the top bit (the sign bit) is 1, the number is negative. The same bits can be read as signed or unsigned:

```rust
assert_eq!(0xFFu8 as i8, -1);
assert_eq!(-1i32 as u32, 0xFFFF_FFFF);
```
'''
see = ["two's complement", "unsigned", "sign bit"]

[[term]]
term = "usize"
aliases = ["isize"]
short = "Rust's integer type with the size of an address: 8 bytes on a 64-bit computer. Used for lengths and indexes."
see = ["32-bit", "pointer"]

[[term]]
term = "dword"
aliases = ["double word"]
short = "Assembly name for a 4-byte value, like a u32 or i32. A word is 2 bytes, a byte is 1."
see = ["qword"]

[[term]]
term = "qword"
aliases = ["quad word"]
short = "Assembly name for an 8-byte value, like a u64, i64 or a pointer."
text = '''
`mov qword ptr [rsp+0x30], 0` stores the 8-byte number 0 in memory. `dword ptr` would store 4 bytes, `byte ptr` 1 byte.
'''
see = ["dword"]

[[term]]
term = "overflow"
aliases = ["overflows", "integer overflow", "overflowed"]
short = "When the result of a calculation does not fit in the number's size. The bits that do not fit are dropped."
text = '''
255 + 1 does not fit in a `u8`. A debug build of Rust panics ("attempt to add with overflow"); a release build, like the CPU itself, wraps around to 0.
'''
see = ["wrapping"]

[[term]]
term = "wrapping"
aliases = ["wrapping_add", "wraps around", "wrap around", "wrapping arithmetic"]
short = "Overflow that continues from the other end, like an odometer: 255u8 + 1 becomes 0."
text = '''
```rust
assert_eq!(255u8.wrapping_add(1), 0);
assert_eq!(250u8.wrapping_add(10), 4);   // 260 - 256
```

This is the CPU's normal behavior, and the reason two's complement works.
'''
see = ["overflow", "two's complement"]

[[term]]
term = "two's complement"
short = "The way computers store negative numbers: -n is stored as 2^bits - n, so -1 in a byte is 0xFF."
text = '''
Two ways to calculate it, for 8 bits:

- 256 - n: -5 is 256 - 5 = 251 = `0xFB`;
- flip all bits of n and add 1: 5 = `0000_0101`, flipped `1111_1010`, plus 1 = `1111_1011` = `0xFB`.

Small negative numbers look like a row of Fs: -1 is `0xFF`, `0xFFFF`, `0xFFFFFFFF` depending on the size. The same addition works for signed and unsigned numbers.
'''
see = ["signed", "sign bit", "wrapping"]

[[term]]
term = "sign bit"
short = "The top bit of a signed number: 1 means negative."
see = ["two's complement", "signed"]

[[term]]
term = "sign extension"
aliases = ["sign-extend", "sign-extended", "sign-extends"]
short = "Making a signed number bigger by filling the new bits with copies of the sign bit, so the value stays the same."
text = '''
```rust
assert_eq!(-1i8 as i32, -1);   // 0xFF becomes 0xFFFF_FFFF
```
'''
see = ["zero extension", "sign bit"]

[[term]]
term = "zero extension"
aliases = ["zero-extend", "zero-extended", "zero-extends"]
short = "Making an unsigned number bigger by filling the new bits with zeros."
text = '''
```rust
assert_eq!(0xFFu8 as u32, 0x0000_00FF);   // 255 stays 255
```
'''
see = ["sign extension"]

[[term]]
term = "truncation"
aliases = ["truncate", "truncated", "truncates"]
short = "Making a number smaller by cutting off its upper bytes: 0x1234u16 as u8 is 0x34."
see = ["zero extension"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- text

[[term]]
term = "ASCII"
short = "The basic code table that gives English letters, digits and symbols the numbers 0 to 127: 'A' is 0x41."
text = '''
Useful landmarks: space `0x20`, `'0'` to `'9'` = `0x30` to `0x39`, `'A'` to `'Z'` = `0x41` to `0x5A`, `'a'` to `'z'` = `0x61` to `0x7A`. A lower-case letter is its upper-case letter plus `0x20`.

```rust
assert_eq!(b'A', 0x41);
assert_eq!(b'7' - b'0', 7);
```
'''
see = ["UTF-8", "control character"]

[[term]]
term = "control character"
aliases = ["control characters"]
short = "A non-printable character code below 0x20, such as newline (0x0A), carriage return (0x0D) and tab (0x09)."
see = ["ASCII", "line ending", "NUL"]

[[term]]
term = "line ending"
aliases = ["line endings", "newline", "carriage return"]
short = "The character(s) that end a line of text: \\n (0x0A) on Linux and macOS, \\r\\n (0x0D 0x0A) on Windows."
text = '''
When you type a password and press Enter, the program receives the line ending too. That is why the crackmes remove it with `strip_suffix('\n')` and `strip_suffix('\r')`.
'''
see = ["control character"]

[[term]]
term = "NUL"
aliases = ["null byte", "zero byte", "NUL byte", "string terminator"]
short = "The byte 0x00. C strings end with it."

[[term]]
term = "Unicode"
aliases = ["code point", "code points"]
short = "The standard that gives every character of every writing system a number, its code point, such as U+20AC for the euro sign."
see = ["UTF-8", "UTF-16"]

[[term]]
term = "UTF-8"
short = "The most common way to store Unicode text as bytes: ASCII characters take 1 byte, others 2 to 4. Rust strings are always UTF-8."
text = '''
```rust
assert_eq!("A".as_bytes(), [0x41]);
assert_eq!("é".as_bytes(), [0xC3, 0xA9]);
assert_eq!("héllo".len(), 6);   // len() counts bytes, not characters
```
'''
see = ["Unicode", "ASCII", "UTF-16"]

[[term]]
term = "UTF-16"
aliases = ["wide string", "wide strings"]
short = "A way to store text with 2 bytes per character (sometimes 4). Windows uses it for its wide strings."
text = '''
For English text every second byte is zero: `"Hi"` is stored as `48 00 69 00` (little-endian). In the text column of a hex view it looks like `H.i.`. The Strings view of ORRESS marks such strings as UTF-16.
'''
see = ["UTF-8", "endianness"]

[[term]]
term = "C string"
aliases = ["C strings", "null-terminated string", "null-terminated strings", "NUL-terminated"]
short = "Text that ends with a zero byte (NUL) instead of having a stored length. Used by C and most operating system functions."
text = '''
```text
"hi" as a Rust &str:  68 69       (length 2 stored separately)
"hi" as a C string:   68 69 00
```

In Rust you build one with `std::ffi::CString`.
'''
see = ["NUL", "string literal"]

[[term]]
term = "string literal"
aliases = ["string literals"]
short = "Text written directly in the source code, like \"Wrong password\". It is stored in the program file's read-only data."
text = '''
String literals survive compiling, which is why the Strings view is often the first place a reverser looks. Rust literals have no end marker, so they are stored back to back and a strings tool may show two of them as one: `Password: Wrong password. Try again!`.
'''
see = ["C string", "UTF-8"]

[[term]]
term = "endianness"
aliases = ["byte order", "little-endian", "big-endian", "little endian", "big endian"]
short = "The order in which the bytes of a number are stored. x86-64 and ARM are little-endian: lowest byte first."
text = '''
```rust
let n: u32 = 0x1234_5678;
assert_eq!(n.to_le_bytes(), [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]);  // little-endian
assert_eq!(n.to_be_bytes(), [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78]);  // big-endian
```

To read a little-endian number from a hex dump, reverse the order of its bytes. Network protocols and some file formats use big-endian.
'''
see = ["byte", "Inspector"]

[[term]]

A value of several bytes has the address of its first byte. A `u32` at `0x1000` covers `0x1000` to `0x1003`, and the next value can start at `0x1004`. Every process has its own addresses (virtual memory).

```

In machine code, references, `Box` and raw pointers are all just addresses.
'''
see = ["address", "dereference", "Rust reference"]

[[term]]

[[term]]

A `Vec` or `String` is three 8-byte numbers: a pointer to the elements, the capacity and the length (24 bytes in total). The order is chosen by the compiler.

[[term]]

The stack is fast and needs no bookkeeping, but the size of everything on it must be known when compiling. The CPU has special instructions for it; Level 1 explains them.

The program asks for a block of heap memory (allocation) and gives it back later. In Rust this happens automatically: a `Vec` frees its heap block when it is dropped.

[[term]]

[[term]]

[[term]]

Address `0x1000` in one process and `0x1000` in another are different bytes, so processes cannot see each other's memory. An address only has a meaning inside one process.

Common optimizations are constant folding (`2 + 3` becomes `5`), inlining (copying a small function into its caller) and removing dead code. Optimized code often looks quite different from the source.

[[term]]

short = "The address where the operating system starts running a program. It runs start-up code, which later calls main."
text = '''
The entry point is stored in the program's header. In a Rust program on Windows the chain is roughly: entry point -> C runtime start-up -> Rust's `lang_start` -> your `fn main`. The **Info** view shows the entry point; **Go > Go to main** skips the start-up code.
'''
see = ["start-up code", "main function", "header"]

[[term]]
term = "start-up code"
aliases = ["startup code", "C runtime", "CRT"]
short = "Code from the C runtime and Rust's standard library that runs before main: it prepares the program and then calls main."
see = ["entry point", "main function"]

[[term]]
term = "main function"
aliases = ["fn main", "main()"]
short = "The function where the programmer's own code begins. ORRESS finds it for you with Go to main (Ctrl+Shift+M)."
see = ["entry point", "start-up code"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- executable files

[[term]]
term = "magic bytes"
aliases = ["magic number", "magic numbers", "file signature"]
short = "Fixed bytes at the start of a file that identify its format, like 4D 5A (MZ) for Windows programs."
text = '''
| format | first bytes |
|---|---|
| PE (Windows) | `4D 5A` (`MZ`) |
| ELF (Linux) | `7F 45 4C 46` (`.ELF`) |
| Mach-O (macOS, 64-bit) | `CF FA ED FE` |
'''
see = ["header", "executable"]

[[term]]
term = "header"
aliases = ["headers"]
short = "A block of fields at a fixed place in a file that describes the rest of the file."
text = '''
An executable's headers say which CPU it is for, whether it is 32- or 64-bit, where the entry point is, which sections there are and where the import table is. The **Info** view reads them for you.
'''
see = ["magic bytes", "section", "entry point"]

[[term]]
term = "section"
aliases = ["sections"]
short = "A named block of an executable, such as .text for code or .rdata for read-only data, loaded into memory as one area."
text = '''
Each section has a start in the file, a start in memory, a size and permissions (read, write, execute). Typical Windows sections are `.text`, `.rdata`, `.data`, `.pdata` and `.reloc`. The **Sections** view lists them.
'''
see = ["header", "executable"]

[[term]]
term = "program loader"
aliases = ["operating system's loader", "Windows loader"]
short = "The part of the operating system that reads an executable, copies its sections into memory, connects its imports and starts it."
see = ["operating system", "entry point"]

`academy/glossary/1-assembly.toml`:

```toml
# Level 1: Reading assembly. Terms first used in the Level 1 lessons.
# General computer terms (CPU, register, instruction, byte, address, pointer, stack ...)
# are in 0-foundations.toml.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- registers

[[term]]
term = "general-purpose register"
aliases = ["general-purpose registers"]
short = "One of the 16 registers of an x86-64 CPU that programs can use for any value: rax, rbx, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, rbp, rsp and r8 to r15."
text = '''
Each general-purpose register holds 64 bits, like a Rust `u64`. Think of them as 16 variables built into the CPU:

```rust
let mut rax: u64 = 0;
let mut rbx: u64 = 0;
// ... 16 in total
```

"General purpose" means any instruction can use them for any value, but conventions give some of them a usual job: `rax` holds results, `rcx`/`rdx`/`r8`/`r9` carry function arguments on Windows, and `rsp` always points at the top of the stack.
'''
see = ["register", "rax", "rsp", "sub-register", "calling convention"]

[[term]]
term = "rax"
aliases = ["eax", "ax", "al", "ah"]
short = "The first general-purpose register. Holds the result of calculations and the return value of functions. eax, ax and al are its lower 32, 16 and 8 bits."
text = '''
`rax` is where a function leaves its **return value**, on Windows and on Linux. The smaller names give access to its lower part:

| Name | Bits | Rust type it typically holds |
|---|---|---|
| `rax` | all 64 | `u64`, `usize`, a pointer |
| `eax` | lower 32 | `u32`, `i32` |
| `ax` | lower 16 | `u16` |
| `al` | lowest 8 | `u8`, `bool` |
| `ah` | bits 8 to 15 | (rare) |

Example: if `rax` is `0x1122334455667788`, then `eax` is `0x55667788`, `ax` is `0x7788` and `al` is `0x88`. A function returning `bool` puts it in `al`, which is why `test al, al` follows so many calls.
'''
see = ["sub-register", "return value", "general-purpose register"]

[[term]]
term = "rbx"
aliases = ["ebx", "bx", "bl"]
short = "A general-purpose register with no fixed job. On Windows and Linux it is non-volatile: a function that uses it must restore it."
see = ["general-purpose register", "non-volatile register"]

[[term]]
term = "rcx"
aliases = ["ecx", "cx", "cl"]
short = "A general-purpose register. On Windows it carries the first argument of a function; compilers also like it as a loop counter."
text = '''
Under the Windows x64 calling convention, `rcx` holds the first argument when a function starts. `mov ecx, 1` followed by `call` means "call with 1 as the first argument". On Linux (System V) `rcx` is the fourth argument. Its historical name is "counter register".
'''
see = ["Windows x64 calling convention", "argument", "loop counter"]

[[term]]
term = "rdx"
aliases = ["edx", "dx", "dl"]
short = "A general-purpose register. On Windows it carries the second argument of a function (on Linux the third)."
text = '''
For a slice argument `&[u8]` on Windows, `rcx` holds the address of the bytes and `rdx` the length. That is why a password check often starts with `cmp rdx, N`: the length check. Some functions also return a second value in `rdx`, next to `rax`.
'''
see = ["Windows x64 calling convention", "slice", "argument"]

[[term]]
term = "rsi"
aliases = ["esi", "sil"]
short = "A general-purpose register. Non-volatile on Windows; on Linux it carries the second argument of a function."
see = ["System V calling convention", "non-volatile register"]

[[term]]
term = "rdi"
aliases = ["edi", "dil"]
short = "A general-purpose register. Non-volatile on Windows; on Linux and macOS it carries the first argument of a function."
see = ["System V calling convention", "non-volatile register"]

[[term]]
term = "rbp"
aliases = ["ebp", "base pointer", "frame pointer"]
short = "The base pointer: often holds a fixed address inside the current function's stack frame, so local variables can be found at [rbp-8], [rbp-16] ..."
text = '''
A classic prologue sets it up:

```text
push rbp          ; save the caller's rbp
mov  rbp, rsp     ; rbp = fixed reference point for this function
sub  rsp, 16      ; room for locals at [rbp-8] and [rbp-16]
```

Optimised code often does not use `rbp` this way and uses it as an ordinary register instead.
'''
see = ["stack frame", "prologue", "rsp"]

[[term]]
term = "rsp"
aliases = ["esp", "stack pointer"]
short = "The stack pointer: always holds the address of the top of the stack. push, pop, call and ret change it."
text = '''
The stack grows downward, so `push` makes `rsp` 8 smaller and `pop` makes it 8 bigger. `sub rsp, 0x28` reserves 0x28 bytes of stack space; `add rsp, 0x28` gives them back. Local variables are often addressed relative to it, like `[rsp+0x20]`. `rsp` is never used for anything other than the stack.
'''
see = ["stack", "push", "pop", "stack frame"]

[[term]]
term = "rip"
short = "The x86-64 name of the instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction. Jumps, calls and returns change it."
text = '''
You never write `rip` directly. After each instruction the CPU adds the instruction's length to it; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` set it to a new address. It also appears inside brackets in rip-relative addressing, which ORRESS shows already resolved to a full address.
'''
see = ["instruction pointer", "jump instruction", "rip-relative addressing"]

[[term]]
term = "r8 to r15"
aliases = ["r8", "r9", "r10", "r11", "r12", "r13", "r14", "r15", "r8d", "r9d", "r8b"]
short = "Eight more general-purpose registers, numbered instead of named. r8 and r9 carry the 3rd and 4th argument on Windows."
text = '''
Their smaller parts use a letter at the end: `r8d` is the lower 32 bits, `r8w` the lower 16, `r8b` the lowest 8. On Windows, `r8`-`r11` are volatile and `r12`-`r15` non-volatile. The Academy's CPU simulator has them, but its Registers pane shows only the first eight registers.
'''
see = ["general-purpose register", "Windows x64 calling convention"]

[[term]]
term = "sub-register"
aliases = ["sub-registers", "partial register", "partial registers"]
short = "A smaller part of a 64-bit register, under its own name: eax is the lower half of rax, al its lowest byte."
text = '''
Using `eax` is like `rax as u32` in Rust. One surprising rule: **writing a 32-bit sub-register clears the upper 32 bits** of the full register (`mov eax, 1` makes all of `rax` equal to 1). Writing an 8-bit or 16-bit part (`al`, `ax`) leaves the other bits alone.
'''
see = ["rax", "general-purpose register"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- reading instructions

[[term]]
term = "mnemonic"
aliases = ["mnemonics"]
short = "The short name of an instruction's operation, like mov, add or jmp."
text = '''
In `add rax, 5`, `add` is the mnemonic and `rax` and `5` are the operands. Mnemonics are abbreviations: `mov` = move (copy), `cmp` = compare, `jne` = jump if not equal, `lea` = load effective address. With Explain Mode on, hover over a mnemonic in the Disassembly view to see what it does.
'''
see = ["operand", "instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "operand"
aliases = ["operands"]
short = "A value an instruction works on: a register, an immediate number, or a memory location in square brackets."
text = '''
In Intel syntax the first operand is the **destination** and the second the **source**: `mov rbx, rax` is `rbx = rax;`. Most instructions take two operands, some one (`inc rcx`, `push rax`) and some none (`ret`).
'''
see = ["destination operand", "source operand", "immediate value", "memory operand"]

[[term]]
term = "destination operand"
aliases = ["destination"]
short = "The first operand in Intel syntax: where the result is written. In add rax, rbx it is rax."
see = ["operand", "source operand", "Intel syntax"]

[[term]]
term = "source operand"
aliases = ["source operands"]
short = "The second operand in Intel syntax: the value that is read. In mov rbx, rax it is rax."
see = ["operand", "destination operand"]

[[term]]
term = "immediate value"
aliases = ["immediate", "immediate values", "immediates"]
short = "A number written directly inside an instruction, like the 5 in mov rax, 5."
text = '''
The number is part of the instruction's bytes, not stored elsewhere in memory. That is why a password compared character by character (`cmp byte ptr [rax], 0x52`) never shows up in the Strings view: the characters are immediate values inside the code.
'''
see = ["operand", "machine code"]

[[term]]
term = "Intel syntax"
short = "The way of writing x86 assembly that ORRESS uses: mnemonic, then destination, then source (mov rax, 5)."
text = '''
Read every two-operand instruction as `destination = destination (op) source`: `sub rax, 1` is `rax -= 1;`. Windows tools and most reverse engineering tools use Intel syntax.
'''
see = ["AT&T syntax", "destination operand"]

[[term]]
term = "AT&T syntax"
aliases = ["AT&T"]
short = "Another way of writing x86 assembly, common on Linux: source first, registers with %, numbers with $ (movq $5, %rax)."
see = ["Intel syntax"]

[[term]]
term = "assembler"
aliases = ["assemblers", "assemble"]

[[term]]

Open it with Ctrl+D or from the Project panel. Useful keys (they need the view to have keyboard focus): **N** rename, **;** comment, **X** cross-references, **Space** graph, **Ctrl+F** find, **Ctrl+G** go to an address, **Esc** go back. Click a name or address in an instruction to go there; hover over a number to see it in decimal and as a character.
'''
see = ["disassembler", "Find bar"]

Open it from **Learn > Academy: CPU Simulator**. Buttons: **Step** (one instruction), **Run** (to the end), **Step back** (undo a step), **Reset** (start again; also needed to edit after running). '''

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- moving and arithmetic

[[term]]
term = "mov"
aliases = ["`mov`"]
short = "Copy a value into a register or memory: mov rax, rbx is rax = rbx. The source keeps its value."
text = '''
Forms you will see: `mov rax, 42` (a number), `mov rbx, rax` (a register), `mov rax, [rsp+8]` (load from memory), `mov [rsp+8], rax` (store to memory). There is no memory-to-memory form, and `mov` never changes the status flags.
'''
see = ["operand", "memory operand", "movzx"]

[[term]]
term = "arithmetic instruction"
aliases = ["arithmetic instructions", "`add`"]
short = "An instruction that calculates: add, sub, inc, dec, neg, imul. The first operand is input and output (add rax, 5 is rax += 5)."
text = '''
| Instruction | Rust |
|---|---|
| `add rax, rbx` | `rax += rbx;` |
| `sub rax, 5` | `rax -= 5;` |
| `inc rcx` / `dec rcx` | `rcx += 1;` / `rcx -= 1;` |
| `neg rax` | `rax = -rax;` |
| `imul rax, rbx` | `rax *= rbx;` |

All of them update the status flags. Results that do not fit wrap around.
'''
see = ["sub", "inc", "imul", "status flags", "wrapping"]

[[term]]
term = "sub"
aliases = ["`sub`"]
short = "Subtract: sub rax, 5 is rax -= 5. sub rsp, N reserves N bytes of stack space."
see = ["arithmetic instruction", "cmp", "rsp"]

[[term]]
term = "inc"
aliases = ["`inc`"]
short = "Increment: add 1 to a register or memory value (inc rcx is rcx += 1). Leaves the carry flag unchanged."
see = ["dec", "loop counter"]

[[term]]
term = "dec"
aliases = ["`dec`"]
short = "Decrement: subtract 1 (dec rcx is rcx -= 1). Sets ZF when the result is 0, so dec + jnz makes a count-down loop."
see = ["inc", "loop", "ZF"]

[[term]]
term = "neg"
aliases = ["`neg`", "negate"]
short = "Negate: change the sign of a value (neg rax is rax = -rax), using two's complement."
see = ["two's complement", "bitwise NOT"]

[[term]]
term = "imul"
aliases = ["`imul`"]
short = "Signed multiply: imul rax, rbx is rax *= rbx; imul rax, rbx, 4 is rax = rbx * 4."
text = '''
Compilers avoid multiplying when they can: `x * 2` may become `add rax, rax`, `x * 8` a shift (`shl rax, 3`), and `x * 3` a `lea`. All compute the same result.
'''
see = ["arithmetic instruction", "shift", "lea"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- bits

[[term]]
term = "bitwise operation"
aliases = ["bitwise operations", "bitwise"]
short = "An operation that works on each bit position separately: AND, OR, XOR, NOT and the shifts."
text = '''
| Rust | Instruction |
|---|---|
| `a & b` | `and` |
| `a \| b` | `or` |
| `a ^ b` | `xor` |
| `!a` | `not` |
| `a << n`, `a >> n` | `shl`, `shr` |

Programs that hide or check secrets (passwords, keys, flags) use these constantly.
'''
see = ["bitwise AND", "bitwise OR", "XOR", "bitwise NOT", "shift", "mask"]

[[term]]
term = "bitwise AND"
aliases = ["`and`", "and instruction"]
short = "A result bit is 1 only where both input bits are 1. With a mask it keeps some bits and clears the rest: and eax, 0xF keeps the last hex digit."
text = '''
Rust `x & 0xF`. Common uses: `x & 1` (is it odd?), `x & 0xFF` (the lowest byte), and `x % 8` for unsigned `x`, which compilers turn into `and eax, 7`.
'''
see = ["mask", "bitwise operation", "test instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "bitwise OR"
aliases = ["`or`", "or instruction"]
short = "A result bit is 1 where at least one input bit is 1. With a mask it switches bits on: x | 0x20 makes an ASCII letter lower case."
see = ["mask", "bitwise operation"]

[[term]]
term = "XOR"
aliases = ["exclusive or", "`xor`", "xor eax, eax"]
short = "Exclusive or: a result bit is 1 where the two input bits differ. XOR with the same key twice gives the original back."
text = '''
Two facts make XOR important for reverse engineers:

- **Any value XOR itself is 0.** `xor eax, eax` is the usual way to write `rax = 0`.
- **XOR twice with the same key undoes it.** `(x ^ key) ^ key == x`, so the same operation hides and reveals data:

```rust
let hidden = b'K' ^ 0x5A;   // 0x11
let back = hidden ^ 0x5A;   // b'K' again
```

That is why XOR is the most common way to hide passwords and text in crackmes and malware.
'''
see = ["XOR cipher", "bitwise operation", "mask"]

[[term]]
term = "bitwise NOT"
aliases = ["`not`", "not instruction"]
short = "Flip every bit: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. Rust's !x for integers. not 0 is -1 (all bits set)."
see = ["bitwise operation", "neg"]

[[term]]
term = "shift"
aliases = ["shifts", "shl", "shr", "sar", "shift left", "shift right"]
short = "Move all bits left (shl) or right (shr). Shifting left by n multiplies by 2 to the power n; shifting right divides (unsigned)."
text = '''
`shl rax, 3` is `rax * 8`, `shr rax, 4` is `rax / 16` for an unsigned value. `sar` (shift arithmetic right) keeps the sign bit, for signed division. Compilers turn multiplications and divisions by powers of two into shifts.
'''
see = ["bitwise operation", "imul"]

[[term]]
term = "mask"
aliases = ["masks", "bit mask", "bitmask"]
short = "A constant used with AND, OR or XOR to pick bits: its 1 bits select which bits are kept, set or flipped."
text = '''
`x & 0x0F` keeps the lowest 4 bits, `x | 0x20` sets bit 5, `x ^ 0xFF` flips the lowest 8 bits. Combined with a shift, a mask extracts a field: `(x >> 4) & 0xF` is the second-lowest hex digit.
'''
see = ["bitwise AND", "bitwise OR", "XOR"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- flags, compare, jump

[[term]]
term = "status flags"
aliases = ["CPU flags", "flags register", "rflags"]
short = "Single bits the CPU sets after arithmetic and comparisons (ZF, SF, CF, OF). Conditional jumps read them."
text = '''
Arithmetic and bit instructions (`add`, `sub`, `and`, `xor`, `cmp`, `test` ...) update them; `mov`, `lea`, `push` and `pop` do not. They live together in the register `rflags`. The simulator shows them in its **Flags** row.
'''
see = ["ZF", "SF", "CF", "OF", "conditional jump"]

[[term]]
term = "ZF"
aliases = ["zero flag"]
short = "Zero flag: 1 when the last result was 0. After cmp a, b it means a == b; je jumps when it is 1."
see = ["status flags", "je", "cmp"]

[[term]]
term = "SF"
aliases = ["sign flag"]
short = "Sign flag: 1 when the last result was negative (its top bit is 1)."
see = ["status flags", "sign bit"]

[[term]]
term = "CF"
aliases = ["carry flag"]
short = "Carry flag: 1 when the last result did not fit as an unsigned number (a carry, or a borrow in a subtraction). After cmp a, b: a < b unsigned."
see = ["status flags", "unsigned jump", "overflow"]

[[term]]
term = "OF"
aliases = ["overflow flag"]
short = "Overflow flag: 1 when the last result did not fit as a signed number. Signed jumps (jl, jg ...) read it."
see = ["status flags", "signed jump", "overflow"]

[[term]]
term = "cmp"
aliases = ["`cmp`", "compare instruction"]
short = "Compare: calculates a - b only to set the status flags, and throws the result away. Usually followed by a conditional jump."
text = '''
`cmp rax, 7` is the first half of `if rax == 7` (or `<`, `>` ...); the jump after it says which comparison. Example:

```text
cmp rdx, 7
jne wrong      ; if rdx != 7 goto wrong
```
'''
see = ["conditional jump", "test instruction", "status flags"]

[[term]]
term = "test instruction"
aliases = ["`test`", "test al, al", "test rax, rax", "test eax, eax"]
short = "test a, b calculates a AND b only to set the flags. test rax, rax asks \"is rax zero?\" (ZF = 1 if so)."
text = '''
Right after a call, `test al, al` + `je` means "if the function returned false". `test rax, rax` checks for a zero value: a null pointer, an `Option` that is `None`, an `Ok` result, or a count of 0.
'''
see = ["cmp", "ZF", "return value"]

[[term]]
term = "jump instruction"
aliases = ["jmp", "`jmp`", "unconditional jump", "jumps"]
short = "An instruction that makes the CPU continue somewhere else. jmp always jumps; conditional jumps only when the flags say so."
see = ["conditional jump", "label", "rip"]

[[term]]
term = "conditional jump"
aliases = ["conditional jumps", "jcc"]
short = "A jump that only happens if a condition on the status flags is true, like je (equal) or jl (less). Together with cmp it makes an if."
text = '''
| Jump | After `cmp a, b`, jumps if |
|---|---|
| `je` / `jz` | a == b |
| `jne` / `jnz` | a != b |
| `jl` / `jle` / `jg` / `jge` | a < b, <=, >, >= (signed) |
| `jb` / `jbe` / `ja` / `jae` | a < b, <=, >, >= (unsigned) |

Compiled `if` statements usually jump *over* the body, so the jump's condition is the opposite of the Rust condition.
'''
see = ["je", "jne", "signed jump", "unsigned jump", "inverted condition", "cmp"]

[[term]]
term = "je"
aliases = ["jz", "`je`"]
short = "Jump if equal (also written jz, jump if zero): jumps when ZF = 1."
see = ["conditional jump", "ZF", "jne"]

[[term]]
term = "jne"
aliases = ["jnz", "`jne`"]
short = "Jump if not equal (also written jnz, jump if not zero): jumps when ZF = 0."
see = ["conditional jump", "ZF", "je"]

[[term]]
term = "signed jump"
aliases = ["signed jumps", "jl", "jle", "jg", "jge"]
short = "A conditional jump for signed numbers (i32, i64 ...): jl less, jle less or equal, jg greater, jge greater or equal."
text = '''
After `mov rax, -1` and `cmp rax, 1`, `jl` jumps (-1 < 1), but the unsigned `jb` does not (as unsigned, `0xffffffffffffffff` is huge). Which kind of jump the compiler used tells you whether the variable was signed.
'''
see = ["unsigned jump", "conditional jump", "signed"]

[[term]]
term = "unsigned jump"
aliases = ["unsigned jumps", "jb", "jbe", "ja", "jae"]
short = "A conditional jump for unsigned numbers (u32, usize ...): jb below, jbe below or equal, ja above, jae above or equal."
text = '''
Memory aid: **b**elow and **a**bove are unsigned, **l**ess and **g**reater are signed. Lengths and indexes in Rust are `usize`, so bounds checks and `for i in 0..n` loops use `jb` and `jae`.
'''
see = ["signed jump", "conditional jump", "unsigned", "bounds check"]

[[term]]
term = "inverted condition"
aliases = ["inverted conditions"]
short = "Compiled if statements jump over their body, so the jump tests the opposite of the Rust condition: if x == 7 becomes cmp + jne."
see = ["conditional jump"]

[[term]]
term = "label"
aliases = ["labels"]
short = "A name for a place in a program that jumps can go to, written as a name with a colon (done:). ORRESS names them loc_ plus the address."
see = ["jump instruction", "generated name"]

[[term]]
term = "loop"
aliases = ["loops"]
short = "Code that runs repeatedly. In assembly: a label, a body, a comparison and a conditional jump back up to the label."
text = '''
```text
again:
    add rax, rcx
    inc rcx
    cmp rcx, 6
    jne again      ; jump back: this makes it a loop
```

In the Graph view a loop is an arrow that points back up to an earlier block.
'''
see = ["loop counter", "back edge", "conditional jump", "infinite loop"]

[[term]]
term = "loop counter"
aliases = ["loop counters"]
short = "The variable that counts the rounds of a loop, often kept in rcx or ecx and changed with inc or dec."
see = ["loop", "inc", "dec"]

[[term]]
term = "infinite loop"
aliases = ["endless loop", "loop that never ends"]
short = "A loop whose exit condition never becomes true, so it runs forever. The simulator stops it after 10 000 steps."
see = ["loop"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- memory

[[term]]
term = "memory operand"
aliases = ["memory operands", "square brackets"]
short = "An operand in square brackets: the value stored in memory at that address. [rsp+8] means \"the value at address rsp + 8\"."
text = '''
`mov rax, rbx` copies the register; `mov rax, [rbx]` reads memory at the address in `rbx`, like `*p` in Rust. Inside the brackets: a register, plus or minus a displacement, optionally plus a second register times 1, 2, 4 or 8: `[rcx+rdx*8]`. Only one operand of an instruction can be in memory.
'''
see = ["displacement", "byte ptr", "lea", "dereference"]

[[term]]
term = "displacement"
aliases = ["displacements"]
short = "The fixed number added to a register inside a memory operand: the 8 in [rsp+8] or the -0x10 in [rbp-0x10]."
text = '''
Often it is the offset of a local variable in the stack frame, or of a field inside a struct: `[rcx+0x10]` is "the field 16 bytes into the struct that rcx points to".
'''
see = ["memory operand", "offset"]

[[term]]
term = "byte ptr"
aliases = ["word ptr", "dword ptr", "qword ptr"]
short = "A size word in front of a memory operand: byte ptr = 1 byte, word ptr = 2, dword ptr = 4, qword ptr = 8."
text = '''
`cmp byte ptr [rax+1], 0x33` compares exactly one byte: the second character of a string. The size tells you the type: `byte` for `u8`/`bool`, `dword` for `u32`/`i32`, `qword` for `u64`, `usize` and pointers.
'''
see = ["memory operand", "dword", "qword"]

[[term]]
term = "movzx"
aliases = ["`movzx`"]
short = "Move with zero extension: load a small value (a byte or word) into a bigger register and fill the rest with zeros, like byte as u32."
see = ["zero extension", "mov", "byte ptr"]

[[term]]
term = "lea"
aliases = ["`lea`", "load effective address"]
short = "Load effective address: computes the address in the brackets and stores the address itself, without reading memory. Rust's &x."
text = '''
```text
mov rbx, [rsp+8]   ; rbx = the value at rsp+8      (let v = x;)
lea rbx, [rsp+8]   ; rbx = the address rsp+8        (let p = &x;)
```

`lea rcx, [0x1400183d0]` loads the address of a string. Compilers also use `lea` as a fast calculator: `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*2]` is `rcx * 3`.
'''
see = ["memory operand", "pointer", "rip-relative addressing"]

[[term]]
term = "scaled index"
aliases = ["scale factor", "scale"]
short = "The register-times-number part of a memory operand, like rdx*8 in [rcx+rdx*8]. The number (1, 2, 4 or 8) is usually the size of an array element."
see = ["memory operand", "byte ptr"]

[[term]]
term = "rip-relative addressing"
aliases = ["rip-relative"]
short = "Addressing data by its distance from the next instruction ([rip+0x172c4]), so code works wherever it is loaded. ORRESS shows the resolved address."
see = ["rip", "lea", "ASLR"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the stack and functions

[[term]]
term = "push"
aliases = ["`push`", "pushes", "pushed"]
short = "Put a value on top of the stack: rsp goes down by 8, then the value is stored at [rsp]."
text = '''
`push rax` is the same as `sub rsp, 8` followed by `mov [rsp], rax`. Functions push the non-volatile registers they use in their prologue, and pop them in the epilogue.
'''
see = ["pop", "stack", "rsp"]

[[term]]
term = "pop"
aliases = ["`pop`", "pops", "popped"]
short = "Take the top value off the stack into a register: read [rsp], then rsp goes up by 8."
text = '''
The stack is last in, first out: after `push rax` and `push rbx`, the first `pop` returns the value of `rbx`. Every push must be matched by a pop, or the next `ret` takes the wrong value as its return address.
'''
see = ["push", "stack", "balanced stack"]

[[term]]
term = "stack frame"
aliases = ["stack frames"]
short = "The part of the stack that belongs to one running function: its saved registers, local variables and the return address."
see = ["prologue", "epilogue", "rbp", "local variable"]

[[term]]
term = "prologue"
aliases = ["prologues", "function prologue"]
short = "The first instructions of a function, which set up its stack frame: push registers, sub rsp, N (and maybe push rbp; mov rbp, rsp)."
see = ["epilogue", "stack frame"]

[[term]]
term = "epilogue"
aliases = ["epilogues", "function epilogue"]
short = "The last instructions of a function, which undo its prologue in reverse order: add rsp, N, pop registers, ret."
see = ["prologue", "ret"]

[[term]]
term = "balanced stack"
aliases = ["balanced"]
short = "A stack where everything a function pushed or reserved has been removed again, so that ret finds the return address on top."
see = ["push", "pop", "return address"]

[[term]]
term = "call instruction"
aliases = ["`call`", "call instructions"]
short = "call f pushes the return address (the address of the next instruction) and jumps to f."
text = '''
Before a `call`, look at which argument registers are set (on Windows `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`); after it, look at how `rax` (the return value) is used. A call to a function that never returns (a panic, `exit`) is followed by `ud2`.
'''
see = ["ret", "return address", "calling convention"]

[[term]]
term = "ret"
aliases = ["`ret`", "return instruction"]
short = "Return from a function: pop the return address from the stack and jump there."
see = ["call instruction", "return address", "epilogue"]

[[term]]
term = "return address"
aliases = ["return addresses"]
short = "The address a function goes back to when it returns: the instruction after the call. call pushes it, ret pops it."
text = '''
A `call` at `0x140001122` that is 5 bytes long pushes `0x140001127`. In a debugger, the return addresses on the stack tell you which functions called the current one. The Academy's simulator pushes the position of the next line instead of a real address.
'''
see = ["call instruction", "ret", "call stack"]

[[term]]
term = "call stack"
aliases = ["backtrace", "stack trace"]
short = "The chain of return addresses on the stack: one for every function that is still running. A panic backtrace prints it."
see = ["return address", "stack frame"]

[[term]]
term = "calling convention"
aliases = ["calling conventions", "convention"]
short = "The rules for calling functions: which registers carry the arguments and the result, and which registers a function must save."
see = ["Windows x64 calling convention", "System V calling convention", "volatile register", "non-volatile register"]

[[term]]
term = "Windows x64 calling convention"
aliases = ["Windows x64 convention", "Windows convention", "Microsoft x64 calling convention"]
short = "On Windows: arguments in rcx, rdx, r8, r9, then on the stack; the result in rax; 32 bytes of shadow space for every call."
text = '''
```text
mov rcx, a     ; 1st argument
mov rdx, b     ; 2nd
mov r8,  c     ; 3rd
mov r9,  d     ; 4th
call f         ; the result comes back in rax
```

Volatile: `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`-`r11`. Non-volatile: `rbx`, `rbp`, `rdi`, `rsi`, `rsp`, `r12`-`r15`. Every PE file for x86-64 uses it.
'''
see = ["System V calling convention", "shadow space", "volatile register", "PE"]

[[term]]
term = "System V calling convention"
aliases = ["System V", "SysV"]
short = "On Linux and macOS: arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9, then on the stack; the result in rax."
text = '''
Memory aid for the order: "**Di**d **Si**r **D**on **C**ook?" (`rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`), then `r8` and `r9`. ELF and Mach-O programs use it; there is no shadow space.
'''
see = ["Windows x64 calling convention", "ELF"]

[[term]]
term = "argument"
aliases = ["arguments", "parameter", "parameters"]
short = "A value passed to a function. On x86-64 the first few arguments go in registers, as the calling convention says."
see = ["calling convention", "return value"]

[[term]]
term = "return value"
aliases = ["return values"]
short = "The result a function gives back. On x86-64 it is in rax (or eax for a u32, al for a bool or u8)."
see = ["rax", "calling convention", "test instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "shadow space"
aliases = ["home space"]
short = "On Windows, 32 bytes of stack space that the caller reserves before every call, for the called function to store its four argument registers."
text = '''
It explains the typical `sub rsp, 0x28` at the start of Windows functions: 0x20 bytes of shadow space for the functions it calls, plus 8 bytes so that `rsp` stays a multiple of 16. A fifth argument is stored just above it, at `[rsp+0x20]`, right before the call.
'''
see = ["Windows x64 calling convention", "stack alignment"]

[[term]]
term = "volatile register"
aliases = ["volatile registers", "caller-saved", "caller-saved register"]
short = "A register that any called function may change (on Windows rax, rcx, rdx, r8-r11). The caller must save it if it needs the value later."
see = ["non-volatile register", "calling convention"]

[[term]]
term = "non-volatile register"
aliases = ["non-volatile registers", "callee-saved", "callee-saved register"]
short = "A register a function must give back unchanged (on Windows rbx, rbp, rdi, rsi, rsp, r12-r15). A function that uses one pushes it first."
see = ["volatile register", "prologue", "push"]

[[term]]
term = "stack alignment"
aliases = ["16-byte alignment", "aligned stack"]
short = "The rule that rsp must be a multiple of 16 at every call. Functions reserve \"a multiple of 16, plus 8\" bytes because the return address adds 8."
see = ["shadow space", "rsp"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Rust patterns

[[term]]
term = "slice"
aliases = ["slices", "&[u8]", "&str"]
short = "A view into a sequence of elements: a fat pointer made of the address of the first element and the number of elements."
text = '''
A `&[u8]` or `&str` is 16 bytes: an address and a length. Passed to a function on Windows it takes two registers: `rcx` = address, `rdx` = length. Stored in memory it is two 8-byte slots side by side. `s.len() != 7` becomes `cmp rdx, 7` + `jne`; `s[2]` becomes `byte ptr [rax+2]`.
'''
see = ["fat pointer", "bounds check", "rdx"]

[[term]]
term = "bounds check"
aliases = ["bounds checks", "bounds checking", "index out of bounds"]
short = "Rust's check that an index is smaller than the length before s[i] is accessed. Compiled as cmp + jb/jae to code that panics."
text = '''
```text
cmp  rdx, 2          ; is the length at least 2?
jb   panic_block     ; no: panic "index out of bounds"
cmp  byte ptr [rax+1], 0x33   ; the real work: s[1]
```

The panic block calls a function with the index (`ecx`), the length (`rdx`) and the source location (`r8`), and ends in `ud2`. C programs have no such checks, so they are a sign of Rust. When reading for logic, skip them.
'''
see = ["panic", "ud2", "unsigned jump"]

[[term]]
term = "panic"
aliases = ["panics", "panic!", "panicked"]
short = "Rust stopping the program because of a bug or failed check (unwrap on None, index out of bounds ...). Panic code never returns."
see = ["bounds check", "ud2"]

[[term]]
term = "ud2"
aliases = ["`ud2`"]
short = "An instruction that crashes on purpose. Compilers place it after calls that never return (panics, exit), so a block ending in ud2 is a dead end."
see = ["panic", "call instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "memcmp"
short = "A C runtime function that compares two blocks of memory: memcmp(a, b, n) returns 0 if the n bytes are equal. Rust's == on strings often calls it."
text = '''
A Rust string comparison compiles to: compare the lengths, then `call memcmp` with `rcx` = first address, `rdx` = second address, `r8` = length, then `test eax, eax` (0 means equal). Because it is imported from a library, it keeps its name in stripped programs.
'''
see = ["import", "slice", "test instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "cmove"
aliases = ["cmovne", "cmovcc", "conditional move"]
short = "Conditional move: a mov that only happens if a flag condition is true (cmove: if ZF = 1). A small if without a jump."
see = ["mov", "conditional jump", "setcc"]

[[term]]
term = "setcc"
aliases = ["sete", "setne"]
short = "Set a byte register to 1 if a flag condition is true, else to 0: sete al makes al = (a == b) after a cmp. Often how a bool result is made."
see = ["cmove", "return value"]

[[term]]
term = "nop"
aliases = ["`nop`", "no operation"]
short = "An instruction that does nothing. Compilers use it as padding; reverse engineers overwrite unwanted instructions with it when patching."
see = ["instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "black_box"
aliases = ["std::hint::black_box"]
short = "A Rust function that hides a value from the optimiser, so the compiler cannot precompute or merge code that uses it. The crackmes use it to keep checks readable."
see = ["optimization"]

[[term]]
term = "byte literal"
aliases = ["byte literals", "byte string"]
short = "Rust's way of writing a byte as a character: b'R' is the u8 value 0x52. A byte string b\"abc\" is a &[u8; 3]."
see = ["ASCII", "immediate value"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- ORRESS views used in Level 1

[[term]]
term = "Strings view"
aliases = ["Strings tab"]
short = "ORRESS's list of all readable text in a file, with a filter box and a Refs column that jumps to the code using each string."
text = '''
Open it from the Project panel or with Ctrl+Shift+S. Type in the filter box to narrow the list (case-insensitive). Click the number with `»` in the **Refs** column to jump to the first instruction that uses the string. Rust stores its string literals back to back, so one row can hold several literals glued together.
'''
see = ["string literal", "Find bar", "Disassembly view"]

[[term]]
term = "Find bar"
short = "The search bar of the Disassembly view (Ctrl+F): finds text in instructions, names and comments. Next (F3) and Previous (Shift+F3) move between matches."
