`academy/glossary/2-static-analysis.toml`:

```toml
# Level 2: static analysis. File formats, navigating a program, the graph view, the
# decompiler, XOR encoding and keygens.

[[term]]
term = "static analysis"
aliases = ["statically", "static analysis tools"]
short = "Understanding a program by reading its file, without running it."
text = '''
Static analysis means you look at the bytes, the instructions and the data of a program,
but you never start it. It is like reading the source code of a Rust project instead of
running `cargo run` and watching what it prints.

It is safe (nothing runs, so a harmful program cannot do anything), and it shows *every*
path through the code, not only the one a single run takes. Its limit: values that only
exist while the program runs (what you type, what a server answers) are not in the file.
'''
see = ["decompiler", "cross-reference"]

[[term]]
term = "executable format"
aliases = ["executable formats", "binary format", "file formats"]
short = "The fixed layout an operating system expects a program file to have: PE, ELF or Mach-O."
text = '''
A program file is not a shapeless pile of machine code. It follows a format that the
operating system knows: a header first, then a table of sections, then the sections
themselves. Windows uses **PE**, Linux and Android use **ELF**, macOS and iOS use
**Mach-O**. The ideas are the same in all three; only the names and the exact byte layout
differ.
'''
see = ["PE", "ELF", "Mach-O"]

[[term]]
term = "PE"
aliases = ["Portable Executable", "PE file", "PE files", "PE format"]
short = "Portable Executable: the file format of Windows programs (.exe), libraries (.dll) and drivers (.sys)."
text = '''
A PE file starts with a small **DOS header** (the letters `MZ`), which points to the
**PE header** (the letters `PE` followed by two zero bytes). After it come the optional
header (image base, entry point, data directories) and the section table. Every program
the Academy gives you is a PE file.
'''
see = ["DOS header", "PE header", "optional header", "section table"]

[[term]]
term = "ELF"
aliases = ["ELF file", "ELF files", "Executable and Linkable Format"]
short = "The executable format of Linux, Android and most other Unix systems."
text = '''
An ELF file starts with the four bytes `7F 45 4C 46` (`\x7fELF`). It has the same ideas as
PE with other names: code is in `.text`, constants in `.rodata`, and library functions are
reached through small stubs in `.plt` and addresses in `.got`. ELF files also have
**segments** (also called program headers): the parts the loader actually maps into memory.
'''
see = ["PE", "import stub"]

[[term]]
term = "Mach-O"
aliases = ["Mach-O file", "MachO"]
short = "The executable format of macOS and iOS."
text = '''
Mach-O files start with a "magic" number such as `CF FA ED FE` (64-bit). Sections live inside
segments, and their names look different: `__TEXT,__text` for code, `__DATA,__data` for
data, `__cstring` for text. A "universal" (fat) Mach-O holds versions for several CPUs at once.
'''
see = ["PE", "ELF"]

[[term]]
term = "DOS header"
aliases = ["MZ header", "DOS stub"]
short = "The first 64 bytes of every PE file, starting with `MZ`; today it mainly points to the PE header."
text = '''
In the 1980s Windows programs had to say something sensible when started under MS-DOS, so
every PE file still starts with a tiny DOS program: the letters `MZ`, some old fields, and a
"stub" that prints *This program cannot be run in DOS mode.* The one field that still
matters is **e_lfanew** at offset `0x3C`: the file offset of the real PE header.
'''
see = ["e_lfanew", "PE header"]

[[term]]
term = "e_lfanew"
short = "The 4-byte number at file offset 0x3C of a PE file: where the PE header starts."
text = '''
To find the PE header, Windows reads the 4 bytes at offset `0x3C` as a little-endian
number. In the Academy's crackmes they are `E8 00 00 00`, so the PE header starts at
offset `0xE8`. In Rust terms:
`let pe = u32::from_le_bytes(file[0x3C..0x40].try_into().unwrap());`
'''
see = ["DOS header", "PE header"]

[[term]]
term = "PE header"
aliases = ["PE signature", "COFF header", "file header", "NT headers"]
short = "The part of a PE file that starts with `PE\\0\\0` and says which CPU the program is for and how many sections it has."
text = '''
After the four signature bytes `50 45 00 00` ("PE" and two zeros) come 20 bytes called the
COFF file header: the machine type (`64 86` = 0x8664 = x86-64), the number of sections, a
time stamp and the size of the optional header that follows.
'''
see = ["optional header", "section table"]

[[term]]
term = "optional header"
short = "The large PE header part (not optional at all for programs) that holds the image base, the entry point and the data directories."
text = '''
Despite its name every program has one. The fields a reverser cares about most:
`AddressOfEntryPoint` (the RVA where execution starts), `ImageBase` (the preferred load
address), `Subsystem` (console or GUI program) and the data directories (where the import
table, export table and other tables are).
'''
see = ["image base", "RVA", "data directory"]

[[term]]
term = "data directory"
aliases = ["data directories"]
short = "A list in the PE optional header that says where tables like the imports and exports are."
text = '''
Each entry is an RVA and a size. Entry 1 is the import table, entry 0 the export table,
entry 12 the Import Address Table. Tools such as ORRESS read these entries to fill the
Imports view.
'''
see = ["import", "IAT"]

[[term]]
term = "section table"
aliases = ["section headers", "section header"]
short = "The list of sections in a program file: for each one its name, size, file offset, address and permissions."
text = '''
Every row of the Sections view is one entry of this table. It is the "map" that tells the
loader which bytes of the file go to which addresses in memory, and it is what lets you
convert between a file offset and an address.
'''
see = ["file offset", "virtual address", "section permissions"]

[[term]]
term = ".text"
aliases = ["text section", "code section"]
short = "The section that holds the program's machine code."
text = '''
The name is an old Unix word for code. It is readable and executable (R-X) but not
writable. On macOS the code section is called `__text`.
'''
see = [".rdata", "section permissions"]

[[term]]
term = ".rdata"
aliases = [".rodata", "read-only data"]
short = "The section with constants: string literals, tables and other read-only data."
text = '''
Windows calls it `.rdata`, Linux `.rodata`. Every `"text"` literal in your Rust code ends up
here, which is why the Strings view finds most messages in this section. On Windows the
import tables usually live at its start too.
'''
see = [".text", ".data"]

[[term]]
term = ".data"
aliases = ["data section"]
short = "The section with global variables that have a starting value and can be changed."
text = '''
A Rust `static mut COUNTER: u32 = 5;` lives here. It is readable and writable (RW-), but
not executable.
'''
see = [".bss", ".rdata"]

[[term]]
term = ".bss"
short = "Global variables that start as zero; the section takes space in memory but not in the file."
text = '''
There is no point in storing a million zero bytes in the file, so the section table only
says "reserve this much memory and fill it with zeros". That is why a `.bss` section has a
memory size but a file size of 0.
'''
see = [".data"]

[[term]]
term = ".pdata"
short = "A 64-bit Windows section that lists where every function starts and ends, for exception handling."
text = '''
Windows needs it to unwind the stack when a panic or crash happens. For a reverser it is a
gift: it is a list of function start addresses, even in a stripped program.
'''
see = [".text"]

[[term]]
term = ".reloc"
aliases = ["relocations", "relocation", "relocation table"]
short = "The list of places in a program that must be fixed when it is loaded at another address than the image base."
text = '''
Some instructions and data contain full addresses. If Windows loads the program somewhere
else (which ASLR does on purpose), it adds the difference to every place listed here.
'''
see = ["image base", "ASLR"]

[[term]]
term = "section permissions"
aliases = ["permissions column", "R-X", "RW-", "RWX"]
short = "Whether a section may be read (R), written (W) and executed (X) when the program runs."
text = '''
Code is `R-X`, constants `R--`, variables `RW-`. A section that is both writable and
executable (`RWX`) is rare in normal programs: it often means the program writes new code
into memory while it runs, as packers and some malware do.
'''
see = [".text", "DEP"]

[[term]]
term = "image base"
aliases = ["ImageBase", "base address"]
short = "The memory address a program prefers to be loaded at; every other address is image base + RVA."
text = '''
For 64-bit Windows programs it is usually `0x140000000`. The disassembly shows addresses as
if the program is loaded there, so `0x140001100` means "RVA `0x1100` from the start of the
loaded program".
'''
see = ["RVA", "virtual address"]

[[term]]
term = "virtual address"
aliases = ["virtual addresses", "VA", "memory address", "load address"]
short = "Where a byte is in memory when the program runs; the addresses the disassembly shows."
text = '''
"Virtual" because every process has its own private address space (Level 0). A virtual
address = image base + RVA. Do not confuse it with the file offset: the same byte is at
different numbers in the file and in memory.
'''
see = ["image base", "RVA", "file offset"]

[[term]]
term = "RVA"
aliases = ["relative virtual address", "RVAs"]
short = "Relative virtual address: an address counted from the image base, so it stays valid wherever the program is loaded."
text = '''
PE headers store almost every address as an RVA. Convert with plain additions:

```rust
let va = image_base + rva;            // 0x140000000 + 0x1100 = 0x140001100
let rva = va - image_base;
```
'''
see = ["image base", "virtual address", "file offset"]

[[term]]
term = "file offset"
aliases = ["file offsets", "raw offset", "offset in the file"]
short = "The position of a byte in the file on disk, counted from 0; what the Hex view shows on the left."
text = '''
Sections are placed differently in the file than in memory, so a file offset and an RVA of
the same byte differ. The section table gives the conversion:

```rust
// for the section that contains the byte:
let offset = rva - section.rva + section.file_offset;
// .text: RVA 0x1000 is at file offset 0x400, so RVA 0x1100 is at 0x500
```
'''
see = ["RVA", "section table", "virtual address"]

[[term]]
term = "import"
aliases = ["imports", "imported function", "imported functions", "import table"]
short = "A function from another file (a DLL or shared library) that a program uses; listed by name in the program."
text = '''
Your Rust program calls `println!`, which in the end calls Windows' `WriteConsoleW` in
`KERNEL32.dll`. That code is not in your `.exe`; the file only lists "I need WriteConsoleW
from KERNEL32.dll". The list of imports shows what a program can do before you read any
code: `ReadConsoleW` reads input, `memcmp` compares memory, `socket` means networking.
'''
see = ["DLL", "IAT", "export"]

[[term]]
term = "export"
aliases = ["exports", "exported function", "export table"]
short = "A function a file offers to other programs, listed by name; DLLs export, normal programs usually do not."
text = '''
The other side of an import: `KERNEL32.dll` exports `WriteConsoleW`, your program imports
it. A Rust library built as a `cdylib` exports its `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn`s.
'''
see = ["import", "DLL"]

[[term]]
term = "DLL"
aliases = ["DLLs", "dynamic-link library", "shared library", "shared libraries"]
short = "A library file (.dll on Windows, .so on Linux, .dylib on macOS) whose functions programs use while they run."
text = '''
Instead of copying the code of `WriteConsoleW` into every program, Windows keeps it in one
file, `KERNEL32.dll`, and loads it next to every program that imports it.
'''
see = ["import", "export"]

[[term]]
term = "IAT"
aliases = ["Import Address Table", "import slot", "import slots"]
short = "Import Address Table: a list of pointers that Windows fills with the real addresses of imported functions at load time."
text = '''
The program does not know where `WriteConsoleW` will be in memory, so it calls *through* a
pointer: `call [0x140018xxx]`. When the program starts, the loader writes the real address
of each imported function into its slot in the IAT. ORRESS shows such a call with the
import's name, e.g. `call WakeByAddressSingle`.
'''
see = ["import", "import stub"]

[[term]]
term = "import stub"
aliases = ["import stubs", "thunk", "thunks", "PLT", "PLT stub"]
short = "A tiny function whose only job is to jump to an imported function."
text = '''
On Linux every call to a library function goes through a stub in `.plt` (`puts@plt`); on
Windows some compilers add thunks like `jmp [IAT slot]`. They all look the same, so the
Functions view hides them unless you tick **Show import stubs**.
'''
see = ["IAT", "import"]

[[term]]
term = "Rich header"
short = "Hidden Microsoft linker data in many PE files that lists the tools (compiler versions) used to build the file."
text = '''
It sits between the DOS stub and the PE header. It is not documented by Microsoft, but it
reliably tells you the program was linked with Microsoft's linker, which is how ORRESS
detects "Microsoft Visual C++" even in a Rust program.
'''
see = ["DOS header"]

[[term]]
term = "subsystem"
aliases = ["console subsystem", "GUI subsystem"]
short = "A PE header field that says whether a program is a console program (text window) or a GUI program (its own windows)."
see = ["optional header"]

[[term]]
term = "TLS callback"
aliases = ["TLS callbacks", "TLS directory"]
short = "A function a PE file asks Windows to run before the entry point, for thread-local storage set-up."
text = '''
Rust and the C runtime use them for normal reasons. Because they run before the entry
point, crackmes and malware sometimes hide checks in them; that is why ORRESS shows a tip
when a file has them.
'''
see = ["optional header"]

[[term]]
term = "ASLR"
aliases = ["address space layout randomization"]
short = "Address Space Layout Randomization: Windows loads the program at a random address each run, to make attacks harder."
text = '''
For static analysis it changes nothing: ORRESS shows addresses as if the program is loaded
at its image base. In a debugger the real addresses differ from run to run, but the RVA
(address minus base) stays the same.
'''
see = ["image base", "RVA", ".reloc"]

[[term]]
term = "DEP"
aliases = ["NX", "DEP / NX", "data execution prevention", "non-executable"]
short = "Data Execution Prevention: memory that holds data (stack, heap) may not be run as code."
text = '''
It stops attacks that write machine code into a buffer and jump to it. For you as a
reverser it mostly means that code lives in sections marked X, and data in sections without X.
'''
see = ["section permissions", "ASLR"]

[[term]]
term = "Control Flow Guard"
aliases = ["CF Guard", "GUARD_CF"]
short = "A Windows protection that checks the target of every indirect call before jumping there."
text = '''
When it is on, indirect calls go through a small check function first. It makes the
disassembly a little noisier, but it does not hide anything from you.
'''
see = ["ASLR", "DEP"]

[[term]]
term = "code signature"
aliases = ["digital signature", "code signing", "Authenticode"]
short = "A certificate stored in a file that proves who published it and that it was not changed since."
text = '''
Windows system files and most commercial software are signed; crackmes and most malware
are not. After you patch a signed file, its signature is no longer valid.
'''

[[term]]
term = "entropy"
aliases = ["Shannon entropy"]
short = "A number from 0 to 8 that says how random the bytes of a file or section look."
text = '''
Text and padding are low (0-4), machine code is in the middle (5-6.5), and compressed or
encrypted data is close to 8. A section near 8 means "you cannot read this yet: it must be
unpacked or decrypted first".
'''

[[term]]
term = "lang_start"
aliases = ["rust_runtime_main", "std::rt::lang_start", "lang_start_internal"]
short = "The Rust standard library function that sets up a Rust program and then calls your `main`."
text = '''
When you write `fn main()`, the compiler also writes a small hidden function that passes a
pointer to your `main` to `std::rt::lang_start`. It sets up the panic handler and
`std::env::args`, calls your `main`, and turns its result into an exit code. ORRESS finds
this hidden function, names it `rust_runtime_main`, and follows the pointer
(`lea rax,[main]`) to find your `main`, even in a stripped program.
'''
see = ["generated name"]

[[term]]
term = "generated name"
aliases = ["generated names", "sub_ name", "sub_ names", "loc_ label", "loc_ labels", "auto-generated name"]
short = "A name ORRESS invents when the file has none: `sub_` + address for functions, `loc_` + address for jump targets."
text = '''
`sub_1400012c0` means "a subroutine (function) that starts at address 0x1400012c0".
`loc_1400012d0` is a location inside a function that some jump goes to. The decompiler
names unknown variables in a similar way: `local_28` is a variable on the stack at offset
0x28, `a1` is the first argument. Replace these names with your own (N) as soon as you know
what something does.
'''
see = ["annotation"]

[[term]]
term = "annotation"
aliases = ["annotations", "rename", "renamed", "renaming"]
short = "Something you add to a program while analysing it: a name for a function or address, or a comment."
text = '''
Annotations never change the program file. ORRESS keeps them next to your analysis and
shows them everywhere: in the disassembly, the graph, the decompiler and the Functions
view. Press **N** to rename and **;** to comment.
'''
see = ["generated name"]

[[term]]
term = "cross-reference"
aliases = ["cross-references", "xref", "xrefs"]
short = "A place in the code that uses an address: a call to a function, a jump to a label, or an instruction that reads a string."
text = '''
Cross-references answer "who uses this?". For a function they are its callers; for a string
they are the instructions that load it. Following them is how you get from a message like
*Invalid licence code.* to the code that decides whether to print it. Press **X** in the
disassembly to see them.
'''
see = ["static analysis"]

[[term]]
term = "navigation history"
aliases = ["Go Back", "Go Forward"]
short = "The list of places you jumped to, so you can go back (Alt+Left or Esc) and forward (Alt+Right) like in a web browser."
see = ["cross-reference"]

[[term]]
term = "basic block"
aliases = ["basic blocks"]
short = "A run of instructions that always executes from top to bottom: one way in at the top, one way out at the bottom."
text = '''
A block ends at every jump, and a new block starts at every place a jump can land. Inside a
block nothing can branch, so you can read it as one small step. In Rust terms, the body of
an `if` without any further `if`s or loops inside it is roughly one basic block.
'''
see = ["control-flow graph", "graph edge"]

[[term]]
term = "control-flow graph"
aliases = ["control flow graph", "CFG", "flow graph", "flow chart"]
short = "A function drawn as boxes (basic blocks) joined by arrows (the jumps between them)."
text = '''
The graph view draws it. Shapes tell you the structure at a glance: a box that splits in two
and joins again is an `if`/`else`; an arrow that goes back up to an earlier box is a loop;
a long ladder of boxes that each can jump to the same exit is a chain of checks.
'''
see = ["basic block", "graph edge", "back edge"]

[[term]]
term = "graph edge"
aliases = ["edges", "graph arrow", "graph arrows"]
short = "An arrow in the graph view: a possible way from the end of one basic block to the start of another."
text = '''
ORRESS colours them: **green** when a conditional jump is taken (the condition is true),
**red** when it is not taken and execution falls through, **blue** for unconditional jumps
and plain fall-through.
'''
see = ["control-flow graph", "fall-through"]

[[term]]
term = "back edge"
aliases = ["back edges", "back-edge"]
short = "A graph arrow that goes back to an earlier block: the sign of a loop."
see = ["control-flow graph", "graph edge"]

[[term]]
term = "fall-through"
aliases = ["fall through", "falls through", "fallthrough"]
short = "What happens when a conditional jump is not taken: the CPU continues with the next instruction below."
see = ["graph edge"]

[[term]]
term = "decompiler"
aliases = ["decompile", "decompiled", "decompiling", "decompilation"]
short = "A tool that turns machine code back into readable code with `if`, loops, variables and calls."
text = '''
A compiler goes from Rust to machine code; a decompiler goes the other way. It cannot get
the original source back, because names, comments and most types are thrown away during
compiling. What it gives you is **pseudocode**: code that does the same thing, with guessed
names and types. ORRESS's decompiler writes that pseudocode in Rust syntax.
'''
see = ["pseudocode", "Rust port"]

[[term]]
term = "pseudocode"
aliases = ["pseudo-code"]
short = "Code that reads like a programming language and shows what a function does, but is not meant to compile."
see = ["decompiler"]

[[term]]
term = "Rust port"
aliases = ["Rust port mode", "port mode"]
short = "The decompiler mode that turns a function into compilable Rust, keeping instructions it cannot translate as inline assembly."
text = '''
Pseudocode is for reading; the Rust port is a starting point for re-writing a function in
Rust (porting it). It adds a small helper prelude and wraps anything it cannot lift in
`asm!` blocks, so the result can still be compiled and tested.
'''
see = ["decompiler", "pseudocode"]

[[term]]
term = "loop unrolling"
aliases = ["unrolled", "unrolls", "unroll", "unrolling"]
short = "A compiler optimisation that repeats the body of a short loop instead of jumping back, so no loop is left in the machine code."
text = '''
If a loop always runs 8 times, the compiler may write the body 8 times in a row, once for
each value of `i`. You then see eight almost identical blocks instead of one loop. Read
them as one loop again: the parts that change from copy to copy are the index and the
constants for that index.
'''
see = ["basic block"]

[[term]]
term = "XOR cipher"
aliases = ["XOR encryption", "XOR-encoded", "XOR encoding", "XOR-encrypted", "XOR'd"]
short = "Hiding data by XORing every byte with a key; XORing again with the same key gives the original back."
text = '''
XOR has a special property: `(x ^ k) ^ k == x` for every `x` and `k`. So the same
operation both hides and reveals:

```rust
let secret = b"hi";
let key = 0x5A;
let hidden: Vec<u8> = secret.iter().map(|b| b ^ key).collect();   // [0x32, 0x33]
let back: Vec<u8> = hidden.iter().map(|b| b ^ key).collect();     // b"hi" again
```

It is not real encryption: anyone who finds the key (and it is always inside the program)
can undo it. Programs use it to keep passwords and messages out of the Strings view.
'''
see = ["XOR key", "ciphertext", "plaintext", "repeating key"]

[[term]]
term = "XOR key"
aliases = ["encryption key", "decryption key", "the key bytes"]
short = "The bytes a value is XORed with to hide it, and XORed with again to recover it."
see = ["XOR cipher", "repeating key"]

[[term]]
term = "repeating key"
aliases = ["rolling key", "repeating-key XOR", "multi-byte key"]
short = "A key of several bytes that is used over and over: byte i of the data is XORed with key byte i % key length."
text = '''
With the 4-byte key `[0x5A, 0x1C, 0x7E, 0x33]`, data byte 0 uses `0x5A`, byte 1 uses
`0x1C`, ..., byte 4 uses `0x5A` again. In Rust: `data[i] ^ KEY[i % KEY.len()]`.
'''
see = ["XOR cipher", "XOR key"]

[[term]]
term = "plaintext"
aliases = ["plain text", "cleartext"]
short = "Data in its readable, original form, before it is encoded or encrypted."
see = ["ciphertext", "XOR cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "ciphertext"
aliases = ["cipher text", "encoded bytes", "encrypted bytes"]
short = "Data after encoding or encryption: what the program stores instead of the readable plaintext."
see = ["plaintext", "XOR cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "known-plaintext attack"
aliases = ["known plaintext"]
short = "Recovering a key because you know (part of) the plaintext: for XOR, key = ciphertext ^ plaintext."
text = '''
If you know a flag starts with `flag{`, XOR the first five ciphertext bytes with `flag{` and
you have the first five key bytes. The Workbench operation **XOR key from known text** does
exactly this.
'''
see = ["XOR cipher", "plaintext"]

[[term]]
term = "Workbench"
aliases = ["Workbench recipe", "recipe"]
short = "The ORRESS tool (Tools > Workbench, Ctrl+Shift+W) that decodes data with a chain of operations such as hex, base64 and XOR."
text = '''
You put bytes in **Input**, add operations from the **Operations** list to the **Recipe**,
and read the result in **Output**. The same recipe also works on the command line:
`orress-cli recipe "from_hex | xor key=0x5a1c7e33" file`.
'''
see = ["XOR cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "keygen"
aliases = ["keygens", "key generator", "key generators"]
short = "A small program that computes valid keys or serial numbers for a program, by doing what its check does."
text = '''
Instead of finding one password, you rebuild the program's check and turn it around, so
that you can produce a valid key for any input (for example for any name). Writing one is
the proof that you fully understood the algorithm.
'''
see = ["keygen-me", "serial number", "inverse operation"]

[[term]]
term = "keygen-me"
aliases = ["keygenme", "keygen-mes"]
short = "A crackme whose key is computed from something you type (often a name), so the goal is a keygen, not one password."
see = ["keygen", "serial number"]

[[term]]
term = "serial number"
aliases = ["serial", "serials", "licence key", "license key", "licence code", "license code"]
short = "A code a program asks for to prove you may use it; its check is an algorithm you can read."
see = ["keygen", "checksum"]

[[term]]
term = "checksum"
aliases = ["checksums"]
short = "A number computed from data (for example the sum of its bytes) to check that the data is right."
text = '''
The simplest checksum adds up all bytes: `data.iter().map(|&b| b as u32).sum::<u32>()`.
Licence checks often require that a checksum of your code has one particular value.
'''
see = ["serial number"]

[[term]]
term = "inverse operation"
aliases = ["inverse", "inverses"]
short = "The operation that undoes another one: subtract undoes add, XOR with k undoes XOR with k."
text = '''
To turn a check like `transform(input) == target` into a generator, apply the inverse of
every step to `target`, in reverse order. Some operations have no clean inverse (a sum
throws information away, a hash is built to have none); then you search for an input
instead, or build one that fits.
'''
see = ["keygen"]

[[term]]
term = "brute force"
aliases = ["brute-force", "brute forcing", "brute-forcing"]
short = "Finding a value by trying every possibility until one works."
text = '''
Fine for small spaces (a 1-byte XOR key has only 256 values; the Workbench tries them all
with **XOR brute force**), hopeless for large ones (an 8-character password).
'''
see = ["XOR key"]

`academy/glossary/3-dynamic-analysis.toml`:

```toml
# Level 3: dynamic analysis. The debugger, breakpoints and stepping, reading and changing
# a running program, patching, emulation, and anti-debugging.

[[term]]
term = "debugger"
aliases = ["debuggers"]
short = "A tool that runs another program under its control, so you can stop it, look at it, and change it while it runs."
text = '''
A **debugger** runs a program and keeps control of it. It can stop the program at an
instruction you choose, show you the real registers and memory at that moment, run one
instruction at a time, and even change a value before letting the program go on.

Think of debugging your own Rust code: you set a breakpoint on a line, run, and execution
pauses so you can inspect your variables. A debugger for a compiled program is the same
idea, one *instruction* instead of one source line, and it works on a program you have no
source code for.

A debugger runs the program for real, on your computer, so you only debug code you trust.
'''
see = ["debuggee", "breakpoint", "stepping", "emulator", "dynamic analysis"]

[[term]]
term = "debuggee"
aliases = ["debuggees"]
short = "The program that is being run under a debugger."
text = '''
The **debuggee** is the program the debugger is controlling. On Windows, the debugger asks
the operating system to start the program in a special way, and from then on Windows reports
what happens in the debuggee to the debugger and freezes it whenever the debugger asks.
'''
see = ["debugger", "process"]

[[term]]
term = "breakpoint"
aliases = ["breakpoints"]
short = "A stop point you place on an instruction: the program pauses there every time it is about to run it."
text = '''
A **breakpoint** tells the debugger to stop the program at a particular instruction. Each
time the program is about to run that instruction, it pauses and hands control back to you,
so you can read registers and memory, step forward, or change something.

In ORRESS you set a breakpoint in the Disassembly view with **F9**, or by clicking the
gutter at the left of the line. A red dot marks it, and it also appears in the Breakpoints
list. Breakpoints are saved with the program, so they are still there next time you open it.
'''
see = ["debugger", "software breakpoint", "stepping"]

[[term]]
term = "software breakpoint"
aliases = ["software breakpoints", "int3", "0xCC"]
short = "The usual kind of breakpoint: the debugger writes a special byte (0xCC) over the instruction to make the CPU stop there."
text = '''
A **software breakpoint** is how a debugger usually stops a program. It temporarily replaces
the first byte of the target instruction with `0xCC` (the `int3` instruction). When the CPU
reaches it, it traps into the debugger, which puts the original byte back, shows you the
stopped program, and restores the breakpoint when you continue.

This leaves a trace: a program can scan its own code for `0xCC` bytes to notice it is being
debugged. That is one of the anti-debugging tricks.
'''
see = ["breakpoint", "anti-debugging"]

[[term]]
term = "runtime address"
aliases = ["runtime addresses", "runtime base"]
short = "The address an instruction or byte actually has while the program runs, after the operating system has loaded it somewhere."
text = '''
A **runtime address** is where something really is in memory while the program runs. Because
of ASLR, the operating system loads the program at a random base each time, so runtime
addresses change from run to run.

ORRESS shows file addresses (as if the program were at its image base), but the debugger's
registers and status line show runtime addresses. To convert:

```text
runtime address = file address - image base + runtime base
```

The runtime base always ends in several zeros, so the **last four hex digits** of a runtime
address match the file address. That is the quickest way to tell which instruction you are on.
'''
see = ["file address", "ASLR", "image base"]

[[term]]
term = "file address"
aliases = ["file addresses", "file virtual address"]
short = "The address ORRESS shows for an instruction or byte, as if the program were loaded at its image base."
text = '''
A **file address** is the address ORRESS uses throughout the Disassembly, Hex and other
views: the address the program *would* have if it were loaded at its image base, the preferred
load address in its header. File addresses are stable, so you can note one down and it still
means the same instruction next time.

The debugger lets you work in file addresses (breakpoints and the Breakpoints list use them)
even though the running program is somewhere else, because it translates to runtime addresses
for you.
'''
see = ["runtime address", "image base", "ASLR"]

[[term]]
term = "exit code"
aliases = ["exit codes", "return code", "status code"]
short = "A number a program hands to the operating system when it ends: 0 for success, non-zero for a problem."
text = '''
Every program ends with an **exit code**, a number for whoever started it. By convention `0`
means success and anything else means something went wrong; the program decides what each
non-zero number means. The Academy crackmes use `0` for the correct password and `1` for a
wrong one.

In Rust, returning normally from `main` gives exit code `0`, and `std::process::exit(1)` ends
with `1`. ORRESS shows the exit code in the Debugger's "Last run:" line, so you can tell
success from failure even if the program's console window closed too fast to read.

(A program that crashes ends with a large, strange code instead, such as `0xC0000005`, which
is Windows' code for an access violation.)
'''
see = ["process", "debugger"]

[[term]]
term = "emulator"
aliases = ["emulators"]
short = "A CPU built in software that runs machine code itself, instead of running it on your real processor."
text = '''
An **emulator** is a simulated CPU: a program that reads machine code and carries out each
instruction itself. ORRESS has one built in. Because the code runs on the simulated CPU and
not your real one, you can run just a single function, feed it inputs, and read exactly what
it computes, without launching the whole program and without even needing the same operating
system it was built for.

Emulation has no real side effects (system calls are intercepted, not performed), so it
cannot harm your computer. Its limit is that it models only a subset of instructions and
almost none of the operating system, so it is best for self-contained computation: a decoder,
a hash, a password check.
'''
see = ["emulation", "debugger"]

[[term]]
term = "emulation"
aliases = ["emulate", "emulated", "emulating"]
short = "Running code on a simulated CPU instead of a real one."
text = '''
**Emulation** is running machine code on a CPU that is simulated in software rather than on
a real processor. It lets you run one piece of a program in isolation, on any operating
system, with full visibility and no real side effects. In ORRESS the Emulator view runs a
chosen function with arguments you provide.
'''
see = ["emulator"]

[[term]]
term = "patch"
aliases = ["patching", "patched", "patches"]
short = "Changing a program's instructions (its bytes) so it behaves differently; a permanent change, unlike setting a register for one run."
text = '''
To **patch** a program is to change its actual instructions. Most patches are tiny: remove
one instruction, or flip one jump. The three common moves are to **NOP** an instruction (skip
it), **invert** a conditional jump (take the other branch), or make a jump **always** happen.

In ORRESS the patch bar in the Disassembly view does these. Patches are kept as an overlay
with your work; the file on disk is never changed. To run the modified program you "Save
patched file", which writes a copy with the changes baked in. Patching makes permanent what
changing a register does for a single run.
'''
see = ["NOP", "conditional jump", "debugger"]

[[term]]
term = "anti-debugging"
aliases = ["anti-debug", "anti-debug check", "anti-debug checks", "debugger detection"]
short = "Tricks a program uses to notice it is being debugged and change what it does to throw off an analyst."
text = '''
**Anti-debugging** is any trick a program uses to detect a debugger and then misbehave:
exit, take a fake path, decode a decoy, or hide its real work. Crackmes use it to frustrate
you; malware uses it to evade analysis.

The common detections are an API call (`IsDebuggerPresent`), reading the PEB's debugger flag
directly, a `ptrace` self-check on Linux, a timing check, or scanning for `0xCC` breakpoint
bytes. They all share one weakness: the result feeds a branch. Find that branch and you can
patch past it, or sidestep the whole thing by emulating the part you care about.
'''
see = ["IsDebuggerPresent", "PEB", "timing check", "patch", "emulation"]

[[term]]
term = "IsDebuggerPresent"
short = "A Windows API a program can call to ask whether it is being debugged."
text = '''
`IsDebuggerPresent` is a Windows function that returns non-zero when the calling program is
being debugged. It is the simplest anti-debugging check, and the easiest to spot: it appears
in the import table, so ORRESS's Triage flags it and you can cross-reference it to the exact
branch it controls. Under the hood it just reads the same PEB flag you could read yourself.
'''
see = ["anti-debugging", "PEB"]

[[term]]
term = "PEB"
aliases = ["Process Environment Block", "BeingDebugged"]
short = "A Windows structure describing the running process; it holds a flag that says whether a debugger is attached."
text = '''
The **PEB** (Process Environment Block) is a structure Windows keeps for every running
process, with details about how it was started and the modules it loaded. It contains a
`BeingDebugged` byte that is set when a debugger is attached.

A program can read this byte itself, with ordinary instructions (`mov rax, gs:[0x60]` to get
the PEB, then the flag byte), so there is no API call to spot. That makes a PEB check harder
to notice than `IsDebuggerPresent`: you have to see it in the code.
'''
see = ["anti-debugging", "IsDebuggerPresent", "process"]

[[term]]
term = "timing check"
aliases = ["timing checks"]
short = "An anti-debug trick that times a short piece of code; a debugger that is stepping makes it take far too long."
text = '''
A **timing check** reads a high-resolution clock before and after a short block of code and
compares the gap against a threshold. Run normally, the block takes microseconds. Under a
debugger where someone is single-stepping, it takes seconds, so a large gap betrays the
debugger. Like every anti-debug trick, the result just feeds a branch you can defeat.
'''
see = ["anti-debugging"]

[[term]]
term = "decoy"
aliases = ["decoy password", "decoys"]
short = "A fake answer a program shows on purpose to mislead an analyst who triggered a protection."
text = '''
A **decoy** is a wrong answer a program produces deliberately, to punish careless analysis.
Crackme #12, for example, decodes a decoy password instead of the real one if any of its
anti-debug guards fire, and still answers "Wrong". If you read the decoded buffer under the
debugger without beating the guards first, you read the decoy and never know it. The lesson:
check *where* a value comes from, and prefer a method (like emulating the real decode
function) that no guard can taint.
'''
see = ["anti-debugging", "emulation"]

[[term]]
term = "gutter"
aliases = ["margin"]
short = "The narrow strip at the far left of the Disassembly view, where breakpoint dots and the current-instruction marker appear."
text = '''
The **gutter** is the thin column on the left edge of the Disassembly view, left of the
address. Clicking it toggles a breakpoint on that line (a red dot). While debugging, a green
triangle in the gutter marks the instruction that will run next.
'''
see = ["breakpoint", "debugger"]

```

`academy/glossary/4-intermediate-ctf.toml`:

```toml
# Level 4: Intermediate CTF. Terms first used in the 04-* lessons.

# --- CTF practice -------------------------------------------------------------

[[term]]
term = "leetspeak"
aliases = ["leet"]
short = "Writing words with look-alike digits and symbols, such as 0 for o, 3 for e and 4 for a."
text = '''
CTF flags are usually written in leetspeak: `flag{r3v3rs1ng_1s_fun}`. It makes flags hard to guess
but easy to read once you have them. When a decoded text looks like leetspeak, you have probably
found the flag.
'''
see = ["CTF flag"]

[[term]]
term = "check function"
aliases = ["check functions", "validation function"]
short = "The function that decides whether your input (password, key, flag) is accepted."
text = '''
In a crackme, `main` reads your input, calls the check function, and prints "Correct!" or "Wrong"
depending on its result. Finding it is step 2 of every reversing challenge: start at the success
or failure message and look for the call whose result decides between them.

```rust
if check_password(input) { println!("Correct!"); } else { println!("Wrong"); }
```
'''
see = ["crackme"]

# --- encodings -----------------------------------------------------------------

[[term]]
term = "encoding"
aliases = ["encodings", "encode", "encoded", "encodes", "decode", "decoded", "decodes", "decoding"]
short = "Writing the same data in a different form, such as hex or base64. Anyone can undo it; no key is needed."
text = '''
An encoding is a fixed, public rule for writing bytes differently. Hex writes each byte as two
digits, base64 packs bytes into 64 safe characters, URL encoding writes special characters as
`%41`. Encodings hide nothing; they only make data look unreadable at first glance.

Compare with encryption (needs a key) and hashing (cannot be undone at all).
'''
see = ["encryption", "hash function", "base64"]

[[term]]
term = "hex text"
aliases = ["hex string", "hex strings", "hex encoding", "hex-encoded"]
short = "Bytes written as hexadecimal digits, two characters per byte, for example 666c6167 for flag."
text = '''
Hex text uses only `0-9` and `a-f`, has an even length, and is twice as long as the data it
holds. In Rust: `format!("{:02x}", byte)` for each byte. The Workbench's **From hex** step turns it
back into bytes.
'''
see = ["hexadecimal", "encoding"]

[[term]]
term = "base64"
aliases = ["base-64"]
short = "An encoding that writes every 3 bytes as 4 characters from A-Z, a-z, 0-9, + and /, often ending with =."
text = '''
Base64 cuts the input into groups of 3 bytes (24 bits), splits each group into four 6-bit numbers,
and looks each number up in a 64-character alphabet. Example: `Man` becomes `TWFu`. A missing byte
at the end is marked with `=` padding.

Recognise it by its alphabet, a length that is a multiple of 4, and `=` at the end. `Zmxh` at the
start is base64 for `fla`, the start of a flag. Undo it with the Workbench's **From base64**.
'''
see = ["encoding", "base32"]

[[term]]
term = "base32"
short = "An encoding like base64 but with only 32 characters: uppercase letters and the digits 2 to 7."
see = ["base64"]

[[term]]
term = "URL encoding"
aliases = ["percent-encoding", "URL-encoded", "URL decode"]
short = "Writing special characters as % followed by two hex digits, as in web addresses: a space becomes %20."
see = ["encoding"]

[[term]]
term = "ROT13"
aliases = ["ROT-13"]
short = "Replacing every letter with the letter 13 places further in the alphabet. Applying it twice gives the original back."
text = '''
`a` becomes `n`, `f` becomes `s`, so `flag{` becomes `synt{`. Digits and punctuation do not
change. Because the alphabet has 26 letters, ROT13 undoes itself. It is a Caesar cipher with a
shift of 13.
'''
see = ["Caesar cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "Caesar cipher"
aliases = ["Caesar shift", "Caesar"]
short = "Shifting every letter by a fixed number of places in the alphabet. Only 25 possible shifts, so it is trivial to break."
see = ["ROT13"]

[[term]]
term = "Magic button"
aliases = ["auto-decoder", "Magic auto-decoder"]
short = "The Workbench button that tries chains of common decodings and lists the most readable results."
text = '''
Magic tries hex, base64, base32, URL decoding, zlib, gzip, single-byte XOR, ROT13, UTF-16 and more,
in chains of up to 3 steps, and scores the results by how readable they are. Click **Use** to load
a result's recipe. On the command line: `orress-cli magic FILE`.
'''
see = ["Workbench", "encoding"]

[[term]]
term = "orress-cli"
aliases = ["ORRESS command line"]
short = "ORRESS's command-line tool: strings, disassembly, decompiling, Workbench recipes and more, without the window."
text = '''
Examples: `orress-cli recipe "from_base64 | rot13" FILE` runs a Workbench recipe on a file,
`orress-cli magic FILE` runs Magic, `orress-cli strings FILE` lists strings. Run
`orress-cli --help` for the full list.
'''
see = ["Workbench"]

[[term]]
term = "zlib"
aliases = ["gzip", "DEFLATE"]
short = "Common compression formats. zlib data usually starts with 78 9C, gzip with 1F 8B. Compressed data looks random, like encrypted data."
see = ["entropy"]

[[term]]
term = "bit rotation"
aliases = ["rotation", "rotations", "rotate_left", "rotate_right", "rol", "ror"]
short = "Shifting the bits of a value and moving the bits that fall off one end back in at the other end."
text = '''
`0b1000_0001u8.rotate_left(1)` is `0b0000_0011`: the top bit wrapped around to the bottom. Unlike
a shift, a rotation loses no bits, so it can always be undone by rotating the other way. The x86
instructions are `rol` and `ror`.
'''
see = ["shift"]

# --- cryptography -------------------------------------------------------------

[[term]]
term = "cryptography"
aliases = ["crypto", "cryptographic"]
short = "The science of protecting information: encryption, hashing, signatures."
text = '''
For a reverse engineer, cryptography is mostly about recognition: identify the standard
algorithm, find its key and data, and use a ready-made implementation. You almost never need its
mathematics.
'''
see = ["encryption", "hash function", "magic constant"]

[[term]]
term = "encryption"
aliases = ["encrypt", "encrypts", "encrypted", "encrypting", "decrypt", "decrypts", "decrypted", "decrypting", "decryption"]
short = "Scrambling data with a key so that only someone with the key can turn it back (decrypt it)."
text = '''
```rust
let ciphertext = encrypt(plaintext, key);
let plaintext  = decrypt(ciphertext, key);
```

A program that decrypts something must contain or receive the key, so a reverse engineer can
usually find it. Compare with encoding (no key) and hashing (no way back).
'''
see = ["cipher", "plaintext", "ciphertext", "secret key"]

[[term]]
term = "cipher"
aliases = ["ciphers"]
short = "An algorithm that encrypts and decrypts data with a key, such as AES, TEA or RC4."
see = ["block cipher", "stream cipher", "encryption"]

[[term]]
term = "secret key"
aliases = ["cipher key", "crypto key", "secret keys"]
short = "The input that controls a cipher. The same plaintext with a different key gives completely different ciphertext."
text = '''
Modern ciphers are public; their security comes only from the key. In a program, look for it
where the data goes into the cipher function: a string (crackme13 keeps `t1ny_crypt0_k3y!` as
text), a byte array, or a value computed at run time. TEA and AES-128 keys are 16 bytes.
'''
see = ["cipher", "XOR key"]

[[term]]
term = "block cipher"
aliases = ["block ciphers"]
short = "A cipher that encrypts fixed-size chunks (blocks), such as 8 bytes for TEA or 16 bytes for AES."
text = '''
In code: a loop over the data in steps of 8 or 16 bytes, and inside it many rounds of shifts,
XORs, additions and table lookups. Ciphertext from a block cipher is a whole number of blocks long.
'''
see = ["stream cipher", "cipher round", "AES", "TEA"]

[[term]]
term = "stream cipher"
aliases = ["stream ciphers"]
short = "A cipher that generates a keystream from the key and XORs it into the data byte by byte, such as RC4 or ChaCha20."
see = ["keystream", "block cipher", "RC4"]

[[term]]
term = "keystream"
aliases = ["key stream"]
short = "The long sequence of pseudo-random bytes a stream cipher makes from its key; data XOR keystream = ciphertext."
see = ["stream cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "cipher round"
aliases = ["rounds", "cipher rounds"]
short = "One repetition of a cipher's mixing steps. Ciphers repeat them many times: TEA 32 cycles, AES 10 to 14 rounds."
see = ["block cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "S-box"
aliases = ["S-boxes", "sbox", "substitution box"]
short = "A lookup table that replaces each byte with another byte, used by ciphers to mix data. AES's starts 63 7C 77 7B."
text = '''
```rust
let out = SBOX[input as usize];
```

A 256-byte table in a program's data is a strong hint of a cipher. AES's S-box is the most famous;
its first bytes are `63 7C 77 7B F2 6B 6F C5`.
'''
see = ["AES", "magic constant"]

[[term]]
term = "AES"
aliases = ["AES-128", "AES-256", "Rijndael"]
short = "The Advanced Encryption Standard, the most used block cipher: 16-byte blocks, 16-, 24- or 32-byte keys."
text = '''
Recognise it by its S-box (`63 7C 77 7B ...`) in the data. Decrypting needs the key, the mode
(ECB, CBC, CTR ...) and, for most modes, a 16-byte IV. The Workbench has **AES decrypt**.
'''
see = ["S-box", "block cipher mode", "IV"]

[[term]]
term = "block cipher mode"
aliases = ["ECB", "CBC", "CTR", "cipher mode"]
short = "How a block cipher handles data longer than one block: ECB encrypts each block alone, CBC and CTR chain them with an IV."
see = ["AES", "IV"]

[[term]]
term = "IV"
aliases = ["initialization vector", "initialisation vector", "nonce"]
short = "A starting value that makes encryption of the same data come out different each time. Needed to decrypt CBC and CTR."
see = ["block cipher mode"]

[[term]]
term = "TEA"
aliases = ["Tiny Encryption Algorithm"]
short = "A small block cipher (8-byte blocks, 16-byte key, 32 cycles), easy to recognise by its constant 0x9E3779B9."
text = '''
Popular in CTFs and malware because it fits in a few lines. Its key is four 32-bit words, read
little-endian in most programs. The Workbench has **TEA decrypt** with an `endian` setting. The
decompiler may show its constant as `-= 0x61c88647`, the same number in two's complement.
'''
see = ["TEA delta", "XTEA", "block cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "XTEA"
aliases = ["eXtended TEA"]
short = "TEA's successor with a slightly different key schedule; same delta constant 0x9E3779B9."
see = ["TEA"]

[[term]]
term = "TEA delta"
aliases = ["delta", "0x9E3779B9", "0x61C88647"]
short = "The constant 0x9E3779B9, derived from the golden ratio, used by TEA and XTEA. Stored as the bytes b9 79 37 9e."
see = ["TEA", "magic constant"]

[[term]]
term = "RC4"
aliases = ["ARC4", "ARCFOUR"]
short = "An old, simple stream cipher popular in malware. Recognised by a loop that fills a 256-byte array with 0 to 255."
text = '''
RC4 has no numeric magic constant. Look for its key-scheduling algorithm: a loop writing 0..255
into a buffer, then 256 swaps driven by the key. Encryption and decryption are the same operation.
The Workbench has **RC4**; on the command line `orress-cli rc4`.
'''
see = ["key-scheduling algorithm", "stream cipher"]

[[term]]
term = "key-scheduling algorithm"
aliases = ["KSA", "key schedule"]

see = ["RC4"]

[[term]]
term = "ChaCha20"
aliases = ["ChaCha", "Salsa20"]
short = "A modern stream cipher, recognisable by the 16-character text expand 32-byte k in its data."
see = ["stream cipher", "magic constant"]

[[term]]
term = "hash function"
aliases = ["hash", "hashes", "hashing", "hashed", "hash functions", "digest", "digests"]
short = "A function that turns any input into a short, fixed-size fingerprint (the digest) that cannot be turned back."
text = '''
The same input always gives the same digest, a tiny change gives a completely different one, and
there is no way back from digest to input. Digest sizes identify the hash: CRC32 4 bytes, MD5 16,
SHA-1 20, SHA-256 32. A program that hashes your password and compares the digest can only be
beaten by guessing (or by patching the comparison).
'''

[[term]]

[[term]]

short = "An old hash function with 16-byte digests. Recognised by the start values 0x67452301, 0xEFCDAB89, 0x98BADCFE, 0x10325476."
see = ["hash function", "SHA-1"]

[[term]]
term = "SHA-1"
aliases = ["SHA1"]
short = "A hash function with 20-byte (40 hex digit) digests. Shares MD5's four start values and adds 0xC3D2E1F0."
see = ["hash function", "MD5"]

[[term]]
term = "SHA-256"
aliases = ["SHA256", "SHA-2"]

see = ["hash function"]

[[term]]
term = "CRC32"
aliases = ["CRC-32", "CRC"]
short = "A 4-byte checksum used by zip and PNG to detect damage. Recognised by 0xEDB88320 or its 1 KB lookup table."
see = ["checksum", "hash function"]

[[term]]
term = "magic constant"
aliases = ["magic constants", "crypto constant", "crypto constants"]
short = "A fixed number or table that is part of an algorithm's definition, so finding it identifies the algorithm."
text = '''
Examples: `0x9E3779B9` (TEA), `0x67452301` (MD5, SHA-1), `0x6A09E667` (SHA-256), `0xEDB88320`

# --- symbolic execution ---------------------------------------------------------

[[term]]
term = "symbolic execution"
aliases = ["symbolic", "symbolically", "symbolic solver", "symbolic solve"]
short = "Running code with unknowns instead of numbers, collecting the conditions on the way to a block, and solving them."
text = '''
Every operation builds a formula (`x ^ 0x5a`) instead of a value, and every branch that depends
on the input adds a constraint (`x ^ 0x5a == 0x15`). Solve the constraints of the path to the
success block and you have an input that reaches it. In ORRESS: the **Symbolic solve** section of
the Emulator.
'''
see = ["symbolic variable", "constraint", "SMT solver", "path explosion"]

[[term]]
term = "concrete value"
aliases = ["concrete", "concrete values", "concretely", "concrete execution"]
short = "A real, known number, as opposed to a symbolic unknown. Normal execution is concrete execution."
see = ["symbolic execution"]

[[term]]
term = "symbolic variable"
aliases = ["symbolic variables", "symbolic byte", "symbolic bytes"]
short = "An unknown, like x in algebra, that stands for an input byte during symbolic execution."
see = ["symbolic execution"]

[[term]]
term = "constraint"
aliases = ["constraints"]
short = "A condition the input must satisfy, for example input[0] ^ 0x5a == 0x15."
see = ["path constraint", "SMT solver"]

[[term]]
term = "path constraint"
aliases = ["path constraints"]
short = "All constraints collected on the way to one block: the input reaches that block exactly when all of them hold."
see = ["constraint", "symbolic execution"]

[[term]]
term = "SMT solver"
aliases = ["solver", "solvers", "constraint solver", "SAT solver"]
short = "A program that finds values satisfying a list of constraints over integers and bits, or proves that none exist."
text = '''
You give it constraints; it answers **sat** (with a solution), **unsat** (impossible) or
**unknown**. z3 is the best known. ORRESS has a small built-in solver for byte-wise checks and
exports SMT-LIB2 for z3.
'''
see = ["z3", "SMT-LIB2", "satisfiable"]

[[term]]
term = "z3"
short = "Microsoft Research's SMT solver, the standard tool for solving the constraints of a crackme."
see = ["SMT solver", "SMT-LIB2"]

[[term]]
term = "SMT-LIB2"
aliases = ["SMT-LIB", "smt2"]
short = "The standard text language for SMT constraints: declare-const for unknowns, assert for conditions."
text = '''
```text
(declare-const x (_ BitVec 8))
(assert (= (bvxor x #x5a) #x15))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```

ORRESS shows the collected constraints in this format under **SMT-LIB2 (for external z3)**.
'''
see = ["z3"]

[[term]]
term = "satisfiable"
aliases = ["sat", "unsat", "unsatisfiable"]
short = "A set of constraints is satisfiable (sat) when some input makes all of them true, unsatisfiable (unsat) when none does."
see = ["SMT solver"]

[[term]]
term = "path explosion"
aliases = ["state explosion"]
short = "The number of paths doubling with every branch, which makes exploring all of them impossible for large functions."
see = ["symbolic execution"]

[[term]]
term = "target address"
aliases = ["target block", "success block"]
short = "In ORRESS's symbolic solve: the block the input must reach, usually the one that leads to Correct!."
see = ["avoid address", "symbolic execution"]

[[term]]
term = "avoid address"
aliases = ["avoid addresses", "avoid block", "failure block"]
short = "In ORRESS's symbolic solve: a block that means failure. Branches toward it are steered the other way."
see = ["target address"]

[[term]]
term = "symbolic address"
aliases = ["symbolic memory address"]
short = "A memory address that depends on the unknown input, such as TABLE[input[0]]. ORRESS's symbolic solver stops on these."
see = ["symbolic execution", "S-box"]

# --- side channels --------------------------------------------------------------

[[term]]
term = "side channel"
aliases = ["side channels", "side-channel", "side-channel attack", "side-channel solve"]
short = "Information that leaks through how a program works (time, power, instruction count) instead of through its output."
text = '''
A check that stops at the first wrong character does less work for a worse guess. Measure the
work and you learn how many leading characters are right. ORRESS's **Side-channel solve** in the
Emulator counts executed instructions to do this byte by byte.
'''
see = ["early exit", "instruction counting", "timing attack", "constant-time code"]

[[term]]
term = "early exit"
aliases = ["early-exit", "early return"]
short = "Leaving a loop or function as soon as the answer is known, for example at the first mismatching byte."
text = '''
Efficient, and a classic leak: the amount of work then depends on how much of the secret you got
right.

```rust
for i in 0..n { if a[i] != b[i] { return false; } }   // early exit
```
'''
see = ["side channel", "constant-time code"]

[[term]]
term = "oracle"
aliases = ["oracles"]
short = "Something you can query that reveals more about a secret than it should, such as a check that leaks how far it got."
see = ["side channel"]

[[term]]
term = "timing attack"
aliases = ["timing attacks", "timing side channel"]
short = "A side channel that measures how long an operation takes. Real-world timing is noisy, so measurements are repeated and averaged."
see = ["side channel", "instruction counting"]

[[term]]
term = "instruction counting"
aliases = ["instruction count", "instruction counts", "counting instructions"]
short = "Counting how many instructions a function executes in an emulator: a noise-free stand-in for timing."
see = ["side channel", "timing attack"]

[[term]]
term = "charset"
aliases = ["character set", "charsets"]
short = "The set of characters a solver tries at each position, such as printable ASCII (95 characters) or digits (10)."
see = ["side channel"]

[[term]]
term = "constant-time code"
aliases = ["constant-time", "constant time"]
short = "Code that does the same work for every secret value, so a side channel has nothing to measure."
text = '''
```rust
let mut diff = 0u8;
for i in 0..a.len() { diff |= a[i] ^ b[i]; }   // no early exit
diff == 0
```
'''
see = ["early exit", "side channel"]

[[term]]
term = "cache attack"
aliases = ["cache attacks", "Flush+Reload"]
short = "A side channel that learns which memory another program used from the processor's cache, leaking table lookups."
see = ["side channel"]

[[term]]
term = "power analysis"
aliases = ["DPA", "differential power analysis"]
short = "A hardware side channel: measuring the power a chip draws while it encrypts to recover its key."
see = ["side channel"]

[[term]]
term = "minification"
aliases = ["minified", "minify", "minifier"]
short = "Shrinking source code by removing whitespace and shortening names to a, b, c. A beautifier puts the layout back."
see = ["JavaScript", "beautify"]

[[term]]
term = "beautify"
aliases = ["beautifier", "beautified", "pretty-print"]

[[term]]
