`academy/glossary/5-advanced.toml`:

```toml
# Glossary terms introduced at Level 5 (Advanced): obfuscation, control-flow
# flattening, virtual-machine protections, packers, self-modifying code, and other
# CPU architectures. Terms taught in earlier levels (bytecode, entropy, register,
# stack, basic block, disassembly, emulator ...) are defined there and reused here.

[[term]]
term = "obfuscation"
aliases = ["obfuscated", "obfuscate", "obfuscator", "obfuscators"]
short = "Rewriting a program so it still does the same thing but is much harder to read."
text = '''
**Obfuscation** transforms a program into an equivalent one that is painful to
understand. The behaviour is unchanged; only the *form* is scrambled. It is used to
protect commercial software and licence checks, to hide malware from analysts, and by
CTF authors to make a challenge harder.

Common tricks: renaming everything to noise, inserting code that does nothing
(**junk code**), guarding real code with conditions that are always true or false
(**opaque predicates**), chopping a function into a dispatch loop (**control-flow
flattening**), and replacing the code with bytecode for a made-up CPU (**VM-based
obfuscation**).
'''
see = ["deobfuscation", "junk code", "opaque predicate", "control-flow flattening", "VM-based obfuscation"]

[[term]]
term = "deobfuscation"
aliases = ["deobfuscate", "deobfuscated", "deobfuscating"]
short = "Undoing obfuscation to get code back into a readable form."
text = '''
**Deobfuscation** reverses obfuscation: it recovers code you can actually read. Some of
it is automatic — ORRESS's decompiler folds away opaque predicates and undoes
control-flow flattening, printing a `// deobfuscated by ORRESS` note when it does — and
some is manual, like reversing a custom VM by hand.
'''
see = ["obfuscation", "control-flow flattening", "devirtualization"]

[[term]]
term = "control-flow flattening"
aliases = ["flattening", "flattened", "flatten", "unflatten", "unflattening", "control flow flattening"]
short = "Obfuscation that turns a function's branches into one big dispatcher loop driven by a state variable."
text = '''
Normal code flows like a straight line with `if`s and loops. **Control-flow flattening**
destroys that shape: every original basic block becomes one arm of a single `switch`
inside a loop, and each arm sets a **state variable** that chooses the next arm. The
real order is hidden inside the state numbers, so you can no longer read the logic top to
bottom. The compiler toolchain OLLVM is a well-known source of it.

To **unflatten** by hand: read each arm, note which state it jumps to next, and relink
the arms into their real order. ORRESS's decompiler does this automatically.
'''
see = ["dispatcher", "state variable", "deobfuscation"]

[[term]]
term = "dispatcher"
aliases = ["dispatch loop", "dispatch", "dispatches"]
short = "The central block a flattened function or a VM interpreter jumps back to, to pick what runs next."
text = '''
A **dispatcher** is the switchboard at the heart of a flattened function or a bytecode
interpreter. It reads a value (a state number, or the next opcode), and jumps to the
block that handles it. Every arm runs, then jumps back to the dispatcher for the next
one, so in a control-flow graph the dispatcher is a single block that *many* other blocks
branch back to — it has a very high **fan-in**.
'''
see = ["state variable", "fan-in", "handler", "fetch-decode-execute"]

[[term]]
term = "state variable"
aliases = ["state variables"]
short = "The number a flattened function keeps to remember which block runs next."
text = '''
In a control-flow-flattened function the **state variable** holds the number of the block
to run next. Each arm of the dispatcher ends by setting the state variable, which sends
control back to the dispatcher and on to the chosen arm. Recovering the mapping from
state number to block is how you unflatten the function by hand.
'''
see = ["control-flow flattening", "dispatcher"]

[[term]]
term = "opaque predicate"
aliases = ["opaque predicates"]
short = "A condition that always evaluates the same way but is written so it looks like it might go either way."
text = '''
An **opaque predicate** is a test the obfuscator knows the answer to in advance but which
is not an obvious constant — for example `(x | 1) != 0` (always true) or `(x & 1) == 2`
(always false). It adds fake branches and dead arms to confuse you. ORRESS proves many of
them with a known-bits analysis and folds them away, deleting the bogus branch.
'''
see = ["obfuscation", "junk code", "deobfuscation"]

[[term]]
term = "junk code"
aliases = ["junk instructions"]
short = "Instructions inserted only to pad and confuse; they have no effect on the result."
text = '''
**Junk code** is filler the obfuscator adds — instructions that compute values nobody
uses, or that cancel each other out. Its only purpose is to bulk up the function and hide
the few lines that matter. Spotting that a value is never used lets you ignore the junk.
'''
see = ["obfuscation", "opaque predicate"]

[[term]]
term = "VM-based obfuscation"
aliases = ["VM obfuscation", "VM protection", "virtualization", "virtualized", "virtualize", "VM-based protection"]
short = "Obfuscation that replaces a function's machine code with bytecode for a made-up CPU, plus an interpreter that runs it."
text = '''
**VM-based obfuscation** (virtualization) is the strongest common protection. It takes a
function, compiles it to **bytecode for an invented instruction set**, and ships a small
**interpreter** that executes that bytecode. Your disassembler now shows the interpreter,
not the logic — the real algorithm has become *data*. Commercial protectors VMProtect and
Themida do this, and CTF authors love hand-rolling tiny versions.
'''
see = ["bytecode VM", "interpreter", "devirtualization", "VMProtect", "Themida"]

[[term]]
term = "bytecode VM"
aliases = ["bytecode interpreter", "bytecode virtual machine", "custom VM", "custom virtual machine"]
short = "A made-up CPU defined in software: a blob of bytecode plus an interpreter that runs it."
text = '''
A **bytecode VM** is a CPU built out of code rather than silicon. It has a blob of
**bytecode** (the program, in a custom instruction set), a **virtual program counter**
that points into it, some **virtual state** (a stack or virtual registers), and a
**fetch-decode-execute** loop that runs it. Real examples include the JVM and CPython; in
obfuscation, a tiny custom one hides the protected logic.
'''
see = ["VM-based obfuscation", "fetch-decode-execute", "stack machine", "register machine", "virtual program counter"]

[[term]]
term = "interpreter"
aliases = ["interpreters"]
short = "The code that reads bytecode one instruction at a time and carries out each one."
text = '''
An **interpreter** runs a program written for a virtual machine: it reads the next
instruction, works out what it means, does it, and moves on. In a VM-protected binary the
interpreter is the only native code you can see, so finding and understanding it is the
first step to recovering the hidden logic.
'''
see = ["bytecode VM", "dispatcher", "handler"]

[[term]]
term = "handler"
aliases = ["handlers"]
short = "The block of code that carries out one virtual instruction (one opcode) in an interpreter."
text = '''
In an interpreter each **handler** implements one opcode: one does addition, one does a
push, one does a compare, and so on. The dispatcher jumps to the right handler for the
current opcode; the handler does its work and jumps back. Reversing every handler tells
you what each opcode means — that is the VM's instruction set.
'''
see = ["dispatcher", "opcode table", "interpreter"]

[[term]]
term = "opcode table"
aliases = ["handler table"]
short = "The list that maps each virtual opcode number to the handler and operation it stands for."
text = '''
The **opcode table** is the map from opcode number to what it does: `0 -> push input
byte`, `1 -> push immediate`, `2 -> xor`, and so on. You build it by reversing each
handler. Once you have it, you can read any bytecode written in that instruction set —
exactly what ORRESS's VM report recovers for you.
'''
see = ["handler", "bytecode VM", "devirtualization"]

[[term]]
term = "fetch-decode-execute"
aliases = ["fetch-decode-execute loop", "fetch decode execute"]
short = "The interpreter's core loop: read the next opcode, work out what it is, do it, repeat."
text = '''
**Fetch-decode-execute** is the heartbeat of every CPU and interpreter. *Fetch* the
opcode the virtual program counter points at; *decode* it (pick the handler); *execute*
that handler; advance the counter; loop. Recognising this loop in native code is how you
spot an interpreter.
'''
see = ["dispatcher", "virtual program counter", "interpreter"]

[[term]]
term = "stack machine"
aliases = ["stack machines", "stack-based"]
short = "A virtual machine that works on a stack: operations pop their inputs and push their result."
text = '''
A **stack machine** keeps its working values on a stack. `ADD` pops two values and pushes
their sum; `PUSH n` puts `n` on top. The JVM and CPython are stack machines. There are no
named registers, so handlers are short and the bytecode reads like reverse-Polish
arithmetic.
'''
see = ["register machine", "bytecode VM"]

[[term]]
term = "register machine"
aliases = ["register-based", "register machines"]
short = "A virtual machine that works on a fixed set of virtual registers instead of a stack."
text = '''
A **register machine** holds its values in a small set of numbered **virtual registers**
rather than on a stack. Instructions name the registers they read and write, like
`ADD r0, r1`. Real CPUs are register machines, and a VM author may pick this style to look
less like a classic stack interpreter.
'''
see = ["stack machine", "virtual register", "bytecode VM"]

[[term]]
term = "virtual program counter"
aliases = ["vpc", "virtual pc"]
short = "The interpreter's index into the bytecode: which virtual instruction runs next."
text = '''
The **virtual program counter** (vpc) is the interpreter's own program counter: an index
into the bytecode blob that says where the next virtual instruction is. Each step the
interpreter reads the opcode at the vpc and advances it past the opcode and its operands.
'''
see = ["bytecode VM", "fetch-decode-execute"]

[[term]]
term = "virtual register"
aliases = ["virtual registers"]
short = "A storage slot a register-based VM uses, held in a buffer the interpreter owns."
text = '''
A **virtual register** is one of the slots a register machine computes with. They are not
real CPU registers — they live in a small array the interpreter keeps in memory — but the
bytecode treats them the way machine code treats real registers.
'''
see = ["register machine", "bytecode VM"]

[[term]]
term = "devirtualization"
aliases = ["devirtualize", "devirtualizing", "devirtualized"]
short = "Turning a VM's bytecode back into readable code by mapping its opcodes and reading its program."
text = '''
**Devirtualization** is the payoff of reversing a VM: you map every handler to its
operation (the opcode table), locate the bytecode, and translate it back into normal
operations — recovering the algorithm the virtualization hid. ORRESS's VM report does the
first stages automatically and even solves the recovered check.
'''
see = ["VM-based obfuscation", "opcode table", "lifting"]

[[term]]
term = "lifting"
aliases = ["lift", "lifted", "lifts"]
short = "Translating low-level or virtual instructions up into a higher-level, readable form."
text = '''
**Lifting** means raising code to a higher level: walking a VM's bytecode and emitting the
equivalent real operation for each opcode, so the hidden program reads like ordinary code.
More generally, a decompiler lifts machine instructions into expressions and statements.
'''
see = ["devirtualization", "opcode table"]

[[term]]
term = "fan-in"
aliases = ["high fan-in"]
short = "How many different blocks branch into one block; a dispatcher has very high fan-in."
text = '''
**Fan-in** is the number of places that jump to a given block. A dispatcher is the one
block that every handler returns to, so it has unusually high fan-in — dozens of incoming
edges inside a single loop. That shape is the fingerprint ORRESS looks for when it flags a
VM or a flattened function.
'''
see = ["dispatcher", "VM-based obfuscation"]

[[term]]
term = "packer"
aliases = ["packers", "packing", "packed", "pack"]
short = "A tool that compresses or encrypts a program into a blob and glues on a stub that restores it at run time."
text = '''
A **packer** takes a finished program, squeezes its real code and data into a blob, and
attaches a small **unpacking stub**. Running the file runs the stub first: it restores the
original program into memory and jumps to it. Packing shrinks files (UPX) and hides code
from scanners (malware). On disk the real program isn't readable — only the stub and the
blob are.
'''
see = ["unpacking stub", "OEP", "dumping", "UPX"]

[[term]]
term = "unpacking stub"
aliases = ["unpacker", "unpacking", "unpack", "unpacks"]
short = "The small loader a packer adds that restores the real program into memory and jumps to it."
text = '''
The **unpacking stub** is the only code that runs at first in a packed file. It
decompresses or decrypts the original program into memory, rebuilds its import table, and
then performs a **tail jump** into the restored code at its **OEP**. Analysts let the stub
run, then capture the now-unpacked program.
'''
see = ["packer", "tail jump", "OEP"]

[[term]]
term = "OEP"
aliases = ["Original Entry Point"]
short = "The Original Entry Point: where the real program starts, after the unpacking stub finishes."
text = '''
The **OEP** (Original Entry Point) is the address the real program begins at once it has
been unpacked. The stub ends by jumping to it. Finding the OEP tells you when unpacking is
done and the memory image is worth dumping and re-analysing.
'''
see = ["unpacking stub", "packer", "dumping"]

[[term]]
term = "dumping"
aliases = ["memory dump", "dumped"]
short = "Copying a program's in-memory image out to a file so you can analyse the unpacked bytes."
text = '''
**Dumping** means snapshotting a running program's memory to a file. For a packed binary
you run it to the OEP, so the real code is decrypted in memory, then dump that image and
analyse the dump — now the disassembly, strings and imports are all present.
'''
see = ["OEP", "packer"]

[[term]]
term = "tail jump"
aliases = ["tail-jump"]
short = "The jump at the end of an unpacking stub into the freshly unpacked code (the OEP)."
text = '''
A **tail jump** is the stub's final instruction: a jump (or call) into the section it just
unpacked — control leaving the stub and entering what looked like data on disk. Its target
is the OEP, so breaking on the tail jump is a classic way to catch the program the moment
it is unpacked.
'''
see = ["unpacking stub", "OEP"]

[[term]]
term = "UPX"
aliases = []
short = "A popular, open-source packer; its sections are named UPX0/UPX1 and `upx -d` unpacks it."
text = '''
**UPX** (the Ultimate Packer for eXecutables) is the best-known packer. It is not
malicious in itself and is used widely to shrink files. You recognise it by its `UPX0` and
`UPX1` section names, and because it unpacks in one step with `upx -d`. Malware sometimes
uses UPX, often after tampering so the stock unpacker refuses.
'''
see = ["packer", "unpacking stub"]

[[term]]
term = "VMProtect"
aliases = []
short = "A commercial protector that virtualizes code into a custom VM."
text = '''
**VMProtect** is a commercial protector that turns chosen functions into bytecode for a
custom virtual machine, among other tricks. It is a real-world example of VM-based
obfuscation; the method you learn on tiny CTF VMs is the same one used against it, only
larger.
'''
see = ["VM-based obfuscation", "Themida"]

[[term]]
term = "Themida"
aliases = []
short = "A commercial protector known for heavy virtualization and anti-analysis."
text = '''
**Themida** is another commercial protector that virtualizes code and layers on
anti-debugging and anti-VM tricks. Like VMProtect, it is a production-scale version of the
VM obfuscation you practise here.
'''
see = ["VM-based obfuscation", "VMProtect"]

[[term]]
term = "self-modifying code"
aliases = ["SMC", "self-modifying", "self modifying code"]
short = "Code that writes new instructions into its own code at run time, then runs them."
text = '''
**Self-modifying code** (SMC) rewrites its own instructions while running — decrypting,
patching or generating them — then executes the result. Until the writer runs, the real
instructions aren't there, so the static disassembly of that region is meaningless. The
tell is a store whose destination lands inside an executable section: code writing code.
'''
see = ["writer loop", "packer"]

[[term]]
term = "writer loop"
aliases = ["decode loop", "decoder loop"]
short = "The loop in self-modifying code that produces the real instructions by writing into the code region."
text = '''
The **writer loop** is the part of self-modifying code that builds the real instructions:
it reads bytes, transforms them (XOR, ADD, ROL), stores them back into the code region,
and counts. Running past it with the emulator applies every write, so the region then
holds the decoded instructions, ready to disassemble.
'''
see = ["self-modifying code"]

[[term]]
term = "RISC"
aliases = ["reduced instruction set"]
short = "A CPU family with fixed-width, simple instructions and a load/store rule (ARM64, MIPS, RISC-V)."
text = '''
**RISC** (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) designs use fixed-width instructions, a small
regular instruction set, many registers, and a **load/store** rule: arithmetic happens
only between registers, and memory is touched only by dedicated load/store instructions.
ARM64, MIPS and RISC-V are RISC. Fixed width makes disassembly reliable.
'''
see = ["CISC", "load/store architecture", "ARM64", "fixed-width instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "CISC"
aliases = ["complex instruction set"]
short = "A CPU family with variable-length, complex instructions that can work on memory directly (x86)."
text = '''
**CISC** (Complex Instruction Set Computer) designs, above all x86, use variable-length
instructions (1 to 15 bytes), many complex operations, and arithmetic that can read and
write memory directly (`add rax, [rbx+8]`). Code is compact but harder to decode, because
you must work out each instruction's length before you can read the next.
'''
see = ["RISC", "fixed-width instruction"]

[[term]]
term = "ARM64"
aliases = ["AArch64", "ARM"]
short = "The 64-bit ARM architecture: a RISC ISA in phones, Apple Silicon and many servers."
text = '''
**ARM64** (also called **AArch64**) is the 64-bit ARM architecture. It is RISC:
fixed-width 4-byte instructions, a load/store model, and 31 general registers named
`x0`-`x30`, plus a dedicated **link register**. ORRESS decodes ARM64 alongside x86 and
x86-64, so the disassembly, graph and decompiler views work the same way.
'''
see = ["RISC", "load/store architecture", "x0-x30", "link register"]

[[term]]
term = "load/store architecture"
aliases = ["load/store", "load/store model", "load-store architecture"]
short = "A design where arithmetic works only on registers; memory is reached only by load and store instructions."
text = '''
In a **load/store architecture** the CPU cannot do arithmetic straight on memory. To
change a value in memory it must *load* it into a register, compute there, then *store* it
back. This is a defining RISC trait, and it is why ARM64 code shuffles values through
registers with explicit loads and stores around every computation, where x86 folds the
memory access into the operation.
'''
see = ["RISC", "ARM64"]

[[term]]
term = "x0-x30"
aliases = ["x0", "x30", "w0"]
short = "ARM64's 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers (their 32-bit halves are w0-w30)."
text = '''
**x0-x30** are ARM64's 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers; `w0`-`w30` name their lower
32-bit halves. By convention `x0`-`x7` pass arguments and return values. There is no
`x31`: that encoding means either the zero register or the stack pointer, depending on the
instruction.
'''
see = ["ARM64", "link register"]

[[term]]
term = "link register"
aliases = ["lr"]
short = "The ARM64 register (x30) that holds the return address for a function call."
text = '''
On ARM64 a call (`bl`) does not push the return address to the stack like x86's `call`.
Instead it stores the return address in the **link register** (`x30`, also written `lr`),
and the function returns with `ret`, which jumps to it. A function that calls others saves
`lr` to the stack in its prologue so the nested call can reuse the register.
'''
see = ["ARM64", "x0-x30"]

[[term]]
term = "fixed-width instruction"
aliases = ["fixed-width", "fixed width", "fixed-length instruction"]
short = "An instruction encoding where every instruction is the same number of bytes (4 bytes on ARM64)."
text = '''
A **fixed-width instruction** set gives every instruction the same size — 4 bytes on
ARM64, MIPS and base RISC-V. You never have to guess where the next instruction starts, so
linear disassembly just works. x86, by contrast, is variable-length (1 to 15 bytes), so a
disassembler must decode each instruction to learn its length.
'''
see = ["RISC", "CISC", "ARM64"]

[[term]]
term = "MIPS"
aliases = []
short = "A RISC architecture common in routers and older embedded gear, often big-endian."
text = '''
**MIPS** is a RISC architecture found in routers and other embedded devices. It is
fixed-width and load/store like other RISC chips, and is frequently **big-endian**, so
bytes and words can read reversed from what an x86 analyst expects. ORRESS does not decode
MIPS yet; the method in the architectures lesson is how you would approach it.
'''
see = ["RISC", "RISC-V"]

[[term]]
term = "RISC-V"
aliases = ["riscv"]
short = "An open, royalty-free RISC architecture used in microcontrollers and research."
text = '''
**RISC-V** is an open, royalty-free RISC architecture. Its base instructions are
fixed-width and load/store, with a small core set plus optional extensions. It turns up in
microcontrollers and increasingly elsewhere. ORRESS does not decode it yet, but it is a
textbook RISC target for the general method.
'''
see = ["RISC", "MIPS"]

```

`academy/glossary/6-malware.toml`:

```toml
# Level 6 glossary: malware analysis. Terms defined here are the malware-specific ones the
# Level 6 lessons introduce. General terms taught earlier (hashing, entropy, XOR, PE, imports,
# strings, sandbox in the emulator sense) belong to their earlier levels and are reused here.
# Every `see` reference stays inside this file so it validates on its own.

[[term]]
term = "malware"
aliases = ["malicious software"]
short = "Software written to do harm: steal, spy, destroy, extort or take control."
text = '''
**Malware** (malicious software) is any program built to act against the interests of the
person running it: stealing data, encrypting files for ransom, spying, or handing control to an
attacker. Malware analysis is the work of taking such a program apart to learn what it does, how
to detect it and how to clean it up. In Rust terms it is still just a compiled program like the
crackmes you have reversed -- the difference is intent, and the care you must take not to run it
carelessly.
'''
see = ["malware analysis", "triage"]

[[term]]
term = "malware analysis"
short = "Taking a suspicious program apart to learn what it does and how to detect it."
text = '''
The discipline this whole level teaches: combining static reading, safe execution and detection
writing to turn an unknown file into a classified, documented threat with a plan attached.
'''
see = ["malware", "triage", "behaviour analysis", "report"]

[[term]]
term = "malware family"
aliases = ["malware families"]
short = "A group of malware samples built from the same code base or by the same author."
text = '''
Samples rarely appear alone. A **family** is a set of related samples -- different builds,
campaigns or variants of the same underlying code (for example "Emotet" or "AgentTesla").
Recognising the family tells you most of what a new sample does before you even open it. The
imphash and YARA rules are tools for grouping samples into families.
'''
see = ["imphash", "YARA rule", "malware variant"]

[[term]]
term = "malware variant"
aliases = ["malware variants"]
short = "A modified build of a known malware family -- same core, small changes."
text = '''
Authors tweak their malware constantly to dodge detection: a new C2 address, a renamed mutex, a
recompile. Each is a **variant** of the family. A good YARA rule catches the family and its
variants by keying on things that rarely change, not on the bytes an author edits every build.
'''
see = ["malware family", "YARA rule"]

[[term]]
term = "trojan"
aliases = ["trojans", "trojan horse"]
short = "Malware disguised as something harmless so the victim runs it willingly."
text = '''
A **trojan** pretends to be a legitimate program -- a game, an installer, a document -- so the
victim runs it. Unlike a worm it does not spread on its own; it relies on the disguise. Once
running it can do anything its author chose: drop a backdoor, steal data, install a loader.
'''
see = ["worm", "backdoor", "dropper"]

[[term]]
term = "ransomware"
short = "Malware that encrypts the victim's files and demands payment for the key."
text = '''
**Ransomware** encrypts a victim's documents (or whole disks) and demands payment, usually in
cryptocurrency, for the decryption key. Its behaviour is unmistakable in a sandbox: heavy file
reading and writing, often a dropped ransom note and a changed desktop. In ATT&CK terms its goal
is *Impact* (data encrypted).
'''
see = ["behaviour analysis", "ATT&CK"]

[[term]]
term = "RAT"
aliases = ["remote access trojan", "remote-access trojan"]
short = "A Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker hands-on remote control of the machine."
text = '''
A **RAT** (Remote Access Trojan) gives its operator interactive remote control: run commands,
browse files, watch the screen, log keystrokes, turn on the webcam. It talks to a C2 server and
waits for instructions. Its config usually contains the C2 address and a campaign id, which is
exactly what a config extractor pulls out.
'''
see = ["C2", "config extractor", "keylogger", "backdoor"]

[[term]]
term = "backdoor"
aliases = ["backdoors"]
short = "Hidden remote access an attacker leaves behind to get back in later."
text = '''
A **backdoor** is a way back into a compromised machine that bypasses normal authentication --
a listening port, a hidden account, a callback to C2. It is how an attacker keeps access after
the initial break-in. Closely related to a RAT, which is essentially an interactive backdoor.
'''
see = ["RAT", "C2", "persistence"]

[[term]]
term = "worm"
aliases = ["worms"]
short = "Malware that spreads to other machines by itself, with no user action."
text = '''
A **worm** copies itself to new machines automatically -- across the network, over USB, through
a vulnerability -- without anyone running it. This self-spreading is why worms must never be run
outside an isolated lab: on a connected network they hunt for neighbours.
'''
see = ["network isolation", "lateral movement"]

[[term]]
term = "malware loader"
aliases = ["malware loaders"]
short = "A small first-stage program whose only job is to fetch and run the real payload."
text = '''
A **loader** is a lightweight first stage. It does little on its own: it unpacks or downloads
the real malware (the second stage) and runs it, often straight into memory to stay off disk.
Analysing a loader means finding where the next stage comes from.
'''
see = ["dropper", "second stage", "downloader"]

[[term]]
term = "dropper"
aliases = ["droppers"]
short = "Malware that carries its payload inside itself and writes it to disk to run it."
text = '''
A **dropper** carries the next stage embedded in its own file (often encrypted) and *drops* it
to disk, then executes it. Where a downloader fetches the payload from the network, a dropper
already has it. In a sandbox a dropper shows up as a File-domain event: a new executable
appearing on disk.
'''
see = ["malware loader", "downloader", "second stage"]

[[term]]
term = "downloader"
aliases = ["downloaders"]
short = "Malware whose job is to fetch the next stage from the network and run it."
text = '''
A **downloader** reaches out to a URL, pulls down the real payload and runs it. Its story in a
sandbox is Network + File + Process: resolve a host, download, write, execute. ATT&CK calls the
fetch *Ingress Tool Transfer* (T1105).
'''
see = ["malware loader", "dropper", "C2", "second stage"]

[[term]]
term = "second stage"
aliases = ["second-stage", "next stage", "payload"]
short = "The real malware that a loader, dropper or downloader brings in after the first stage."
text = '''
Malware often arrives in stages. The **first stage** (a loader/dropper/downloader) is small and
disposable; its job is to bring in the **second stage** -- the payload that does the real work.
Splitting it up lets the author swap payloads and slip past detection that only saw the first
stage.
'''
see = ["malware loader", "dropper", "downloader"]

[[term]]
term = "botnet"
short = "A network of infected machines ('bots') an attacker controls together through C2."
text = '''
A **botnet** is a fleet of compromised machines all taking orders from the same C2
infrastructure. The attacker can command them in bulk -- to send spam, mine coins, or launch a
denial-of-service attack. Each bot typically beacons to C2 waiting for instructions.
'''
see = ["C2", "beacon"]

[[term]]
term = "C2"
aliases = ["C&C", "command and control", "command-and-control"]
short = "Command and Control: the attacker's server a sample talks to for orders and data."
text = '''
**C2** (Command and Control) is the attacker-controlled server a sample contacts to receive
commands and send back stolen data. Finding the C2 address -- in a string, in a decoded config,
or by watching the sample beacon in a sandbox -- is a central goal of analysis, because blocking
it cuts the malware off. ATT&CK groups all of this under the *Command and Control* tactic.
'''
see = ["beacon", "config extractor", "IOC", "ATT&CK"]

[[term]]
term = "beacon"
aliases = ["beaconing", "beacons"]
short = "A sample's periodic check-in to its C2 server to ask for commands."
text = '''
A **beacon** is the regular "I'm here, any orders?" message a sample sends to its C2, often at a
fixed interval. Spotting the beacon -- the host it calls, how often, what it sends -- is how you
map the C2 channel in a sandbox, and the interval itself can be a detection signal.
'''
see = ["C2", "network isolation"]

[[term]]
term = "persistence"
aliases = ["persist", "persistent"]
short = "Mechanisms malware uses to survive a reboot and keep running."
text = '''
**Persistence** is how malware makes sure it runs again after the machine restarts or the user
logs back in. The classic trick is a registry Run key, but there are many: scheduled tasks,
services, startup folders. In a sandbox, a copy-to-a-stable-location followed by a Run-key write
is the textbook persistence pattern. ATT&CK tactic: *Persistence*.
'''
see = ["Run key", "ATT&CK"]

[[term]]
term = "Run key"
aliases = ["Run keys", "autostart"]
short = "A registry value that Windows runs automatically at every logon -- a persistence favourite."
text = '''
The Windows registry keys `...\CurrentVersion\Run` (and `RunOnce`) list programs Windows starts
automatically at each logon. Malware writes its own path there so it relaunches after every
reboot. Seeing a write under a Run key in a sandbox log is a strong persistence indicator
(ATT&CK T1547.001).
'''
see = ["persistence", "IOC"]

[[term]]
term = "process injection"
aliases = ["code injection", "inject", "injecting"]
short = "Running your code inside another, trusted process to hide and gain its privileges."
text = '''
**Process injection** means writing code into another running process and making it execute --
so the malicious activity appears to come from a trusted program (like `explorer.exe`) rather
than from the malware. The classic Windows recipe imports `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`
and `CreateRemoteThread`; seeing that trio together is a capability red flag (ATT&CK T1055).
'''
see = ["capability", "ATT&CK"]

[[term]]
term = "keylogger"
aliases = ["keylogging"]
short = "Code that records every key the victim presses, to steal passwords and messages."
text = '''
A **keylogger** captures keystrokes, usually to steal credentials. On Windows it typically
imports `SetWindowsHookEx` or polls `GetAsyncKeyState`. ATT&CK technique T1056.001. It is a
common component of RATs and info-stealers.
'''
see = ["RAT", "capability"]

[[term]]
term = "triage"
aliases = ["triaging"]
short = "The fast first pass that classifies a sample and decides what to do with it."
text = '''
**Triage** is the quick, mostly static first assessment of a suspicious file: what is it, what
can it do, what next. It is about *classifying and prioritising*, not fully understanding --
turning a scary unknown into a labelled sample with a plan. ORRESS's Triage view assembles the
whole first-pass picture (flags, capabilities, IOCs, hashes) in one screen.
'''
see = ["capability", "IOC", "imphash", "report"]

[[term]]
term = "capability"
aliases = ["capabilities", "capa"]
short = "Something a sample CAN do, inferred from its imports and strings (not proof it does it)."
text = '''
A **capability** is a higher-level behaviour a sample is *able* to perform, deduced from the
combination of APIs it imports and strings it contains -- "inject into a process", "persist via
a Run key", "talk HTTP". The open-source tool *capa* popularised this idea, and ORRESS's Triage
view lists capabilities with the evidence behind each and its ATT&CK technique. A capability says
what the sample *can* do; only behaviour analysis proves what it *does*.
'''
see = ["triage", "ATT&CK", "behaviour analysis", "process injection"]

[[term]]
term = "IOC"
aliases = ["IOCs", "indicator of compromise", "indicators of compromise"]
short = "An Indicator of Compromise: a concrete artefact (hash, domain, IP, mutex) that flags the threat."
text = '''
An **IOC** (Indicator of Compromise) is a concrete, checkable artefact tied to a threat: a file
hash, a C2 domain or IP, a URL, a mutex name, a registry key. IOCs are the actionable output of
analysis -- defenders feed them to firewalls and hunting tools to block and find the threat.
ORRESS extracts IOCs from a sample's strings and shows them defanged.
'''
see = ["defang", "C2", "imphash", "report"]

[[term]]
term = "defang"
aliases = ["defanged", "defanging"]
short = "Mangling a dangerous indicator so it stays readable but can't be clicked or run by mistake."
text = '''
**Defanging** rewrites a live indicator into an inert form: `http://evil.com` becomes
`hxxp[://]evil[.]com`, `1.2.3.4` becomes `1[.]2[.]3[.]4`. It is still readable, so you can put it
in a report or chat, but it is no longer a clickable link or a runnable address -- nobody visits
it by accident. ORRESS defangs every network IOC it shows.
'''
see = ["IOC", "report"]

[[term]]
term = "imphash"
short = "A hash of a PE's import table -- samples built from the same code share an imphash."
text = '''
An **imphash** is a hash computed over a PE file's import table (which functions it imports, in
order). Because malware from one family tends to import the same functions the same way, two
samples with the same imphash were probably built from the same source -- so the imphash clusters
a family even when the bytes differ. ORRESS lists it in the Triage Hashes section.
'''
see = ["malware family", "fuzzy hash", "triage"]

[[term]]
term = "fuzzy hash"
aliases = ["fuzzy hashing", "fuzzy hashes"]
short = "A hash where SIMILAR inputs get SIMILAR values, so you can spot near-duplicate samples."
text = '''
An ordinary hash changes completely if one byte changes. A **fuzzy hash** is designed so that
*similar* files produce *similar* hashes, letting you measure how alike two samples are and spot
tweaked variants. TLSH and ssdeep are the two fuzzy hashes ORRESS reports.
'''
see = ["TLSH", "ssdeep", "imphash", "malware variant"]

[[term]]
term = "TLSH"
short = "Trend Micro Locality Sensitive Hash: a fuzzy hash whose distance measures file similarity."
text = '''
**TLSH** (Trend Micro Locality Sensitive Hash) is a fuzzy hash: two similar files get TLSH values
a small "distance" apart, so you can cluster related samples by comparing distances. ORRESS shows
it in the Triage Hashes section alongside ssdeep.
'''
see = ["fuzzy hash", "ssdeep"]

[[term]]
term = "ssdeep"
short = "A context-triggered piecewise fuzzy hash, long the standard for near-duplicate detection."
text = '''
**ssdeep** is a widely used fuzzy hash (context-triggered piecewise hashing). Like TLSH it gives
similar samples similar values, so analysts match a new sample against a known-malware corpus.
ORRESS reports it next to TLSH.
'''
see = ["fuzzy hash", "TLSH"]

[[term]]
term = "config extractor"
aliases = ["configuration extractor", "config extraction"]
short = "Code that finds and decodes a known family's embedded configuration (C2, keys, campaign id)."
text = '''
Many families store their settings -- C2 addresses, encryption keys, a campaign id, a mutex name
-- in an embedded, usually encoded, configuration blob. A **config extractor** recognises that
family's format, decodes the blob and hands back the fields. ORRESS ships a small extractor
framework; its demo `ExampleRAT` extractor finds a marker, reads a length, XOR-decodes the text
and parses `key=value;` pairs. A decoded config is the richest triage result you can get.
'''
see = ["C2", "triage", "RAT"]

[[term]]
term = "mutex"
aliases = ["mutexes", "named object"]
short = "A named system object malware creates so it can tell it is already running on a machine."
text = '''
A **mutex** is a named synchronisation object. Malware often creates one with a fixed, unusual
name as an "infection marker": if the mutex already exists, a copy is already running, so the new
one exits. That fixed name is distinctive, so it makes an excellent IOC and YARA string. Named
objects live under `Global\` or `Local\`.
'''
see = ["IOC", "YARA string"]

[[term]]
term = "MITRE ATT&CK"
aliases = ["ATT&CK", "ATTACK"]
short = "A public catalogue of attacker tactics and techniques, giving analysts a shared vocabulary."
text = '''
**MITRE ATT&CK** is a free, structured knowledge base of how attackers behave, organised into
*tactics* (the goal, e.g. Persistence) and *techniques* (the method, e.g. T1547.001 Registry Run
Keys). Tagging each behaviour you find with its ATT&CK technique lets every reader -- in any
team, any company -- understand your report the same way. ORRESS labels capabilities and import
groups with their ATT&CK technique.
'''
see = ["ATT&CK tactic", "ATT&CK technique", "TTP", "report"]

[[term]]
term = "ATT&CK tactic"
aliases = ["tactic", "tactics"]
short = "The attacker's goal at one stage, e.g. Persistence, Execution, Exfiltration, Impact."
text = '''
In ATT&CK a **tactic** is the *why* -- the objective of a step, such as Initial Access,
Persistence, Defense Evasion, Command and Control, Exfiltration or Impact. Each tactic groups
many techniques that achieve it.
'''
see = ["MITRE ATT&CK", "ATT&CK technique"]

[[term]]
term = "ATT&CK technique"
aliases = ["ATT&CK techniques"]
short = "A specific method for achieving a tactic, with an ID like T1055 (Process Injection)."
text = '''
An ATT&CK **technique** is the *how* -- a concrete method, identified by a `T####` number (with
optional `.###` sub-technique), such as T1055 Process Injection or T1547.001 Registry Run Keys.
You cite techniques in a report so everyone knows exactly which behaviour you mean.
'''
see = ["MITRE ATT&CK", "ATT&CK tactic"]

[[term]]
term = "TTP"
aliases = ["TTPs"]
short = "Tactics, Techniques and Procedures: the characteristic way a given actor operates."
text = '''
**TTPs** (Tactics, Techniques and Procedures) is the shorthand for *how an adversary operates* --
the patterns that tend to stay the same even as tooling changes. ATT&CK is the standard way to
describe the tactics and techniques; the "procedures" are the specific implementation details.
'''
see = ["MITRE ATT&CK", "ATT&CK tactic", "ATT&CK technique"]

[[term]]
term = "YARA"
short = "A pattern-matching engine and language for describing and detecting files of interest."
text = '''
**YARA** is the de-facto standard tool for writing *detection rules* for files. A rule describes
bytes, strings and logic; the engine tells you which files match. Analysts use it to hunt a known
threat across a whole fleet, classify samples into families, and share detections. ORRESS has a
built-in YARA workbench powered by the pure-Rust YARA-X engine.
'''
see = ["YARA rule", "YARA string", "YARA condition"]

[[term]]
term = "YARA rule"
aliases = ["YARA rules"]
short = "One detection: a meta block, a strings block and a condition that decides a match."
text = '''
A **YARA rule** has three parts: `meta` (informational -- author, description), `strings` (the
patterns to look for, each named `$name`) and `condition` (the boolean logic that decides whether
the file matches). Point the engine at files and it reports which ones satisfy the condition.
'''
see = ["YARA", "YARA string", "YARA condition"]

[[term]]
term = "YARA string"
aliases = ["YARA strings"]
short = "A pattern in a rule: a text literal, a hex byte pattern, or a regular expression."
text = '''
Inside a rule's `strings:` block each pattern is named (`$a`, `$dos`, ...) and can be a **text**
literal (`"run in DOS mode"`, with modifiers like `nocase`, `wide`, `fullword`), a **hex
pattern** of raw bytes (`{ 4D 5A }`, with `??` wildcards), or a **regular expression**
(`/evil[0-9]+\.com/`). The condition then refers to these by name.
'''
see = ["hex pattern", "YARA anchor", "YARA condition"]

[[term]]
term = "hex pattern"
aliases = ["hex patterns"]
short = "A YARA string written as raw bytes, e.g. { 4D 5A }, with ?? for bytes that vary."
text = '''
A **hex pattern** matches raw bytes rather than text -- ideal for magic numbers, opcode
sequences and binary structures. Wildcards let bytes vary: `{ 4D ?? 5A }` matches any middle
byte, and jumps like `{ 4D 5A [2-4] 50 }` allow a gap. Perfect for matching code, which has no
readable text.
'''
see = ["YARA string", "YARA anchor"]

[[term]]
term = "YARA anchor"
aliases = ["anchor", "anchored"]
short = "A position constraint in a rule, e.g. `$mz at 0`, pinning a match to an exact offset."
text = '''
An **anchor** ties a pattern to a position. `$mz at 0` requires the pattern at the very first
byte; `$x in (0..100)` restricts it to a range. Anchoring makes a rule both faster and more
precise -- for instance checking a file *starts* with the `MZ` signature, not merely contains it.
'''
see = ["YARA condition", "hex pattern"]

[[term]]
term = "YARA condition"
aliases = ["YARA conditions"]
short = "The boolean logic of a rule that decides a match, referring to the strings by name."
text = '''
The **condition** is where a rule gets its precision. It combines the named strings with boolean
logic (`and`, `or`, `not`), counts (`#a > 3`), positions (`at`, `in`), size (`filesize`) and
shorthands (`any of them`, `2 of ($a*)`). `$mz at 0 and $dos` matches only when both hold. Tune
the condition to catch the family and its variants without ever firing on clean files.
'''
see = ["YARA string", "YARA anchor", "false positive"]

[[term]]
term = "YARA module"
aliases = ["YARA modules"]
short = "A plug-in that lets a rule reason about file structure, e.g. pe.imphash() or hash.md5()."
text = '''
A YARA **module** exposes structured, format-aware data to a rule. The `pe` module lets you write
`pe.imports("kernel32.dll", "CreateRemoteThread")` or `pe.entry_point`; the `hash` and `math`
modules give `hash.md5(...)` and `math.entropy(...)`. Modules make rules far more precise than raw
byte matching. ORRESS's YARA-X engine ships the `pe`, `elf`, `macho`, `hash`, `math` and `string`
modules.
'''
see = ["YARA rule", "imphash"]

[[term]]
term = "false positive"
aliases = ["false positives"]
short = "A detection that fires on a clean file -- the main thing a good YARA rule must avoid."
text = '''
A **false positive** is a rule (or scanner) flagging a benign file as malicious. False positives
erode trust and waste responders' time, so you always test a rule both ways: it must match the
sample (a true positive) *and* stay silent on a pile of clean files. Keying on distinctive
strings rather than compiler boilerplate is how you avoid them.
'''
see = ["true positive", "YARA condition"]

[[term]]
term = "true positive"
aliases = ["true positives"]
short = "A detection that correctly fires on a file that really is the threat."
text = '''
A **true positive** is the rule doing its job: matching a file that genuinely belongs to the
threat you wrote it for. A useful rule maximises true positives (catching the family and its
variants) while keeping false positives at zero.
'''
see = ["false positive", "malware variant"]

[[term]]
term = "behaviour analysis"
aliases = ["behavior analysis", "behavioural analysis", "behavioral analysis"]
short = "Watching what a sample actually DOES when it runs, inside a safe lab."
text = '''
**Behaviour analysis** is dynamic: you run the sample in a safe, isolated lab and record the
actions it takes -- processes started, files written, registry keys set, network calls made.
Where static triage shows what a sample *can* do, behaviour analysis proves what it *does*, and
catches packed or obfuscated logic that only reveals itself at run time.
'''
see = ["dynamic analysis", "detonate", "ETW", "capability"]

[[term]]
term = "dynamic analysis"
short = "Analysis that runs the sample (in isolation) and observes it, as opposed to static reading."
text = '''
**Dynamic analysis** means executing the sample and watching it, rather than only reading its
bytes. It is powerful -- it defeats packing and obfuscation -- but dangerous, so it happens only
inside an isolated lab you can reset. Behaviour analysis is dynamic analysis focused on the
sample's actions.
'''
see = ["behaviour analysis", "detonate", "network isolation", "snapshot"]

[[term]]
term = "detonate"
aliases = ["detonation", "detonating"]
short = "To deliberately run a malware sample in a controlled lab so you can watch it act."
text = '''
Analysts "**detonate**" a sample: run it on purpose in an isolated, monitored, resettable
environment so its real behaviour comes out. The word is a reminder of the care it needs -- you
detonate inside a sealed lab, with monitors armed and a clean snapshot to revert to.
'''
see = ["dynamic analysis", "snapshot", "network isolation"]

[[term]]
term = "snapshot"
aliases = ["snapshots"]
short = "A saved, restorable state of a VM, so you can roll back to clean after each run."
text = '''
A **snapshot** captures a virtual machine's entire state so you can return to it instantly. The
analysis loop is: snapshot the clean VM, detonate the sample, collect what you need, then revert
to the snapshot -- so no sample ever contaminates the next analysis.
'''
see = ["detonate", "network isolation"]

[[term]]
term = "network isolation"
aliases = ["isolated network", "network containment", "contained network"]
short = "Keeping a lab's traffic off the real internet while still letting you observe it."
text = '''
**Network isolation** cuts the lab off from the real internet so a detonated sample cannot phone
home, spread or exfiltrate -- while still letting you *see* the traffic. Tools like INetSim and
FakeNet sit on the isolated network and answer the sample's DNS and HTTP requests, logging every
one, so you capture C2 behaviour without a single packet escaping.
'''
see = ["FakeNet", "INetSim", "C2", "beacon"]

[[term]]
term = "FakeNet"
aliases = ["fake network"]
short = "A tool that simulates internet services on an isolated network and logs every request."
text = '''
**FakeNet** (and the similar INetSim) pretends to be the whole internet: it answers the sample's
DNS lookups and serves fake HTTP responses, so the malware thinks it reached its C2 while nothing
leaves the lab. Every request is logged, giving you the domains, URLs and beacons the sample
used. ORRESS's Sandbox view includes a built-in fake-network responder.
'''
see = ["network isolation", "INetSim", "C2"]

[[term]]
term = "INetSim"
short = "An internet-services simulator used to contain and observe lab network traffic."
text = '''
**INetSim** is a well-known Linux tool that simulates common internet services (DNS, HTTP, SMTP,
and more) for a malware lab. Like FakeNet, it answers the sample's requests on an isolated
network and records them, so you watch C2 behaviour safely.
'''
see = ["FakeNet", "network isolation"]

[[term]]
term = "ETW"
aliases = ["Event Tracing for Windows"]
short = "Event Tracing for Windows: the kernel facility ORRESS's monitor uses to log a sample's actions."
text = '''
**ETW** (Event Tracing for Windows) is Windows' built-in, high-volume tracing system. ORRESS's
Sandbox activity monitor subscribes to ETW to record a running sample's process, file, registry,
network and image-load events. It needs administrator rights and traces the whole system, so you
filter by the sample's process id to cut the noise.
'''
see = ["behaviour analysis", "dynamic analysis"]

[[term]]
term = "lateral movement"
short = "Spreading from the first compromised machine to others across the network."
text = '''
**Lateral movement** is how an attacker, having landed on one machine, reaches others on the same
network -- stealing credentials, abusing remote-execution tools, exploiting internal services. It
is why a worm or a hands-on intrusion must be studied only on an isolated network.
'''
see = ["worm", "network isolation"]

[[term]]
term = "anti-analysis"
aliases = ["anti-analysis checks", "evasion"]
short = "Tricks malware uses to detect a lab or analyst and hide its real behaviour."
text = '''
**Anti-analysis** (or evasion) is everything malware does to avoid being understood: detecting a
VM or debugger and staying dormant, delaying execution, checking the user-name or screen size.
The practical lesson for behaviour analysis: a sample that does nothing may simply have detected
your lab -- a quiet sample is not always a safe one.
'''
see = ["behaviour analysis", "snapshot"]

[[term]]
term = "report"
aliases = ["malware report", "reporting"]
short = "The written deliverable that turns analysis into something defenders can act on."
text = '''
The **report** is the point of the whole exercise: analysis that stays in your head helps nobody.
A good malware report has a predictable skeleton -- summary, identification (hashes), capabilities
and behaviour mapped to ATT&CK, defanged IOCs, your YARA detection, and recommendations -- each
section aimed at a reader. ORRESS's Triage view exports a Markdown skeleton to build on.
'''
see = ["IOC", "MITRE ATT&CK", "YARA rule", "triage"]

[[term]]
term = "SOC"
aliases = ["security operations center", "security operations centre"]
short = "A Security Operations Centre: the team that monitors and responds to threats, often 24/7."
text = '''
A **SOC** (Security Operations Centre) is the team watching an organisation's defences around the
clock. They are a key reader of your report: during an incident they need the IOCs and detections
up front so they can block and hunt immediately.
'''
see = ["report", "IOC", "threat hunting", "incident response"]

[[term]]
term = "incident response"
aliases = ["incident responder", "incident responders"]
short = "The work of containing, scoping and cleaning up an active compromise."
text = '''
**Incident response** is the hands-on work of dealing with a live breach: contain it, work out
how far it spread, remove it, recover. Responders read your report to scope the damage -- what the
malware does tells them where to look -- so clear behaviour and IOCs matter most to them.
'''
see = ["SOC", "report", "IOC"]

[[term]]
term = "threat hunting"
aliases = ["threat hunter", "threat hunters"]
short = "Proactively searching a fleet for signs of a threat, often using IOCs and YARA rules."
text = '''
**Threat hunting** is looking for a threat across many machines before an alert fires -- running
your YARA rules over files, searching for your IOCs in logs, pivoting on an imphash. It turns one
analysed sample into fleet-wide detection, which is why a report's detections and indicators are
so valuable.
'''
see = ["IOC", "YARA rule", "imphash", "report"]

`academy/glossary/7-expert.toml`:

```toml
# Glossary terms introduced in Level 7 (Expert). Lower levels define the basics
# (register, stack, basic block, keygen, XOR, emulator, decompiler, ...); this file
# only adds the words this level brings in. Terms and aliases are unique across all
# glossary files, so nothing here repeats a lower level's term.

[[term]]
term = "time-travel debugging"
aliases = ["TTD", "time travel debugging", "reverse debugging", "debugging backward"]
short = "Recording a program's execution once and then stepping backward and forward through the recording."
text = '''
A normal debugger only moves forward: to see an earlier moment you must restart the program. Time-travel debugging records every instruction of a run first, then lets you move to any point in that recording, backward as easily as forward. It is the fastest way to answer "which instruction caused this value?".
'''
see = ["execution trace", "deterministic replay", "step back"]

[[term]]
term = "execution trace"
aliases = ["trace"]
short = "The recording saved during a run: one entry per instruction, holding its address and the registers after it ran."
text = '''
A trace is produced during a single run. Each entry holds the address of the instruction that ran and the register values just after it. ORRESS saves registers, not memory, which keeps traces small. Moving through the trace is how time-travel debugging shows you the past without running the program again.
'''
see = ["time-travel debugging", "deterministic replay"]

[[term]]
term = "deterministic replay"
aliases = ["deterministic"]
short = "The property that a recorded run does exactly the same thing every time you look at it."
text = '''
Because the emulator is deterministic, a recorded run never changes: step 193 holds the same values no matter how often you jump away and come back. This is what makes time-travel debugging reliable, unlike re-running code that behaves differently each time. To see memory at a step (the trace keeps only registers), run the function again with the same input.
'''
see = ["execution trace", "time-travel debugging"]

[[term]]
term = "step back"
aliases = ["stepping back", "step backward", "reverse step"]
short = "Moving to the previous snapshot in a trace, so you see the state before an instruction ran."
text = '''
Stepping back shows an earlier entry of the recorded trace; nothing is executed in reverse. Following a wrong value backward, one step at a time, to the instruction that wrote it is the core move of root cause analysis.
'''
see = ["execution trace", "root cause"]

[[term]]
term = "root cause"
aliases = ["root cause analysis"]
short = "The first instruction or input that introduced a wrong value, found by tracing an effect back to its source."
text = '''
Root cause analysis starts at a symptom (a crash, a wrong return value) and works backward along the data: find where the bad value was written, then where its inputs came from, until you reach an input byte, a constant, or a table. Time-travel debugging makes this straightforward.
'''
see = ["step back", "time-travel debugging"]

[[term]]
term = "binary diffing"
aliases = ["binary diff", "diffing"]
short = "Comparing two related binaries function by function to see what is the same, changed, added or removed."
text = '''
Recompiling shifts addresses, so comparing two builds byte-for-byte is useless. Binary diffing instead matches functions by an address-independent signature and labels each one identical, changed, added or removed. It is how patches and malware variants are compared.
'''
see = ["function matching", "function signature", "patch diffing"]

[[term]]
term = "patch diffing"
aliases = ["patch diff"]
short = "Binary-diffing a program against its patched version to find exactly what a security update changed."
text = '''
The functions that come back "changed" (and any "added" helpers) are where the vendor altered something, very often a security fix. Defenders use patch diffing to judge how urgent an update is; attackers use it to exploit the bug before systems update.
'''
see = ["binary diffing", "1-day"]

[[term]]
term = "1-day"
aliases = ["one-day", "1-days"]
short = "A vulnerability that is already patched but still exploitable on systems that have not installed the update."
text = '''
Once a patch ships, anyone can diff it to learn the bug. Systems that have not applied the update yet are open to attack during that window. The bug is a "1-day" (as opposed to a 0-day, which has no patch yet).
'''
see = ["patch diffing"]

[[term]]
term = "function matching"
short = "Pairing each function in one binary with its counterpart in another, by name, code or shape."
text = '''
ORRESS matches functions in rounds of decreasing certainty: by real name, then identical opcode hash, then identical shape, then the most similar remaining pair. Functions left unmatched are "added" or "removed".
'''
see = ["function signature", "similarity score", "binary diffing"]

[[term]]
term = "function signature"
aliases = ["fingerprint"]
short = "An address-independent description of a function: its shape plus an opcode hash."
text = '''
A signature captures what a function does, not where it lives: counts of instructions, basic blocks, edges and calls, plus an opcode hash that leaves out addresses. Two functions with the same signature are the same code even at different addresses.
'''
see = ["opcode hash", "function matching"]

[[term]]
term = "opcode hash"
short = "A hash of a function's instructions with every address replaced by a placeholder."
text = '''
ORRESS feeds each mnemonic and its operands into a hash, but replaces jump targets, call targets, data references and large numbers with a placeholder. So relocating the code does not change the hash, while a real change (a different constant, jz becoming jnz) does.
'''
see = ["function signature"]

[[term]]
term = "similarity score"
aliases = ["similarity"]
short = "A number from 0 to 1 saying how alike two matched functions are (1 means identical code)."
text = '''
For a changed pair, ORRESS reports a similarity from the weighted comparison of their shapes (instructions 40%, blocks 30%, edges 20%, calls 10%). A high but not perfect score means a small change, which is often exactly the fix you are looking for.
'''
see = ["function matching"]

[[term]]
term = "user mode"
short = "The limited privilege level where ordinary programs run, isolated from each other and the hardware."
text = '''
User-mode code (ring 3) cannot touch hardware, read other programs' memory, or change the system. When it tries, the CPU stops it. A crash there ends one program, not the machine. It is like safe Rust: the rules are enforced.
'''
see = ["kernel mode", "privilege ring", "system call"]

[[term]]
term = "kernel mode"
aliases = ["kernel"]
short = "The most privileged level, where the operating system core and drivers run with full control of the machine."
text = '''
Kernel-mode code (ring 0) can read and write any memory, talk to hardware and change any process. A mistake crashes the whole system (a blue screen). It is like one huge unsafe block that owns the computer, which is why rootkits want to get there.
'''
see = ["user mode", "ring 0", "driver", "rootkit"]

[[term]]
term = "privilege ring"
aliases = ["ring", "rings", "privilege rings", "privilege level"]
short = "A hardware privilege level on x86, numbered 0 (most) to 3 (least)."
text = '''
The CPU stores the current ring and blocks privileged instructions and kernel memory outside ring 0. Windows and Linux use only ring 0 (kernel) and ring 3 (user); rings 1 and 2 go unused.
'''
see = ["ring 0", "ring 3", "kernel mode", "user mode"]

[[term]]
term = "ring 0"
short = "The most privileged CPU ring: kernel mode."
text = '''
"Running at ring 0" means having full control of the machine. The kernel and drivers run here.
'''
see = ["privilege ring", "kernel mode"]

[[term]]
term = "ring 3"
short = "The least privileged CPU ring: user mode, where normal programs run."
see = ["privilege ring", "user mode"]

[[term]]
term = "driver"
aliases = ["drivers", "device driver"]
short = "Kernel-mode code that controls a device or adds a system feature; on Windows a .sys file."
text = '''
Drivers run in ring 0 and are the legitimate way to extend the kernel. The kernel calls into a driver through its entry point (DriverEntry) and its request-handling (dispatch) routines. Bugs in a driver can hand an attacker kernel power.
'''
see = [".sys", "DriverEntry", "dispatch routine", "kernel mode"]

[[term]]
term = ".sys"
aliases = ["sys file"]
short = "The file extension of a Windows kernel driver (a PE file, like an .exe, but loaded into the kernel)."
text = '''
A .sys file is a normal PE file with tell-tale traits: the Native subsystem, a DriverEntry entry point, and imports from the kernel (ntoskrnl.exe, hal.dll) rather than user-mode DLLs.
'''
see = ["driver", "Native subsystem", "DriverEntry"]

[[term]]
term = "Native subsystem"
aliases = ["Native (driver or boot program)"]
short = "The PE subsystem value that marks a driver or boot program, instead of Console or GUI."
text = '''
ORRESS's "What Is This File?" view shows the subsystem. For a normal app it reads Console or GUI; for a driver it reads "Native (driver or boot program)", a quick way to tell you are looking at kernel-mode code.
'''
see = [".sys", "driver"]

[[term]]
term = "DriverEntry"
short = "The entry point of a Windows driver, the first routine the kernel runs when the driver loads."
text = '''
Where a normal program starts at the C runtime startup before main, a driver starts at DriverEntry. It sets the driver up and registers the dispatch routines that will handle requests.
'''
see = ["driver", "dispatch routine"]

[[term]]
term = "IRP"
aliases = ["IRPs", "I/O request packet"]
short = "An I/O Request Packet: the structure the kernel uses to pass a request to a driver."
text = '''
When user-mode code asks a device to read, write or do something custom, the kernel packages the request as an IRP and hands it to the driver's matching dispatch routine. IRP handling is where a driver's real behaviour lives.
'''
see = ["driver", "dispatch routine"]

[[term]]
term = "dispatch routine"
aliases = ["dispatch routines", "IRP dispatch"]
short = "A driver function that handles one kind of request (one IRP type) from user mode."
text = '''
A driver registers dispatch routines in DriverEntry, one per request type (create, read, write, device control). They are the driver's interface to the rest of the system and the first place to read when reversing one.
'''
see = ["driver", "IRP", "DriverEntry"]

[[term]]
term = "SSDT"
aliases = ["system-call table", "system call table"]
short = "The System Service Descriptor Table: the kernel's list of which routine handles each system call."
text = '''
When a syscall arrives, the kernel looks up its number in the SSDT to find the routine to run. Overwriting an SSDT entry (an SSDT hook) lets a rootkit make the kernel run its code for a system call instead of the real one.
'''
see = ["system call", "hook", "rootkit"]

[[term]]
term = "hook"
aliases = ["hooks", "hooking"]
short = "Redirecting a call so your code runs in place of, or before, the original."
text = '''
A hook can overwrite an entry in a table (such as the SSDT) or patch the first bytes of a function to jump elsewhere. Rootkits hook the kernel's own routines so that queries like "list the processes" return doctored answers.
'''
see = ["SSDT", "rootkit", "DKOM"]

[[term]]
term = "DKOM"
aliases = ["Direct Kernel Object Manipulation"]
short = "Direct Kernel Object Manipulation: hiding things by editing the kernel's own data structures."
text = '''
Instead of hooking code, DKOM edits data: for example unlinking a process's record from the kernel's list of processes so tools that walk the list never see it. The process still runs; it just does not appear.
'''
see = ["rootkit", "hook"]

[[term]]
term = "rootkit"
aliases = ["rootkits"]
short = "Malware that loads into the kernel to hide itself and tamper with the system from underneath."
text = '''
A rootkit runs at ring 0, so it can hook kernel routines or use DKOM to make hidden processes, files and connections invisible to tools that run above it, including antivirus. Analysing one safely means static analysis first, and any dynamic work only in a disposable VM with kernel debugging.
'''
see = ["kernel mode", "hook", "DKOM", "SSDT", "blue screen"]

[[term]]
term = "blue screen"
aliases = ["BSOD", "blue-screen", "bug check"]
short = "The full-system crash Windows shows when kernel-mode code fails."
text = '''
A user-mode crash ends one program; a kernel-mode fault cannot be contained, so Windows stops the whole machine with a blue screen (a "bug check"). It is why kernel bugs are so serious and why kernel work is done in a throwaway VM.
'''
see = ["kernel mode", "ring 0"]

[[term]]
term = "analysis pass"
aliases = ["pass", "passes", "analysis passes"]
short = "A reusable, automated procedure that runs an analysis routine over one or many binaries."
text = '''
Instead of clicking through views for every file, you write the routine once (as a script, or a chain of MCP tool calls) and run it over a whole folder or feed. An analysis pass is how one analyst keeps up with many samples.
'''
see = ["Rhai", "MCP", "script"]

[[term]]
term = "script"
aliases = ["scripts", "scripting"]
short = "A short program you run against the open binary's analysis to automate a query or a transform."
text = '''
In ORRESS, scripts are written in Rhai and run in the Scripting console or from the command line. They read the analysis (functions, strings, bytes, disassembly) only, cannot touch your disk or network, and are stopped if they run too long.
'''
see = ["Rhai", "analysis pass"]

[[term]]
term = "Rhai"
short = "The small, Rust-like scripting language ORRESS runs for its scripts."
text = '''
Rhai reads much like Rust without the types: let, if, for, functions, numbers, strings and arrays. ORRESS exposes its analysis to Rhai through a handful of built-in functions such as functions(), read(addr, len) and disasm(addr, n).
'''
see = ["script", "analysis pass"]

[[term]]
term = "MCP"
aliases = ["Model Context Protocol"]
short = "A simple text protocol that lets AI agents and tools call a program's features in a uniform way."
text = '''
ORRESS ships an MCP server (orress-mcp) that offers its analyses as tools (triage, strings, disassemble, detect_vm, binary_diff, deobfuscate_js, archive_list). Each takes a file path and returns structured results a program can read, so an agent or pipeline can drive ORRESS.
'''
see = ["AI Assistant", "analysis pass"]

[[term]]
term = "AI Assistant"
short = "ORRESS's in-app helper that answers plain-language questions about the open binary."
text = '''
The Assistant drives the same analysis engine the MCP server exposes. It runs on your own Claude plan through the Claude Code tool (no API key), offers an offline static-only mode, and only sends the binary's context to the model if you opt in.
'''
see = ["MCP"]

[[term]]
term = "extension"
aliases = ["extensions", "add-on"]
short = "An add-on that gives ORRESS a new capability, loaded in a sandbox (including Zed-compatible add-ons)."
text = '''
ORRESS has an extension host that can load themes, syntax grammars and language-server adapters, including ones built for the Zed editor. Extension code runs confined to its own folder, so a bad or hostile extension cannot reach the rest of your system.
'''
see = []

text = '''
Welcome! This Academy teaches you **reverse engineering** from the very beginning.

You only need to know some **basic Rust**: variables, functions, `if`, `loop`, `match`, `Vec`, `String` and `cargo run`. Everything else is explained here, in order, before you need it. You do not need to know anything about hexadecimal numbers, processors, assembly or debuggers yet.

The course has eight levels:

- **Level 0, Foundations** (this level): how a computer runs a program, how numbers and text are stored, what a compiler produces, and a first tour of ORRESS.
- **Level 1**: reading the instructions a processor runs, and cracking your first practice programs.
- **Levels 2 to 7**: more and more powerful techniques, up to the tools experts use.

Each lesson is a list of short **steps**. Read a step, do what it asks, and continue. You see your position in the row of dots at the top of this panel: click a dot to go back to an earlier step at any time.

Take your time. There is no timer, and you can stop and continue later: your progress is saved automatically.

Press **Next** below to continue.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Building forward, reversing backward"
goal = "Understand the basic idea of reverse engineering."
text = '''
When you write a Rust program, you write **source code**: text that people can read.

```rust
fn main() {
    let password = "swordfish";
    let input = std::env::args().nth(1).unwrap_or_default();
    if input == password {
        println!("Welcome!");
    } else {
        println!("Wrong password");
    }
}
```

`cargo build` gives that text to the **compiler**. The compiler translates it into **machine code**: a long list of numbers that the processor of your computer can run directly. The result is a program file, such as `myapp.exe` on Windows.

The program file does not contain your source code. Your variable names, your comments and the nice structure of your code are mostly gone. What is left are numbers.

**Reverse engineering** is going the other way. You only have the program file, and you work out what it does: by reading its machine code, by looking at the text and data inside it, and by watching it run. Step by step you rebuild an understanding of the original logic. For the program above, a reverser would find the text `swordfish` inside the file and the place where the input is compared with it.

People who do this are called **reversers**. ORRESS is a tool for reversers, and this Academy teaches you to use it.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Reverse engineering is much older than software. Engineers have always taken apart machines made by others to learn how they work. For software the idea is the same, but the "taking apart" is done with tools that show you the bytes, the instructions and the behavior of a program.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Why people reverse programs"
goal = "Know the main reasons for reverse engineering."
text = '''
Reverse engineering is used for many good reasons:

- **CTF competitions.** CTF stands for *Capture The Flag*. In a CTF, teams solve security puzzles for points. In the "reversing" puzzles you get a program that hides a secret text, the *flag*, which looks like `flag{y0u_f0und_m3}`. You find the flag by understanding the program.
- **Malware analysis.** **Malware** is software made to do harm, such as viruses or programs that steal passwords. Analysts reverse it to learn what it does, so that it can be detected, blocked and cleaned up.
- **Security research.** Researchers look for mistakes (bugs) in programs whose source code they do not have, so the bugs can be fixed before criminals find them.
- **Compatibility.** Sometimes the only documentation of an old file format or a device is the program that uses it. Reversing it lets new software work with old data.
- **Learning.** Reading what a compiler made from your own code is one of the best ways to understand how computers really work.

Most of what you learn in this Academy is useful for all of these. The practice programs in this course are small CTF-style puzzles called **crackmes**: programs that ask for a password and are made to be reversed. You will open the first one at the end of this level.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "What is a flag?"
goal = "Check that you know the goal of a reversing challenge."
text = '''
Let us check the most important idea from the previous step.

In a CTF reversing challenge, you receive a program. Somewhere in its logic a secret is hidden, the flag. Sometimes the flag is printed when you type the right password; sometimes the flag *is* the password; sometimes it is calculated from your input. Your job is to understand the program well enough to get the flag, and then submit it on the CTF website for points.

Which of these describes the goal of a reversing challenge?
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Legal and ethical use"
goal = "Know what is allowed and what is not."
text = '''
Reverse engineering itself is a normal, legal skill that is taught at universities and used by security companies every day. What you *do* with it is what matters.

**Fine:**

- reversing CTF challenges and crackmes: they are made to be reversed;
- reversing your own programs;
- analyzing malware samples inside a safe, isolated lab (Level 6 shows you how to set one up);
- security research done according to the rules of the software maker or a bug bounty program.

**Not fine:**

- removing the license check from software so you do not have to pay for it, or sharing such a "cracked" copy;
- breaking into systems or accounts that are not yours;
- running malware on your everyday computer or on a work or school network, where it can spread.

Laws differ per country, and license agreements can add rules. When in doubt, ask, or stick to material that was made for practice, like the programs in this Academy.

Which of these is fine?
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Two ways to look at a program"
goal = "Know the difference between static and dynamic analysis."
text = '''
Reversers have two basic ways to study a program, and you will learn both.

**Static analysis** means looking at the program file *without running it*. You read the text inside it, the numbers, and the machine code turned into readable form. ORRESS has many views for this. It is safe (nothing runs), and you can look at every part of the program, also the parts that rarely run.

**Dynamic analysis** means *running* the program and watching what it does: which values it calculates, which files it opens, what it prints. A **debugger** is the classic tool for this: it can pause a running program and show you its memory. Dynamic analysis answers questions quickly, but it only shows the paths the program actually takes, and running unknown programs can be dangerous.

Good reversers switch between the two all the time. Level 2 of this Academy is about static analysis, Level 3 about dynamic analysis.

You suspect a program contains a password as plain text. You open it in ORRESS and search the text inside the file, without starting the program. Which kind of analysis is that?
'''
