    "Add the length of the instruction, 5 bytes. (Or look at the address of the next line.)",
    "Type the result as a hex number starting with `0x` and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0x140001127"], number = true }

    "The return address is the address of the instruction right after the call.",
    "0x140001122 + 5 = 0x140001127.",
]
success = '''
`0x140001127`, the address of the next line. When a debugger (Level 3) stops inside a function, the stack shows return addresses like this one, and they tell you who called the function.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Watch a call on the stack"
goal = "Step through `call` and `ret` and watch the return address."
text = '''
The simulator loaded the `triple` example:

```text
    mov rax, 3
    call triple
    ret              ; end of the program
triple:
    mov rbx, rax
    add rax, rbx
    add rax, rbx
    ret              ; back to the caller
```

1. `mov rax, 3`: the argument.
2. `call triple` pushes the return address and jumps to the label `triple`.
3. Inside `triple`: copy `rax` to `rbx`, then add it twice. 3 + 3 + 3.
4. The `ret` of `triple` pops the return address and jumps back, to the line after the call.
5. That line is the program's own `ret`, which returns to the end-of-program value.

The simulator does not have real addresses. As its return address it pushes the **position** of the next instruction in its program, counting from 0: here `0x2`, because the instruction after the call is the third one. On a real CPU it would be an address like `0x140001127`.

Step through it slowly. After `call triple`, look at the top of the **Stack** pane: `0x2` sits above the end-of-program value. After the `ret` inside `triple`, it is gone again.

What is in `rax` when the program has finished?
'''

A function can call another function. Each `call` pushes one more return address, and each `ret` pops one. [[steps]]
title = "Functions in ORRESS"
goal = "Know how ORRESS shows functions and where a program really starts."
text = '''
In a compiled program every Rust function becomes a piece of machine code that starts at some address and ends with `ret`. ORRESS finds these pieces by following every `call` instruction. Where you will see them:

- **Functions view** (in the **Project** panel, or with **Ctrl+Shift+F**): every function found, with its address, size and the number of places that call it ("callers").
- **Disassembly view**: a thin line across the view marks the start of each function, with its name.
- **Names**: stripped programs have no names, so ORRESS invents `sub_<address>`. A few names it can still find: functions imported from Windows DLLs (like `memcmp` or `WakeByAddressSingle`), and functions it recognises, like `main` and `rust_runtime_main`.

Where does a Rust program start? Not in your `main`. Windows starts the program at its **entry point** (Level 0), which runs setup code from the C runtime. That calls Rust's runtime start function, which calls your `main`, and `main`'s `ret` goes back into that runtime code, which then ends the process. ORRESS's **Go to main** (**Ctrl+Shift+M**, or the **Go** menu) skips all of that and takes you straight to your own `main`.

When you read a function, use its call and ret to orient yourself:

- the lines right before a `call` prepare the arguments;
- the lines right after it use the result.

Which registers carry those arguments and the result is fixed by a set of rules. That is the next lesson.
'''
success = '''
You know how functions work at the machine level. Next: the rules that say where arguments and results go, so you can read any call in a real program.
'''

`academy/lessons/01-09-calling-conventions.toml`:

```toml
id = "l1-calling-conventions"
level = 1
order = 9
title = "Calling conventions"
summary = "Which registers carry the arguments and the result on Windows and Linux, shadow space and saved registers."
goals = [
    "name the argument registers and the return register on Windows x64",
    "know how Linux and macOS (System V) differ",
    "write a function that follows the Windows convention",
    "read the arguments and the result around a real `call`",
    "explain shadow space and which registers a function must save",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Rules for calling"
goal = "Know why calling conventions exist and the two you will meet."
text = '''
In the last lesson the argument and the result were both in `rax`, because we decided so. Real programs need fixed rules: a function compiled today must work with a caller compiled last year, maybe by a different compiler. The rules that say where arguments go, where the result comes back, and which registers a function may change, are called a **calling convention**.

Two conventions matter on x86-64:

| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | more | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Windows x64** | `rcx` | `rdx` | `r8` | `r9` | on the stack | `rax` |
| **System V** (Linux, macOS) | `rdi` | `rsi` | `rdx` | `rcx` | `r8`, `r9`, then the stack | `rax` |

So on Windows, a call to `f(a, b)` looks like this:

```text
mov rcx, a     ; first argument
mov rdx, b     ; second argument
call f
               ; the result is now in rax
```

Smaller arguments use the smaller register names: a `u32` as first argument goes in `ecx`, a `bool` in `cl`. A `bool` or `u32` result comes back in `al` or `eax`.

Rust guarantees these conventions only for `extern "C"` functions. Ordinary Rust functions use Rust's own, unstable convention. In practice it is very close: small arguments go in the same registers in the same order. So use the table as your first guess, and check it by looking at which registers are set before the call and used at the start of the function.

The crackmes in this Academy are Windows programs, so the Windows column is the one you will use most.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Which register holds the first argument?"
goal = "Apply the Windows convention to a Rust function."
text = '''
Look at this Rust function, compiled for Windows:

```rust
fn f(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 {
    a * 2 + b
}
```

When `f` starts, its arguments are already in registers: the caller put them there just before the `call`. The compiled function might look like this:

```text
f:
    lea rax, [rdx+rcx*2]    ; rax = b + a * 2  (lea used as a calculator, Lesson 6)
    ret
```

A tiny function like this does not even need a stack frame. It reads the two argument registers, calculates the result straight into the return register, and returns.

Reading functions like this is how you recover a function's **signature**: which registers it reads without setting them first are its arguments; what it leaves in `rax` before `ret` is its result.

On Windows, which register holds `a` when `f` starts?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = ["rax", "rcx", "rdi", "rsp"], correct = 1, explain = [
    "rax is where the result goes. It does not carry an argument.",
    "On Windows x64 the first argument is in rcx, the second in rdx. The lea reads both.",
    "rdi is the first argument on Linux and macOS (System V), not on Windows.",
    "rsp is the stack pointer. It is never used for an argument.",
] }
hints = [
    "Look at the Windows x64 row of the table on the previous page.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "The same function on Linux"
goal = "Know the System V argument order."
text = '''
Compile the same Rust function for Linux or macOS and the registers change, because those systems use the **System V** convention:

```text
f:
    lea rax, [rsi+rdi*2]    ; rax = b + a * 2
    ret
```

The instruction is the same, only the registers differ: `rdi` and `rsi` instead of `rcx` and `rdx`. The result is still in `rax`, as on Windows.

A simple way to remember System V's order: "**Di**d **Si**r **D**on **C**ook?" for `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, followed by `r8` and `r9`.

So the first question when you reverse a function is: **which platform was it compiled for?** ORRESS's **Info** view tells you: a PE file is a Windows program (Windows convention), an ELF file is a Linux program (System V), and a Mach-O file is a macOS program (System V too). Getting this wrong makes you read the arguments in the wrong order.

Compiled for Linux, which register holds `a` when `f` starts?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = ["rcx", "rsi", "rdi", "rdx"], correct = 2, explain = [
    "rcx is the first argument on Windows. On Linux it is the fourth.",
    "rsi is the second argument on Linux: here it holds b.",
    "System V passes the first argument in rdi.",
    "rdx is the third argument on Linux (and the second on Windows).",
] }
hints = [
    "Did Si(r) ...: the first is Di.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Exercise: a Windows function"
goal = "Write a function that follows the Windows x64 convention."
text = '''
Write this Rust function the way a Windows compiler would:

```rust
fn area(width: u64, height: u64) -> u64 {
    width * height
}

let a = area(6, 7);
```

Following the Windows convention:

- the caller puts `width` in `rcx` and `height` in `rdx`, then calls;
- the function computes the result in `rax`, then returns.

The simulator already contains the caller. You write the body of `area`. A good way: copy the first argument into `rax`, multiply `rax` by the second argument, return.

Notice that the function must not change `rcx` or `rdx` to compute the result *in* them: the result must be in `rax`, because that is where the caller looks for it.
'''

]

area:

    mov rcx, 6
    mov rdx, 7
    call area
    ret
area:
    mov rax, rcx
    imul rax, rdx
    ret
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Arguments in a real program"
goal = "Read the arguments before a real `call`."
text = '''
Here are two calls from crackme #1's `main`, as ORRESS shows them:

```text
140001250  lea  rcx, [0x140018428]   ; "Correct! You cracked your first program."
140001257  mov  edx, 0x53
14000125c  call sub_1400059b0
```

The lines before the `call` fill the argument registers: `rcx` gets the address of the message (first argument), `edx` a number (second argument; Rust's printing code uses it to describe the text, it is related to the text's length). So `sub_1400059b0` is the function that prints a message: `println!` in the Rust source.

```text
1400012cc  mov  ecx, 1
1400012d1  call sub_140004f80
1400012d6  ud2
```

Here only one argument is set. `ud2` after the call is an instruction that crashes on purpose: the compiler puts it after a call that **never returns**. A function that never returns and gets one small number... In the source it is `std::process::exit(1)`.

This is the core skill of reading calls: look at which argument registers are set right before the `call`, and with what. Often that is enough to guess what an unnamed function does. Rename it (**N**) as soon as you know.

What number does `main` pass as the first argument to `sub_140004f80`?

[[steps]]
title = "Return values: rax, eax and al"
goal = "Read the result of a call, especially a `bool`."
text = '''
The result of a function comes back in `rax`, or in the part of `rax` that fits the type:

| Rust return type | Register |
|---|---|
| `u64`, `usize`, a pointer, a reference | `rax` |
| `u32`, `i32` | `eax` |
| `bool`, `u8` | `al` |

A `bool` is one byte: 0 for `false`, 1 for `true`. This is the pattern you will see in almost every crackme, right after the password check is called. From crackme #2's `main`:

```text
140001413  call sub_140001100     ; the password check, returns a bool in al
140001418  test al, al            ; is al zero? (ZF = 1 if false)
14000141a  je   loc_140001487     ; jump if it was false
```

`test al, al` (Lesson 4) sets ZF when `al` is 0. So `je` means "jump if the function returned `false`", and `loc_140001487` prints *Wrong password. Try again!*. The Rust was:

```rust
if check_password(line.as_bytes()) {
    println!("Correct! ...");
} else {
    println!("Wrong password. Try again!");
    std::process::exit(1);
}
```

When does this code jump to `loc_140001487`?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "When the check function returns true",
    "When the check function returns false",
    "Always, after the call",
    "When al is 1",
], correct = 1, explain = [
    "If it returns true, al is 1, `test al, al` gives a non-zero result, ZF = 0 and `je` does not jump.",
    "false is al = 0. `test al, al` sets ZF, and je jumps: to the Wrong password message.",
    "je is conditional. It jumps only when ZF is 1.",
    "al = 1 means true. Then ZF is 0 and je does not jump.",
] }
hints = [
    "test al, al sets ZF exactly when al is 0.",
]
deep_dive = '''
Results larger than 8 bytes but at most 16 often come back in two registers: `rax` and `rdx`. For example, `read_line` returns an `io::Result<usize>`, and in crackme #1 you can see `main` store both halves right after the call: `mov [rsp+0x50], rax` and `mov [rsp+0x58], rdx`. Larger results (big structs) are returned through memory: the caller passes a pointer to a free space as a hidden first argument, and the function writes the result there.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Which registers a function may change"
goal = "Know volatile and non-volatile registers."
text = '''
A calling convention also says which registers a function may freely change, and which it must give back unchanged:

- **Volatile** registers (also called **caller-saved**) may be changed by any function you call. On Windows: `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, `r10`, `r11`. If the caller still needs a value in one of these after the call, the caller must save it first.
- **Non-volatile** registers (also called **callee-saved**) must have the same value when the function returns as when it was called. On Windows: `rbx`, `rbp`, `rdi`, `rsi`, `rsp`, `r12` to `r15`. A function that wants to use one of them must save it first (`push`) and restore it before returning (`pop`).

This explains a lot of what you see at the start and end of functions. A function that pushes `rbx`, `rsi` and `rdi` in its prologue is telling you: "I am going to use these three registers for my own long-lived values". And after a `call`, values in `rbx` or `rsi` are still valid, while `rcx` and `rdx` are not.

(On Linux, `rdi` and `rsi` are volatile, because they carry arguments there.)

Crackme #1's `main` starts with `push rsi` and ends with `pop rsi`. Why?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "rsi holds main's first argument",
    "rsi is non-volatile on Windows: main uses it, so it must restore the caller's value",
    "push rsi reserves room for the local variables",
    "rsi holds the return value",
], correct = 1, explain = [
    "On Windows the first argument is in rcx. rsi is not an argument register on Windows.",
    "main uses rsi (it keeps a pointer in it across several calls), so it saves the caller's rsi in the prologue and restores it in the epilogue.",
    "Room for locals is reserved by `sub rsp, 0x60`, the next instruction.",
    "The return value is in rax.",
] }
hints = [
    "Is rsi in the volatile or in the non-volatile list on Windows?",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Shadow space and more arguments"
goal = "Understand `sub rsp, 0x28` and arguments on the stack."
text = '''
The Windows convention has one more rule that shows up in every function: **shadow space**. Before every `call`, the caller must leave 32 bytes (`0x20`) of free stack space right above the return address. The called function may use those 32 bytes to store its four argument registers if it wants to (for example, to free the registers for other work).

That is why so many Windows functions start with `sub rsp, 0x28` or `sub rsp, 0x38`. Take the password check of crackme #2, which begins with `sub rsp, 0x38`:

- `0x20` (32) bytes: shadow space for the functions *it* calls;
- the rest: its own local variables, plus padding.

The padding exists because of another rule: `rsp` must be a multiple of 16 at every `call`. The return address pushed by the call adds 8 bytes, so functions usually reserve "a multiple of 16, plus 8". `0x28` = 40 = 32 + 8, `0x38` = 56 = 48 + 8.

**More than four arguments**: argument 5 and further go on the stack, just above the shadow space. Right before the call you see them stored at `[rsp+0x20]`, `[rsp+0x28]`, and so on:

```text
mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x20], rax   ; 5th argument
mov  r9, ...                     ; 4th
mov  r8, ...                     ; 3rd
mov  rdx, ...                    ; 2nd
mov  rcx, ...                    ; 1st
call some_function
```

What are the 32 bytes right above the return address for?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The function's return value",
    "Shadow space: room where the called function may store its four argument registers",
    "The fifth argument",
    "Nothing; it is a mistake of the compiler",
], correct = 1, explain = [
    "The return value comes back in rax, not on the stack.",
    "That is the Windows shadow space: 0x20 bytes the caller reserves for the callee.",
    "The fifth argument goes just above the shadow space, at [rsp+0x20] at the time of the call.",
    "It is a rule of the Windows x64 calling convention. Every Windows program follows it.",
] }
hints = [
    "The name of this space was on this page, in bold.",
]
success = '''
You now know the full Windows x64 calling convention: rcx, rdx, r8, r9 for arguments, rax for the result, shadow space, and which registers survive a call. With this you can read any call in the crackmes. Next: what typical Rust code looks like in assembly.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Why Rust code looks the way it does"
goal = "Know what extra code Rust adds, so it does not surprise you."
text = '''
You can now read every instruction in the first two crackmes. What remains is recognising **patterns**: groups of instructions that together mean one Rust idea. Once you know them, a page of assembly turns into a few lines of Rust in your head.

Rust programs have some patterns that C programs do not have, because Rust adds safety and richer types:

- **Fat pointers.** A slice `&[u8]`, a `&str` and a `&mut [T]` are not one address but two values: an address and a length.
- **Bounds checks.** Every `s[i]` checks that `i` is smaller than the length, and panics if not.
- **Panics.** Code that handles a panic never returns; it is marked with `ud2`.
- **Enums like `Option` and `Result`.** Testing them often looks like a test for zero.
- **`String` and `Vec`.** Three values: capacity, pointer and length.
- **Drops.** At the end of a scope, the compiler frees heap memory: you see a check "capacity != 0?" and a call to the deallocation function.

All the examples in this lesson come from the two crackmes you are about to crack, exactly as ORRESS shows them (with comments added). So this lesson is also a preview of what you will see.

A tip before you start: you do not need to understand every line of a function. Reverse engineers skip what is clearly bookkeeping (bounds checks, drops, error handling) and look for the parts that matter, like the comparison that decides *Correct!* or *Wrong*.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Slices: a pointer and a length"
goal = "Recognise a slice argument in two registers."
text = '''
In Rust, a slice `&[u8]` or a `&str` is a **fat pointer**: two 8-byte values, the address of the first byte and the number of bytes. You can check this yourself in Rust: `std::mem::size_of::<&[u8]>()` is 16, twice the size of a normal pointer.

When a slice is passed to a function, it takes **two** argument registers. On Windows:

```rust
fn check_password(s: &[u8]) -> bool { ... }
```

- `rcx` = the address of the bytes (`s.as_ptr()`)
- `rdx` = the length (`s.len()`)

The password check of crackme #2 starts like this:

```text
140001100  sub  rsp, 0x38
140001104  cmp  rdx, 7
140001108  jne  loc_14000125b
```

`rdx` is the second argument register, so it holds the slice's length. The function compares the length with 7 and, if it is not equal, jumps away. (`loc_14000125b` is `xor eax, eax` followed by a return: it returns `false`.)

In Rust, this is:

```rust
if s.len() != 7 {
    return false;
}
```

What does this tell you about the password?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The password must be 7 characters long",
    "The password must contain the digit 7",
    "The function is called 7 times",
    "The password starts at address 7",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "rdx is the length of the slice. Any input that is not exactly 7 bytes is rejected at once.",
    "The 7 is compared with rdx, the length, not with any character.",
    "The length check runs once per call. Nothing here counts calls.",
    "The address of the bytes is in rcx, not rdx.",
] }
hints = [
    "rdx is the second register of the slice. Which half of a slice is that?",
]
success = '''
The password is 7 characters long. You know something about it without seeing it. A length check at the very start of a check function is extremely common, and it is often the first clue.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Reading the bytes of a slice"
goal = "Turn `byte ptr [rax+N]` into `s[N]`."
text = '''
To read `s[i]`, the code needs the slice's address in a register. In crackme #2 the address is first stored on the stack together with the length (`black_box` in the source forces this), and then loaded again:

```text
14000110e  mov  [rsp+0x28], rcx            ; store the slice: address ...
140001113  mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x30], 7    ; ... and length (7)
...
1400011f0  mov  rax, [rsp+0x28]            ; rax = the address of the bytes
1400011f5  cmp  byte ptr [rax+4], 0x72     ; compare s[?] with 0x72
1400011f9  jne  loc_14000125b              ; not equal: return false
```

(The `...` hides the checks of the first four characters, which look the same.)

Notice how the slice looks in memory: two 8-byte slots side by side, address first (`[rsp+0x28]`), length second (`[rsp+0x30]`). Whenever you see a pair like that, think "slice".

`byte ptr [rax+4]` reads one byte, 4 bytes after the start of the slice. Since the first byte is at `[rax+0]`, this is the byte with **index 4**, `s[4]`. So the Rust is:

```rust
if s[?] != 0x72 { return false; }
```

0x72 is a character code (Level 0). You will look it up in the last lesson of this level.

Which index does `cmp byte ptr [rax+4], 0x72` read?
'''
instructions = [
    "Look at the offset inside the brackets of the `cmp` line.",
    "Remember that `[rax+0]` is index 0.",
    "Type the index in the answer box and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["4"], number = true }
hints = [
    "The byte at rax+0 is s[0], at rax+1 is s[1], ...",
    "rax+4 is s[4].",
]
success = '''
`s[4]`, the fifth character. For bytes the offset is the index. For bigger elements, divide the offset by the element size (Lesson 6): `[rax+0x10]` in a `[u64]` is index 2.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Bounds checks"
goal = "Recognise Rust's index check and its panic call."
text = '''
Rust checks every index. `s[1]` panics with *index out of bounds* if the slice has fewer than 2 elements. The compiler writes that check as a comparison before the access:

```text
14000114e  mov  rdx, [rsp+0x30]       ; rdx = s.len()
140001153  cmp  rdx, 2                ; is the length at least 2?
140001157  jb   loc_140001274         ; below 2 (unsigned): go and panic
14000115d  mov  rax, [rsp+0x28]
140001162  cmp  byte ptr [rax+1], 0x33  ; the actual check of s[1]
```

and at `loc_140001274`:

```text
140001274  lea  r8, [0x140019400]     ; 3rd argument: where in the source the panic is
14000127b  mov  ecx, 1                ; 1st argument: the index (1)
140001280  call sub_140017e73         ; 2nd argument rdx: the length. Panic!
140001285  ud2
```

Read it with the calling convention: the panic function gets the index in `ecx`, the length in `rdx` and a pointer to the source location (file `crackmes\crackme02.rs`, line and column) in `r8`. That is everything it needs to print *index out of bounds: the len is 7 but the index is 1*. The Strings view contains both texts.

Here the check can never fail (the length was already checked to be 7), but because of `black_box` the compiler cannot know that. In most Rust programs you will see many of these checks. They are a strong sign that a program was written in Rust (C has no bounds checks), and you can **skip them** when reading: a `cmp` with a length, a `jb` or `jae` to a block that calls something and ends in `ud2`.

What does the `jb loc_140001274` jump to?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The next character check",
    "Code that panics because the index is out of bounds",
    "The start of a loop",
    "The return address",
], correct = 1, explain = [
    "The next character check comes right after the jb, when the jump is NOT taken.",
    "loc_140001274 calls the bounds-check panic with the index and the length, and never returns (ud2).",
    "It is a forward jump to a block that ends in ud2, not a backward jump.",
    "Only `ret` uses the return address. jb jumps to a label.",
] }
hints = [
    "Look at what the code at loc_140001274 does, and how it ends.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Panics and ud2"
goal = "Know that code ending in `ud2` never returns."
text = '''
`ud2` is an instruction that is **undefined on purpose**: if the CPU ever runs it, the program crashes. Compilers place it right after calls to functions that can never return, such as:

- panics (`panic!`, `unwrap()` on `None`, bounds checks, overflow checks in debug builds),
- `std::process::exit` and `std::process::abort`,
- `unreachable!()`.

Rust knows these functions have the return type `!` ("never"). The `ud2` is a safety net: there is no code after it, because there is nothing to come back to. ORRESS's decompiler even writes `unreachable!(); // execution stops here` for it.

For you as a reader, `ud2` is a gift. It tells you: "the block that ends here is an error path". In a graph, those blocks are dead ends. When you look for the code that decides whether a password is right, you can ignore every block that ends in `ud2`. In crackme #2's check function, seven of its blocks are bounds-check panics like the one on the previous page, all ending in `ud2`: one for each index from 1 to 6, plus one for index 0 (in case the slice is empty).

The Strings view helps here too. Rust programs contain many panic messages and source paths, like `index out of bounds: the len is` and `crackmes\crackme02.rs`. The code that uses them is error handling, not the logic you are looking for. The path also tells you the name of the source file the program was built from.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "String: capacity, pointer, length"
goal = "Recognise a `String` (or `Vec`) by its three fields."
text = '''
A `String` (and a `Vec<T>`) is three 8-byte values: the **capacity** (how many bytes are reserved on the heap), a **pointer** to those bytes, and the **length** (how many are used). Here is `let mut input = String::new();` from crackme #1's `main`:

```text
14000114f  mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x30], 0   ; capacity = 0
140001158  mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x38], 1   ; pointer  = 1  (a placeholder, see below)
140001161  mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x40], 0   ; length   = 0
```

Three values side by side on the stack: that is the `String`. An empty `String` has nothing on the heap, so Rust stores a placeholder pointer (here 1, an address that is never used) instead of a real one. Rust lays out the three fields in whatever order it prefers; in this program it is capacity, pointer, length.

Later, after `read_line` filled the string, the code loads the pointer and the length into registers:

```text
1400011da  mov  rcx, [rsp+0x38]    ; rcx = input.as_ptr()
1400011df  mov  r8,  [rsp+0x40]    ; r8  = input.len()
```

and at the end of `main` the string is **dropped**:

```text
140001261  mov  rdx, [rsp+0x30]    ; capacity
140001266  test rdx, rdx           ; capacity == 0?
140001269  je   loc_14000127c      ; nothing on the heap: nothing to free
14000126b  mov  rcx, [rsp+0x38]    ; pointer
140001270  mov  r8d, 1             ; alignment
140001276  call sub_140001330      ; free the heap memory
```

Which stack slot holds the `String`'s pointer to its bytes?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "[rsp+0x30]",
    "[rsp+0x38]",
    "[rsp+0x40]",
    "[rsp+0x48]",
], correct = 1, explain = [
    "[rsp+0x30] is the capacity: the drop code tests it for 0 before freeing.",
    "[rsp+0x38] is loaded into rcx before the input is used, and passed as the pointer to the free function.",
    "[rsp+0x40] is the length: it starts at 0 and is loaded into r8 as a count.",
    "[rsp+0x48] is not one of the String's three fields; the String uses 0x30, 0x38 and 0x40.",
] }
hints = [
    "Which slot is passed in rcx to the function that frees the memory?",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Comparing strings: length, then memcmp"
goal = "Read the code behind `==` on two `&str`."
text = '''
How does Rust compile `line == "open_sesame_101"`? Two strings are equal when they have the same length **and** the same bytes. So the compiler checks the length first (cheap), and only then compares the bytes. From crackme #1:

```text
14000121a  lea  rdx, [0x1400183fe]          ; address of "open_sesame_101..."
140001221  mov  [rsp+0x20], rdx             ; store the &str: address ...
140001226  mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x28], 0xf   ; ... and length 15
...
140001234  cmp  r8, [rsp+0x28]              ; same length as the input?
140001239  jne  loc_1400012a5               ; no: Wrong password
14000123b  mov  rdx, [rsp+0x20]             ; 2nd argument: the password's bytes
...                                         ; (rcx = your input's bytes, r8 = the length)
140001247  call memcmp                      ; compare r8 bytes
14000124c  test eax, eax                    ; memcmp returns 0 when equal
14000124e  jne  loc_1400012a5               ; not 0: Wrong password
```

You already know every piece: a `&str` as an address and a length side by side on the stack, a length comparison, arguments in `rcx`, `rdx` and `r8`, and a result in `eax`.

`memcmp` is a function from the C runtime library. Because the program imports it from a DLL, it keeps its name even though the program is stripped. It compares two blocks of memory and returns 0 if they are equal. (A negative or positive result says which one is "smaller", which `==` does not need.)

So the program shows *Wrong password* if the lengths differ **or** if `memcmp` returns something other than 0.

After `call memcmp`, the code does `test eax, eax` and `jne loc_1400012a5`. When is that jump taken?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "When the two strings are equal",
    "When the two strings are different",
    "When the input is empty",
    "Never",
], correct = 1, explain = [
    "Equal strings make memcmp return 0. test eax, eax then sets ZF, and jne does not jump.",
    "Different bytes make memcmp return a non-zero value, ZF = 0, and jne jumps to the Wrong password message.",
    "An empty input already failed the length check before memcmp was called.",
    "jne jumps whenever eax is not zero, which happens for every wrong password of the right length.",
] }
hints = [
    "memcmp returns 0 for equal. test eax, eax sets ZF when eax is 0.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Option and Result"
goal = "See how `Option` and `Result` are tested."
text = '''
Rust's enums often compile to something very small. An `Option<&T>` needs no extra space at all: a reference is never 0, so Rust uses the value 0 to mean `None`. Testing it is a test for zero.

Crackme #1 calls `strip_suffix('\n')`, which returns an `Option<&str>`. The compiler inlined it (put its code directly into `main`):

```text
1400011e4  xor   eax, eax                   ; result = None (0)
1400011e6  test  r8, r8                     ; is the input empty?
1400011e9  je    loc_1400011f5              ; then it stays None
1400011eb  cmp   byte ptr [rcx+r8-1], 0xa   ; is the last byte '\n'?
1400011f1  cmove rax, rcx                   ; if equal: result = Some(address)
```

There is one new instruction: `cmove` (conditional move) is a `mov` that only happens if ZF = 1, like a tiny `if` without a jump. And `[rcx+r8-1]` is "address + length - 1": the last byte. Afterwards the code tests `rax` for zero to see whether it got `Some`.

A `Result` usually needs an explicit marker that says which variant it is. Right after `read_line`:

```text
140001194  call sub_1400092b0               ; stdin.read_line(&mut input)
140001199  mov  [rsp+0x50], rax             ; the result, in two registers
14000119e  mov  [rsp+0x58], rdx
1400011a3  test rax, rax                    ; which variant?
1400011a6  jne  loc_1400012b8               ; not 0: Err -> ... exit(1)
```

The Rust was `if stdin.read_line(&mut input).is_err() { exit(1) }`. In this program `rax` = 0 means `Ok`.

In `strip_suffix`'s code above, what value of `rax` means `None`?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "0",
    "1",
    "0xa",
    "The length of the input",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "None is 0. A real address is never 0, so Rust can use 0 for None without any extra field.",
    "Here 1 has no special meaning. (It was the placeholder pointer of an empty String, a different thing.)",
    "0xa is the character '\\n' that the code compares with.",
    "The length is in r8 and stays there.",
] }
hints = [
    "Look at the first line: `xor eax, eax` sets the starting value.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Your pattern cheat sheet"
goal = "Have every pattern of this level in one place."
text = '''
Here is everything in one table. Come back to it while you crack the next two programs.

| You see | It means |
|---|---|
| `xor eax, eax` | `= 0` |
| `mov rax, rcx` + arithmetic on `rax` | one Rust expression on the first argument |
| `cmp` / `test` + `jcc` | an `if` (with the condition inverted) |
| a conditional jump back up | a loop |
| `lea rcx, [0x...]  ; "text"` | a pointer to a string literal |
| `lea rcx, [rsp+0x..]` before a call | passing a reference to a local variable |
| `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9` set before `call` | arguments 1 to 4 (Windows) |
| `test al, al` + `je` after a call | `if !function(...)`: the function returned a `bool` |
| two slots side by side: address, length | a slice or `&str` |
| three slots: capacity, pointer, length | a `String` or `Vec` |
| `cmp` with a length + `jb`/`jae` to a block ending in `ud2` | a bounds check: skip it |
| `call ...` + `ud2` | a call that never returns (panic, exit) |
| compare lengths, then `call memcmp`, `test eax, eax` | `a == b` on strings or slices |
| `cmp byte ptr [rax+N], 0x..` | `s[N] == b'?'`: a character check |
| `push` / `sub rsp` at the start, `add rsp` / `pop` / `ret` at the end | a function's prologue and epilogue |

You do not have to learn this table by heart. You will recognise these patterns more and more by yourself, as you read more code. The next two lessons put it all to work on real programs.
'''
success = '''
You know enough to crack your first programs. Next lesson: crackme #1.
'''

fn check_password(s: &[u8]) -> bool {

}
```

`b'a'` is a byte literal: the number 97. In the compiled program, these numbers end up inside `cmp` instructions, as immediate values, not as text in the data. So you have to read the code. Everything you learned in this level comes together here.

title = "Find the decision"
goal = "Find the call whose result decides Correct or Wrong."
text = '''
Now scroll down through `main`. Much of it you have seen in crackme #1 and in Lesson 10: printing the prompt, `String::new()` (three `mov qword ptr` lines), `read_line`, and then the two `strip_suffix` calls, which compare the last byte with `0xa` (`'\n'`) and `0xd` (`'\r'`).

Right after that comes the part that matters. In crackme #1 the comparison was written directly in `main`. Here `main` calls a function instead, and then uses its `bool` result. You know this pattern from Lesson 9:

```text
call sub_????????     ; the password check: returns a bool in al
test al, al           ; false?
je   loc_140001487    ; then: "Wrong password. Try again!"
```

The Find bar gets you there quickly: search for `test al`.

Remember that the `sub_` name is made of the function's address. That address is what you need now. Which function does `main` call right before `test al, al`? Type its address.

Renaming is the most important habit in reverse engineering: the name then appears everywhere the function is used (in every `call`, in the Functions view, in the decompiler), and ORRESS saves it with your work. Over time, the unnamed program turns into a readable one.

In the Disassembly view, the key **N** renames. On a line with a `call`, it renames the function that is called, so you do not have to go inside first.

A good name says what the function does. Rust's naming style (snake_case) works well: `check_password`. If you give a name that is already used, ORRESS tells you.

[[steps]]
title = "Inside check_password"
goal = "Follow the call and get an overview of the check."
text = '''
Now go inside: **click the name** `check_password` in the `call` line. ORRESS jumps to the first instruction of the function. (**Esc** brings you back to where you were, like a browser's Back button.)

You will recognise its beginning from Lesson 10:

```text
sub  rsp, 0x38            ; prologue: room for locals and shadow space
cmp  rdx, 7               ; s.len() == 7 ?
jne  loc_14000125b        ; no: return false
```

`rcx` holds the address of your input, `rdx` its length: the two halves of the slice `&[u8]`. Then the function checks the characters one by one. Each check has the same shape:

```text
mov  [rsp+0x28], rcx            ; (black_box: store the slice ...)
mov  qword ptr [rsp+0x30], 7    ; (... and its length)
...                             ; (a bounds check: cmp rdx, N / jb -> panic)
mov  rax, [rsp+0x28]            ; rax = address of the input
cmp  byte ptr [rax+1], 0x33     ; s[1] == 0x33 ?
jne  loc_14000125b              ; no: return false
```

Scroll through the function. Count the instructions that compare one byte of the input with a number: the lines with `cmp byte ptr [rax...]`. How many are there?
'''
instructions = [
    "In the Disassembly view, click the name `check_password` in the line `call check_password`.",
    "Scroll down through the function until you reach the `ret` lines and the blocks that end in `ud2`.",
    "Count the lines that start with `cmp byte ptr [rax`. Type the number and press **Check**.",
]
spotlight = "view.Disassembly"
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["7"], number = true }
hints = [
    "Use Ctrl+F with `byte ptr [rax` and press Next repeatedly, counting the matches in this function.",
    "There is one comparison per character, and the length check said how many characters there are.",
    "Seven: one for each character of a 7-character password.",
]
success = '''
Seven comparisons for seven characters: one for `[rax]`, then `[rax+1]` up to `[rax+6]`. The last one is followed by `sete al` (set `al` to 1 if equal) instead of a jump: its result is the function's return value.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Read the characters"
goal = "Turn the seven numbers into characters."
text = '''
Now write the seven comparisons down in order, by the offset in the brackets:

| offset | compared with | character |
|---|---|---|
| `[rax]` | `0x52` | ? |
| `[rax+1]` | `0x33` | ? |
| `[rax+2]` | ... | ? |
| ... | ... | ... |
| `[rax+6]` | ... | ? |

Skip the lines in between: the `mov [rsp+0x28], rcx` and `mov qword ptr [rsp+0x30], 7` lines are `black_box` storing the slice, and every `cmp rdx, N` followed by `jb` is a bounds check (Lesson 10). Only the `cmp byte ptr` lines matter.

To turn a number into a character, you have two tools:

- **Hover** over the number in the Disassembly view. ORRESS shows it in hex and decimal, and *as a character*, for example `as a character: 'R'`.
- The **ASCII table** below: find the hex code, read the character next to it.

Remember from Level 0 that digits are characters too: `'0'` is `0x30`, `'1'` is `0x31`, and so on. A password can mix letters and digits.

When you have the whole table, read the characters from top to bottom: that is the password. Continue to the next step to enter it.
'''
instructions = [
    "In the Disassembly view, find each `cmp byte ptr [rax...], 0x..` line of `check_password`.",
    "Hover over the number on each of those lines and write down the character ORRESS shows.",
    "Put the seven characters in the order of the offsets, from `[rax]` to `[rax+6]`.",
]
spotlight = "view.Disassembly"
widget = "ascii_table"
hints = [
    "The offsets [rax], [rax+1], [rax+2] ... give the order.",
    "0x52 is 'R' and 0x33 is '3'.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Enter the password"
goal = "Prove that you read the check correctly."
text = '''
Put the seven characters together and type the password below.

Check yourself before you press **Check**:

- it has exactly 7 characters (the length check said so);
- the first character is the one compared at `[rax]`, the last the one at `[rax+6]`;
- upper and lower case matter: `0x52` is `'R'`, while `'r'` is `0x72`. Both appear in this password.

If it is not accepted, go back to the table and look at each number again. A common mistake is reading a digit as a letter: `0x33` is the digit `'3'`, not the letter `'e'` (which is `0x65`).

You could also test your answer without the lesson: run `crackme02.exe` from a terminal, the way the last step of the previous lesson described, and type the password. If it prints *Correct! You read the password byte by byte.*, you got it.

instructions = [
    "Type the seven characters in the answer box, in order, without spaces.",
    "Press **Check**.",
]

check = { kind = "secret", sha256 = "2bfa401089ad1adbbf882bbd49236b2043d5e6f0f1c9a4d7bea8f7bef5f7f3ea" }

    "It looks like the word 'Reverse', with the e's written as 3.",
    "R3v3rs...",

success = '''
That is the password. You read it directly out of the machine code, character by character, even though it was never stored as text. That is real reverse engineering.
'''

`academy/lessons/02-01-static-analysis.toml`:

```toml

order = 1
title = "Static analysis: a first look"
summary = "What static analysis is, and a fixed routine for your first five minutes with any unknown program."
goals = [

    "read the Info view of a program: format, architecture, detections and protections",

[[steps]]
title = "Reading without running"
goal = "Know what static analysis is and why you start with it."
text = '''
In Level 1 you read assembly line by line. Real programs are much bigger than one
function, so now you learn to find your way around a whole program. That is
**static analysis**: understanding a program by reading its file, **without running it**.

Think of a Rust project you did not write. You could run `cargo run` and watch what it
prints. Or you could open `src/main.rs` and read. Reading takes longer, but it shows you
everything: every `if`, every error message, also the paths that one run never takes.
Static analysis is the "open the source and read" approach, except that the "source" is
the machine code inside the `.exe`.

Static analysis has three big advantages:

- **It is safe.** Nothing runs, so even a harmful program cannot do anything.
- **It is complete.** You can see every path through the code.
- **It needs only the file.** No special computer, no debugger.

It also has a limit. Values that only exist while the program runs are not in the file:
what you type, what a server answers, data the program decrypts in memory. For those you
will run the program under a debugger in Level 3 (that is *dynamic analysis*).

Experienced reversers always start statically, and ORRESS is built for it. In this level
you learn the tools: the Info view, the file format, navigation, names and comments, the
graph view and the decompiler. At the end you decode a hidden password and write a key
generator.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Meet crackme #10"
goal = "Open the practice program for the first six lessons of this level."

For the next six lessons you work with one program: **crackme #10**, a small "licence
checker" written in Rust. It asks for a licence code and answers *Licence accepted* or
*Invalid licence code.* By the end of the decompiler lesson you will know exactly which
codes it accepts, without ever guessing.

Each lesson uses this program to practise one skill. That is how real analysis works too:
you come back to the same program again and again, and every visit adds to what you know.

When you press the button, ORRESS copies the program to its configuration folder (in a
subfolder `academy/crackmes`) and opens it. It does not run it. The program is harmless: it
only reads one line and prints one answer. If you want to try codes later, you can run
`crackme10.exe` from a terminal in that folder.
'''
instructions = [
    "Press the **Open crackme10** button below.",
    "Wait a moment: the tabs `crackme10.exe · Hex` and `crackme10.exe · Info` open in the middle of the window.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "A routine for the first five minutes"
goal = "Learn the fixed checklist you will use on every new program."
text = '''
Faced with an unknown program, beginners click around at random. Professionals follow a
short, fixed routine, a kind of **first look** (malware analysts call it *triage*). It
answers five questions in five minutes:

1. **What is it?** Which file format, which processor, is it a program or a library?
2. **Who made it?** Which language and compiler? Is it packed (squeezed and hidden)?
3. **How is it protected?** Which security features are on? Does it have function names?
4. **What does it say?** Which messages and other text are inside?
5. **What can it do?** Which library functions does it use (its imports)?

The answers decide what you do next. A program written in Rust needs different habits than
one written in C#. A packed program must be unpacked first. A program that imports network
functions talks to the internet.

The **Info** view answers questions 1 to 3 on one page, and it gives tips for 4 and 5. The
**Strings** view answers question 4, the **Imports** view question 5. In the next steps
you work through the routine on crackme #10, one question at a time.

Remember the order. You will use it for every program in this course, and for every
program after it.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "What is it?"
goal = "Read the format and the processor from the Info view."
text = '''
Look at the first card of the Info view, **What is this file?**. It shows:

- the **format** in large text, with one line explaining it. *PE (Windows executable)*
  means a Windows program. Linux programs say *ELF*, macOS programs *Mach-O*.
- **Size**: the file size in bytes.
- **Kind**: a program you run (*Executable program*), a library other programs use, or an
  object file (a half-finished piece of a program).
- **Architecture**: the processor the machine code is written for, and the byte order.
- **Image base** and **Entry point**: two addresses you will meet in the next lesson.
- **Imports / exports** and **Symbols**: how many library functions it uses, how many it
  offers, and how many names are stored in the file.
- **Entropy**: how random the bytes look, from 0 to 8 (more about it in the deep dive).

Hover over any label with Explain Mode on and ORRESS explains it.

The architecture matters most: assembly for an ARM64 phone looks completely different from
the x86-64 assembly you learned in Level 1. Read it off the card.
'''
deep_dive = '''
**Entropy** measures how unpredictable the bytes are. English text uses few different
byte values and scores about 4 to 5. Machine code scores about 6. Compressed or encrypted
data uses all 256 byte values evenly and scores close to 8. The **Entropy graph** card at
the bottom of the Info view draws it along the file. One part near 8 means "this cannot
be read yet": it is packed or encrypted, and you must find the code that unpacks it.
'''
instructions = [
    "Click the tab **crackme10.exe · Info** in the middle of the window (it is probably already in front).",

    "Type the processor name (the part before the dot) in the answer box below and press **Check**.",
]

    "Type `x86-64`.",

x86-64: the 64-bit PC processor, little-endian (the lowest byte of a number is stored
first). Everything you learned in Level 1 applies. Good to know before you read a single

[[steps]]
title = "Who made it?"
goal = "Understand what the Detected card tells you about the compiler."
text = '''
Scroll down to the card **Detected**. ORRESS recognises languages, compilers and packers by
traces they leave in the file. Each line shows the kind of detection, the name, and the
evidence in brackets.

For crackme #10 you see two lines:

- **Language: Rust**, because the file contains paths like `/rustc/...`. The Rust standard
  library keeps its source file names for panic messages, and they survive compiling.
- **Compiler: Microsoft Visual C++**, because of a *Rich header*: hidden data that
  Microsoft's linker writes into every file it builds.

A Rust program built by Microsoft Visual C++? Both are true. `rustc` compiles your Rust
code, but on Windows it uses Microsoft's **linker** to glue the pieces into an `.exe`, and
Microsoft's C runtime start-up code runs before your `main`. So you will meet some
Microsoft code before you reach the Rust code.

Why does the language matter? Because every language leaves typical patterns. In Rust you
will see slices passed as a pointer plus a length, bounds checks before indexing, and
`String`s made of a capacity, a pointer and a length. In C you would see zero-terminated
strings instead. Knowing the language tells you which patterns to expect.
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The Rust code was compiled by rustc, and Microsoft's linker and C runtime start-up code put the .exe together",
    "Someone rewrote the Rust program in C++",
    "ORRESS made a mistake: a file can only be one of the two",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "That is how every Rust program on Windows is built. Expect some Microsoft start-up code before your main.",
    "Nobody rewrote anything. The C++ detection comes from the linker's Rich header, not from C++ code.",
    "Both detections are right: they describe different tools in the build chain.",

[[steps]]
title = "How is it protected?"
goal = "Know what each protection means for you as a reverser."
text = '''
The card **Protections** lists security features of the file, with **yes**, **no** or
**partial** and a short detail. For crackme #10:

- **ASLR: yes.** Windows loads the program at a random address each time. In ORRESS
  addresses are always shown as if it were loaded at its preferred address, so this does
  not bother you now.
- **DEP / NX: yes.** Data in memory (stack, heap) may not be run as code. Normal for every
  modern program.
- **Control Flow Guard: no.** An extra check on indirect calls. When it is on, the
  disassembly gets a bit noisier, nothing more.
- **Signed: no.** No certificate that proves who published it. Crackmes and most malware
  are not signed; Windows itself is.
- **Stripped: yes.** The file contains no names for its own functions, only the names of
  the library functions it imports.

For a reverser the last line is the most important one. A stripped program shows its
functions with generated names such as `sub_1400012c0`: "the function at address
0x1400012c0". Naming them is your job, and you will learn it in lesson 4.
'''
deep_dive = '''
These protections were made against attackers who exploit bugs, not against reversers.
None of them hides code from static analysis. Protections that *do* fight reversers are
packers, obfuscation and anti-debugging tricks; the Info view warns about those under
**Detected** and **Observations and tips** when it finds them. Level 3 and Level 5 teach
you to beat them.
'''

```toml
id = "l2-file-formats"
level = 2
order = 2
title = "Inside an executable: the PE format"
summary = "Headers, sections, imports and the difference between a file offset and an address, read from a real Windows program."
goals = [
    "find the DOS header, the PE header and the section table in the raw bytes",
    "read the image base and the entry point, and explain what an RVA is",
    "convert between a file offset and a memory address with the section table",
    "explain what imports, exports and the Import Address Table are",
    "recognise the same ideas in ELF (Linux) and Mach-O (macOS) files",
]
badge = "Format Reader"

[[steps]]
title = "A file with a fixed layout"
goal = "See an executable as a structure with known fields, like a Rust struct."
text = '''
When you double-click an `.exe`, the Windows **program loader** reads the file, copies its parts
into memory, connects it to the libraries it needs and jumps to its first instruction. To
do that, the file must have a layout the program loader understands: an **executable format**.
Windows uses **PE** (Portable Executable), Linux uses **ELF**, macOS uses **Mach-O**.

You can think of a PE file as a Rust struct written to disk, field after field:

```rust
struct PeFile {
    dos_header: DosHeader,       // starts with "MZ"; says where the PE header is
    pe_header: PeHeader,         // "PE\0\0", processor type, number of sections
    optional_header: OptHeader,  // image base, entry point, where the tables are
    sections: Vec<SectionHeader>,// the section table: name, offset, size, address
    // ... then the sections themselves: .text, .rdata, .data, ...
}
```

The headers are small (crackme #10's take about 0x400 bytes, out of 136 KB). Most of the
file is the sections: code in `.text`, constants in `.rdata`, variables in `.data`.

Level 0 gave you the big picture of headers, sections, file offsets and imports. In this
lesson you read them yourself, in the raw bytes and in the Info, Sections and Imports
views, so you know exactly where every number in ORRESS comes from. Keep crackme #10 open; if you closed it, open it again in the next step.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Open crackme #10"
goal = "Have the practice program open."
text = '''
This lesson reads the headers of crackme #10. If it is still open from the previous
lesson, pressing the button opens it again; that does no harm.
'''

]

[[steps]]
title = "MZ: the DOS header"
goal = "Find where the PE header starts, using the bytes at offset 0x3C."
text = '''
Every PE file starts with the two bytes `4D 5A`, the letters `MZ`. They begin the
**DOS header**, a leftover from MS-DOS in the 1980s: if you start the program under DOS,
a tiny program in it prints *This program cannot be run in DOS mode.* (find that text near
the top of the Hex view).

Only one field of the DOS header still matters. At **file offset 0x3C** (60 bytes from the
start) are 4 bytes called **e_lfanew**: a little-endian `u32` with the file offset of the
real PE header. In Rust the program loader does this:

```rust
let pe_offset = u32::from_le_bytes([file[0x3C], file[0x3D], file[0x3E], file[0x3F]]);
```

Remember little-endian from Level 0: the lowest byte comes first. The bytes `10 01 00 00`
mean 0x00000110 = 0x110.

Read e_lfanew of crackme #10 yourself. The **Hex** view shows the offset of each row on the
left (`00000030` is the row with offsets 0x30 to 0x3F) and 16 bytes per row. The toolbar
shows `cursor 0x...`: the offset of the byte the cursor is on.

[[steps]]
title = "PE: the file header"
goal = "Read the processor type and the number of sections from the PE header."
text = '''
At offset 0xE8 you find the **PE header**. It starts with a signature of 4 bytes:
`50 45 00 00`, which is `P`, `E` and two zero bytes. Then come 20 bytes of the COFF file
header. The first two fields are:

| Offset | Size | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0xE8 | 4 | Signature | `50 45 00 00` = "PE\0\0" |
| 0xEC | 2 | Machine | the processor: `64 86` = 0x8664 = x86-64 |
| 0xEE | 2 | NumberOfSections | how many entries the section table has |

`64 86` is little-endian again: the number is 0x8664, Microsoft's code for x86-64. A
32-bit x86 program has 0x014C, an ARM64 program 0xAA64. This is where the Info view got
"x86-64" from.

Go to offset 0xE8 and read the number of sections: the two bytes right after `64 86`.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Image base, entry point and RVAs"
goal = "Understand the image base and the RVA of the entry point."
text = '''
After the COFF header comes the **optional header** (it is not optional for programs). Two
of its fields are on the Info view:

- **Image base**: the address where the program would like to be loaded in memory. For
  64-bit Windows programs it is almost always `0x140000000`.
- **Entry point**: the address of the first instruction that runs.

The header does not store the entry point as a full address. It stores an **RVA**, a
*relative virtual address*: the distance from the image base. The full address (the
*virtual address*, or VA) is a sum:

```rust
let image_base = 0x1_4000_0000u64;
let entry_rva = 0x1_63A0u64;            // what the header stores
let entry_va = image_base + entry_rva;  // 0x1400163A0: what ORRESS shows
```

Why relative? Because of **ASLR**, Windows may load the program at a different address on
each run. An RVA stays correct wherever the program lands; only the image base changes.
That is also why ORRESS shows every address as if the program sat at its image base: those
numbers match the file.

Read **Image base** and **Entry point** on the Info view, and compute the RVA of the entry
point: entry point minus image base.
'''
instructions = [
    "Click the tab **crackme10.exe · Info**.",
    "In the **What is this file?** card, read **Image base** and **Entry point**. Leading zeros do not matter: `0x0000000140000000` is `0x140000000`.",
    "Subtract: entry point - image base. Type the result in hex, for example `0x1234`.",
]
spotlight = "view.Info"
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0x163A0"], number = true }
widget = "number_converter"
hints = [
    "The entry point is `0x1400163A0` and the image base is `0x140000000`.",
    "Subtracting 0x140000000 removes the leading `14000` part.",
    "0x1400163A0 - 0x140000000 = 0x163A0.",
]
success = '''
RVA 0x163A0. Note that this entry point is **not** your `main`: it is the start-up code of
Microsoft's C runtime and of Rust's standard library, which runs first and calls `main`
later. The next lesson shows how ORRESS finds `main` from here.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "The section table"
goal = "Read what each section is for and where it is."
text = '''
After the optional header comes the **section table**: one entry per section, with its
name, where it is in the file and where it goes in memory. The **Sections** view shows it
as a table:

- **Name**: chosen by the compiler. `.text` is code, `.rdata` read-only data (string
  literals, constants, and on Windows the import tables), `.data` global variables,
  `.pdata` a list of functions for exception handling, `.reloc` relocations (fixes for
  when the program is not loaded at its image base).
- **Offset** and **Size**: where the section's bytes are in the **file**.
- **Address** and **Mem size**: where they go in **memory**.
- **Perms**: R = readable, W = writable, X = executable. Code is `R-X`, constants `R--`,
  variables `RW-`.
- **Entropy** and **Usually contains**: how random the bytes are, and what such a section
  normally holds.

Compare the **Offset** and **Address** of `.text`. The section starts at file offset
0x400, but it is loaded at address 0x140001000 (RVA 0x1000). The file packs sections
tightly, in steps of 0x200 bytes; memory uses steps of 0x1000 bytes (one memory page), so
the numbers do not match. Click a row to see that section's bytes in the Hex view.

Which section is both readable and writable?
'''
instructions = [
    "In the **Project** panel on the left, click **Sections**.",
    "Read the **Perms** column for every row.",
    "Type the name of the section with the permissions `RW-` (with its dot) in the answer box.",
]
spotlight = "tree.Sections"
check = { kind = "answer", answers = [".data", "data"] }
hints = [
    "Only one row has a W.",
    "It holds the global variables.",
    "Type `.data`.",
]
success = '''
`.data` is the only writable section: global variables live there. Code is never writable
in a normal program, and data is never executable. A section with `RWX` would be a
warning sign: the program may write new code into memory while it runs, as packers do.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "File offset or address?"
goal = "Convert an address to a file offset with the section table."
text = '''
Every byte has two numbers:

- its **file offset**: where it is in the file (the Hex view, the Strings view's
  **Offset** column);
- its **virtual address**: where it is in memory (the disassembly, the debugger, the
  Strings view's **Address** column).

The section table connects them. For a byte inside a section:

```rust
// offset -> address
let va = section.address + (offset - section.offset);
// address -> offset
let offset = section.offset + (va - section.address);
```

**Worked example.** Where in the file is the entry point, 0x1400163A0? It is in `.text`
(that section covers 0x140001000 up to 0x140017FEE). `.text` starts at address
0x140001000 and at file offset 0x400. So:

```text
offset = 0x400 + (0x1400163A0 - 0x140001000)
       = 0x400 + 0x153A0
       = 0x157A0
```

Check it yourself. On the Info view, next to **Entry point**, there is a small button
**show bytes**. It opens the Hex view at the entry point's file offset. The Hex view's
toolbar then says `cursor 0x...`: the file offset of the cursor. The **Inspector** tab in
the dock on the right shows both numbers for the byte under the cursor: **Offset** and
**Address**.
'''
instructions = [
    "Click the tab **crackme10.exe · Info**.",
    "Next to **Entry point**, click **show bytes**. The Hex view opens with the cursor on the first byte of the entry point.",
    "Read the file offset in the Hex view's toolbar, after the word `cursor`.",
    "Type that file offset in the answer box, in hex.",
    "Optional: in the dock on the right, click the **Inspector** tab to see **Offset** and **Address** of the same byte. Click the **Lesson** tab to come back here.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0x157A0"], number = true }
hints = [
    "The worked example above computes it.",
    "Type `0x157A0`.",
]
success = '''
The same byte: offset 0x157A0 in the file, address 0x1400163A0 in memory. Mixing up the
two is the most common beginner mistake in reverse engineering. When a number "does not
work" in a view, ask yourself first: is this an offset or an address?
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Imports: borrowed functions"
goal = "See which library functions the program uses."
text = '''
Your Rust code calls `println!`, which in the end asks Windows to write text with a
function called `WriteConsoleW`. That function is not inside `crackme10.exe`. It is in a
**DLL** (dynamic-link library), `KERNEL32.dll`, that Windows loads next to every program.
The `.exe` only contains a list: "I need `WriteConsoleW` from `KERNEL32.dll`". That list is
the **import table**, and each entry is an **import**.

The **Imports** view groups the imports by DLL. Functions ORRESS knows get a coloured
category (Input, Comparison, Anti-debugging, Network, ...) and an explanation when you
hover them. The link **N »** after a function jumps to the places that call it.

Imports are the quickest way to learn what a program can do: `ReadConsoleW` reads input,
`memcmp` compares memory, `CreateFileW` opens files, `connect` talks to the network. A
small Rust program imports around 90 functions, almost all for the standard library's own
use.

Under the group header you can see how many functions come from each DLL. How many
functions does crackme #10 import from `KERNEL32.dll`?
'''

[[steps]]
title = "How a call reaches a DLL"
goal = "Understand the Import Address Table."
text = '''
When the program is built, nobody knows where `KERNEL32.dll` will be in memory. So the
program cannot contain `call 0x7FF812345678`. Instead it calls **through a pointer**:

```text
call qword ptr [0x140018xxx]    ; "call the address stored at 0x140018xxx"
```

The pointers live in the **Import Address Table** (**IAT**), one slot per import. In the
file the slots hold placeholders. When the program starts, the program loader looks up each
imported function and writes its real address into its slot. In Rust terms, the IAT is a
`static mut IAT: [fn(); N]` that Windows fills before `main` runs.

ORRESS knows which slot belongs to which import, so instead of a bare pointer you read
`call WakeByAddressSingle` in the disassembly. In crackme #10 the IAT is at the very start
of `.rdata` (RVA 0x18000).

The other side of imports are **exports**: functions a file offers to others. DLLs export
functions; normal programs usually export nothing. Look at the bottom of the Imports view:
crackme #10 has **Exports (0)**.

Why does the program call an imported function through a pointer?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The DLL's address is only known when the program runs, so the program loader fills the pointer in at start-up",
    "Calls through pointers are faster than direct calls",
    "To hide the function name from reversers",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. The IAT slot is filled by the program loader, so the same .exe works wherever Windows puts the DLL.",
    "They are not faster; they are needed because the address is unknown when the file is built.",
    "The name is not hidden at all: it is in the import table, and ORRESS shows it in the disassembly.",
] }
hints = [
    "What does the program not know when it is compiled?",
    "Think about ASLR: DLLs move too.",
]

[[steps]]
title = "ELF and Mach-O"
goal = "Recognise the same ideas in Linux and macOS programs."
text = '''
Linux and macOS programs use other formats, but the ideas are the same. When you meet one,
translate:

| Idea | PE (Windows) | ELF (Linux) | Mach-O (macOS) |
|---|---|---|---|
| First bytes | `MZ` | `7F 45 4C 46` (`\x7fELF`) | `CF FA ED FE` (64-bit) |
| Code | `.text` | `.text` | `__TEXT,__text` |
| Constants | `.rdata` | `.rodata` | `__TEXT,__cstring` / `__const` |
| Variables | `.data` | `.data`, `.bss` | `__DATA,__data` |
| Imported functions | import table + IAT | `.plt` stubs + `.got` | `__stubs` + `__la_symbol_ptr` |
| Typical base | `0x140000000` | `0x0` (PIE) or `0x400000` | `0x100000000` |

On Linux a call to a library function goes to a small stub, `puts@plt`, which jumps
through an address in the `.got` table, the same trick as the IAT with another name. ELF
files also have **segments** (program headers): the larger parts the program loader actually maps,
each covering one or more sections. ORRESS shows them under **Segments** at the bottom of
the Sections view.

ORRESS reads all three formats, and every view you learn in this level works the same for
them.

Test yourself: which format starts with the bytes `7F 45 4C 46`?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "ELF (a Linux program)",
    "PE (a Windows program)",
    "Mach-O (a macOS program)",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right: 7F 45 4C 46 is \\x7fELF, the start of every ELF file.",
    "A PE file starts with 4D 5A (MZ).",
    "A 64-bit Mach-O file starts with CF FA ED FE.",
] }
hints = ["Look at the row **First bytes** of the table."]
deep_dive = '''
If you are curious about the full PE layout: Microsoft documents it as the
"PE Format" specification, and the optional header of crackme #10 starts at offset 0x100
with the magic number `0B 02` (0x20B), which means PE32+, the 64-bit variant.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "What you can read now"
goal = "Summarise the structure of an executable."
text = '''
You now know what is inside a program file, and where each ORRESS view gets its data:

- **DOS header** (`MZ`) -> **e_lfanew** at 0x3C -> **PE header** (`PE\0\0`, machine,
  number of sections): the **Info** view's format and architecture.
- **Optional header**: **image base** and **entry point** (an RVA): the Info view's
  addresses.
- **Section table**: the **Sections** view, and the key to converting between **file
  offsets** and **virtual addresses**.
- **Import table** and **IAT**: the **Imports** view, and the names you see on calls in
  the disassembly.

Three formulas to remember:

```rust
va = image_base + rva;
va = section.address + (offset - section.offset);
offset = section.offset + (va - section.address);
```

Next lesson: you leave the headers behind and go into the code. You will find `main`
starting from the entry point, use the Functions view, and follow cross-references from
the *Invalid licence code.* message to the check.
'''
success = "Lesson complete. You can read an executable's structure like a reverser."

Open the program (again) with the button.

instructions = ["Press the **Open crackme10** button below."]
check = { kind = "open_crackme", name = "crackme10" }

[[steps]]
title = "The entry point is not main"
goal = "Understand what runs between the entry point and your main."
text = '''
In Rust, your program starts in `fn main()`. The processor does not know that. It starts
at the **entry point** from the PE header (0x1400163A0 in crackme #10), and that is
start-up code you never wrote:

1. **Microsoft's C runtime** starts at the entry point. It sets up the heap, the
   command-line arguments and some security features, and then calls a function named
   `main`, as every C program expects.
2. That `main` is not yours. `rustc` writes it for you, and it looks roughly like this:

```rust
// generated by rustc, not by you:
extern "C" fn main(argc: i32, argv: *const *const u8) -> i32 {
    std::rt::lang_start(your_main, argc, argv)  // pass a pointer to YOUR main
}
```

3. **`std::rt::lang_start`**, in Rust's standard library, sets up panics, threads and
   `std::env::args()`, then calls `your_main()`, and finally turns its result into the
   program's exit code.

So between the entry point and your code there are three layers of start-up code. In a
stripped program none of them has a name. ORRESS recognises the rustc-generated function
by its shape, names it `rust_runtime_main`, and follows the pointer it passes to
`lang_start` to find the real `main`.

C, C++ and Go programs have similar layers. That is why "Go to main" is the first thing
you press in almost every program.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Visit the entry point"
goal = "See with your own eyes that the entry point is start-up code."
text = '''
Have a look at the entry point anyway, so you know what start-up code looks like.

The **Disassembly** view has a **Go to** bar: press **Ctrl+G** while the disassembly has
focus and type an address (in hex, without `0x` if you like) or a name. ORRESS knows the
name `entry` for the entry point.

At the entry point you will find only four instructions: it makes room on the stack,
calls one function, gives the room back, and then **jumps** to another function. The
called function sets up a security value (the "stack cookie"); the jump goes to the C
runtime's main start-up routine. No message, no input, no check: nothing of your
program.

Which function does the entry point jump to at its end?
'''
instructions = [
    "Press **Ctrl+D** to open the **Disassembly** view of crackme10.exe.",
    "Click once inside the disassembly so it has keyboard focus.",
    "Press **Ctrl+G**, type `entry` in the **Go to** box and press **Enter**.",
    "Read the four instructions under `entry:`. The last one is a `jmp`.",
    "Type the name after `jmp` in the answer box (it starts with `sub_`).",
]
spotlight = "view.Disassembly"
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["sub_140016224", "0x140016224", "140016224"] }
hints = [

[[steps]]
title = "How ORRESS finds main"
goal = "See the pointer to main in the generated function."
text = '''
Now look at the function in the middle: `rust_runtime_main`, the one rustc generated. It
is short. The interesting instruction is:

```text
lea      rax,[main]
```

`lea` means *load effective address*: it computes an address and puts it in a register,
without reading memory (Level 1). Here the address is the start of your `main`. The
function stores that pointer on the stack and calls the standard library's `lang_start`
(a `sub_` function), exactly like the Rust sketch in the previous step:
`std::rt::lang_start(your_main, argc, argv)`.

ORRESS saw that pattern and named the target `main`. That is how it can find your `main`
in a program without any names.

What does `rust_runtime_main` do with your `main`?
'''
instructions = [
    "Click inside the disassembly and press **Ctrl+G**.",
    "Type `rust_runtime_main` and press **Enter**.",
    "Find the line `lea rax,[main]` and look at what happens to `rax` and which function is called after it.",
]
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "It puts the address of main in a register, stores it, and passes it to another function that calls main later",
    "It calls main directly with a call instruction",
    "It copies the machine code of main to another place",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. main is called later, by lang_start in the standard library, through that pointer.",
    "There is no `call main` here. The call goes to a standard-library function, which gets main's address as an argument.",
    "lea only computes an address. Nothing is copied.",
] }
hints = [
    "`lea` loads an address, not the bytes at that address.",
    "Look at the `call` near the end of the function: it is not `call main`.",
]

id = "l2-naming"
level = 2
order = 4
title = "Making code readable: names and comments"
summary = "Rename functions as you understand them, leave comments, and why naming as you go is the core habit of reverse engineering."
goals = [
    "rename a function with N, and see the name appear in every view",
    "work out what a small function does and give it a fitting name",
    "add a comment with ; to record a fact you found",
    "use names as hypotheses that you improve as you learn more",

[[steps]]
title = "Code without names"
goal = "Feel why generated names slow you down."
text = '''
Imagine reading this Rust code:

```rust
fn sub_1400012f0(a1: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if a1.len() != 6 { return false; }
    if a1[0] != b'K' { return false; }
    sub_1400012c0(a1) == 500
}
```

And now this:

```rust
fn is_valid(code: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if code.len() != 6 { return false; }
    if code[0] != b'K' { return false; }
    checksum(code) == 500
}
```

Same code, but the second one you understand at a glance. A stripped program is the first
version, times four hundred functions. Every `sub_` name is a small puzzle your brain has
to solve again each time it sees it.

The fix is the single most important habit in reverse engineering: **as soon as you
understand something, give it a name**. Once you rename `sub_1400012f0` to `is_valid`,
every call to it, in every view, reads `is_valid`. You never solve the same puzzle twice,
and the program slowly turns from machine code into something that reads like source.

In this lesson you name the two functions you found in crackme #10 and leave a comment
for your future self.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Open crackme #10"
goal = "Have the practice program open."
text = '''
Names and comments belong to one file. ORRESS saves them for you automatically, in its
own configuration folder, linked to the exact file (by its SHA-256 hash). The program file
itself is never changed. Close ORRESS, open the same file next week, and your names are
still there.

Open crackme #10 with the button.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Read the helper"
goal = "Work out what sub_1400012c0 does from its instructions."
text = '''
`is_valid` calls one helper, `sub_1400012c0`. Before you can name it, you have to know
what it does. Here is the whole function (you can also see it with **Ctrl+G** `1400012c0`):

```text
sub_1400012c0:
  push  rax
  xor   eax,eax            ; eax = 0            (the result)
  test  rdx,rdx            ; is the length 0?
  je    loc_1400012eb      ;   then return 0
  lea   r8,[rsp+7]
  xor   r9d,r9d            ; r9 = 0             (the index i)
loc_1400012d0:
  movzx r10d,byte ptr [rcx+r9]  ; r10 = code[i]
  mov   [rsp+7],r10b       ; (a black_box detour through the stack)
  movzx r10d,byte ptr [rsp+7]
  add   eax,r10d           ; result += code[i]
  inc   r9                 ; i += 1
  cmp   rdx,r9             ; i == length?
  jne   loc_1400012d0      ;   no: loop again
loc_1400012eb:
  pop   rcx
  ret                      ; return result (in eax)
```

It gets a slice (pointer in `rcx`, length in `rdx`), starts a result at 0, and walks over
every byte, adding it to the result. In Rust:

```rust
fn sub_1400012c0(code: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    let mut sum = 0;
    for &b in code { sum += b as u32; }
    sum
}
```

What does this function compute?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The sum of all byte values of the code: a checksum",
    "The length of the code",
    "Whether the code is equal to a stored password",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. It adds every byte to eax and returns it. A number computed from data like this is called a checksum.",
    "The length is already in rdx when the function starts. The loop adds the bytes themselves (add eax, r10d).",
    "There is no second string and no compare between bytes: only an add in a loop.",
] }
hints = [
    "Look at what happens to eax inside the loop.",
    "`add eax, r10d` with r10 = one byte of the code.",
]

[[steps]]

A number computed from data to check it, like the sum of its bytes, is called a

This time rename it from a *call*: put the cursor on the line `call sub_1400012c0` inside
`is_valid` and press **N**. Because that line contains an address, **N** renames the

After the rename, look at `is_valid` again. It now reads like a sentence: `call checksum`,

converter below: it is the value every valid code must add up to.

instructions = [

    "Press **N**, check that the window says **Rename 0x1400012c0**, type `checksum` and press **Enter**.",

[[steps]]

Good comments say **why** or **what it means**, not what the instruction already says:

| Weak comment | Good comment |
|---|---|
| `compare eax with 0x1f4` | `checksum must be 500` |

Write a comment on the checksum comparison in `is_valid`.

[[steps]]
title = "Names are hypotheses"
goal = "Learn how professionals name things they only partly understand."
text = '''
You will often see a function and only *guess* what it does. Name it anyway. A guess you
write down is better than a guess you forget. Mark how sure you are:

- `maybe_parse_number` or `parse_number?` for a guess (ORRESS allows `?` in names);
- `check_password` when you are sure;
- `unk_big_loop` (unknown) for "I looked, it is big, I did not understand it yet";
- `std_memcpy`, `std_alloc` for library helpers you recognised: you know you can skip them.

When you learn more, rename again. A name is not a promise; it is your current best
understanding.

Labels inside a function can have names too. Put the cursor on a label line such as
`loc_140001297:` in `main` and press **N**: a name like `fail` turns every
`je loc_140001297` into `je fail`. Try it if you like; it is not needed for this step.

A last tip: work **from the known outward**. Start with what you are sure of (the strings,
the imports, `main`), name it, and use those names to understand the code around them.
Each name makes the next one easier.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Names are not only for you. ORRESS can share them with your team in real time (the
**Collaboration** panel, View > Open View > Collaboration), so a team at a CTF can split
a big program and still see each other's names. The Assistant and scripts also see your
names, which makes their answers better.
'''
