`academy/lessons/03-07-emulation.toml`:

```toml
id = "l3-emulation"
level = 3
order = 7
title = "Emulation"
summary = "Run one function on a simulated CPU inside ORRESS. Feed crackme #2's check the password and read its yes/no answer, with no real execution and no operating system."
badge = "CPU Whisperer"
goals = [
    "say what an emulator is and how it differs from a debugger",
    "name the kind of code emulation is best for",
    "run a single function in the Emulator with an input you choose",
    "read the function's return value from RAX",
    "know the emulator's limits",
]

[[steps]]
title = "Running on a simulated CPU"
goal = "Understand what an emulator does."
text = '''
A debugger runs the program on your **real** processor. An **emulator** runs it on a **simulated** one: a CPU built in software that reads the machine code and carries out each instruction itself. ORRESS has one built in. You met a simple version in Level 1, the CPU simulator; the emulator is the same idea for real x86-64 code from a file.

Why fake the CPU when you could just run the program? Because an emulator can run **just a piece** of it. You point it at a single function, hand it some inputs, and read exactly what it produces, without launching the whole program, without its files or network, and without even needing the same operating system the program was built for.

For understanding one routine, a decoder, a hash, a password check, that isolation is a superpower. You saw it already in the last-but-one lesson, where you ran crackme #11's builder on its own and read the decoded password out of the scratch buffer. This lesson looks at the tool itself.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Emulation next to debugging"
goal = "Compare the two ways of running code."
text = '''
You now know both ways to run code. They complement each other:

- **A debugger** runs the **whole program** on the **real** CPU and OS. It is the real thing: real input, real behaviour, real side effects. It needs the right operating system (Windows, for these crackmes), and anything the program does really happens.
- **An emulator** runs **one piece** on a **simulated** CPU, inside ORRESS. Nothing it does reaches your computer: system calls are intercepted, not performed, so no file, network or registry is touched. It runs the same on any operating system, because it never asks the real one to do anything.

Three things fall out of that:

- **No environment needed.** Run a Windows function on Linux, or code for another setup, without that setup.
- **No real side effects.** Running a snippet cannot harm your machine.
- **Deterministic and fully visible.** Same inputs, same result, every time, and you can read every register and byte afterwards.

The trade-off: the emulator models a **subset** of instructions and almost none of the operating system. A whole GUI app that makes thousands of OS calls will not "just run". Emulation shines on **self-contained computation**.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "What is it good for?"
goal = "Pick the emulator's sweet spot."
text = '''
Given those strengths and limits, what is the emulator best at?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "Running one self-contained routine on inputs you choose, to see exactly what it computes",
    "Making the whole program run faster than it normally would",
    "Building the program from its source code",
    "Replacing the debugger for a full-screen GUI application",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. Feed a decoder, hash or check function an input and read precisely what it returns or writes, with no environment to set up.",
    "A simulated CPU is slower than the real one, not faster. Speed is not the point; isolation and control are.",
    "The emulator runs existing machine code; it does not compile source. Compiling is the opposite direction.",
    "A GUI app makes thousands of OS calls the emulator does not model. It is for self-contained routines, not whole interactive programs.",
] }
hints = [
    "Think about the one-function-in-isolation strength, not whole-program execution.",
    "Feed a routine an input and read its output, with no environment to set up.",
]
success = '''
The emulator is for running a self-contained routine on chosen inputs and reading exactly what it produces. Now use it on crackme #2's password check.
'''

[[steps]]

'''

[[steps]]
title = "Workflow and limits"
goal = "Know when to reach for the emulator and when not to."
text = '''
Put the emulator to work:

1. **Confirm what a routine does.** Feed it an input, Run, and read **RAX** and the **Scratch buffer after run**. Returning a `bool`? Decoding bytes in place? The output tells you, without your reading every instruction.
2. **Run code you otherwise could not.** Wrong operating system, missing libraries: none of it stops the emulator from running a self-contained function. This is the Linux and macOS path through much of this level.
3. **It powers the solvers.** The same engine underlies the side-channel and symbolic solvers and the time-travel recorder you meet in later levels. Emulation is the foundation they build on.

Know the edges too. The emulator models a large but not complete set of instructions (integer, branch, stack, memory and the common SSE2 used for slice comparisons) and almost none of the OS, so heavy system calls, threads or GUI code will not run. When it cannot proceed, it stops and tells you, for example an unsupported instruction or a memory fault. Aim it at **self-contained computation** and it rarely lets you down.

So: **debugger** for the whole program on a real CPU; **emulator** for one function on a simulated CPU. Reach for whichever fits the question.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "What you can do now"
goal = "Sum up emulation."
text = '''
You can now run a function in isolation:

- open the **Emulator** (**F7**) and point it at a **function address**;
- pass an **input** (as a pointer) and, when the function needs it, its **length**;
- press **Run** and read the **return value in RAX** (its low byte `al` for a `bool`) and the **scratch buffer**;
- sweep inputs quickly, because the simulated CPU is deterministic and has no side effects;
- and run self-contained code on any operating system, while knowing the emulator's limits.

That is three ways to run code under your control: the debugger, patching, and the emulator. In the last two lessons of this level you use them against programs that try to stop you: crackme #4, which notices the debugger, and crackme #12, which stacks three such tricks.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Programs that fight back"
goal = "Know what anti-debugging is and why programs do it."
text = '''
Some programs notice when they are being debugged and **change what they do** to throw you off: they exit, take a fake path, quietly corrupt the answer, or just do nothing interesting. Crackmes do it to frustrate you; malware does it to **hide its real behaviour** from an analyst.

This is **anti-debugging**, the last core dynamic-analysis skill in this level. The tricks look intimidating, but they share one fatal weakness, and once you see it, most of them fall in a single patch.

The job is always the same two steps: **recognise** the check, then **neutralise** it.

In this lesson you take crackme #4. Run it under the debugger and it always says "Debugger detected", even when your password is right. You will find the check, find the password, and patch past the trap so you can analyse it like any other program.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "How a program spots a debugger"
goal = "Learn the common detection tricks."
text = '''
The usual ways a program detects a debugger:

- **API calls.** On Windows, `IsDebuggerPresent`, `CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent`, or `NtQueryInformationProcess` (asking for the debug port). The program just asks the operating system.
- **Reading the PEB directly.** The debugger flag lives in a structure the process owns (the Process Environment Block). A program can read the `BeingDebugged` byte there itself, with **no API call** to spot.
- **ptrace.** On Linux, a process tries to `ptrace` itself; if that fails, something else is already tracing it.
- **Timing.** Read the clock before and after a short block of code. Under a debugger that is single-stepping, the gap is huge, which gives the debugger away.
- **Breakpoint scanning.** The program checks its own code for the `0xCC` byte that a software breakpoint leaves behind.

Different mechanisms, same end: each produces a yes/no "is a debugger here?" that the program then acts on.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "The weakness they share"
goal = "See what makes every anti-debug check beatable."
text = '''
However a check detects the debugger, the result is useless to the program unless it *does something* with it. What is the weakness every anti-debug trick shares?
'''

[[steps]]
title = "An anti-debugging playbook"
goal = "Have a repeatable plan for anti-debugging."
text = '''
A plan that works on most anti-debugging:

1. **Recognise it.** Triage flags it, or the program behaves differently under a debugger than when run normally.
2. **Locate the check.** Cross-reference the anti-debug APIs, or look for a PEB read, a timing pair, or a `ptrace` call near a suspicious branch.
3. **Read the branch.** Work out which way is "detected" and which is "clean".
4. **Neutralise it.** Usually one of:
   - **Patch and go.** NOP or invert the branch so it always takes the clean path (what you just did).
   - **Change a register.** Stop after the check and set its result to "no debugger", as in the changing-registers lesson.
   - **Emulate** the routine you care about, where there is no real debugger and timing is deterministic. For crackme #4 you can run `check_password` (`0x140001100`) in the Emulator (**F7**) with `n0_debugger_here` and **pass input length** ticked: it returns `1` in `al`, confirming the password on any operating system, with no debugger for the guard to detect.
5. **Verify.** Confirm the program behaves the same debugged as not.

Watch for **stacked** checks: a program can carry several, so find them all. That is exactly the next lesson, where crackme #12 stacks three different debugger checks and hides the real password behind them. Anti-debugging is a speed bump, not a wall.

The source of crackme #4 appears below. Compare `debugger_present` and the branch in `main` with what you found and patched.
'''

[[steps]]

This is the practice lesson for the whole level. Crackme #12 does not play fair. It stacks **three different debugger checks**, and it adds a nasty twist: if any of them fires, it does not just say "detected". It silently decodes a **decoy** password instead of the real one, then always answers "Wrong". So a careless debugger session shows you a password that looks real and is not.

Everything you have learned applies. But the clever move is not to fight all three guards one by one. It is to notice which single function actually computes the password, and run just that function in a place where no guard can see you: the **Emulator**.

By the end you will have the real password and a feel for the general lesson: when a program defends itself, find the smallest piece that holds the secret and run that piece in isolation.
'''

[[steps]]

[[steps]]
title = "The three guards"
goal = "Tell the three detection methods apart."
text = '''
In the Disassembly view, `main` calls three small functions one after another, just before it decodes the password. Each is one of the detection tricks from the last lesson:

- **An API check.** It calls `IsDebuggerPresent` and asks Windows directly. Easy to spot: the call goes to an imported function by name.
- **A PEB check.** It reads `gs:[0x60]` to get the Process Environment Block, then reads the debugger flag byte itself. There is **no API call** to cross-reference; just a `mov` from `gs:[0x60]` and a byte read.
- **A timing check.** It reads a high-resolution counter before and after a short loop and compares the gap against a threshold. Under a debugger that is stepping, the gap is far too large.

The program combines all three results with `or` into a single "was I watched?" flag, and checks that flag once near the end.

Of the three, which one needs **no operating-system API call at all**, so it would not show up if you only looked at the imports?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The PEB check: it reads gs:[0x60] and the flag byte directly, calling nothing",
    "The API check: IsDebuggerPresent is not really an API",
    "The timing check: reading a counter never involves the operating system",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. Reading gs:[0x60] and the byte in the PEB is done with ordinary instructions, so there is no import to find. You have to spot it in the code.",
    "The API check is exactly the one that does call an API (IsDebuggerPresent); that is how Triage flagged the program.",
    "The timing check reads a counter through a system call (a high-resolution timer), so it does involve the operating system.",
] }
hints = [
    "Which method reads a process structure with plain instructions instead of asking Windows?",
    "gs:[0x60] is read directly; no import is involved.",
]
success = '''
The PEB check hides from the imports, because it reads the flag itself. That is why reading the code matters: a program can check for a debugger without any tell-tale API call.

[[steps]]
title = "The decoy twist"
goal = "Understand why a naive debugger session misleads you."
text = '''
Now the twist that makes guessing dangerous. Here is the shape of the end of `main`:

```text
  ... compute "watched" = guard1 OR guard2 OR guard3 ...
  mov   dl, watched
  call  decode_secret        ; decode_secret(out, decoy = watched)
  call  check_password
  test  bl, bl               ; bl = watched
  jne   wrong                ; if watched, go to "Wrong"
  test  al, al               ; al = password correct?
  je    wrong
  ...                        ; "Correct!"
```

Look at how the "watched" flag is used. It is passed to `decode_secret` as the **decoy** argument. So if any guard fired, the program decodes the **wrong** password and *also* takes the "Wrong" branch. If you run this under the debugger and read the decoded buffer in memory (as you did in lesson 4), you will read the **decoy**, not the real password, and never know the difference.

That is why patching just the final `jne` is not enough here: by the time you reach it, `decode_secret` has already built the decoy. You would have to defeat all three guards *before* the decode, so that `watched` is 0 and the real password is produced.

There is a much simpler way.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Beat them all with the Emulator"
goal = "Recover the real password without triggering any guard."
text = '''
The guards only run in `main`. The function that actually builds the password, `decode_secret`, does not check anything: it just decodes. Its second argument decides which password to build, the real one (`decoy = 0`) or the decoy (`decoy = 1`).

So run `decode_secret` on its own in the **Emulator**. No `main`, no guards, and you control the decoy argument. `decode_secret` is at `0x140001190`. The Emulator passes your **Input** as the first argument (the output buffer) and, only if you tick **pass input length**, the length as the second argument. Leave that box **unticked**, and the second argument is `0`: `decoy = 0`, the **real** password.

Open the Emulator (**F7**), set the **Function address** to `0x140001190`, type sixteen characters as the **Input** (for example `AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA`, so the scratch buffer is sixteen bytes long), leave **pass input length as arg1** unticked, and press **Run**. The **Scratch buffer after run** line shows the real password.

Type the password it reveals.
'''
instructions = [

]

'''

[[steps]]
title = "Level 3 complete"
goal = "Look back at what you can do now."
text = '''
That is the end of Dynamic Analysis. You can now:

- **watch a program run** and know when it is safe to;
- **drive the debugger**: start, breakpoints, stepping, registers, flags, stack and memory;
- **read secrets at runtime** that are nowhere in the file;
- **change a running program** by setting a register to steer a branch;
- **patch** a program's bytes and save a copy that behaves the new way;
- **emulate** a single function on a simulated CPU, on any operating system;
- **beat anti-debugging**, including stacked guards and a decoy, by recognising the checks and either neutralising the branch or sidestepping it entirely.

The deepest habit of this level is the one you just used: **know what you are looking for, find the smallest piece that holds it, and run that piece where nothing can interfere.** A debugger, a patch and an emulator are three ways to do that.

Level 4 moves from cracking single programs to the CTF workflow: encodings, the Workbench, recognising crypto, and automatic solvers that build on the very emulator you used here.

The source of crackme #12 appears below. Read the three guard functions and the decoy logic in `main`, and see how closely the code matches what you worked out.
'''

```

You can now read assembly, use the decompiler, run a program under the debugger, patch it and emulate a single function. That is a full toolbox. This level teaches you to use it on **CTF** challenges, the way people practise reverse engineering all over the world.

**CTF** stands for **Capture The Flag**. It is a competition (or a practice website) with many small puzzles called *challenges*. Each challenge hides a secret text, the **flag**. When you find the flag, you type it into the website and you get points.

Challenges come in categories. The ones in this course belong to the **reversing** category (often called "rev" or "RE"): you get a program, and the flag is hidden inside it. Usually the program asks for a password or a key, and the flag is that password, or the program prints the flag once you give the right input.

Other categories you will meet on CTF websites:

- **crypto**: break a cipher (you will learn to *recognise* ciphers in this level),
- **pwn**: find a bug in a program and use it to take control,
- **web**: attack a web site,
- **forensics**: find data hidden in files, disk images or network captures.

Reversing skills help in all of them, because every category ends with "understand what this code does".

Many CTF websites keep their challenges online all year, so you can practise any time. This level gives you the skills for intermediate challenges: decoding hidden text, recognising cryptography, letting a solver find a password for you, and reading programs that are not machine code at all.
'''
success = "Let's look at what a flag looks like, so you recognise one the moment you see it."

[[steps]]
title = "What a flag looks like"
goal = "Recognise the usual flag formats."
text = '''
Most CTFs use a fixed **flag format**: a short prefix, curly braces, and a secret inside. For example:

```text
flag{x0r_is_not_encrypti0n}
CTF{this_one_is_from_a_big_event}
picoCTF{some_letters_and_digits}
```

The prefix tells you which event the flag belongs to. The part between the braces is usually lowercase letters, digits and underscores, with letters often swapped for digits that look alike: `0` for `o`, `1` for `i` or `l`, `3` for `e`, `4` for `a`. That style is called "leetspeak". It makes flags hard to guess but easy to read once you have them.

Why does the format matter to a reverse engineer?

1. **It tells you when you are done.** Text that starts with `flag{` and ends with `}` is almost certainly the answer.
2. **It is a known piece of the secret.** If a program hides the flag, you already know its first five characters: `f`, `l`, `a`, `g`, `{`. In the next lesson you will use exactly this to break an XOR key.
3. **Tools can search for it.** ORRESS's Strings view and Workbench mark text that looks like a flag.

Some challenges do not use a format at all: the flag is just "the password the program accepts". The practice programs in this Academy are like that. Their passwords are the flags.
'''

    "flag{w3_l0v3_r3v3rs1ng}",

[[steps]]
title = "The plan that solves most challenges"
goal = "Learn a fixed order of work, so you never wonder what to do next."
text = '''
Experienced players do not start by reading every instruction. They follow the same plan every time:

1. **Look around.** Open the program and read the **Info** view (what kind of file is it?), the **Strings** view (messages, URLs, suspicious text) and the **Imports** (which library functions does it use?). Ten minutes here often saves hours.
2. **Find the check.** Search the strings for the success and failure messages ("Correct!", "Wrong"), jump to the code that uses them, and find the `if` that decides between them. The function that computes that condition is the **check function**.
3. **Understand the transformation.** Read the check function in the decompiler. What does it do to your input before it compares? Nothing (a plain compare)? An XOR? Arithmetic? A real cipher?
4. **Choose your attack.** The answer to step 3 picks the tool:
   - a plain compare: read the expected value (Level 1);
   - a reversible transformation such as XOR: undo it by hand or write a keygen (Level 2);
   - a check you cannot read easily: run it in the emulator or debugger and watch (Level 3);
   - many tangled conditions: let a **solver** compute the input (this level);
   - a byte-by-byte compare with an early exit: a **side channel** (this level);
   - a known cipher: find the key and decrypt (this level).
5. **Verify.** Give your answer to the real program. It must say "Correct!".

Notice step 3. Most of this level is about recognising *what kind* of transformation you are looking at, because that decides everything after it.
'''
success = "Keep this plan in mind. Every practice program in this level follows it."

[[steps]]
title = "Pick the attack"
goal = "Match a check to the right tool."
text = '''
Here is a check function, as the decompiler might show it in Rust syntax:

```rust
fn check(input: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if input.len() != 6 {
        return false;
    }
    let key = [0x10, 0x20, 0x30, 0x10, 0x20, 0x30];
    let expected = [0x63, 0x13, 0x53, 0x62, 0x13, 0x44];
    for i in 0..6 {
        if input[i] ^ key[i] != expected[i] {
            return false;
        }
    }
    true
}
```

Each input byte is XORed with a key byte and compared with an expected byte. You learned in Level 2 that XOR undoes itself: if `a ^ k == e`, then `a == e ^ k`. So every byte of the password can be computed directly from two numbers you can see.
'''

], correct = 0, explain = [

Use the same check function as in the previous step:

```rust
let key = [0x10, 0x20, 0x30, 0x10, 0x20, 0x30];

// accepted when input[i] ^ key[i] == expected[i] for every i
```

Because XOR undoes itself, `input[i] = expected[i] ^ key[i]`. Here is the first character worked out completely:

- `expected[0]` is `0x63`, `key[0]` is `0x10`.
- In binary: `0110 0011` XOR `0001 0000`. XOR gives 1 where the bits differ: `0111 0011`.
- `0111 0011` is `0x73`, which is 115 in decimal: the ASCII code of `s`.

So the password starts with `s`. Now do the other five positions the same way. The **Number converter** below shows a number in hex, decimal and binary, and the **ASCII table** in Level 0 maps codes to characters (`0x30` to `0x39` are the digits `0` to `9`, `0x61` to `0x7a` are the lowercase letters `a` to `z`).

[[steps]]
title = "Disguised data: three different things"
goal = "Tell encoding, encryption and hashing apart."
text = '''
Programs that hide a flag transform it. There are three very different kinds of transformation, and beginners mix them up all the time:

| | What it does | Needs a secret key? | Can you get the original back? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Encoding** | Writes the same data in another form, e.g. as hex digits or base64 text | No | Yes, always |
| **Encryption** | Scrambles data with a **key**, so only someone with the key can read it | Yes | Yes, *with the key* |
| **Hashing** | Computes a short fingerprint of the data | No | No, never |

Think of them in Rust terms:

- **Encoding** is like `format!("{:02x}", byte)`: a different way to write the same value. Anyone who knows the format can read it back. Base64, hex and URL encoding are encodings. They hide *nothing*; they only make data look unreadable at first sight.
- **Encryption** is like a lock: `encrypt(data, key)` gives scrambled bytes, and only `decrypt(scrambled, key)` gives the data back. AES, RC4 and TEA are encryption algorithms. In a program the key must be *somewhere*, so a reverse engineer can often find it.
- **Hashing** is like a fingerprint: `sha256(data)` always gives the same 32 bytes for the same input, but you cannot turn those 32 bytes back into the input. MD5 and SHA-256 are hash functions. A program that hashes your password and compares the result never needs to store the password itself.

So the first question about any strange-looking data is: *which of the three is this?* The next two lessons teach you to answer it.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Simple "ciphers" like ROT13 (shift every letter 13 places) or XOR with a fixed byte sit between encoding and encryption. Technically they use a key (the shift, the XOR byte), but the key is so small that you can try every possible one in a fraction of a second. CTF players treat them like encodings: something to peel off, not something to break.
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "Encoding (for example base64): anyone can decode it, no key needed",
    "Encryption (for example AES): you need the key",
    "Hashing (for example SHA-256): it cannot be reversed",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. A flag that was only base64-encoded is hidden from a quick glance, but anyone can decode it in a second. That is why encoding is not protection.",
    "Encryption does need a key. But the question asks which one needs no key at all to undo.",
    "Hashing cannot be undone at all, with or without a key, so it is not the answer either.",
] }
hints = [
    "Which row of the table says 'No' for the key and 'Yes, always' for getting the data back?",
]
success = "Encoding needs no key. When you meet data that looks random, try decoding it before you think about breaking anything."

[[steps]]

goal = "Use the properties of each kind to pick an attack."

Two challenges, side by side.

**Challenge A** contains this Rust logic (as the decompiler shows it):

let digest = sha256(input);
if digest == [0x5e, 0x88, 0x48, 0x98, /* ... 28 more bytes ... */] {

let plain = aes_decrypt(STORED_BYTES, KEY);
if input == plain {
    println!("Correct!");
}
```

In challenge B, the program itself decrypts the secret with a key it carries. Everything needed to read the flag is inside the program: the stored bytes and the key. You can find both and decrypt them yourself, or stop the program in the debugger right after `aes_decrypt` and read `plain` from memory.

In challenge A, the program only keeps a fingerprint. Nobody can turn a SHA-256 fingerprint back into the input. Your only way in is to *guess* inputs, hash each guess and compare. That works when the password is short or is a common word (a list of common passwords is called a dictionary), and it is hopeless for a long random flag.

Which challenge can you solve without guessing?
'''

    "You do not need source code. The program contains the data and the code that uses it, and that is enough.",
] }

    "Encryption can be undone with the key. Hashing cannot be undone.",
]

`academy/lessons/04-02-encodings-workbench.toml`:

```toml
id = "l4-encodings"
level = 4
order = 24
title = "Encodings and the Workbench"
summary = "Hex, base64, ROT13 and XOR: how they work, how to spot them, and how to peel them off in ORRESS's Workbench."
goals = [
    "explain how hex and base64 turn bytes into text",
    "recognise base64, ROT13 and XOR-scrambled data",
    "decode data with a Workbench recipe",
    "recover an XOR key from a known start such as flag{",
    "let Magic find a chain of decodings for you",
]
badge = "Decoder Ring"

[[steps]]
title = "Why programs disguise text"
goal = "Understand why a flag is rarely stored as plain text."
text = '''
In Level 1 you found passwords with the **Strings** view: the password was stored as plain text, so it showed up in the list. Challenge authors know that too. So they disguise the flag before they put it in the program, and the program undoes the disguise at run time (or disguises your input the same way and compares).

The cheapest disguise is an **encoding**: the same bytes written in a different form. Here is the idea in Rust:

```rust
let secret = "flag{hi}";
let disguised = to_base64(secret);   // "ZmxhZ3toaX0="
// The program stores only "ZmxhZ3toaX0=".
// At run time it calls from_base64 and compares with your input.
```

In the Strings view you would now see `ZmxhZ3toaX0=`, which does not look like a flag at all. But anyone who recognises base64 can decode it in a second. Encodings are not protection, they only stop a quick glance.

In this lesson you learn the four disguises you will meet most often in CTFs:

1. **hex**: every byte written as two hex digits,
2. **base64**: bytes written with 64 safe characters,
3. **ROT13**: every letter shifted 13 places in the alphabet,
4. **XOR** with a short key.

For each one you learn how it works, how to recognise it, and how to undo it in ORRESS's **Workbench**, a tool that chains decoding steps together.
'''
success = "Let's start with the one you already know from Level 0: hex."

[[steps]]
title = "Hex as text"
goal = "Decode hex digits back into characters."
text = '''
You know hexadecimal from Level 0: one byte is two hex digits, from `00` to `ff`. When a program writes bytes as hex **text**, each byte becomes two characters. The byte `0x66` becomes the two characters `6` and `6`.

So the 4-byte text `flag` becomes the 8-character text `666c6167`:

| character | `f` | `l` | `a` | `g` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASCII code (hex) | `66` | `6c` | `61` | `67` |

**How to recognise hex text:** it uses only the digits `0`-`9` and the letters `a`-`f` (or `A`-`F`), its length is even, and it is often split into pairs by spaces. A long string like `0c0b5df889a72f01` is almost certainly hex.

**How to decode it:** split it into pairs, turn each pair into a byte, and read the bytes as ASCII. Try it on this one:

```text
72 33 76
```
'''
instructions = [
    "Look up each pair in the ASCII table below: `72`, then `33`, then `76`.",
    "Type the three characters into the answer box and press **Check**.",
]
widget = "ascii_table"
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["r3v"], case_sensitive = true }
hints = [
    "0x30 to 0x39 are the digits 0 to 9, so 0x33 is a digit.",
    "0x72 is r and 0x76 is v.",
    "The answer is r3v.",
]
success = "`r3v`. Hex text doubles the size of the data and uses only 16 different characters. Those two facts give it away."

[[steps]]
title = "How base64 works"
goal = "Understand why base64 text looks the way it does."
text = '''
Hex is wasteful: two characters per byte. **Base64** packs data more tightly. It uses 64 different characters, the **alphabet**:

```text
A-Z  (values 0-25)   a-z  (26-51)   0-9  (52-61)   +  (62)   /  (63)
```

64 is 2 to the power 6, so each character carries exactly **6 bits**. Base64 takes the input **3 bytes at a time** (3 x 8 = 24 bits) and cuts those 24 bits into **4 pieces of 6 bits**. Each piece is a number from 0 to 63, which picks one character.

Worked example: the text `Man`.

1. The bytes: `M` = `0x4d`, `a` = `0x61`, `n` = `0x6e`.
2. In bits: `01001101 01100001 01101110`.
3. Cut into four 6-bit groups: `010011 010110 000101 101110`.
4. As numbers: 19, 22, 5, 46.
5. Look them up: 19 = `T`, 22 = `W`, 5 = `F`, 46 = `u`.

So `Man` becomes `TWFu`. Every 3 bytes become 4 characters.

When the input length is not a multiple of 3, the last group is padded and the output ends with one or two `=` signs. That is why base64 text so often ends in `=` or `==`.

**How to recognise base64:** only the characters `A-Z a-z 0-9 + /`, a length that is a multiple of 4, and maybe `=` at the end. Text starting with `Zmxh` is a gift: it is base64 for `fla`, the start of `flag{`.
'''
deep_dive = '''
In Rust you would write the core of a base64 encoder like this:

```rust
const ALPHABET: &[u8; 64] =
    b"ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/";

fn encode3(b: [u8; 3]) -> [u8; 4] {
    let n = (b[0] as u32) << 16 | (b[1] as u32) << 8 | b[2] as u32;
    [
        ALPHABET[(n >> 18 & 63) as usize],
        ALPHABET[(n >> 12 & 63) as usize],
        ALPHABET[(n >> 6 & 63) as usize],
        ALPHABET[(n & 63) as usize],
    ]
}
```

When you see a 64-byte table like `ALPHABET` in a program's data, the program contains its own base64 code. Some challenges use a *shuffled* alphabet so that normal decoders fail. The Workbench's **From base64** step has an `alphabet` field for exactly that case: copy the program's table into it.
'''
success = "Three bytes in, four characters out. Keep that ratio in mind for the next question."

[[steps]]
title = "Base64 by the numbers"
goal = "Use the 3-to-4 rule."
text = '''
Base64 turns every group of **3 bytes** into **4 characters**. When the input fills whole groups exactly, there is no `=` padding at the end.

A program stores a 24-byte flag as base64 text. 24 bytes is exactly 8 groups of 3 bytes.

How many characters long is the base64 text?
'''
instructions = [
    "Count the groups: 24 bytes divided by 3 bytes per group.",
    "Multiply the number of groups by 4 characters per group.",
    "Type the result and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["32"], number = true }

    "24 / 3 = 8 groups.",

The Workbench has three columns:

1. **Operations** (left): every step you can add, grouped into categories such as *Encoding*, *Text*, *Bitwise*, *Crypto* and *Hashes*. A search box at the top filters the list. Click an operation to add it to the end of the recipe. Hover over it to read what it does.
2. **Recipe** (middle): the steps, top to bottom. Each step has a tick box (untick it to skip the step), `^` and `v` to move it, `x` to remove it, and fields for its settings, such as a key. Below the steps, **As text** shows the same recipe as one line, for example `from_base64 | rot13`, and the **Clear** button removes all steps.
3. **Input and Output** (right): type or paste the data into the **Input** box. The **text / hex** switch says whether you type characters or hex bytes. The **Output** box shows the result after all steps, and says **This looks like a flag!** when it finds one. The **Magic** button at the bottom tries to find a recipe for you.

Open it now.
'''
instructions = [

[[steps]]
title = "ROT13: shifting letters"
goal = "Undo a letter-shift cipher."
text = '''
**ROT13** ("rotate by 13") replaces every letter with the letter 13 places further in the alphabet, wrapping around from `z` to `a`. Digits, punctuation and braces stay as they are.

```text
a b c d e f g h i j k l m      (letters 0-12)
n o p q r s t u v w x y z      (letters 13-25)
```

So `a` becomes `n`, `f` becomes `s`, and `n` becomes `a` again. The alphabet has 26 letters, so shifting by 13 twice brings every letter back: **ROT13 undoes itself**. In Rust:

```rust
fn rot13(c: char) -> char {
    match c {
        'a'..='z' => (((c as u8 - b'a' + 13) % 26) + b'a') as char,
        'A'..='Z' => (((c as u8 - b'A' + 13) % 26) + b'A') as char,
        _ => c,
    }
}
```

**How to recognise ROT13:** the text keeps the shape of the original (same length, braces and underscores in the same places), but the words are nonsense. `flag{` becomes `synt{`. When you see `synt{`, think ROT13.

ROT13 is a special case of the **Caesar cipher**, which shifts by any amount. The Workbench has both: **ROT13** and **Caesar shift** (with a `shift` setting), in the *Text* category.

Decode this one:

```text
synt{ebg13_vf_whfg_n_fuvsg}
```
'''
instructions = [
    "Copy the string above with the copy icon of its grey box.",
    "In the Workbench, click **Clear** in the middle column.",
    "In the left column, search for `rot` and click **ROT13**.",
    "Click into the **Input** box, press `Ctrl+A`, then `Ctrl+V`.",
    "Type the flag from the **Output** box into the answer box and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "secret", sha256 = "cb4a012c5138f0733609e8e69811c04a6401dd04264b517c365cf41140cbfbca" }

    "If the output still says synt{, the recipe is empty or the step is unticked.",

]
success = "ROT13 hides text from a human reader for about two seconds. Like base64 it needs no key: knowing the method is enough."

[[steps]]
title = "XOR and the known start"
goal = "Recover an XOR key from the text you know the flag starts with."
text = '''
You met XOR in Level 2: `a ^ k` flips the bits of `a` where `k` has a 1, and XOR with the same `k` again gives `a` back. Programs often XOR a flag with a short **repeating key**: byte 0 with key byte 0, byte 1 with key byte 1, and so on, starting over when the key runs out.

```rust
fn xor(data: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    data.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, b)| b ^ key[i % key.len()]).collect()
}
```

If you know the key, decoding is the same function again. But what if you do not know the key?

Here is the trick. You know the flag starts with `flag{`. XOR has a third useful property: `plain ^ key == cipher` means `cipher ^ plain == key`. So XOR the first scrambled bytes with `f`, `l`, `a`, `g`, `{` and the key falls out.

Worked example with the first byte below: `0x25 ^ 0x66` (the code of `f`) = `0x43`, which is the character `C`. That is the first key byte.

This kind of attack is called a **known-plaintext attack**: knowing part of the original text reveals the key. The Workbench automates it with the operation **XOR key from known text**. It tries every key length up to the length of the known text, finds the key, decrypts, and prints the key on the first output line.

Here is a flag XORed with a short key, written as hex:

```text
25 38 27 24 2f 2d 2d 64 31 2d 0b 36 2f 60 77 2d 20 75 3b 20 19 34 65 28 30 29
```

What is the key?
'''
instructions = [

    "Check that the `known` field of the XOR step says `flag{` (that is the default).",

[[steps]]
title = "Chains and Magic"
goal = "Let the Workbench find a recipe for you."
text = '''
Challenge authors like to stack disguises: ROT13 first, then base64 on top, or XOR, then hex. You undo them in **reverse order**: the last disguise added is the first one you remove. In Rust terms:

```rust
let stored = to_base64(rot13(flag));   // ROT13 first, base64 on top
let flag   = rot13(from_base64(stored)); // undo base64 first, then ROT13
```

You could try combinations by hand, but the Workbench has a button for it: **Magic**. Magic tries the common decodings (hex, base64, base32, URL, zlib, gzip, XOR with one byte, ROT13, UTF-16 and more) in chains of up to 3 steps. It scores each result by how readable it is and lists the best ones, each with its recipe, a preview, and the reason it was chosen ("looks like a flag!", "readable text"). Click **Use** next to a result to load its recipe.

Magic does not know the program. It only looks at the data, so it is a starting point: always check that the result makes sense.

Try it on this stacked disguise:

```text
c3ludHt6NHQxcF9zMWFxZl9ndTNfcHU0MWF9
```
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Recognising disguises: a summary"
goal = "Have a checklist for strange-looking data."
text = '''
When a challenge gives you strange text, or the Strings view shows something odd, go through this list:

| You see | It is probably | Undo it with |
|---|---|---|
| only `0-9 a-f`, even length, maybe pairs with spaces | hex | **From hex** |
| `A-Z a-z 0-9 + /`, length a multiple of 4, maybe `=` at the end; starts with `Zmxh` | base64 | **From base64** |
| uppercase and `2-7` only, `=` padding | base32 | **From base32** |
| `%41%42` | URL encoding | **URL decode** |
| `synt{`, words of the right length but nonsense | ROT13 | **ROT13** |
| random-looking bytes, and you know how the text starts | XOR with a short key | **XOR key from known text** |
| random-looking bytes, one-byte key suspected | XOR with one byte | **XOR brute force** |
| bytes starting `78 9c` or `1f 8b` | zlib or gzip compression | **Zlib decompress**, **Gzip decompress** |
| none of the above | maybe real encryption | the next lesson |

You can also run every recipe outside the app. The **Copy as command** button under the recipe copies a command for `orress-cli`, ORRESS's command-line tool, for example `orress-cli recipe "from_base64 | rot13" FILE`, and `orress-cli magic FILE` runs Magic on a file. That is handy when you have many files to decode.

And if Magic finds nothing readable, the data may be truly encrypted. Encrypted data looks random, and its **entropy** (a measure of randomness from 0 to 8, which the Workbench shows under the output) is close to 8. That is the topic of the next lesson.
'''
success = "You can now peel off every common encoding. Next: real ciphers, and how to recognise them inside a program."

```toml

[[steps]]
title = "The words of cryptography"
goal = "Learn the five words every crypto challenge uses."
text = '''
**Cryptography** is the science of hiding information so that only the right people can read it. You do not need its mathematics to reverse engineer it. You need its vocabulary and the ability to recognise its algorithms.

A **cipher** is an algorithm that encrypts and decrypts. In Rust terms, every cipher looks like this:

```rust
fn encrypt(plaintext: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>;   // gives the ciphertext
fn decrypt(ciphertext: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>;  // gives the plaintext back
```

- The **plaintext** is the readable data, for example the flag.
- The **ciphertext** is the scrambled result. Without the key it looks like random bytes.
- The **secret key** is the input that controls the scrambling. Same plaintext, different key: completely different ciphertext.

Modern ciphers are public. Everybody knows exactly how AES works; its security comes only from the key. For you as a reverse engineer that is great news:

1. If you can **name** the algorithm, you do not have to understand its code. A tested implementation already exists, for example in the Workbench.
2. A program that decrypts something must have the **key** somewhere: in its data, computed by its code, or typed by the user.

So the job is: recognise the algorithm, find the key, find the ciphertext, decrypt. This lesson teaches the recognising. The next lesson does the rest on a real program.
'''
success = "Recognise, then decrypt. Never re-derive a cipher by hand."

[[steps]]
title = "Block ciphers and stream ciphers"
goal = "Know the two big families of ciphers and how they look in code."
text = '''
Ciphers come in two families.

A **block cipher** encrypts a fixed-size chunk, a *block*, at a time. AES uses 16-byte blocks, TEA uses 8-byte blocks. Longer data is cut into blocks. In code you recognise a block cipher by:

- a loop over the data in steps of 8 or 16 bytes,
- an inner loop of **rounds**: the same mixing steps repeated many times (TEA: 32 cycles, AES: 10 to 14 rounds),
- lots of shifts, XORs, additions, and sometimes a table lookup.

A **stream cipher** produces a long sequence of pseudo-random bytes from the key, the **keystream**, and XORs it with the data, byte by byte:

```rust
for i in 0..data.len() {
    out[i] = data[i] ^ keystream[i];   // the same as the XOR from the last lesson
}
```

Encryption and decryption are the same operation. RC4 and ChaCha20 are stream ciphers. You recognise them by a byte-by-byte XOR at the end, fed by a generator that keeps internal state between bytes.

Note how this connects to the last lesson: XOR with a repeating key is a stream cipher with a terrible keystream (it repeats every few bytes). A real stream cipher never repeats, so the known-plaintext trick only reveals the keystream for the bytes you know, not the key.
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "A loop that generates one byte of pseudo-random state per step and XORs it with the next data byte",
    "A loop that takes 16 bytes at a time and runs 10 rounds of mixing on each chunk",
    "A function that turns any input into exactly 32 bytes",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. One keystream byte per data byte, combined with XOR: that is a stream cipher such as RC4.",
    "Fixed 16-byte chunks with rounds of mixing: that is a block cipher, and 16 bytes with 10 rounds is exactly AES-128.",
    "A fixed-size output for any input is a hash function, the topic of the next step.",
] }
hints = [
    "Which option XORs a generated sequence with the data, one byte at a time?",
]
success = "Stream ciphers XOR a keystream into the data; block ciphers mix fixed-size blocks in rounds."

[[steps]]
title = "Hash functions and checksums"
goal = "Recognise hashes by the size of their output."
text = '''
A **hash function** turns input of any length into a short, fixed-size **digest**. The same input always gives the same digest, a tiny change of the input changes the digest completely, and you cannot compute the input back from the digest (it is a **one-way function**).

The common ones, with the size of their digest:

| Hash | Digest size | As hex text |
|---|---|---|
| **CRC32** | 4 bytes | 8 hex digits |
| **MD5** | 16 bytes | 32 hex digits |
| **SHA-1** | 20 bytes | 40 hex digits |
| **SHA-256** | 32 bytes | 64 hex digits |

**CRC32** is a *checksum*, not a security hash: it detects accidental damage (zip files and PNG images use it) but is easy to fool on purpose. **MD5** and **SHA-1** are old and broken for some purposes but still everywhere. **SHA-256** is the current standard.

You have seen digests already: the **Info** view shows the MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 of every file you open. The Workbench can compute them too (category *Hashes*).

The size of a digest tells you which hash it probably is. That works for a string of hex digits in the Strings view and for a byte array in the decompiler.

A program contains this hex text in its strings and compares it with something computed from your input:

```text
5baa61e4c9b93f3f0682250b6cf8331b7ee68fd8
```

Which hash is it most likely?
'''
instructions = [
    "Count the hex digits in the string (or count pairs: each pair is one byte).",
    "Look up that length in the table.",
    "Type the name of the hash (for example `MD5`) and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["SHA-1", "SHA1", "SHA 1"] }
hints = [
    "The string has 40 hex digits.",
    "40 hex digits = 20 bytes.",
    "20 bytes is the digest size of SHA-1.",
]
success = "40 hex digits, 20 bytes: SHA-1. (This one is the SHA-1 of the word `password`. Common passwords are exactly what a dictionary attack tries first.)"

[[steps]]
title = "Magic constants: the fingerprints"
goal = "Know why fixed numbers give an algorithm away."
text = '''
The best way to recognise an algorithm is by its **magic constants**: fixed numbers and tables that are part of its definition. Every implementation of the algorithm in every language contains them, and almost nothing else does. Finding one is close to proof.

Here is the TEA block cipher in Rust. Look at the first line inside the function:

```rust
fn tea_encrypt(v: &mut [u32; 2], k: &[u32; 4]) {
    const DELTA: u32 = 0x9E37_79B9;           // the fingerprint
    let (mut v0, mut v1) = (v[0], v[1]);
    let mut sum = 0u32;
    for _ in 0..32 {
        sum = sum.wrapping_add(DELTA);
        v0 = v0.wrapping_add((v1 << 4).wrapping_add(k[0]) ^ v1.wrapping_add(sum) ^ (v1 >> 5).wrapping_add(k[1]));
        v1 = v1.wrapping_add((v0 << 4).wrapping_add(k[2]) ^ v0.wrapping_add(sum) ^ (v0 >> 5).wrapping_add(k[3]));
    }
    v[0] = v0;
    v[1] = v1;
}
```

`0x9E3779B9` comes from the golden ratio. Any program that contains it almost certainly uses TEA, XTEA or a relative. The constants to remember:

| Algorithm | Magic constant | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| **TEA / XTEA** | `0x9E3779B9` (delta) | an immediate in the code |
| **MD5** | `0x67452301`, `0xEFCDAB89`, `0x98BADCFE`, `0x10325476` | start values in the code |
| **SHA-1** | the same four as MD5, plus `0xC3D2E1F0`; round constant `0x5A827999` | code |
| **SHA-256** | start values `0x6A09E667`, `0xBB67AE85`; round table starting `0x428A2F98` | code or a 256-byte table |
| **CRC32** | `0xEDB88320`, or a 1 KB table starting `00 00 00 00 96 30 07 77` | code or data |
| **AES** | the **S-box**, a 256-byte table starting `63 7C 77 7B F2 6B 6F C5` | data |
| **ChaCha20 / Salsa20** | the text `expand 32-byte k` | the Strings view |
| **RC4** | no constant, but a loop that fills a 256-byte array with 0, 1, 2, ... 255 | code |

An **S-box** ("substitution box") is a lookup table that replaces each byte with another byte: `out = SBOX[input as usize]`. Block ciphers use S-boxes to mix data in a way that is hard to undo without the key.
'''
deep_dive = '''
RC4's setup, the **key-scheduling algorithm (KSA)**, is short enough to learn by heart. In Rust:

```rust
let mut s: [u8; 256] = core::array::from_fn(|i| i as u8);   // 0, 1, 2, ... 255
let mut j = 0u8;
for i in 0..256 {
    j = j.wrapping_add(s[i]).wrapping_add(key[i % key.len()]);
    s.swap(i, j as usize);
}
```

In the disassembly this shows up as a loop that writes 0 to 255 into a buffer, followed by a loop that swaps two of its bytes 256 times. When you see those two loops, it is RC4. The Workbench's **RC4** operation decrypts it once you have the key.

Why do these constants exist? Designers pick numbers that nobody can suspect of a hidden weakness, such as digits of pi, square roots of primes, or the golden ratio. That makes them trustworthy, and it also makes them perfectly recognisable.
'''
success = "A table of magic numbers to come back to. You do not need to memorise all of them: you need to know that they exist and where to look them up."

]

To search a program for a constant, you need to know how its bytes are stored. You learned in Level 0 that x86-64 is **little-endian**: a multi-byte number is stored with its **lowest** byte first.

Worked example with CRC32's constant `0xEDB88320`:

1. Split it into bytes: `ED B8 83 20`.
2. Reverse the order: `20 83 B8 ED`.

So in the file you search for the bytes `20 83 b8 ed`.

In Rust you can check this with `0xEDB88320u32.to_le_bytes()`, which gives `[0x20, 0x83, 0xb8, 0xed]`.

Now do the same for TEA's delta, `0x9E3779B9`. Which four bytes do you search for?

[[steps]]
title = "Read the cipher's code"
goal = "Confirm the algorithm in the disassembly and the decompiler."
text = '''
Jump to the function and read it. In the **Disassembly** you will find two instructions that use the constant:

```text
mov      r11d,0x9e3779b9      ; sum = DELTA
...
add      r11d,0x9e3779b9      ; sum += DELTA, once per cycle
```

Compare with the Rust code of TEA from step 4: `sum` starts at `DELTA` (the compiler did the first `wrapping_add` for you) and grows by `DELTA` in every cycle. Between them you see the `shl ...,4` and `shr ...,5` of `(v1 << 4)` and `(v1 >> 5)`, and the XORs.

Above the loop, another register is set to the number of cycles and counts down with `dec` until it reaches zero.

How many cycles does the loop run?
'''

[[steps]]
title = "The same number, written differently"
goal = "Recognise a constant when the decompiler writes it as a subtraction."
text = '''
Now press `F5` with the cursor in this function to open the **Decompiler**. You will see a line like:

```rust
r11 = 0x9e3779b9;
...
r11 -= 0x61c88647;
```

The disassembly said `add r11d,0x9e3779b9`, but the decompiler says `-= 0x61c88647`. Both are true, because 32-bit numbers wrap around at 2^32:

```text
0x9e3779b9 + 0x61c88647 = 0x1_0000_0000  (which is 0 in 32 bits)
```

So adding `0x9e3779b9` and subtracting `0x61c88647` give the same 32-bit result. In Rust: `x.wrapping_add(0x9e3779b9) == x.wrapping_sub(0x61c88647)` for every `u32` x. This is the **two's complement** idea from Level 0: `0x61c88647` is the negative of `0x9e3779b9`.

Compilers and decompilers pick whichever form they like. So remember both forms of a constant, or convert it yourself.

Which algorithm does crackme13 use?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = ["TEA", "AES", "RC4", "SHA-256"], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. The delta 0x9E3779B9 (or 0x61C88647 subtracted), 32 cycles, shifts by 4 and 5 on two 32-bit halves of an 8-byte block: TEA.",
    "AES would show a 256-byte S-box starting 63 7C 77 7B in the data, and 16-byte blocks.",
    "RC4 has no such constant; it starts with a loop that fills 256 bytes with 0 to 255.",
    "SHA-256 would show 0x6A09E667 and a table of 64 round constants. It also cannot be decrypted, and this program encrypts.",
] }
hints = [
    "Look up 0x9E3779B9 in the table of magic constants.",
]
success = "TEA. You identified a cipher without reading its maths, from one number and a loop count."

[[steps]]
title = "From recognition to attack"
goal = "Know what to do once the algorithm has a name."
text = '''
Naming the algorithm decides the attack:

1. **A cipher with the key inside the program** (TEA, AES, RC4, XOR): find the key and the ciphertext, then decrypt them in the Workbench (**TEA decrypt**, **XTEA decrypt**, **AES decrypt**, **RC4**, **XOR**). That is the next lesson.
2. **A hash of your input compared with a stored digest** (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256): you cannot decrypt. Guess inputs instead: common passwords, short brute force, or whatever the challenge text hints at. Or patch the comparison if the challenge only needs the program to say "Correct".
3. **A custom transformation** (XOR, additions, rotations you cannot name): undo it by hand, or let the symbolic solver compute the input (two lessons ahead).

Two more places that help you recognise crypto:

- The **Imports** view. Programs that use Windows' built-in crypto import functions such as `CryptEncrypt`, `CryptDecrypt`, `BCryptEncrypt` or `BCryptDecrypt`. The **Triage** report then lists them under its capabilities and calls the file a crypto challenge. A program with its own hand-written cipher, like crackme13, imports none of these, so for it you hunt the constants yourself, as you just did.
- The **Strings** view, for text constants like `expand 32-byte k` (ChaCha20), and for keys that are stored as readable text, as you will see next.
'''
success = "Next lesson: you finish crackme13 by finding its key and decrypting the flag."

title = "A key is four numbers"

text = '''
The TEA code from the last lesson takes the key as `k: &[u32; 4]`: four 32-bit numbers, not 16 characters. The program converts the text into numbers like this (from the source, in Rust):

```rust
let mut k = [0u32; 4];
for i in 0..4 {
    k[i] = u32::from_le_bytes([key[4*i], key[4*i+1], key[4*i+2], key[4*i+3]]);
}
```

So every 4 characters become one number, **little-endian**: the first character is the lowest byte.

Worked example with the text `ABCD`: the bytes are `41 42 43 44`. Little-endian means the first byte is the lowest, so the number is `0x44434241`.

This matters because some programs read the words **big-endian** instead (first byte highest). Both versions of TEA exist in the wild, and they give different results with the same key text. The Workbench's **TEA decrypt** has an `endian` setting for exactly this reason. When decryption gives garbage, try the other setting.

2. **Find the key** by following the data into the cipher function.
3. **Find the ciphertext** where the program compares.
4. **Decrypt** with a ready-made implementation.

Harder challenges make steps 2 and 3 harder, never step 4:

- **The key is computed**, for example XORed with a constant or built from several pieces. Then run the code that builds it under the debugger and read the finished key from memory just before the cipher is called. (A breakpoint on the call to the cipher function, then read the register that holds the key pointer: `rdx` for the second argument on Windows.)
- **The ciphertext is not text** but raw bytes in the data section. Select them in the Hex view and use **Hex: Send Selection to Workbench** (`Ctrl+Shift+B`) to load them as input.

- **Modified constants**: authors sometimes change the delta or the number of rounds. Then the ready-made decryptor gives garbage, and you write a small Rust program that copies the decompiled cipher and runs it backwards.

`academy/lessons/04-05-symbolic-execution.toml`:

```toml
id = "l4-symbolic-execution"
level = 4
order = 27
title = "Symbolic execution"
summary = "Let the program solve itself: treat the input as unknowns, collect the conditions a correct input must meet, and let a solver compute it."
goals = [
    "explain concrete and symbolic execution with a Rust example",
    "turn the branches of a check function into constraints",
    "explain what an SMT solver such as z3 does",
    "solve crackme14 with the Emulator's Symbolic solve",
    "know when symbolic execution cannot help",
]
badge = "Constraint Breaker"
reveal_source = "crackme14"

[[steps]]
title = "When guessing is hopeless"
goal = "See why brute force fails for real passwords."
text = '''
Some check functions are too tangled to invert by hand. Every condition mixes several input characters, the operations are a soup of XORs, additions and rotations, and after an hour you still have no idea which input passes.

The obvious fallback is **brute force**: try every possible input until one works. How long would that take? Count the possibilities. A password of printable ASCII characters has 95 choices per character:

| Length | Possible passwords |
|---|---|
| 1 | 95 |
| 2 | 95 x 95 = 9 025 |
| 4 | 81 450 625 |
| 8 | about 6.6 x 10^15 |
| 12 | about 5.4 x 10^23 |

Each extra character multiplies the work by 95. A computer that tests a billion passwords per second needs about 77 days for 8 characters and about 17 million years for 12.

But brute force ignores something important: **you have the check function**. It describes, precisely, which inputs it accepts. Instead of asking it "is this one right?" a trillion times, you can ask a smarter question: "*what* would make you say yes?"

That is what **symbolic execution** does.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Brute force is still the right tool sometimes: for a 4-digit PIN (10 000 possibilities), or when the check is a real hash function, where nothing smarter exists. The skill is to estimate the number of possibilities first and decide.
'''
success = "Exponential growth beats any computer. You need a method that does not guess."

[[steps]]
title = "Concrete and symbolic"
goal = "Understand what it means to run code on unknowns."
text = '''
Normally a program runs with **concrete** values: real numbers. Take this check:

```rust
fn check(x: u8) -> bool {
    let t = x ^ 0x5a;
    if t == 0x15 {
        return true;
    }
    false
}
```

Run it concretely with `x = 0x41`: `t` becomes `0x41 ^ 0x5a = 0x1b`, `0x1b == 0x15` is false, the function returns `false`. You learn that `0x41` is wrong, and nothing else.

Now run it **symbolically**. Do not choose a value for `x`. Keep it as an unknown, a **symbolic variable**, like in algebra at school. Every operation then builds a formula instead of a number:

1. `t = x ^ 0x5a`: `t` is not a number now, it is the formula `x ^ 0x5a`.
2. `if t == 0x15`: we cannot decide true or false, because it depends on `x`. So we write the condition down: to take the `return true` path, `x ^ 0x5a == 0x15` must hold.

That written-down condition is a **constraint**. Every input-dependent branch on the way to "Correct!" adds one. The list of all constraints on the way to a block is the **path constraint** of that block.

Collect the constraints of the path to the success block, find values that satisfy all of them, and you have an input that reaches success. Without guessing.
'''
success = "Run on unknowns, write down the conditions, solve. Next you solve one yourself."

[[steps]]
title = "Solve a constraint by hand"
goal = "Solve the single constraint from the last step."
text = '''
The path to `return true` in the last step has one constraint:

```text
x ^ 0x5a == 0x15
```

To solve it, use the XOR rule from Level 2: XOR with the same value twice cancels out. XOR both sides with `0x5a`:

```text
x ^ 0x5a ^ 0x5a == 0x15 ^ 0x5a
x               == 0x15 ^ 0x5a
```

Compute `0x15 ^ 0x5a`. In binary: `0001 0101` XOR `0101 1010`.

(This is not a made-up example: it is the very first character of crackme03's password check, which you solved in Level 2.)
'''
instructions = [
    "Write `0x15` and `0x5a` in binary (the Number converter below shows both).",
    "XOR them bit by bit: 1 where the bits differ, 0 where they are equal.",
    "Type the result (hex with `0x`, decimal, or the character in quotes like `'A'`) and press **Check**.",
]
widget = "number_converter"
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0x4f"], number = true }
hints = [
    "0x15 = 0001 0101, 0x5a = 0101 1010.",
    "The XOR is 0100 1111.",
    "0100 1111 = 0x4f, the character 'O'.",
]
success = "`0x4f`, the character `O`. A constraint with one unknown and one XOR is easy. Real checks have many unknowns and constraints that mix them, and that is where a machine helps."

[[steps]]
title = "Solvers: z3 and friends"
goal = "Understand what an SMT solver is."
text = '''
A program that finds values satisfying a list of constraints is a **solver**. The kind used in reverse engineering is an **SMT solver** ("satisfiability modulo theories"). Ignore the long name: it means a solver that understands not only true/false logic but also *theories* such as fixed-size integers. It knows that a `u8` wraps at 256, that `<<` loses the top bits, that XOR and rotation work bit by bit.

You give it constraints, it answers one of three things:

- **sat** ("satisfiable"): here are values that make every constraint true,
- **unsat**: no values can satisfy them all (so that path can never be taken),
- **unknown**: it gave up (too hard, or out of time).

The most famous SMT solver is **z3**, from Microsoft Research. CTF players use it all the time, usually from Python. Its language for constraints is called **SMT-LIB2**. The constraint from the last step looks like this in SMT-LIB2:

```text
(declare-const x (_ BitVec 8))
(assert (= (bvxor x #x5a) #x15))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```

`BitVec 8` is an 8-bit number, a `u8`. `bvxor` is XOR. z3 answers `sat` and gives `x = #x4f`.

Solvers are not magic. Internally they search, but cleverly: they learn from every dead end and skip whole families of wrong answers at once. For the kind of constraints a crackme produces they usually finish in well under a second.
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "A list of constraints; it returns values that satisfy all of them, or says that none exist",
    "A compiled program; it returns its source code",
    "A password hash; it returns the password",
    "A list of passwords to try one by one",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. Constraints in, satisfying values (sat) or a proof that there are none (unsat) out.",
    "That would be a decompiler, and even a decompiler cannot give back the original source exactly.",
    "A real hash is a one-way function. A solver cannot invert it in any reasonable time, as you will see at the end of this lesson.",
    "That is brute force with a dictionary. A solver is exactly the thing that avoids trying candidates one by one.",
] }
hints = [
    "Think about the sat / unsat answers.",
]
success = "Constraints in, a solution out. ORRESS has its own small solver built in, and it can also export constraints for z3."

[[steps]]
title = "Meet crackme14"
goal = "Open a program that is hard to solve by hand."
text = '''
**Crackme #14** asks for a 12-character key. Its check function takes the key two characters at a time. For each pair `(a, b)` it computes two values from *both* characters and compares each with a stored byte:

```rust
let x = a ^ KA[j];        // KA: a stored key byte per pair
let y = b ^ 0x3c;
if x ^ y != MIX[j] { return 0; }
if x.rotate_left(1).wrapping_add(y) != ROT[j] { return 0; }
```

Every comparison involves two unknown characters at once. You cannot read one character off one comparison, as you could in crackme03. By hand you would have to solve six small systems of equations. (`rotate_left(1)` shifts all bits one place to the left and moves the top bit around to the bottom.)

This is exactly the situation symbolic execution is made for. Open the program.
'''
instructions = [
    "Click **Open crackme14** below.",
    "Wait until the Project panel lists the views of `crackme14.exe`.",
]
check = { kind = "open_crackme", name = "crackme14" }
hints = ["The button is directly under this text."]
success = "Before you can let ORRESS solve it, you need three addresses: the check function, its success block and its failure block."

[[steps]]
title = "Find the check function"
goal = "Locate the function that decides."
text = '''
Start in `main`, as always. In crackme14's `main` you find this near the end:

```text
cmp      rax,0xc          ; is the key 12 (0xc) characters long?

...
call     sub_1400.....    ; the check function

```

So `main` first checks the length, then calls a function and accepts the key only if that function returns `0x600d` (a hex joke: "good"). That function is the **check function**.

What is its address?
'''
instructions = [
    "Press `Ctrl+Shift+M` (Go to main) to jump to `main` in the Disassembly.",
    "Scroll down to the line `cmp eax,0x600d`.",
    "The line just above it is `call sub_1400.....`. Read the address in that name.",
    "Type it with `0x` in front and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0x1400012c0"], number = true }
hints = [
    "The call is directly above cmp eax,0x600d.",
    "The function is called sub_1400012c0.",
    "Type 0x1400012c0.",

  14000148a  ret
```

text = '''
Under the solve result there is a folded section, **SMT-LIB2 (for external z3)**. Click it to see the constraints ORRESS collected, written in z3's language: one `declare-const` per input byte (`b0` to `b11`) and one `assert` per branch.

Why would you need z3 when ORRESS solved it already? The built-in solver has a limit: it solves each group of bytes that depend on each other by trying combinations, and it gives up when a group gets too big (more than 3 bytes that are all tied together, which means more than 16 million combinations). A check where *every* character influences *every* comparison, for example a hash-like mixing loop over the whole input, creates one giant group. Then the status line is shown in a warning colour and the result is incomplete.

For those, copy the SMT-LIB2 text into a file, add two lines at the end:

```text
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```

and run `z3 file.smt2` (z3 is a separate program you install yourself). z3 reasons about the formulas instead of trying combinations, and solves much bigger problems.
'''
success = "Built-in solver for the common cases, z3 for the tough ones. The constraints are the same."

[[steps]]
title = "Where symbolic execution fails"
goal = "Know the limits."
text = '''
Symbolic execution is powerful, but not almighty. Three classic problems:

1. **Path explosion.** Every input-dependent branch can go two ways. A function with 30 such branches in a row has up to 2^30 (a billion) paths. ORRESS sidesteps this by following only *one* path, steered by your target and avoid addresses, which is why you give it those.
2. **Symbolic addresses.** When the input is used as an *index*, for example `TABLE[input[0] as usize]`, the address read from depends on the unknown. The engine then cannot know which memory it reads. ORRESS stops with `symbolic memory address`. Lookup tables (like an AES S-box) cause this.
3. **One-way functions.** A real hash like SHA-256 is designed so that no formula leads back from the output to the input. The constraints are correct, but no solver can solve them in your lifetime.

Some practical limits of ORRESS's implementation: the input is passed as **one** argument (a pointer). A function that also needs the length in a second argument, like crackme03's `check_password(s: &[u8])`, gets the length 0 from the solver, fails its length check, and the solver reports that it was *forced into an avoided block*. And it runs x86-64 code only.

Which check can symbolic execution **not** crack?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "sha256(input) == STORED_DIGEST",

    "input[0] + input[1] == 0x9b and input[0] - input[1] == 0x15",
    "input.rotate_left(3) == 0x2e (for a single byte)",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. SHA-256 is a one-way function: the constraints exist, but no solver can find an input for a given digest. Only guessing (dictionary, brute force) works there.",
    "Byte-wise XOR and compare: the easiest case for a solver, one tiny constraint per byte.",
    "Two linear equations with two unknowns. A solver handles that instantly.",
    "A rotation of one byte is easy to invert, for a solver and for you: rotate right by 3.",
] }
hints = [
    "Which option contains a function designed to be impossible to invert?",
]
success = "Hashes resist solvers. Everything that is built from XOR, addition, subtraction, multiplication and rotation on a few bytes at a time is fair game. In the next lesson you meet a check that leaks its secret in a completely different way."

```toml
id = "l4-side-channels"
level = 4
order = 28
title = "Side channels"
summary = "A check can leak its secret through how much work it does. Recover crackme03's password one character at a time by counting instructions."
goals = [

    "read the per-position counts and spot where the signal is missing",
    "know the defence: constant-time code",

[[steps]]
title = "Secrets leak sideways"
goal = "Understand the idea of a side channel."
text = '''
A check function gives you one bit of information: right or wrong. "Wrong key. Try again!" is the same for every wrong key. Or is it?

The *output* is the same, but the *work* is not. A program that decides something about a secret often does a different amount of work depending on that secret: it runs longer or shorter, it uses the processor's memory cache differently, it even draws a slightly different amount of electrical power. Anything you can measure from the outside that depends on the secret is a **side channel**: information that leaks *beside* the official output.

Real-world examples:

- **Timing attacks**: a server that checks a password takes a few nanoseconds longer when the first character is right. Measured over many tries, that tiny difference reveals the password.
- **Power analysis**: the power drawn by a smart card while it encrypts reveals the bits of its key.
- **Cache attacks**: which memory a program touched is visible to another program on the same processor.

In this lesson you use the cleanest side channel of all: **instruction counting**. You run the check in ORRESS's emulator and count how many instructions it executes. No noise, no statistics, just one exact number per try.
'''
success = "Next: why a perfectly ordinary comparison loop leaks."

[[steps]]
title = "The early exit"
goal = "See exactly where crackme03's check leaks."
text = '''
Here is crackme03's check function, from its source. You solved this crackme in Level 2 by undoing the XOR:

```rust
fn check_password(s: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if s.len() != CIPHER.len() {
        return false;
    }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < CIPHER.len() {
        if s[i] ^ KEY[i % 4] != CIPHER[i] {
            return false;   // stop at the FIRST wrong character
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}
```

Look at the `return false` inside the loop. It is an **early exit**: the loop stops at the first character that does not match. That is natural and efficient, and it is exactly the leak:

- If the first character is wrong, the loop runs once and stops.
- If the first character is right but the second is wrong, the loop runs twice.
- If the first three are right, it runs four times.

So the **amount of work tells you how many characters at the start are right**. The function was supposed to answer only "yes or no", but by the way it works it answers "how many correct characters at the start", which is much more.

A check that leaks like this is called an **oracle**: something you can ask questions that answers more than it should.
'''
success = "Early exit = leak. Now: how do you use it?"

[[steps]]
title = "One character at a time"
goal = "Turn the leak into a strategy."
text = '''
You can measure how far the loop gets, but you still do not know any character of the password. How do you turn "how far did it get" into the full password?
'''

    "Run the check once with an empty input and read the password from the count",
    "Measure the time of the 'Correct!' message",

    "One measurement gives one number. The leak only says how many leading characters are right, so you need many tries, one position at a time.",

] }

[[steps]]
title = "Measuring without noise"
goal = "Understand why ORRESS counts instructions instead of time."
text = '''
On a real computer you would measure **time**. But time is noisy: other programs run, the processor changes its speed, the operating system interrupts. A difference of a few nanoseconds disappears in that noise, so a real timing attack repeats every measurement thousands of times and averages.

In an **emulator** (Level 3) you do not need any of that. The emulator executes the function one instruction at a time and can simply count them. One more loop iteration means a few more instructions, every time, exactly. That count is a perfect, noise-free stand-in for time.

ORRESS's **Side-channel solve**, in the Emulator tab, does the whole attack for you:

1. It writes a candidate input into memory (unknown positions are filled with zero bytes at first).
2. For position 0, it tries every character of the chosen **Charset** (printable, alphanumeric, or digits), calls the function, and counts the executed instructions.
3. It keeps the character with the highest count, and moves to position 1.
4. At the end it shows the **Recovered input** and a table, **per-position instruction counts**: for every position the chosen byte, its count, and the **runner-up** (the second-highest count).

The runner-up column is your quality check. A clear signal looks like `count 24, runner-up 18`: one character stood out. Equal numbers mean no character made a difference at that position.
'''
success = "Now do it on crackme03."

[[steps]]
title = "When the side channel stays silent"
goal = "Know which checks do not leak."
text = '''
The side channel worked on crackme03 because each character was checked on its own, in order, with an early exit. Try to imagine it on crackme14 from the last lesson, which checks characters in **pairs**:

```rust
if x ^ y != MIX[j] { return 0; }     // x comes from character 2j, y from 2j+1
if x.rotate_left(1).wrapping_add(y) != ROT[j] { return 0; }
```

When the solver varies character 0, character 1 is still a zero byte. Some character 0 may happen to pass the first comparison together with that zero byte, and the solver keeps it. But it is the wrong character, and nothing that follows can fix it. If you run the Side-channel solve on crackme14 (length 12, without the length tick box), it recovers one wrong character and then gives up: all other counts equal their runner-up.

So side channels need a check that tests the secret **piece by piece, in order, and stops early**. Checks that mix pieces need the symbolic solver.

The defence follows directly: **constant-time code**. Compare every byte, even after a mismatch, and combine the results without branching:

```rust
fn equal_constant_time(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool {
    let mut diff = 0u8;
    for i in 0..a.len() {
        diff |= a[i] ^ b[i];   // no early exit
    }
    diff == 0
}
```

This runs exactly the same instructions for every input of the right length, so there is nothing to measure. Cryptography libraries are written this way on purpose.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Real-world side channels go far beyond counting:

- **Remote timing**: password and token checks on web servers have been broken over the network by measuring response times thousands of times.
- **Cache attacks** (Flush+Reload, Prime+Probe): another program on the same processor learns which memory lines a victim used, which leaks table lookups such as an AES S-box.
- **Speculative execution** (Spectre, Meltdown): the processor runs instructions ahead of time, and their traces in the cache leak data across security boundaries.
- **Power and electromagnetic analysis**: on smart cards and microcontrollers, differential power analysis (DPA) recovers keys from the power drawn during encryption.

In CTFs you mostly meet the first kind: a check with an early exit, and sometimes a challenge that literally prints how long the check took.
'''
success = "Side channels: the secret leaks through behaviour, not output. You now have three ways to beat a check: invert it, solve it, or listen to it. Next: programs that are not machine code at all."
