`academy/lessons/06-43-yara-rules.toml`:

```toml
id = "l6-yara-rules"
level = 6
order = 43
title = "Writing YARA rules"
summary = "Turn 'I recognise this malware' into a reusable detection: rule anatomy, string types, conditions, and ORRESS's live YARA workbench."
badge = "Rule Writer"
reveal_source = "crackme15"
goals = [
    "say what YARA is and name the three parts of a rule",
    "tell apart text, hex and regex strings and read an anchor like `at 0`",
    "read a condition's boolean logic and tune its strictness",
    "write a rule in the YARA workbench that matches the training sample",
]

[[steps]]
title = "What is YARA?"
goal = "Understand YARA as a way to turn recognition into reusable detection."
text = '''
You've triaged a sample and recognised something distinctive — a marker string, a config blob, a chunk of code. **YARA** lets you turn that recognition into a **reusable, shareable detection**.

A YARA rule is a small pattern description: "a file matches if it contains *these* bytes or strings in *this* combination." Point the engine at a file (or thousands) and it tells you which ones match. Analysts use YARA to **hunt** a known threat across a whole fleet, **classify** samples into families, and **share** detections with other defenders.

ORRESS has a built-in **YARA workbench** powered by the pure-Rust **YARA-X** engine, so you can write a rule and test it against the open file instantly — no external tool needed.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Anatomy of a rule"
text = '''
Every rule has the same three parts. Here's the example ORRESS starts you with:

```text
rule example {
    meta:
        author = "analyst"
        description = "matches the PE DOS stub"
    strings:
        $dos = "This program cannot be run in DOS mode"
        $mz  = { 4D 5A }
    condition:
        $mz at 0 and $dos
}
```

- **meta** — informational only (author, description, date, references). It doesn't affect matching; it's provenance.
- **strings** — the patterns to look for, each with a `$name`.
- **condition** — the boolean logic that decides whether the file matches, referring to the strings by name.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Three kinds of string"
text = '''
The `strings:` section can describe patterns three ways:

- **Text**: `$dos = "This program cannot be run in DOS mode"` — a literal string. Add `nocase`, `wide` (UTF-16), or `fullword` as modifiers.
- **Hex**: `$mz = { 4D 5A }` — raw bytes, perfect for magic numbers, opcodes, or structures. Wildcards like `{ 4D ?? 5A }` allow bytes that vary.
- **Regex**: `$re = /evil[0-9]+\.com/` — a regular expression, for patterns that aren't fixed.

In the example, `$mz` has the **anchor** `at 0`. What does `$mz at 0` require?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
  "The bytes 4D 5A must appear at offset 0 — the very start of the file",
  "The pattern must appear zero times (i.e. be absent)",
  "The pattern may appear anywhere in the file",
  "The pattern must appear at the end of the file",
], correct = 0 }
hints = [
  "`at <offset>` pins a string to an exact position; 0 is the first byte.",
  "4D 5A at offset 0 is the \"MZ\" signature every PE file begins with.",
]
success = "Right — `at 0` pins the match to the first byte, so this checks the file starts with the MZ signature."

[[steps]]
title = "The condition"
text = '''
The `condition` is where a rule gets its precision. On its own, each string is just "present or not"; the condition combines them into a verdict with boolean logic (`and`, `or`, `not`), counts (`#dos > 3`), positions (`at`, `in`), and helpers like `filesize` or `any of them`.

In the example the condition is:

```text
$mz at 0 and $dos
```

Which single keyword there makes the rule require **both** the MZ signature *and* the DOS-stub string, so that a file with only one of them does **not** match?
'''
instructions = ["Type the single keyword from the condition and press Check."]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["and"], number = false, case_sensitive = false }
hints = ["It's the boolean operator between the two conditions.", "`A and B` is true only when both A and B are true."]
success = "`and` — both must hold. Swap it for `or` and either one alone would match; that's how you tune a rule's strictness."

[[steps]]
title = "The YARA workbench"
text = '''
ORRESS lets you write and test rules live. The **YARA workbench** opens with the example rule, and you can:

- **Edit the rule** and scan the open file — matches show their rule, pattern, offset and a byte preview.
- **Generate a rule** from the sample's distinctive strings as a starting point.
- **Scan a rule folder** — run the open file against every `.yar`/`.yara` rule in a directory (your rule library).

Open the **YARA workbench** now (Ctrl+Shift+Y, the View menu, or the command palette).
'''
instructions = [
    "Press **Ctrl+Shift+Y**, or the **View** menu -> **Open View** -> **Open YARA Workbench**.",
    "(Or **Ctrl+Shift+P** and type \"YARA\".)",
    "Note the example rule in the editor and the **Scan open file** button above it.",
]
check = { kind = "action", id = "view::Yara" }
spotlight = "view.Yara"
hints = ["Ctrl+Shift+Y opens it — or Ctrl+Shift+P and type \"YARA\"."]

[[steps]]
title = "Load the sample to match"
goal = "Open the training sample so your rule has something to scan."
text = '''
Let us write a rule that catches the training sample. First make it the open file: the YARA

    "Click the **Scan open file** button and confirm one match for `$marker`.",
]
check = { kind = "action", id = "view::Yara" }
spotlight = "view.Yara"
hints = [
    "Ctrl+Shift+Y opens the workbench; the editor is at the top.",
    "Paste the rule exactly, keeping the quotes around the marker string.",
    "Scan open file runs the rule against crackme15 -- you want one match.",
]
success = "You wrote a rule, scanned the sample and got a match. That rule is now a reusable, shareable detection: point it at a thousand files and it finds this sample and its variants, while leaving clean files alone."

[[steps]]
title = "Writing rules that last"
goal = "Learn the craft of rules that catch variants without false positives."
text = '''
A good rule catches the family and its variants without ever firing on clean files. The craft:

1. **Pick distinctive, stable strings.** A custom mutex name, a C2 domain, a unique format string — not compiler boilerplate or library code that appears in thousands of benign programs.
2. **Combine several.** Require a handful of markers together in the condition, so one small change by the author doesn't slip past the rule.
3. **Use hex and anchors for code.** Match opcode sequences or structures with `{ .. }` and pin signatures with `at`, allowing wildcards where bytes legitimately vary.
4. **Record provenance in meta.** Author, date, a reference to the report or sample hash — so future analysts trust and maintain it.
5. **Test both ways.** Confirm it matches the sample (true positive) *and* doesn't match a pile of clean files (no false positives). Use ORRESS's "Generate rule" as a draft, then tighten it, and run your whole library with "Scan rule folder".

A tuned rule is a durable asset: you write it once and it hunts the threat across every file you'll ever scan. That's how recognition becomes detection.
'''

`academy/lessons/07-01-time-travel-debugging.toml`:

```toml
id = "l7-time-travel-debugging"
level = 7
order = 1
title = "Time-travel debugging"
summary = "Record a function once, then step backward through it to find exactly which instruction caused a result."
goals = [
    "explain what an execution trace is and why stepping backward is useful",
    "record a trace of one function in the Emulator",
    "move backward and forward through the trace and read the registers at each step",
    "follow a wrong result back to the instruction and the input byte that caused it",
]
badge = "Time Traveller"

[[steps]]
title = "Welcome to the Expert level"
goal = "See why a normal debugger makes some questions hard."
text = '''
Welcome to the last level. You can already read assembly, use the decompiler, the debugger and the emulator, and you have solved crackmes with keygens, solvers and side channels. This level adds four expert skills: **time-travel debugging**, **binary diffing**, kernel **drivers and rootkits**, and **automating ORRESS with scripts**. It ends with a final project that uses everything.

Start with a problem you have probably met. A normal debugger only moves **forward**. You set a breakpoint, run, and step one instruction at a time. Now imagine you step past the interesting moment: the register you wanted to see has already been overwritten. The only way back is to restart the program and stop earlier. If the program behaves a little differently each run (other input, other timing, random values), you may never see the same moment twice.

Most real questions are about the **past**:

- "This function returned `false`. Which comparison failed?"
- "This register holds a strange value. Which instruction wrote it?"
- "The program crashed here. What led up to it?"

Answering them by moving forward means guessing where to stop, again and again. In this lesson you learn a way to answer them directly, by recording the run once and then walking **backward** through it.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Record once, replay as often as you like"
goal = "Understand what a trace is."
text = '''
**Time-travel debugging** works in two phases.

1. **Record.** The program (or one function) runs once. After **every** instruction, the tool saves a small **snapshot**: the address of the instruction that just ran and the values of all registers at that moment. This list of snapshots is called an **execution trace**.
2. **Replay.** You move through the saved list instead of the live program. Stepping forward means "show the next snapshot", stepping backward means "show the previous one". Nothing runs again, so going back is as easy as going forward.

In Rust, a trace is not much more than a `Vec`:

```rust
struct Snapshot {
    addr: u64,       // the instruction that just ran
    regs: [u64; 16], // rax, rcx, rdx, ... r15 after it ran
}

let trace: Vec<Snapshot> = record(function, input);
let now = &trace[193];     // look at step 193
let before = &trace[192];  // "step back" is just index - 1
```

Because the recording never changes, every question you ask gets the same answer, every time. That property is called **deterministic replay**, and it is what makes time travel reliable: you can look at step 193, jump to step 10, and come back to step 193 to find exactly the same values.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Professional tools record whole programs: WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging on Windows, `rr` on Linux, and record-and-replay modes in emulators such as QEMU. They also record memory writes, system calls and thread switches, so a trace of a big program can be gigabytes.

ORRESS records inside its own emulator, one function at a time, and saves the registers (not memory) after each instruction. That keeps traces small and fast. If you need to know what memory looked like at a step, run the same function again with the same input: the emulator is deterministic, so it does exactly the same thing.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "What does stepping back do?"
goal = "Check that the idea of a trace is clear."
text = '''
You recorded a trace and are looking at step 50. You click **step back** once. Think about what really happens inside the tool before you answer.
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "The tool shows the saved snapshot of step 49; nothing is executed again",
    "The CPU runs instruction 50 backwards to undo it",
    "The tool restarts the program and runs it again until step 49",
    "The program's memory is restored from a backup on disk",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. The run was recorded once; stepping back only shows an earlier entry of the recorded list.",
    "A CPU cannot run instructions backwards. Many instructions also destroy information (for example `xor eax, eax` forgets the old value), so undoing them is impossible. That is why the state is saved before it is lost.",
    "That is what you must do with a normal debugger. A trace makes it unnecessary: the earlier step is already saved.",

    "A trace is a list that was filled in during one single run.",

[[steps]]
title = "The program for this lesson"
goal = "Get to know crackme17 and its check function."
text = '''
For this lesson you use a new practice program, **crackme17**, "KeyVault 1.0". It asks for a licence key and prints "Access granted" or "Access denied". The check is done by one function. Written in Rust it looks like this (the expected bytes `ENC` are a secret table in the program's data):

```rust
fn check_key(key: &[u8]) -> bool {
    for &b in key {                       // 1. every byte must be printable
        if !(0x20..=0x7e).contains(&b) { return false; }
    }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < key.len() {                 // 2. compare byte by byte
        if i >= 10 { return false; }
        if (key[i] ^ 0x5c).wrapping_add(i as u8) != ENC[i] {
            return false;                 // stops at the first wrong byte
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}
```

So each key byte is XORed with `0x5c`, its position `i` is added, and the result must equal `ENC[i]`.

The argument `key: &[u8]` is a **slice**: a pointer to the bytes plus their length. On Windows the first two arguments arrive in `rcx` and `rdx`, so `rcx` holds the address of the key and `rdx` holds its length. Remember this, you need it when you start the function in the Emulator.

Click **Open crackme17** below to open the program.

- Step 192, `add esi,r9d`: `rsi` becomes `0xb`. Its inputs were `rsi` and `r9` (7).

[[steps]]
title = "Method and limits"
goal = "Take away a repeatable method and know what ORRESS's trace cannot do."
text = '''
The method you used works on any recorded function:

1. **Record** the function you suspect, with an input that shows the problem. Keep it small: a trace is limited to 100 000 instructions, so record one function, not a whole program.
2. **Start at the symptom.** Go to the last step, or to the step where something looks wrong.
3. **Find the decision.** Step back to the comparison or jump that sent the run the wrong way.
4. **Follow the data.** Step back to the instruction that wrote each value that decision used. Repeat for that instruction's inputs.
5. **Stop at the origin**: an input byte, a constant, or a table in memory. That is the root cause.

Know the limits of ORRESS's trace:

- It saves **registers**, not memory. To see what was in memory at a step, run the function again with **Run**: the emulator is deterministic.
- It runs inside the **emulator**, so it has the emulator's limits: x86-64 only, and calls into Windows are replaced by simple stand-ins. Self-contained functions such as checks, decoders and hash functions work best.
- If the run stops with an error (for example a memory fault), the steps up to the error are kept, and the last line shows `stopped: ...`. That is often exactly what you want to investigate.

In the next lesson you will compare crackme17 with its successor and find what the vendor changed.
'''

`academy/lessons/07-02-binary-diffing.toml`:

```toml
id = "l7-binary-diffing"
level = 7
order = 2
title = "Binary diffing"
summary = "Compare two versions of a program function by function, and find exactly what a security patch changed."
goals = [
    "explain why two builds of a program differ in thousands of bytes even when the code barely changed",
    "describe how function matching works: signatures, opcode hashes and similarity scores",
    "compare two binaries in ORRESS's Binary diff tab and read the result",
    "use patch diffing to find and understand a fixed security bug",
]
badge = "Patch Analyst"

[[steps]]
title = "Two versions of one program"
goal = "See why the difference between two binaries is often the interesting part."
text = '''
Often you do not have one program to understand, but **two related ones**, and the question is what is different between them:

- A program **before and after a security update**. The vendor says "fixed a security issue" and nothing more. What was the bug?
- **Two samples of the same malware family.** What did the authors add in the new version?
- **Two builds of your own program.** Did a compiler update or a small source change do something you did not expect?

Reading both programs completely would take days. **Binary diffing** takes two binaries, pairs up the functions that belong together, and tells you which functions are the same, which changed, which are new and which are gone. You then read only the few functions that matter.

In this lesson you play a security researcher. KeyVault 1.0 (crackme17, from the previous lesson) has a bug that customers reported. The vendor released KeyVault 1.1 (crackme18) "with security improvements". You have no source code. Your task: find out what was fixed, and what an attacker could do with version 1.0.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Why comparing bytes does not work"
goal = "Understand that addresses shift when code changes."
text = '''
Your first idea might be to compare the two files byte by byte, like the `diff` tool compares text files. That fails completely, and the reason is **addresses**.

The compiler places functions one after another. If one function grows by 32 bytes, every function after it moves 32 bytes further. Every `call` and every reference to data now contains a different address. Here is the start of `main` in both versions of KeyVault:

```text
crackme17 (1.0)                          crackme18 (1.1)
140001100  push rsi                      140001120  push rsi
140001101  sub  rsp,0x60                 140001121  sub  rsp,0x60
140001105  lea  rcx,[0x1400193d0]        140001125  lea  rcx,[0x1400193e6]
14000110c  mov  edx,0x67                 14000112c  mov  edx,0x67
140001111  call sub_140005a30            140001131  call sub_140005a70
```

The instructions are the same. Only the addresses differ: `main` itself moved by `0x20` bytes, the text it prints moved, and the function it calls moved. A byte comparison reports thousands of differences that mean nothing.

So diffing tools compare **functions**, and describe each function in a way that does **not** depend on where it is in memory.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "A fingerprint for every function"
goal = "Know what ORRESS compares when it matches functions."
text = '''
ORRESS describes each function with a **function signature** (a fingerprint), made of two parts.

1. **Its shape:** the number of instructions, **basic blocks**, edges between blocks (the arrows in the graph view) and calls.
2. **An opcode hash:** ORRESS walks over the function's instructions and feeds each mnemonic and its operands into a hash, but replaces every **address** (jump targets, call targets, data references, large numbers) with a placeholder. Registers and small numbers stay in.

In Rust it would look like this:

```rust
struct FuncSig {
    insns: u32, blocks: u32, edges: u32, calls: u32, // the shape
    opcode_hash: u64,                                // the instructions, without addresses
}
```

Because addresses are left out, `call sub_140005a30` and `call sub_140005a70` hash the same, and the two `main` functions above get the same fingerprint. But a real change, such as `jz` turned into `jnz`, or `cmp rdx,8` turned into `cmp rdx,10`, changes the hash.
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "A `cmp rdx,8` was changed into `cmp rdx,10`",
    "The whole function moved to a different address",
    "The function now calls a helper that moved to another address",
    "A string the function prints moved to another place in the data",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. 8 and 10 are small numbers, so they are part of the hash. A changed constant is a real change in the logic.",
    "Moving changes only addresses, and addresses are replaced by a placeholder. The hash stays the same.",
    "Call targets are addresses, so they are left out of the hash.",
    "The reference to the string is an address. It is replaced by the placeholder, so the hash does not change.",
] }
hints = [
    "Which of these changes involves something that is not an address?",
    "Small numbers and registers stay in the hash; addresses do not.",
]
success = "That is the key idea of binary diffing: ignore where things are, compare what they do."

[[steps]]
title = "Matching and the four verdicts"
goal = "Understand how functions are paired and what each verdict means."
text = '''
With a fingerprint for every function in both programs, ORRESS **matches** them in rounds, from most to least certain:

1. Same **name** (only real names from symbols or imports, never `sub_...`).
2. Same **opcode hash**, if exactly one function on each side has it.
3. Same **shape**, if exactly one function on each side has it.
4. For what is left: the most similar pair, if the **similarity score** is above 0.5. The score is a weighted comparison of the shapes: instructions count 40%, blocks 30%, edges 20%, calls 10%.

Then every function gets one of four **verdicts**:

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **identical** | matched, and the code is the same |
| **changed** | matched, but the code differs; shown with the similarity, e.g. `~82%` |
| **added** | only in the second binary (B): new code |
| **removed** | only in the first binary (A): code that was deleted |

For **patch diffing**, the **changed** and **added** lists are the gold. A security fix usually changes one or two functions (a new check, a different constant) and sometimes adds a small helper.

A function exists in version 1.1 (B) but has no partner in version 1.0 (A). Which verdict does it get?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
    "Added",
    "Removed",
    "Changed",
    "Identical",
], correct = 0, explain = [
    "Right. It exists only in the second binary, so it is new code.",
    "Removed is the opposite: a function that exists only in the first binary.",
    "Changed needs a partner in the other binary. This function has none.",
    "Identical also needs a partner with the same code.",
] }
hints = [
    "The question is about a function that exists only in version B.",
]
deep_dive = '''
Professional tools such as BinDiff and Diaphora use more features: the call graph (who calls whom), constants, strings, and a comparison of the basic blocks inside each matched pair. ORRESS's matcher is simpler and fast. Its weak spot is step 4: when two unrelated functions happen to have a very similar shape, it can pair the wrong ones. If a match looks strange, open both functions and check them yourself.
'''

Defenders diff patches to judge how urgent an update is; attackers do it to exploit the gap.'''

[[steps]]
title = "A patch-diffing workflow"
goal = "Take away a repeatable method."
text = '''
The method you just used works for any two versions of a program:

1. **Open the old version** and make it the active file (A).
2. **Compare** against the new version (B) in **View > Open View > Binary diff**.
3. **Read the summary.** A few changed or added functions in a big program means a small, targeted change. Hundreds of changes usually mean a different compiler or settings, and the diff is mostly noise.
4. **Read the added functions first.** Small new helpers are often the fix (or, in malware, the new feature).
5. **Compare each changed pair.** Decompile the function in A, then its partner in B, and look for new checks, changed constants and new calls. To see both disassemblies at once, use **View > Split Pane Right** and show one file on each side.
6. **Explain the bug** in one sentence: what could an attacker do with the old version?

The same comparison is available outside the window, too: the `orress-mcp` program offers it as the tool `binary_diff`, so an AI agent or a script can diff many pairs of files. You will meet that in the scripting lesson.
'''
deep_dive = '''
Real patch diffing has some extra hurdles:

- **Symbols help a lot.** Microsoft publishes symbol files (PDB) for Windows system files, so names make matching much more reliable. ORRESS uses names first whenever they exist.
- **Updates contain more than the fix.** A monthly update may change hundreds of functions. Filter by the components named in the security advisory, then sort by similarity: functions with high but not perfect similarity (a small change) are the most likely fixes.
- **Inlining moves code around.** If the compiler copied a small function into its callers, the fix may show up in several changed functions at once.
'''

`academy/lessons/07-03-drivers-and-rootkits.toml`:

```toml
id = "l7-drivers-and-rootkits"
level = 7
order = 3
title = "Drivers and rootkits"
summary = "Reverse-engineering kernel-mode code: how to spot a driver, how rootkits hide, and why ring 0 raises the stakes."
goals = [
    "explain user mode and kernel mode, and the privilege rings",
    "recognise a Windows driver (.sys) by its subsystem, entry point and imports",
    "describe how a driver handles requests through DriverEntry and IRP dispatch routines",
    "name the main tricks rootkits use to hide, and how to analyse kernel code safely",
]
badge = "Ring Zero"

[[steps]]
title = "Down to the kernel"
text = '''
Everything you've reversed so far has been **user mode** — ordinary programs, running with limited privilege, isolated from each other by the operating system. Expert work eventually takes you below that line, into **kernel mode**: device drivers, and the malware that lives alongside them.

Kernel code runs at the processor's highest privilege level with direct access to memory, hardware and every process on the machine. That's where **drivers** operate legitimately — and where a **rootkit** plants itself to hide, persist and tamper with the system from underneath the tools trying to find it.

The reversing skills are the same — it's still disassembly and control flow. What changes is the environment, the APIs, and the stakes.
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Spotting a driver"
text = '''
A Windows kernel driver (a `.sys` file) is a **PE file**, just like an `.exe` — but with tell-tale differences:

- Its **PE subsystem** is **Native**, not Console or GUI.
- Its entry point is **`DriverEntry`**, not the usual C runtime startup.
- It imports from the **kernel**, not the usual user-mode DLLs: functions from `ntoskrnl.exe` and `hal.dll` with prefixes like `Ex`, `Io`, `Ob`, `Ps`, `Rtl` (for example `ExAllocatePool`, `IoCreateDevice`) — never `kernel32`/`user32`.

See those traits together and you're looking at kernel-mode code, which tells you to switch your mental model from "a program with a `main`" to "a driver the kernel calls into."
'''

[[steps]]
title = "Is this a driver?"
text = '''
The quickest check is the file overview. ORRESS's **"What Is This File?"** view reports the PE **subsystem**, among the format, protections and entropy. For a normal app it says *Console* or *GUI*; for a driver it reads **"Native (driver or boot program)"**.

Open the **What Is This File?** view (the command palette, or the File menu) and find the Subsystem field.
'''
instructions = [
    "Make sure a file is open (for example crackme17).",
    "Press **Ctrl+I**, or open the menu **View > This File** and click **File: What Is This File?**.",
    "In the card **Windows details**, find the row **Subsystem**.",
]
check = { kind = "action", id = "file::Info" }
hints = ["Ctrl+Shift+P, then type \"What Is This File\" — or the File menu. Look for the Subsystem row."]

[[steps]]
title = "How rootkits hide"
text = '''
A rootkit's whole purpose is to make the system **lie** — so a hidden process, file or network connection simply doesn't appear to the tools that query it. From the kernel, how does it pull that off?
'''
check = { kind = "choice", options = [
  "By hooking or patching OS code and tables (e.g. the system-call table or a driver's dispatch routines), or unlinking kernel objects (DKOM), so the OS returns doctored answers",
  "By choosing a very long and complex file name",
  "By compressing itself to take up less disk space",
  "By asking the user politely not to look",
], correct = 0 }
hints = [
  "If you control the code that answers 'list the processes', you control what the answer says.",
  "Think SSDT hooks, inline patches on kernel functions, and DKOM (unlinking an EPROCESS from the list).",
]
success = "Right — rootkits intercept or doctor the kernel's own bookkeeping (hooks, patches, DKOM) so the system reports a false picture of itself."

[[steps]]
title = "The stakes of ring 0"
text = '''
Kernel mode is often called by its x86 privilege level, a single-digit number. User-mode apps run at the least-privileged level; the kernel runs at the **most**-privileged one.

What is the privilege-ring number of kernel mode? (One digit.)
'''
instructions = [
    "Type the ring number of kernel mode in the answer box and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0"], number = true }
hints = ["The rings go from 0 (most privileged) to 3 (least). Applications run in ring 3.", "Kernel mode is the most privileged ring."]
success = "Ring 0 — the most privileged level. A mistake here doesn't crash one app; it can blue-screen or compromise the whole machine."

[[steps]]
title = "Analysing kernel code safely"
text = '''
Ring 0 changes how you work:

1. **Confirm it's kernel-mode** — Native subsystem, `DriverEntry`, kernel imports.
2. **Find the entry and dispatch routines.** `DriverEntry` sets up the driver; the **IRP dispatch** routines are its interface to user mode (the requests it handles). Those are where the real behaviour lives.
3. **Map what it touches.** Which kernel objects, tables and functions does it read or write? Writes to the **system-call table**, patches at the **start of kernel functions**, or walks of the **process list** are rootkit fingerprints.
4. **Respect the danger.** A kernel bug or detonation can **blue-screen or fully compromise** the host, and a kernel rootkit can defeat user-mode monitoring entirely — so lean on **static analysis** first, and do any dynamic work in a **disposable VM with kernel debugging**, never on your real machine.

Same disassembly skills, far higher stakes. Ring 0 is the deep end of reverse engineering — and now you know how to recognise it, read it, and stay safe doing so.
'''

ORRESS is built to be driven this way. Its analysis (functions, strings, bytes, disassembly) is not locked inside the window; you can reach it from a small script. In this lesson you write a few, using crackmes you already know.

title = "A pass over every function"
goal = "Write a script that searches all functions for a pattern."
text = '''
Now a real pass: find the function that does the XOR check. In crackme03 the check XORs each input byte with a constant, so its code is full of instructions like `xor al,0x5a`. You can find it by disassembling every function and counting lines that contain both `xor` and `,0x`.

Here is the script. `disasm(f, 60)` gives up to 60 instructions of the function at address `f` as one text; `.split("\n")` turns that into an array of lines; `.contains(...)` tests a line.

```rhai
// Find functions that XOR bytes with constant keys.
for f in functions() {
    let hits = 0;
    for line in disasm(f, 60).split("\n") {
        if line.contains("xor") && line.contains(",0x") {
            hits += 1;
        }
        if line.contains("ret") { break; }   // stop at the end of the function
    }
    if hits >= 4 {
        print(func_name(f) + " at 0x" + f.to_hex() + ": " + hits + " xor-constant lines");
    }
}
```

Type (or paste) it into the console and run it. Exactly one function is reported.
'''

    "In the **Scripting** tab, clear the script box.",
    "Type or paste the script from the text above.",
    "Click **Run**.",
    "The output names one function and its address. Type that address (with `0x`) in the answer box and press **Check**.",
]
check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["0x140001100"], number = true }
hints = [

[[steps]]
title = "A keygen as a script"
goal = "Read the program's own data and compute the password."
text = '''
A script can read the program's bytes, so it can do real work. In the keygen lesson you learned that crackme03 XORs each input byte with a 4-byte key and compares with a fixed ciphertext. XOR is its own inverse, so `password[i] = cipher[i] ^ key[i % 4]`.

Rather than read the key and ciphertext off the screen, pull them straight from the instructions. In `check_password`, the key bytes are the numbers after `xor al,` and the expected bytes are the numbers after `cmp byte ptr [rsp+7],`. This script collects both and recovers the password:

```rhai
// Keygen for crackme03: recover the password from check_password.
fn num(t) {                      // "0x5a" or "9" -> a number
    if t.starts_with("0x") { t.sub_string(2).parse_int(16) } else { t.parse_int() }
}
let keys = [];
let targets = [];
for line in disasm(0x140001100, 60).split("\n") {
    let parts = line.split(",");
    let last = parts[parts.len() - 1];
    if line.contains("xor al,") { keys.push(num(last)); }
    if line.contains("cmp byte ptr [rsp+7],") { targets.push(num(last)); }
    if line.contains("ret") { break; }
}
let charset = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";
let password = "";
for i in 0..targets.len() {
    let code = keys[i] ^ targets[i];
    for c in charset { if c.to_int() == code { password += c; } }
}
print("password: " + password);
```

Run it. The password it prints is the one that unlocks crackme03.
'''
instructions = [

]

(The characters needing single quotes in Rhai are avoided here by looking each byte up in a charset string.)'''

text = '''
Reading a loop in assembly is slow. The **decompiler** turns it back into Rust-like code. Jump to the check and press **F5**. You will see roughly:

```rust
fn sub_1400012e0(a1: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if sub_140001100(a1, a1.len()) != 0 {        // a shape check (length + dashes)
        // ... every byte must be printable ...
        let mut rdx_2 = 0;
        while rdx_2 != 10 {
            if (a1[rdx_2] ^ 92) + rdx_2 != read::<u8>(rdx_2 + &data_140019478) {
                break;                            // wrong byte
            }
            rdx_2 += 1;
        }
    }
}
```

The important line is the comparison. Each key byte `a1[i]` is XORed with `92` (that is `0x5c`), then `i` is added, and the result must equal the `i`-th byte of a table in the program's data, `data_140019478`.

What is done to the key byte **before** `i` is added? Answer in one word.
'''

    "Press **Ctrl+G**, type `1400012e0` and press **Enter** (in the disassembly).",

]

check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["xor", "xored"], number = false, case_sensitive = false }
hints = [
    "`^` in Rust is one specific bitwise operation.",
    "`a1[i] ^ 92` is a bitwise XOR. Type `xor`.",
]
success = '''So the rule is `(key[i] ^ 0x5c) + i == ENC[i]`, where `ENC` is the table at `data_140019478`. Note that name, you need the address `0x140019478` next.'''

[[steps]]
title = "Step 4 - Recover the key"
goal = "Write a keygen script that reads ENC and inverts the rule."
text = '''
You know the rule and where the table is. Invert it: from `(key[i] ^ 0x5c) + i == ENC[i]` it follows that

```text
key[i] = (ENC[i] - i) ^ 0x5c
```

Let a script read the 10 table bytes and compute the key. `read(addr, len)` returns the bytes as numbers. The key is made of letters, digits and dashes, so you can turn each code into a character by looking it up in a small charset string (this avoids character literals):

```rhai
// Keygen for KeyVault 1.1.
let enc = read(0x140019478, 10);
print("ENC table: " + enc);
let charset = "-0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
let key = "";
for i in 0..10 {
    let code = ((enc[i] - i) ^ 0x5c) & 0xff;
    for c in charset { if c.to_int() == code { key += c; } }
}
print("key: " + key);
```

Open the Scripting console and run it.
'''

    "Open **View > Open View > Scripting console**.",

]
spotlight = "view.Script"
check = { kind = "secret", sha256 = "a02124df865a2c5cc9633d5a7ef71f85d3346040060184c4acf548a43944cb0b" }

goal = "Confirm the key, and know how else you could have solved it."
text = '''
To be sure, you would run the program and paste the key: it prints "Access granted". You can do that any time from a terminal.

It is worth knowing the other roads to the same key, all taught in this course, so you can pick the fastest one next time:

- **Side-channel solver** (Level 4): the loop stops at the first wrong byte, so more correct bytes mean more instructions. The Emulator's instruction-counting solver recovers the key one byte at a time, without you reading the rule.
- **Symbolic solver** (Level 4): mark the "granted" block as the target and let the solver find an input that reaches it.
- **Time-travel** (this level): record the check with a near-miss key and read ENC and the loop counter straight from the trace.

You chose to understand the check and invert it, which is the most reliable: it gives the real key, and it tells you *why*.
'''

`crates/orress-academy/build.rs`:

```rs
//! Embeds every lesson (`academy/lessons/*.toml`) and glossary file
//! (`academy/glossary/*.toml`) so adding one needs no code change.

use std::fmt::Write as _;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

fn toml_files(dir: &Path) -> Vec<PathBuf> {
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={}", dir.display());
    let mut files: Vec<PathBuf> = std::fs::read_dir(dir)
        .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("{}: {e}", dir.display()))
        .filter_map(|entry| entry.ok().map(|e| e.path()))
        .filter(|p| p.extension().is_some_and(|x| x == "toml"))
        .collect();
    files.sort();
    for file in &files {
        println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={}", file.display());
    }
    files
}

fn table(name: &str, files: &[PathBuf]) -> String {
    let mut out = format!("pub(crate) const {name}: &[(&str, &str)] = &[\n");
    for file in files {
        let file_name = file.file_name().unwrap().to_string_lossy();
        let path = file.display().to_string().replace('\\', "/");
        writeln!(out, "    ({file_name:?}, include_str!({path:?})),").unwrap();
    }
    out.push_str("];\n");
    out
}

fn main() {
    // Not canonicalized: on Windows that adds a `\\?\` prefix `include_str!` can't take.
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("../../academy");
    let mut out = table("BUILT_IN", &toml_files(&root.join("lessons")));
    out.push_str(&table(
        "GLOSSARY_FILES",
        &toml_files(&root.join("glossary")),
    ));
    let out_dir = Path::new(&std::env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).to_path_buf();
    std::fs::write(out_dir.join("academy_files.rs"), out).unwrap();
    std::fs::write(
        out_dir.join("crackme_files.rs"),
        crackmes(&root.join("crackmes")),
    )
    .unwrap();
}

/// `CRACKMES`: every `crackmes/<name>.rs` that has a built `crackmes/bin/<name>.exe`.
fn crackmes(dir: &Path) -> String {
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={}", dir.display());
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={}", dir.join("bin").display());
    let mut sources: Vec<PathBuf> = std::fs::read_dir(dir)
        .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("{}: {e}", dir.display()))
        .filter_map(|entry| entry.ok().map(|e| e.path()))
        .filter(|p| p.extension().is_some_and(|x| x == "rs"))
        .collect();
    sources.sort();
    let mut out = String::from("pub const CRACKMES: &[Crackme] = &[\n");
    for source in sources {
        let name = source.file_stem().unwrap().to_string_lossy().into_owned();
        let exe = dir.join("bin").join(format!("{name}.exe"));
        if !exe.exists() {
            continue;
        }
        println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={}", source.display());
        println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={}", exe.display());
        let slash = |p: &Path| p.display().to_string().replace('\\', "/");
        writeln!(
            out,
            "    Crackme {{ name: {name:?}, file_name: \"{name}.exe\", \
             bytes: include_bytes!({:?}), source: include_str!({:?}) }},",
            slash(&exe),
            slash(&source)
        )
        .unwrap();
    }
    out.push_str("];\n");
    out
}

```

`crates/orress-academy/src/crackmes.rs`:

```rs
//! Practice programs built into ORRESS. Sources and the build script are in
//! `academy/crackmes/`; adding `crackmeNN.rs` and building it is enough to embed it.

use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

pub struct Crackme {
    pub name: &'static str,
    pub file_name: &'static str,
    pub bytes: &'static [u8],
    pub source: &'static str,
}

// Every `academy/crackmes/<name>.rs` with a built `bin/<name>.exe` (see `build.rs`).
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/crackme_files.rs"));

pub fn find(name: &str) -> Option<&'static Crackme> {
    CRACKMES.iter().find(|c| c.name == name)
}

/// Writes the crackme to `dir` (if not already there) and returns its path.
pub fn extract(crackme: &Crackme, dir: &Path) -> Result<PathBuf, String> {
    std::fs::create_dir_all(dir).map_err(|e| format!("{}: {e}", dir.display()))?;
    let path = dir.join(crackme.file_name);
    let current = std::fs::read(&path).ok();
    if current.as_deref() != Some(crackme.bytes) {
        std::fs::write(&path, crackme.bytes).map_err(|e| format!("{}: {e}", path.display()))?;
    }
    Ok(path)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn crackmes_are_windows_programs() {
        assert!(CRACKMES.len() >= 8);
        for c in CRACKMES {
            assert!(c.bytes.starts_with(b"MZ"), "{} is a PE file", c.name);
            assert!(c.source.contains("fn main"));
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn extract_writes_once() {
        let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("orress-crackmes-{}", std::process::id()));
        let path = extract(&CRACKMES[0], &dir).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(std::fs::read(&path).unwrap(), CRACKMES[0].bytes);
        assert_eq!(extract(&CRACKMES[0], &dir).unwrap(), path);
        std::fs::remove_dir_all(dir).ok();
    }
}

```

`crates/orress-academy/src/glossary.rs`:

```rs
//! The Academy glossary: every technical word the lessons use, explained for a
//! beginner. Files are in `academy/glossary/`, one per level, merged at startup:
//!
//! ```toml
//! [[term]]
//! term = "register"
//! aliases = ["registers"]          # other spellings found in lesson text
//! short = "A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU."
//! text = """Longer Markdown explanation, with an example."""
//! see = ["rax", "stack"]           # related terms
//! ```
//!
//! Lesson steps list the glossary terms that appear in their text automatically, so
//! a learner never meets a word that is not explained somewhere.

use serde::Deserialize;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Term {
    pub term: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub aliases: Vec<String>,
    /// One sentence.
    pub short: String,
    /// Optional longer Markdown explanation.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub text: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub see: Vec<String>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct File {
    #[serde(default)]
    term: Vec<Term>,
}

pub fn parse(source: &str) -> Result<Vec<Term>, String> {
    toml::from_str::<File>(source)
        .map(|f| f.term)
        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())
}

/// All built-in terms, sorted alphabetically (case-insensitive). A broken file is left
/// out (and reported); the tests reject broken files.
pub fn catalog() -> Vec<Term> {
    let mut terms: Vec<Term> = crate::lesson::GLOSSARY_FILES
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|(file, source)| {
            parse(source).unwrap_or_else(|e| {
                eprintln!("built-in glossary {file} skipped: {e}");
                Vec::new()
            })
        })
        .collect();
    terms.sort_by_key(|t| t.term.to_lowercase());
    terms
}

/// Index of the term named `name` (or with that alias), ignoring case.
pub fn find(terms: &[Term], name: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    terms.iter().position(|t| {
        t.term.eq_ignore_ascii_case(name) || t.aliases.iter().any(|a| a.eq_ignore_ascii_case(name))
    })
}

/// Whether `needle` occurs in `haystack` as a whole word (or words), ignoring ASCII case.
fn contains_word(haystack: &str, needle: &str) -> bool {
    if needle.is_empty() {
        return false;
    }
    let hay = haystack.to_ascii_lowercase();
    let needle = needle.to_ascii_lowercase();
    let is_word = |c: char| c.is_alphanumeric() || c == '_';
    let mut from = 0;
    while let Some(pos) = hay[from..].find(&needle) {
        let start = from + pos;
        let end = start + needle.len();
        let before = hay[..start].chars().next_back();
        let after = hay[end..].chars().next();
        if !before.is_some_and(is_word) && !after.is_some_and(is_word) {
            return true;
        }
        from = start + hay[start..].chars().next().map_or(1, char::len_utf8);
    }
    false
}

/// Indices of the terms mentioned in `text`, in glossary order.
pub fn mentioned(terms: &[Term], text: &str) -> Vec<usize> {
    terms
        .iter()
        .enumerate()
        .filter(|(_, t)| {
            contains_word(text, &t.term) || t.aliases.iter().any(|a| contains_word(text, a))
        })
        .map(|(i, _)| i)
        .collect()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn built_in_glossary_is_valid() {
        let terms = catalog();
        assert!(!terms.is_empty());
        let mut names: Vec<String> = terms
            .iter()
            .flat_map(|t| std::iter::once(&t.term).chain(&t.aliases))
            .map(|n| n.to_lowercase())
            .collect();
        let count = names.len();
        names.sort();
        names.dedup();
        assert_eq!(names.len(), count, "glossary terms and aliases are unique");
        for t in &terms {
            assert!(
                !t.short.trim().is_empty(),
                "`{}` has a short explanation",
                t.term
            );
            for see in &t.see {
                assert!(
                    find(&terms, see).is_some(),
                    "`{}` refers to `{see}`, which is not in the glossary",
                    t.term
                );
            }
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn finds_whole_words_only() {
        assert!(contains_word("The Stack grows down.", "stack"));
        assert!(contains_word("a call stack frame", "stack frame"));
        assert!(!contains_word("stacked boxes", "stack"));
        assert!(!contains_word("unstack", "stack"));
        assert!(contains_word("use `rax`.", "rax"));
        assert!(!contains_word("anything", ""));
    }
}

`crates/orress-academy/src/lesson.rs`:

```rs
//! Lesson files.
//!
//! A lesson is a TOML file with Markdown text, in `academy/lessons/`:
//!
//! ```toml
//! id = "l0-numbers"
//! level = 0
//! order = 2
//! title = "Number systems"
//! summary = "Binary, hexadecimal and how computers store negative numbers."
//!
//! goals = ["Read and write hexadecimal numbers", "..."]   # shown when the lesson starts
//!
//! [[steps]]
//! title = "Hexadecimal"
//! goal = "Convert a hex number to decimal."   # one line: what this step is for
//! text = """Markdown explanation..."""
//! instructions = ["Click ...", "Type ... and press Check."]  # numbered "Do this" list
//! deep_dive = """Optional extra depth, folded away under 'Learn more'."""
//! widget = "number_converter"          # optional interactive tool
//! spotlight = "palette"                # optional: highlight a part of the UI
//! check = { kind = "answer", answers = ["42"], number = true }
//! hints = ["a nudge", "a direction", "almost the answer"]
//! success = "Shown after the step is done: why it works."
//! ```

use serde::Deserialize;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
#[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub enum Check {
    /// Just read and press Next.
    Continue,
    /// Run a command (by action id), e.g. open the command palette.
    Action { id: String },
    /// Open (or focus) a view of a file, e.g. "Strings".
    View { view: String },
    /// Open one of the Academy's practice programs.
    OpenCrackme { name: String },
    /// Type an answer. With `number = true`, `42`, `0x2a` and `0b101010` are equal.
    Answer {
        answers: Vec<String>,
        #[serde(default)]
        number: bool,
        #[serde(default)]
        case_sensitive: bool,
    },
    /// Pick one option. `explain`, if given, has one entry per option: why that option is
    /// right or wrong, shown when it is picked.
    Choice {
        options: Vec<String>,
        correct: usize,
        #[serde(default)]
        explain: Vec<String>,
    },
    /// Type a secret (a password). Only its SHA-256 is stored, so reading the lesson
    /// file does not spoil it.
    Secret { sha256: String },
    /// Run a program in the CPU simulator that ends with these register values.
    Sim {
        expect: Vec<(String, i64)>,
        #[serde(default)]
        requires: Vec<String>,
    },
    /// The cursor is inside the detected main function of the open file.
    CursorInMain,
    /// You renamed something in the open file.
    Renamed,
    /// You added a comment in the open file.
    Commented,
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
pub struct Step {
    pub title: String,
    /// One line: what the learner gets out of this step.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub goal: Option<String>,
    pub text: String,
    /// Exactly what to do, one action per entry; shown as a numbered list. Required for
    /// every step with a task other than a multiple-choice question.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub instructions: Vec<String>,
    /// Optional extra depth, folded away under "Learn more".
    #[serde(default)]
    pub deep_dive: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub widget: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub spotlight: Option<String>,
    /// Example program loaded into the CPU simulator for this step.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub sim_code: Option<String>,
    /// Reference solution for simulator steps; shown after all hints, and run by the
    /// tests to prove the exercise can be solved.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub solution: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default = "continue_check")]
    pub check: Check,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub hints: Vec<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub success: Option<String>,
}

fn continue_check() -> Check {
    Check::Continue
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
pub struct Lesson {
    pub id: String,
    pub level: u8,
    pub order: u32,
    pub title: String,
    pub summary: String,
    /// What the learner can do after the lesson; shown at its start.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub goals: Vec<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub badge: Option<String>,
    /// Crackme whose source is shown after the lesson is completed.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub reveal_source: Option<String>,
    pub steps: Vec<Step>,
}

pub const LEVELS: [(&str, &str); 8] = [

// Every `academy/lessons/*.toml` file, as `BUILT_IN: &[(file name, source)]`, plus the
// glossary files (see `build.rs`).
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/academy_files.rs"));

pub fn parse(source: &str) -> Result<Lesson, String> {
    let lesson: Lesson = toml::from_str(source).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    validate(&lesson)?;
    Ok(lesson)
}

fn validate(lesson: &Lesson) -> Result<(), String> {
    if lesson.steps.is_empty() {
        return Err(format!("{}: a lesson needs at least one step", lesson.id));
    }
    for (i, step) in lesson.steps.iter().enumerate() {
        let at = format!("{} step {}", lesson.id, i + 1);
        if step.hints.len() > 3 {
            return Err(format!("{at}: at most 3 hints"));
        }
        match &step.check {
            Check::Choice {
                options, correct, ..
            } if *correct >= options.len() => {
                return Err(format!("{at}: `correct` is out of range"));
            }
            Check::Choice {
                options, explain, ..
            } if !explain.is_empty() && explain.len() != options.len() => {
                return Err(format!("{at}: `explain` needs one entry per option"));
            }
            Check::Answer {
                answers, number, ..
            } => {
                if answers.is_empty() {
                    return Err(format!("{at}: no answers"));
                }
                if *number && answers.iter().any(|a| crate::numbers::parse(a).is_none()) {
                    return Err(format!("{at}: number answers must be numbers"));
                }
            }
            Check::Secret { sha256 } if sha256.len() != 64 => {
                return Err(format!("{at}: sha256 must be 64 hex digits"));
            }
            Check::Sim { expect, .. }
                if expect
                    .iter()
                    .any(|(r, _)| !crate::sim::REGS.contains(&r.as_str())) =>
            {
                return Err(format!("{at}: unknown register in `expect`"));
            }
            Check::OpenCrackme { name } if crate::crackmes::find(name).is_none() => {
                return Err(format!("{at}: unknown crackme `{name}`"));
            }
            _ => {}
        }
        let needs_instructions = !matches!(step.check, Check::Continue | Check::Choice { .. });
        if needs_instructions && step.instructions.is_empty() {
            return Err(format!(
                "{at}: steps with a task need `instructions` that say exactly what to do"
            ));
        }
        if let Some(code) = &step.sim_code {
            crate::sim::Cpu::new(code)
                .map_err(|e| format!("{at}: sim_code line {}: {}", e.line, e.message))?;
        }
        if let Check::Sim { expect, requires } = &step.check {
            let solution = step
                .solution
                .as_ref()
                .ok_or_else(|| format!("{at}: simulator steps need a `solution`"))?;
            let mut cpu = crate::sim::Cpu::new(solution)
                .map_err(|e| format!("{at}: solution line {}: {}", e.line, e.message))?;
            cpu.run();
            if !cpu.finished_ok() {
                return Err(format!("{at}: solution stopped with: {:?}", cpu.halted));
            }
            for (reg, value) in expect {
                if cpu.reg(reg) != Some(*value as u64) {
                    return Err(format!(
                        "{at}: solution leaves {reg} = {:?}, expected {value}",
                        cpu.reg(reg)
                    ));
                }
            }
            if let Some(m) = requires.iter().find(|m| !cpu.uses(m)) {
                return Err(format!("{at}: solution does not use `{m}`"));
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

/// All built-in lessons, sorted by level and order. A broken file is left out (and
/// reported) rather than taking the app down; the tests reject broken files.
pub fn catalog() -> Vec<Lesson> {
    let mut lessons: Vec<Lesson> = BUILT_IN
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|(file, source)| {
            parse(source)
                .map_err(|e| eprintln!("built-in lesson {file} skipped: {e}"))
                .ok()
        })
        .collect();
    lessons.sort_by_key(|l| (l.level, l.order));
    lessons
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    /// Checks every file on its own and lists all problems at once, so one broken file
    /// does not hide the others.
    #[test]
    fn every_lesson_file_is_valid() {
        let errors: Vec<String> = BUILT_IN
            .iter()
            .filter_map(|(file, source)| parse(source).err().map(|e| format!("{file}: {e}")))
            .chain(
                crate::lesson::GLOSSARY_FILES
                    .iter()
                    .filter_map(|(file, source)| {
                        crate::glossary::parse(source)
                            .err()
                            .map(|e| format!("glossary/{file}: {e}"))
                    }),
            )
            .collect();
        assert!(errors.is_empty(), "invalid files:\n{}", errors.join("\n"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn built_in_lessons_are_valid() {
        let lessons = catalog();
        assert_eq!(lessons.len(), BUILT_IN.len());
        let mut ids: Vec<_> = lessons.iter().map(|l| l.id.as_str()).collect();
        ids.sort_unstable();
        ids.dedup();
        assert_eq!(ids.len(), lessons.len(), "lesson ids are unique");
        // ORRESS's default fonts have no glyphs for these; they would show as boxes.
        for (file, source) in BUILT_IN {
            for ch in ['→', '←', '✔', '✓', '●', '○'] {
                assert!(
                    !source.contains(ch),
                    "{file} uses `{ch}`, which the UI font cannot show"
                );
            }
        }
    }

    /// Every spotlight target a lesson names must be one the UI actually marks, or the lesson
    /// points at nothing. The list mirrors the `orress_ui::spotlight::mark` call sites across the
    /// workspace (this crate cannot depend on the view crates, so it is kept here by hand):
    /// - `orress` app: `palette`, `explain_toggle`;
    /// - `orress-academy`: `lesson`, `sim.*`;
    /// - `orress-workspace`: `dock.*`, and `view.<View::name()>` for every document tab;
    /// - `orress-views`: `tree.<View::name()>` in the project tree, plus each tool view's own
    ///   `view.<Name>`.
    #[test]
    fn spotlight_targets_are_marked_somewhere() {
        // `orress_views::View::name()` — marked as `view.<name>` (document tabs) and
        // `tree.<name>` (project tree).
        const DOC_VIEWS: &[&str] = &[
            "Disassembly",
            "Graph",
            "Functions",
            "Info",
            "Hex",
            "Sections",
            "Imports",
            "Strings",
        ];
        const TOOL_VIEWS: &[&str] = &[
            "Archive",
            "Assistant",
            "DebugSource",
            "Debugger",
            "Decompiler",
            "DotNet",
            "Editor",
            "Emulator",
            "Java",
            "Js",
            "Output",
            "Problems",
            "Pyc",
            "Sandbox",
            "Script",
            "Shellcode",
            "Terminal",
            "Triage",
            "Wasm",
            "Yara",
        ];
        const OTHER: &[&str] = &[
            "palette",
            "explain_toggle",
            "lesson",
            "sim.step",
            "sim.run",
            "sim.code",
            "sim.registers",
            "sim.flags",
            "sim.stack",
            "dock.center",
            "dock.left",
            "dock.right",
            "dock.bottom",
        ];
        let mut known: Vec<String> = OTHER.iter().map(|s| s.to_string()).collect();
        for v in DOC_VIEWS {
            known.push(format!("view.{v}"));
            known.push(format!("tree.{v}"));
        }
        known.extend(TOOL_VIEWS.iter().map(|v| format!("view.{v}")));
        // The three named in the audit must be among them.
        for must in ["view.Disassembly", "view.Info", "view.Strings"] {
            assert!(known.iter().any(|k| k == must));
        }

        for lesson in catalog() {
            for step in &lesson.steps {
                if let Some(target) = &step.spotlight {
                    assert!(
                        known.iter().any(|k| k == target),
                        "lesson `{}` step `{}` spotlights `{target}`, which no UI element marks",
                        lesson.id,
                        step.title
                    );
                }
            }
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_bad_lessons() {
        let bad = r#"
            id = "x"
            level = 0
            order = 1
            title = "t"
            summary = "s"
            [[steps]]
            title = "q"
            text = "?"
            check = { kind = "choice", options = ["a"], correct = 3 }
        "#;
        assert!(parse(bad).unwrap_err().contains("out of range"));
        assert!(parse("id = 1").is_err());
    }
}
